commentary.historical_context: The category of 'those who fear the LORD' appears throughout the Psalms and reflects a reality of Second Temple Judaism: the Jewish community was not hermetically sealed. There were always individuals and families who, while not ethnically Jewish, were attracted to monotheism and the worship of Israel's God. Some of these 'god-fearers' (sebomenoi in Greek, from which we get our word 'synagogue') appear in the New Testament (e.g., Cornelius in Acts 10, the Ethiopian eunuch in Acts 8). They represent a category of genuine piety that operates outside ethnic or institutional boundaries. By invoking them explicitly in Psalm 118, the psalmist is asserting that God's covenant mercy extends to all who approach Him with genuine reverence, regardless of genealogy. This is theologically significant because it prevents the psalm from being read as narrowly nationalist; instead, it affirms that God's faithful love is universal in its availability, even if Israel remains particular in its election as covenant bearer.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 13:34, the angel teaches that the gospel will be taken 'to all nations, kindreds, tongues, and people,' echoing the principle that God's covenant mercy is not ethnically or institutionally restricted. The Book of Mormon repeatedly affirms that all who genuinely seek God and fear Him are included in His covenant (see Mosiah 3:18; Alma 24:19-22). The principle extends mercy to those outside the formal covenant structure who nonetheless have sincere hearts.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 138 (the vision of the spirits in paradise) describes spirits from all ages, nations, and kindreds who are counted among the righteous because they feared God and sought truth, even without access to the full gospel. This directly parallels Psalm 118:4's inclusion of 'all them that fear the LORD'—affirming that genuine piety transcends institutional boundaries.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, all who enter are invited to participate in the same ordinances and make the same covenants, regardless of background or prior status. The temple does not distinguish between those born into covenant families and those who have come to the faith later. This universal accessibility of temple blessings reflects the principle that anyone who fears God and enters into covenant is welcomed into the circle of God's people.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus's commission in Matthew 28:19 directs the apostles to teach 'all nations,' affirming that the gospel invitation extends to all who will fear (revere, obey) God. The breaking down of barriers between Jew and Gentile in the New Testament is prefigured by Psalm 118's inclusion of those who fear God regardless of ethnic status. Christ's redemption is offered to all who approach Him with genuine reverence and faith—a universal principle rooted in the democratic structure of Psalm 118. The psalmist's inclusivity anticipates Christ's refusal to restrict God's mercy to any particular group.
commentary.application: This verse fundamentally expands who 'we' are in the covenant community. It invites us to recognize that sincere faith and reverence for God matter more than genealogy, institutional status, or prior religious background. Practically, this means: when we worship and testify, we are joining not just with the formal membership of our wards or stakes but with all people across history and geography who have genuinely feared God. This challenges insularity and parochialism. It also means recognizing that people outside the formal institutional structure of the Church—people with sincere faith, genuine reverence for God, and authentic commitment to righteousness—are already participating in this ancient chorus testifying to God's mercy. In our interactions with others, this verse invites us to listen for authentic piety wherever it appears and to recognize it as valid testimony to God's faithfulness. It also challenges us personally: Does my fear of the Lord—my reverence, awe, and commitment to His will—run deep enough that I can authentically join this chorus?

text_kjv: I called upon the LORD in distress: the LORD answered me, and set me in a large place.

commentary.narrative:
With verse 5, the psalm pivots from the liturgical call to collective testimony into the personal narrative that substantiates it. The psalmist moves from 'we/they' to 'I,' and the focus shifts from affirmation of God's general character to a specific moment of crisis and rescue. The speaker was in metzar ('a narrow place, distress, confinement')—a word that suggests psychological, physical, or spiritual compression. The speaker cried out to God using the intimate form 'Yah' (a shortened, more personal address of God's name), and God answered. But the answer was not merely deliverance from pressure; it was expansion. God brought the psalmist out into merchav ('a wide, open, spacious place')—the opposite of confinement.

This movement from metzar to merchav is the psalm's central redemptive image, and it carries echoes of Israel's foundational story. Egypt was a metzar—a place of bondage, confinement, and oppression. The exodus was God's rescue, bringing Israel out into the wilderness and ultimately to a land of their own. By invoking this language, the psalmist is claiming personal participation in that paradigm of liberation. But more broadly, the text speaks to any experience of confinement—physical imprisonment, grief, sickness, anxiety, spiritual despair—and asserts that God's response is not merely symptomatic relief but fundamental transformation of the space one inhabits. The psalmist is not merely rescued; he is relocated into freedom, possibility, and movement. This verse establishes the narrative foundation for everything the psalm will claim about God's character: He hears, He answers, and He liberates.

word_study.meaning: From the root tzarar, meaning 'to be narrow, to confine, to bind, to press.' Metzar literally denotes a geographical strait or narrow space, but it is used metaphorically for any kind of constriction, distress, or claustrophobia. It can refer to physical imprisonment, psychological anguish, or spiritual bondage. The etymology connects to mitzrayim ('Egypt'), the place of Israel's original bondage.
word_study.significance: The word encapsulates the experience of being trapped, compressed, unable to move or breathe freely. It is more than mere difficulty; it is the sense of being confined, of having no exit or possibility. The use of this word immediately evokes Israel's Egyptian slavery, inviting the reader to see personal rescue as a reenactment of the nation's foundational liberation story.

word_study.meaning: From the root qara, meaning 'to call, to cry out, to summon.' Qarati is the first-person past tense ('I called'). It denotes both a verbal utterance and a deeper cry of the soul—an appeal to God made in urgency and vulnerability.
word_study.significance: This is not prayer as formal ritual but prayer as desperate utterance. The psalmist cried out from genuine need, invoking God's attention and intervention.

word_study.meaning: A shortened form of YHWH, the divine name. While YHWH is the full, formal name of God, Yah is more intimate and personal. It appears often in prayers, hymns, and moments of emotional intensity (see also 'Hallelu-Yah,' 'praise Yah').
word_study.significance: The use of the intimate form 'Yah' rather than the formal 'YHWH' (as appeared in vv. 1-4) signals a shift from liturgical formula to personal relationship. The psalmist is not calling upon a distant God but upon one who is personally accessible, intimate, and responsive to individual cry.

word_study.meaning: From the root anah, meaning 'to answer, to respond, to speak in reply.' Anani is the third-person past tense ('He answered me'). It denotes not silence but active response—God heard and responded to the cry.
word_study.significance: The fundamental claim of the psalm: God's chesed is not abstract but responsive. He hears genuine cries and answers them. This is the experiential grounding for the affirmation of verse 1.

word_study.meaning: From the root rachav, meaning 'to be wide, to be spacious, to be broad.' Merchav denotes open space, room to move, freedom, and possibility. It is the opposite of metzar (narrow). In the Psalms, merchav often symbolizes salvation, freedom, and deliverance (see Psalm 31:8, 81:10).
word_study.significance: God's rescue is not partial or temporary relief but a fundamental relocation of the psalmist's existence. He is moved from confinement to spaciousness, from compression to freedom. This is not merely negative deliverance (removal of the problem) but positive transformation (relocation into something better). The contrast between metzar and merchav is the poem's central metaphor.

cross_references.connection: The exodus account describes God opening the sea to create a way of escape and liberation—the archetypal act of moving people from confinement (Egypt) to freedom (wilderness and ultimately Canaan), which Psalm 118:5 echoes.
Uses the same root as merchav ('Thou hast set my feet in a large room / merchav') to describe God's deliverance, establishing this as a standard image of salvation in the Psalms.
The Lord says, 'I am the LORD thy God...Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it'—using merchav (wide) to describe the space God creates for blessing and freedom.

Lehi describes how the Lord led his family to 'a land of promise, a land which is choice above all other lands,' corresponding to the movement from metzar to merchav—from confinement to freedom and blessing.

The Lord teaches that His power is available to those who approach Him in faith: 'influence and persuasion' rather than coercion—a principle of freedom and spaciousness that contrasts with the metzar of bondage.

commentary.historical_context: The vocabulary of metzar and merchav draws directly from Israel's foundational narrative. Ancient Israelite worshippers would immediately recognize in this verse the echoes of the exodus—the movement from the confinement of Egypt to the freedom of the wilderness and the promised land. Scholars have noted that Psalm 118 was sung during Passover celebrations, specifically during the Hallel ('praise psalms') recited in connection with the Seder meal. In that context, verse 5 takes on particular resonance: the individual psalmist's rescue from metzar to merchav becomes a microcosm of Israel's national redemption. The language also reflects wisdom and prayer traditions in the Ancient Near East, where rescue from constraint and movement into openness was a standard image for divine deliverance. Archaeological evidence from ancient Egypt and the Levant shows that the concept of pharaonic oppression and divine rescue was widely understood across the ancient Near East. The specificity of the metzar-to-merchav transition reflects not merely metaphorical poetry but the actual psychology of oppression and liberation—a movement from psychological confinement to the restoration of agency, possibility, and hope.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 2:2-4, Lehi describes how the Lord commanded him to leave Jerusalem (the metzar of spiritual captivity and danger) and led him toward the promised land (the merchav of freedom and covenant). The Nephite record repeatedly uses this pattern: the people are in bondage or confinement, they cry out to God, and He delivers them into spaciousness. In Alma 26:12, Ammon testifies that God 'has delivered us out of the hands of...the Lamanites.' The movement from confinement to freedom is a recurring narrative arc in the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 6:33 promises: 'Therefore, fear not, little flock; do good; let earth and hell combine against you, for if ye are built upon my rock, they cannot prevail.' This echoes Psalm 118's principle: the psalmist is delivered out of metzar into the protection and freedom of God's covenant. D&C 98:1 similarly affirms that those who keep God's commandments 'shall be filled with joy and gladness.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment ceremony enacts a kind of metzar-to-merchav narrative: the initiate moves through rooms and spaces, progresses from ignorance to knowledge, and experiences an expansion of understanding and spiritual capacity. The temple journey itself mirrors the movement from confinement to spaciousness that Psalm 118:5 describes. The restoration of all things promised in the temple is fundamentally a restoration of freedom and expanded possibility.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus's resurrection is the ultimate metzar-to-merchav transformation. Jesus entered the confinement of death, the grave, and apparent abandonment by God. His resurrection moved Him out of that narrow space into glorified, spacious existence—boundless by time, space, or mortal limitation. His exaltation opened up the possibility of universal resurrection for all of humanity. In Matthew 28:18, the risen Jesus declares, 'All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth'—a statement of ultimate freedom and expanded dominion. Furthermore, Christ's atonement releases humanity from the metzar of sin and death, moving us into the merchav of freedom and eternal possibility. The cross becomes the pivot point of the metzar-to-merchav narrative for all creation.
commentary.application: This verse invites modern members to examine their own experiences of confinement and crisis. What 'narrow place' are you in—emotional, relational, spiritual, financial? The psalmist's testimony is that God hears genuine cries and responds, but His response is not merely symptomatic relief. He relocates us into freedom and possibility. Practically, this means: when facing distress, cry out authentically. Don't suppress the reality of your confinement or pretend everything is manageable. Invoke God's name personally (as the psalmist uses Yah). Then trust that God's answer—whether immediate or gradual—will be a movement into spaciousness, not merely a removal of the immediate problem. This might mean new opportunity, healed relationships, shifted perspective, or the discovery of agency and freedom you didn't know you possessed. The verse also invites us to recognize God's hand in past deliverances. Can you identify a time when God moved you from metzar to merchav? That past testimony becomes the foundation for trust in future trials. Finally, this verse challenges us to extend mercy to others in narrow places. Having experienced being cried out to and answered, we are invited to be a voice of hope and possibility for others experiencing confinement.

text_kjv: The LORD is on my side; I will not fear: what can man do unto me?

commentary.narrative:
The psalmist makes a radical declaration of confidence: God is 'on my side'—a claim that is both theological and existential. This is not abstract assurance but a statement of alignment, allegiance, and active support. Having just narrated rescue from confinement (v. 5), the psalmist now faces potential human opposition and asks a rhetorical question that challenges the entire human dimension of the threat: 'What can any human do to me?' The underlying logic is not that humans are powerless but that their power is insignificant compared to having the LORD as one's ally.

This verse appears to be grounded in a concrete historical situation—the psalmist faces opposition from human enemies or adversaries. But the existential truth runs deeper than the immediate political or personal threat. The question 'What can man do unto me?' encompasses all human opposition: mockery, persecution, betrayal, violence, slander, abandonment. The psalmist's answer is not bravado but a theological claim: because God is on my side, these human-inflicted harms cannot ultimately define or destroy me. The shift in pronouns (from 'I' in v. 5 to 'my' in v. 6) creates intimacy—this is not universal theology but personal relationship. This verse grounds the entire psalm's affirmations in a foundational axis: if God is truly 'on our side,' then the whole structure of human fear collapses. The verse will be quoted in Hebrews 13:6, making it a New Testament anchor for Christian confidence.

word_study.meaning: The Hebrew preposition li means 'for me, to me, on my behalf.' When combined with YHWH ('the LORD'), it creates the phrase YHWH li ('the LORD is for me / the LORD is mine / the LORD is on my behalf'). This is not merely God's existence but God's active stance toward the speaker. It denotes divine favor, alliance, and support.
word_study.significance: This is not abstract theological knowledge but intimate personal assurance. The LORD is not merely present in the universe; He is actively positioned on the side of the psalmist. This personal stance of God is the foundation for the confidence that follows.

word_study.meaning: The root yare means 'to fear, to be afraid, to revere.' Lo ira ('I will not fear') is a resolute negation. The statement is not 'I do not feel fear' but 'I will not allow fear to govern my choices and beliefs.' It is a declaration of will, not merely emotion.
word_study.significance: Fear is the fundamental human response to threat and vulnerability. The psalmist's refusal is not denial of danger but a recalibration of what determines his ultimate allegiance and security. Because God is on his side, fear of human opposition will not rule him.

word_study.meaning: A rhetorical question. Mah ('what') opens an interrogative; ya'aseh ('to do, to make, to accomplish') is a wide-ranging verb of action; adam ('human, mankind, mortal') is the category of being invoked. The question essentially asks: 'What action, what harm, what interference can any mortal inflict upon me that would matter ultimately?'
word_study.significance: This is not a question that expects a literal answer but rather invites the listener to recognize the scale of the threat. What can humans do? In comparison with God's power and commitment, very little that is ultimately destructive. Humans can cause pain, loss, public shame, even death—but they cannot ultimately nullify God's favor toward us or God's purposes for us.

cross_references.connection: The New Testament directly quotes Psalm 118:6 and applies it to Christian confidence: 'The Lord hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee. So that we may boldly say, The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man shall do unto me.' This makes Psalm 118:6 a foundational verse for New Testament faith.
Paul echoes the logic: 'If God be for us, who can be against us?' This is a direct parallel to Psalm 118:6's claim that God's stance on our behalf renders human opposition ultimately insignificant.
Uses similar language: 'The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?' establishing a broader tradition of affirming God's protective presence.

The Lord tells Hyrum Smith: 'Be faithful, be humble before the Lord, reprove betimes with sharpness, when moved upon by the Holy Ghost; and then show forth afterwards an increase of love toward him whom thou hast reproved.' This teaches that God's support enables us to face difficult situations without fear governing our choices.
Mormon testifies: 'Therefore I will cry unto you in the anguish of my soul.' Even in deep distress, the conviction that God is accessible and on one's side sustains faith.

commentary.historical_context: Scholars debate whether Psalm 118 originates from a time of acute political threat (perhaps the Maccabean conflict, when Jewish worshippers faced persecution from Hellenistic rulers) or whether the threat is more general and internal—enemies within the covenant community, perhaps adversaries in legal or cultic disputes. Ancient Near Eastern royal psalms frequently invoke the king's divine backing as a source of confidence against enemies. The phrase 'the god is on my side' appears in Egyptian and Mesopotamian contexts as a standard assertion of divine favor. However, in the Israelite tradition, this phrase takes on particular significance because it is applied not to a king alone but to the psalmist as a member of the covenant community. The rhetorical question 'What can man do unto me?' echoes the confidence of those who have been tried by human opposition and found that God's presence and commitment transcend it. In the context of Second Temple Judaism, where the Jewish community faced repeated threats—Greek Hellenization, Roman occupation, internal sectarian conflict—this verse would have resonated as a defiant assertion that ultimate security rests not in military strength or political power but in God's covenantal stance toward His people.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 26:11-12, Ammon testifies: 'Behold, I have labored without ceasing, that I might bring souls unto repentance; that I might bring them to taste of the exceeding joy of which I do taste. And now I say unto you, I trust I do not boast in saying I have wrought the works which were wrought by the power and blessing of God.' Ammon's confidence that God is on his side sustains him through opposition from the Lamanites. The Book of Mormon repeatedly affirms that those who are aligned with God's purposes cannot be ultimately harmed by human opposition (see Mosiah 3:19, Alma 22:16).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:7-8 teaches the early Saints: 'My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment; And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high.' This affirms the principle of Psalm 118:6—that human-inflicted opposition and adversity are temporary and insignificant compared to God's exaltation of those who remain faithful. D&C 3:8 states: 'Remember, remember that it is not the work of God that is frustrated.' God's work and purposes cannot be thwarted by human opposition.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple covenants, the initiate receives assurance of divine protection and support. The temple veil itself represents the barrier between human and divine; passage through it symbolizes that God is now 'on one's side'—that the individual has entered into sacred relationship with the divine. The temple endowment teaches that those who remain faithful to their covenants will be sustained by divine power. This is the practical application of Psalm 118:6 in the context of saving ordinances.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus exemplifies the ultimate enactment of this verse. Throughout His ministry, He faced opposition—from religious authorities, from political powers, from Satan himself. In Matthew 26:39, in Gethsemane, Jesus prays that the cup be taken from Him, yet He concludes with 'nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.' His confidence rested not in resistance to human opposition but in His absolute alignment with the Father's will. When He stands before the Sanhedrin and later before Pilate, He does not defend Himself against human accusations because His security rests in God's stance toward Him. At the crucifixion, when all human power seems arrayed against Him, Jesus's cry 'Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit' (Luke 23:46) demonstrates ultimate confidence that God is on His side. His resurrection vindicates this confidence: no human power could ultimately hold Him. Furthermore, Christ's victorious stance at the right hand of the Father (Hebrews 1:3, 8:1) is the eternal manifestation of 'the LORD is on my side'—and through His work, all who enter into covenant with Him can make the same claim.
commentary.application: This verse confronts a fundamental question: What determines your security—human approval, political power, economic status, or God's stance toward you? The psalmist's confidence seems naive in a world where humans inflict real harm—violence, betrayal, loss. Yet the verse is not denying human power to hurt but recalibrating the ultimate measure of security and worth. Practically, this means: when you face opposition from others (criticism, rejection, mockery, persecution), the fundamental question is not 'How can I win their approval?' but 'Is God on my side?' This is not permission to be indifferent to others' legitimate concerns but rather a refusal to allow human judgment to determine your ultimate identity and security. If you are genuinely seeking to follow God and live according to your understanding of His will, then human opposition—however painful—cannot nullify your worth or your standing before God. The verse also invites you to examine whether you are truly on God's side. His stance toward you is not automatic but relational; it deepens through covenants kept, through genuine repentance, through alignment with His purposes. Finally, this verse is a prayer. When you are facing opposition, the practice is to consciously affirm: 'The Lord is on my side. I will not fear. What can any human do unto me?' This is not self-deception but a reorientation toward the ultimate source of security and meaning.

text_kjv: The LORD taketh my part with them that help me: therefore shall I see my desire upon them that hate me.

commentary.narrative:
This verse announces the foundational confidence that undergirds the entire psalm: the LORD is not a distant observer but an active participant on behalf of the psalmist. The phrase "the LORD taketh my part" (Hebrew: YHWH li be-ozrai) does not mean God is merely one helper among many equal helpers, but rather that God is the decisive helper whose presence fundamentally changes the calculus of the situation. The psalmist has helpers, but what matters is that the LORD is with them—or more precisely, the LORD is for the psalmist among whoever helps. This is not confidence in human allies; it is confidence rooted in divine alliance.

The second clause shifts from present assurance to future vindication: "therefore shall I see my desire upon them that hate me." The verb "see" (Hebrew: er'eh) in this context means more than mere vision—it carries the sense of seeing victory, seeing enemies defeated, seeing the fulfillment of divine justice. The TCR rendering captures this as "I will look in triumph," emphasizing that the looking itself is an act of vindication, not mere observation. The psalmist will witness the reversal of fortunes that comes when one stands with the LORD against those who stand opposed to God's purposes.

This verse establishes the rhetorical and theological pattern that dominates Psalm 118: affirmation of God's faithfulness, confidence in divine protection, and trust that this confidence will be vindicated in time. For the original psalmist (likely in the post-exilic period, celebrating God's deliverance), this was lived experience. For the New Testament church and for modern readers, this becomes a template for faith in trial—the assurance that God's presence and alliance transform both present circumstances and future outcomes.

word_study.meaning: The LORD is for me among my helpers. The preposition 'li' (to/for me) expresses alliance and protection. 'Be-ozrai' (among my helpers) indicates that God is not alone in helping but is the primary helper whose presence defines all other help. The construction emphasizes God's active stance on behalf of the psalmist.
word_study.significance: This phrase moves beyond passive permission (God allowing help) to active participation (God being for the psalmist). In covenant theology, this recalls the language of God taking Israel's side against enemies (Exodus 14:14; Deuteronomy 20:4). For Latter-day Saints, this parallels the promise that the Holy Ghost will be a comforter and advocate (John 14:16).

word_study.meaning: The verb 'see' carries the connotation of witnessing or beholding a fulfillment. The phrase literally means 'I will see upon/against those who hate me'—implying not just observation but vindication. The enemies are identified not by circumstance but by their hatred (sone'ai), which designates them as those actively opposed to the psalmist's God.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering—'I will look in triumph'—captures the sense that seeing is itself an act of victory. The psalmist's future ability to witness this reversal is not vindictive but vindicating: it confirms that trust in the LORD is justified. This echoes the later Christian understanding of patient endurance rewarded (1 Peter 1:7; Revelation 3:21).

cross_references.connection: Moses tells Israel, 'The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace.' Both verses ground confidence in God's active intervention on behalf of His people.
The law promises that God goes before Israel in battle. This echoes the same assurance that the LORD, not military might alone, determines victory.
Hezekiah tells Jerusalem, 'With him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the LORD our God to help us.' The parallel structure echoes Psalm 118:7's contrast between human and divine support.
Paul writes, 'If God be for us, who can be against us?'—a direct application of the principle established in this verse to Christian assurance.

commentary.historical_context: Psalm 118 is widely understood as a thanksgiving psalm sung in the context of a military or national deliverance. The repeated language of enemies surrounding the psalmist (verses 10–12) suggests a specific historical crisis—possibly the Babylonian siege and exile, or a later threat to the restored community in Judah. The reference to 'all nations' (verse 10) and 'princes' (verse 9) indicates that the threat was not merely personal but involved national powers. In the post-exilic period, such psalms would have been sung during temple festivals (likely Passover or Sukkot) as commemorations of God's faithfulness and deliverance. The cultural context of ANE warfare emphasizes that military victory was attributed to divine intervention—a ruler's success proved divine favor. The psalmist claims this ancient logic but inverts it: the victory belongs not to the psalmist's strength but to alliance with the LORD.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:12 records Ammon's declaration: 'Behold, I say unto you, I do not boast in my own strength, nor in my own wisdom; but behold, my joy is full, yea, my heart is brim with joy, and I will rejoice in my God.' This parallels the psalmist's confidence that God is the source of strength and vindication, not human capability.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 35:8 records the Lord telling Emma Smith, 'Murmur not because of the things which thou hast not seen, for they are withheld from thee and from the world, which is wisdom in me.' This echoes Psalm 118:7's trust that God's alliance is real even when enemies press hard—faith precedes vindication.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Psalm 118 was likely sung as part of the temple liturgy during pilgrimage festivals. The declaration 'the LORD is for me' reflects the covenant renewal that occurred in temple worship—the reaffirmation that God had chosen Israel and taken their part against all adversaries. For modern Latter-day Saints, this verse grounds the assurance that temple covenants bind us to God's protection and vindication.

commentary.christological_typology: In Matthew 21:42, Jesus applies Psalm 118:22–23 to Himself—'The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner.' This suggests that the entire psalm's movement from threat to vindication prefigures Christ's passage through rejection to exaltation. Verse 7's promise that the LORD takes the part of the righteous one foreshadows God the Father's vindication of Christ through resurrection. The enemies who surrounded the psalmist typify the powers that opposed Christ; the LORD's intervention typifies the Atonement and Resurrection.
commentary.application: Modern disciples often face opposition—from secular culture, from personal doubt, from those who ridicule faith. Verse 7 offers a corrective to the anxiety this opposition can generate: the crucial fact is not the size or power of opposition but the identity of one's ally. If the LORD is for you, the outcome is not in doubt, even if the path is unclear. This is not a promise of immediate deliverance from all difficulty (verses 10–12 make clear that encirclement and attack still occur) but of ultimate vindication. The practical application is to align oneself with God's purposes, to seek His guidance through prayer and revelation, and then to trust that His presence transforms the meaning and outcome of opposition. For Latter-day Saints, this means relying on temple covenants, priesthood blessings, and the guidance of living prophets—means by which we consciously align ourselves with the LORD's party.

text_kjv: It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in man.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 8 shifts from narrative assertion to wisdom principle, establishing a fundamental hierarchy of trust that will be reinforced and intensified in verse 9. The Hebrew structure—tov lachsot ba-YHWH mibettoach ba-adam—is not cynical dismissal of human help but rather a clear-eyed statement about ultimate reliability and sufficiency. To 'take refuge' in the LORD (lachsot) is to run toward secure shelter, while to 'trust' (bittoach) in humanity is to place confidence in that which cannot ultimately sustain. The verb lachsot carries the imagery of a hunted animal fleeing to a fortress or cave—it is active, urgent seeking of protection. Bittoach in humans, by contrast, treats a finite being as if they possessed infinite resources.

The wisdom here is not that human help is worthless—verses 7 and 15 reference helpers and the assembly—but that human help cannot be the foundation of confidence. Humans fail due to weakness (mortality), limited knowledge, or conflicting interests. More fundamentally, humans cannot guarantee outcomes; they can only offer their limited power. The LORD, by contrast, is infinite in power, knowledge, and commitment to His covenant people. This principle does not prohibit seeking human counsel or accepting human aid; rather, it establishes the proper hierarchy: human help is good when it is instrumental to a larger trust in God, but destructive when it becomes an alternative to trusting God.

The placement of this principle at verse 8 (early in the psalm's argument) establishes the intellectual foundation for what follows. When verses 10–12 describe enemies surrounding like bees and swarming like fire, the reader has already been primed to understand that military logic (trust in commanders, soldiers, strategy) is secondary to trusting the LORD. The wisdom principle makes the later narrative declarations make sense: confidence in human alliance without divine alliance is misplaced; confidence in divine alliance even in isolation is well-founded.

word_study.meaning: To take refuge, to seek shelter, to flee for protection. The root chacah (חסה) appears frequently in the Psalms and denotes active movement toward a place of safety. The preposition 'ba' (in/into) emphasizes entering into the refuge. Unlike bittoach (passive trust/reliance), lachsot is urgent and active.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering—'take refuge'—better captures the sense of emergency and active seeking than 'trust' alone. For covenantal theology, this imagery recalls God as a fortress, rock, and shield (Psalm 18:2). In LDS context, taking refuge in God parallels entering into covenant and receiving ordinances that bind us to God's protection.

word_study.meaning: To trust, to rely upon, to place confidence in. The verb bittoach is more passive than lachsot—it expresses reliance or dependence. 'Adam' (אדם) is the generic term for humanity—not a specific person but the class of mortals. This breadth is significant: the principle applies to trusting any human being, regardless of rank or competence.
word_study.significance: This word study shows the psalm is not criticizing prudent counsel-seeking but rather the idolatry of placing ultimate confidence in human beings. In political terms, it warns against attributing salvation to human rulers. In personal terms, it warns against making any person (spouse, parent, leader, therapist) into a god.

cross_references.connection: This later psalm reinforces the principle: 'Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help. His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish.' The transience of human help is the logical basis for seeking help elsewhere.

Isaiah's warning—'Cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils: for wherein is he to be accounted of?'—carries the same logic: human breathlessness (mortality, weakness) disqualifies humans as the foundation of hope.
'Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.' This wisdom principle parallels Psalm 118:8 by instructing trust in God's wisdom over human reasoning.
Jeremiah pronounces a curse on 'the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm.' This inverts Psalm 118:8 into a warning about the spiritual consequences of misplaced trust.

Nephi declares, 'O then, if I have seen so great things, if the Lord in his condescension unto the children of men hath visited men in so much mercy, why should my heart weep and my soul linger in the valley of sorrow?' The principle is that God's character and capacity warrant trust more than human compassion or capability.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, political survival often meant calculating which human alliance—which king, which army, which powerful patron—offered the best prospects. The Assyrian Empire's expansion and later the Babylonian threat forced Israel into diplomatic and military alliances that often compromised religious integrity. Prophets like Isaiah and Jeremiah repeatedly condemned Israel's reliance on Egyptian or other foreign military alliances instead of trusting God. Psalm 118 seems to emerge from the post-exilic period when Judah had no king, no standing army, and no political power—only the Temple and faith in God's covenant. In this context, the instruction to trust God rather than 'man' (which could mean princes, military commanders, or foreign rulers) was countercultural wisdom. It asserted that Judah's security lay not in political maneuvering but in faithful covenant with the LORD.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Helaman 5:7–11 records Helaman's teaching to his sons: 'Now my sons, behold I have somewhat to say unto you; for I perceive that ye are in bonds—yea, even in the bonds of iniquity. And now my sons, remember, remember that it is upon the rock of our Redeemer, who is Christ, the Son of God, that ye must build your foundation; that when the devil shall send forth his mighty winds, yea, his shafts in the whirlwind, yea, when all his hail and his mighty storm shall beat upon you, it shall have no power over you to drag you down to the gulf of misery and endless wo, because of the rock upon which ye are built.' This passage teaches the same hierarchy: human allies (symbolized by earthly foundations) fail; only Christ endures.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 78:21 teaches: 'See that ye are not lifted up in the pride of your hearts; for every man that exalteth himself shall be abased, and he that abaseth himself shall be exalted.' The principle in Psalm 118:8 reverses the order of trust that pride establishes—pride trusts in oneself or human allies; humility trusts in God.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple liturgy emphasizes covenant with God as the supreme binding relationship, superseding all earthly alliances and authorities. When a person enters temple covenants, they are making a solemn choice to place their ultimate trust not in government, money, status, or even family relationships, but in God and His restored Church. Verse 8 is the scriptural foundation for this choice.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's earthly ministry repeatedly illustrates this principle. In John 6:15, Jesus withdraws from disciples who want to make Him king by force—He will not compete for the throne or place confidence in human political processes. In Matthew 4:1–11, Christ resists temptations that would require trusting in earthly means (turning stones to bread, throwing Himself from the temple to demonstrate divine rescue through human witnesses) in favor of trusting His Father's provision and timing. Christ is the perfect exemplar of trusting the Father's will over all earthly alliances.
commentary.application: In modern life, Latter-day Saints are constantly pressured to place confidence in human systems: political parties that claim to offer security, financial institutions that promise wealth, medical professionals who claim to solve all problems, therapists who suggest that human relationship alone heals, educational systems that claim to provide all truth. Verse 8 does not prohibit prudent engagement with these systems (medicine, education, wise financial planning are good); rather, it establishes the proper hierarchy. These human systems are tools, not foundations. The foundation is trust in God, expressed through covenant, prayer, and adherence to revealed truth. When a Latter-day Saint faces a decision, the question is not 'What do the experts say?' or 'What does public opinion favor?' but 'What does God's word and the living prophets teach?' Verse 8 consecrates this order of priority as ancient wisdom.

text_kjv: It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in princes.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 9 repeats the structure of verse 8 but escalates the hierarchy of trust by specifying princes (Hebrew: nedivim) rather than generic 'man.' If trusting in ordinary humans is inferior to trusting God, trusting in princes—the most powerful, most resourced, most impressive of humans—is equally and perhaps even more starkly inferior. This escalation is not accidental; it is theologically strategic. The psalmist might have stopped at verse 8, but by adding verse 9, the psalm declares that even the most impressive human power cannot compete with God's power or constancy. A prince has armies, treasuries, intelligence networks, and the authority to command obedience. Yet all of this, the psalm insists, is worth less than trust in the LORD.

The Hebrew word nedivim carries several layers of meaning: 'princes' (rulers), 'nobles' (the wealthy elite), 'willing ones' or 'volunteers' (those who give freely or step forward). In the context of a military or political crisis, nedivim would denote the leaders whose decisions determine outcomes—kings, generals, counselors. The inclusion of this verse suggests that the psalmist was tempted, during some trial, to place hope in powerful human allies. Perhaps during the Babylonian crisis or under Persian or Greek rule, there was pressure to trust in the protection of sympathetic rulers or to seek military alliance with powerful neighbors. The verse warns that this temptation, however reasonable it seems, is spiritually misaligned.

The rhetorical force of verses 8–9 together is to establish a ladder of error: if trusting ordinary people is wrong, then trusting princes (who have more power and resources) is even more wrong in the sense that it represents an even greater misdirection of ultimate confidence. The logical conclusion, which verses 10–12 then illustrate, is that only trusting the LORD makes sense when facing a crisis that exceeds human power to solve.

word_study.meaning: Plural of nadiv, denoting rulers, nobles, or princes—those of elevated status and power. The root ndb (נדב) can also mean 'to volunteer' or 'to give willingly,' suggesting that nedivim might include both those born into power and those who assume leadership through capacity or will. In political contexts, nedivim are the decision-makers whose choices affect the fate of nations.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering preserves 'princes' as the parallel to 'man' in verse 8. This progression—from generic humanity to the most powerful humans—shows that power itself does not make a being trustworthy for ultimate purposes. A prince's power extends only over earthly, temporal matters and is subject to change, death, and divine judgment. Only the eternal God warrants ultimate trust.

cross_references.connection: The near-identical verse establishes the pattern: the parallel structure in verses 8–9 intensifies the principle by moving from generic humans to princes, showing that even the most powerful cannot replace trust in God.
This verse explicitly extends the warning: 'Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.' Psalm 118:9 is an earlier statement of the same principle.

Isaiah condemns those who 'take counsel, but not of me; and that cover with a covering, but not of my spirit, that they may add sin to sin: That walk to go down into Egypt, and have not asked at my mouth; to strengthen themselves in the strength of Pharaoh, and to trust in the shadow of Egypt!' The prophet echoes Psalm 118:9 by warning against trusting in powerful rulers instead of God.

Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego tell Nebuchadnezzar, a supreme prince of their time: 'Be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.' They exemplify trusting God over the most powerful prince of their era.

The Lord warns: 'Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and the prophecies and promises which are in them shall all be fulfilled. What I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken; and I excuse not myself; and though the heavens and the earth pass away, my word shall not pass away, but shall be fulfilled, all fulfilled, one jot and one tittle.'

commentary.historical_context: The post-exilic Judean community faced repeated pressures from powerful foreign rulers: Persian governors, later Greek rulers under the Seleucids, and eventually Roman governors. Throughout this period, there was temptation (sometimes explicit pressure from the ruling power) to compromise religious practice or to seek security through alignment with the current empire. Psalm 118, likely emerging from this context, asserts that the community's security lies not in calculating which empire is strongest or most favorable but in trust in the LORD who transcends all earthly powers. The Maccabean revolt (2nd century BCE) would later exemplify the practical outworking of this principle: a small community choosing religious fidelity over political accommodation, trusting that God's purposes transcend imperial power. In this historical frame, verse 9 is radical theology: it denies what every political calculation of the era would suggest—that trust in princes is the only reasonable course.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 29:25–26 records King Mosiah's abdication and the establishment of judges: 'Now if there should be a king over the land the common people were assured of their rights and privileges of the church, for it were all one that a king should reign; and thus they were depending upon the kings of the earth for their support and for their happiness.' This reflects the danger Psalm 118:9 warns against—depending on earthly rulers (princes) for security and happiness rather than on God's provision and guidance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:5–8 teaches: 'Thus saith the Lord God, who prepareth all things before the foundation of the world: By mine own voice have I decreed it; yea, and the voice of my Only Begotten shall utter the same, even by the voice of his Spirit, saying: Listen to the voice of Jesus Christ, your Redeemer, the Great I AM, whose arm of mercy hath atoned for your sins; Who will gather his people even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, even as many as will hearken to my voice and humble themselves before me.' This reveals that Jesus Christ (not earthly princes) is the true gatherer and protector.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment includes covenants made directly to God, not to any earthly representative or institution. While the Church provides the setting and ordinances, the actual covenant is with God. This dramatizes Psalm 118:9: the temple teaches that the individual's security and exaltation derive from direct relationship with God, not from institutional status or human favor.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's temptation narrative (Matthew 4:8–9) includes Satan's offer of 'all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them' if Christ would worship Satan. Christ's refusal embodies the principle of verse 9: all earthly power and princes are ultimately subject to evil if disconnected from God's authority. Christ's kingship, by contrast, is 'not of this world' (John 18:36) and is established through trust in the Father, not through worldly alliance. His exaltation comes through faithful obedience to God, not through acquisition of earthly power or alignment with earthly princes.
commentary.application: Modern Latter-day Saints encounter this principle in subtle and obvious forms. Subtle forms include placing ultimate hope in political leaders (either conservative or progressive), believing that a particular party's triumph will solve moral and spiritual crises, or trusting that government institutions will protect religious freedom. More obvious forms include idolizing celebrity leaders, business magnates, or even Church leaders as if their wisdom or power could replace God's guidance. Verse 9 cuts through all of this: no matter how brilliant, wealthy, charismatic, or powerful any human being is, they cannot be the foundation of ultimate trust. The practical implication is that Latter-day Saints should engage civically and prudently with political and social systems, but should do so while maintaining clear consciousness that God's purposes transcend all earthly kingdoms. When a policy or leader conflicts with revealed truth, covenant-keeping disciples align with God's word, not with princes.

text_kjv: All nations compassed me about: but in the name of the LORD will I destroy them.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 10 marks a dramatic shift from wisdom principle to narrative testimony. The psalmist has established the hierarchy of trust (verses 1–9); now the psalm illustrates why this hierarchy matters by describing an actual crisis. 'All nations compassed me about' (Hebrew: kol goyim sevavuni) places the psalmist in a position of complete encirclement. To be surrounded by all nations is not merely to face opposition but to face opposition from every direction, with no escape route and no neutral observer. This imagery is not necessarily literal military siege (though it could be); it is the experience of being hemmed in by hostility with no human recourse. The word goyim (nations) is significant—not personal enemies or rival tribes, but organized political entities with armies, wealth, and legitimacy.

The response pivots from the threat to the remedy: 'but in the name of the LORD will I destroy them.' The Hebrew construction (beshem YHWH ki amilam) emphasizes that the power to respond comes not from the psalmist's military capacity but from the name of the LORD—God's revealed character, authority, and power. To invoke the LORD's name is to appeal to His covenant identity, His proven faithfulness, and His authority over all creation. The verb 'destroy' (mul, Hiphil: amil) literally means 'to cut off' or 'to circumcise'—to remove or excise. The psalmist claims that in the name of the LORD, these surrounding nations will be cut off, removed from threat, executed in judgment.

This verse is eschatological in its horizon. It does not describe a battle that has already occurred; it is a declaration of faith that this confrontation will be resolved according to divine will, not human calculation. The pattern—threat, then invocation of God's name, then confidence in the outcome—demonstrates exactly why the hierarchy of trust established in verses 8–9 is crucial. When surrounded by all nations with no earthly help, the only recourse is the name of the LORD. This experience (or this theological claim about the nature of ultimate reality) vindicates the principle that trusting God rather than princes is the only wisdom.

word_study.meaning: All nations encircled me. The verb 'sevav' (סבב) means to go around, to encircle, to surround. 'Kol goyim' (all nations) emphasizes totality—not one enemy but all enemies, suggesting complete vulnerability. This is the language of siege, of being trapped with no exit.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering—'All nations surrounded me'—preserves the sense of encirclement. In covenant theology, this recalls God's protection of Israel against surrounding nations in the wilderness and land conquest. The reversal here is that the psalmist (possibly representing the whole community) is surrounded, not the nations around them. This inverts normal power dynamics and highlights the desperation that makes faith necessary.

word_study.term_english: in the name of the LORD
word_study.meaning: In/by the name of Yahweh. The name (shem) is not merely a label but encompasses the revealed identity, character, and authority of God. To invoke God's name is to appeal to all that God has revealed about Himself—His power, faithfulness, holiness, and covenant commitment. This is not magical thinking but rather reliance on God's nature as the basis for confidence.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'in the name' appears throughout scripture as the basis for efficacy in prayer, blessing, and spiritual authority. In D&C 29:26–27, the Lord says the Comforter 'shall teach you all things' and shall 'bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you.' The name of God—His revealed nature—is the ground of all power and authority. The psalmist's confidence rests not on a wish or hope but on the character of God.

word_study.meaning: I will cut them off, I will remove them. The Hiphil form of mul (מול), which primarily means 'to cut' or 'to circumcise.' In this context, it means to excise, to cut off, to remove completely. The tense is future—the psalmist declares what will happen, not what has already happened.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering—'I cut them off'—preserves the sense of decisive removal. This is not 'I will negotiate with them' or 'I will negotiate terms' but a complete severing of the threat. The confidence is absolute, stated as fact rather than wish or prayer.

cross_references.connection: David declares, 'The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?' and continues, 'Though an host should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear.' This parallel expresses the same confidence in God despite military threat.

'No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper; and every tongue that shall rise against thee in judgment thou shalt condemn.' This promise echoes Psalm 118:10—the assurance that enemies risen up will be cut off.

The Aramean army surrounds Elisha in Dothan, and Elisha's servant fears. Elisha prays, and God opens the servant's eyes to see the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire. The story illustrates the principle of verse 10—even when surrounded by all visible enemies, the LORD's army is infinitely greater.

Nephi declares, 'I will go and do the things which the Lord hath commanded, for I know that the Lord giveth no commandments unto the children of men, save he shall prepare a way for them that they may accomplish the thing which he commandeth them.' The same principle: the Lord's name is sufficient guarantee when trust is placed in His word.

The Lord teaches, 'I am the Lord your God, and I am willing to make you free... Verily, verily, I say unto you, as I said unto Peter, So I say unto you, that whatsoever ye desire which is right ye shall ask in my name being filled with my Spirit.' The name of the Lord is the conduit through which divine power operates.

commentary.historical_context: The image of 'all nations' surrounding the psalmist reflects the ANE political reality of small kingdoms hemmed in by superpowers. Judah, caught between Egypt and Mesopotamian empires, repeatedly faced situations where all surrounding powers were hostile or potentially hostile. The Babylonian siege (587 BCE) would have been a literal fulfillment—all neighboring nations submitted to Babylon while Judah resisted. Later, under Seleucid pressure (2nd century BCE), the Jewish community again faced comprehensive pressure from the ruling empire and its allies. The phrase 'all nations' carries the weight of ANE political powerlessness: a small community with no military option, no allies, no escape. In such situations, faith in divine deliverance became not optional spirituality but the only rational response. The psalm may derive from one specific crisis but was likely sung and reinterpreted through multiple crises, making it a template for community faith in survival.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 60:36 records Moroni's confidence despite being surrounded by enemies: 'I have come unto you with gladness that I might show unto you that ye have erred in your ways.' More directly, Helaman 5:50 describes the people experiencing divine deliverance: 'And it came to pass that the voices came again; and the words which they heard were: Repent ye, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. And again, and again were the voices heard, and by the multitude of them they were overpowered insomuch that they fell to the earth.' Even surrounded, deliverance comes through the word and power of God.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4–6 promises the prophet: 'Wherefore, meaning the church, thou shalt give heed unto all his words and commandments which he shall give unto you as he receiveth them, walking in all holiness before me; For his word ye shall receive, as if from mine own mouth, in all patience and faith. For by doing these things the gates of hell shall not prevail against you; yea, and the Lord God will disperse the powers of darkness from before you, and cause the heavens to shake for your good.' The name of the Lord, working through His servants, becomes the protection against all surrounding opposition.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, the endowment depicts the human soul surrounded by opposition and temptation (represented by Satan and his agents), yet protected by sacred covenants and the name of God invoked through proper authority. The psalmist's experience of being surrounded by all nations parallels the spiritual reality dramatized in temple ordinances—that without divine protection and covenant, we are vulnerable; with it, we are invincible.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's crucifixion fulfills the imagery of verse 10 in reverse: Christ himself is surrounded—by Roman soldiers, by mocking crowds, by disciples who flee. Yet His response is not to invoke military power but to submit to the Father's will and to trust in resurrection. Hebrews 2:14 states that Christ, through His death, 'destroyed' (Greek: katargeo, which can mean 'to reduce to inactivity' or 'to render powerless') death and Satan. The enemies that surrounded Christ (sin, death, and the devil) are cut off through Christ's atonement. Modern disciples, surrounded by opposition, are invited to follow Christ's pattern of trust in the Father's name rather than reliance on worldly power.
commentary.application: Latter-day Saints face crises where all visible options seem to close simultaneously: financial pressures that threaten security on all fronts, health crises that simultaneously affect family members, workplace or social situations where opposition seems universal and coordinated, or spiritual trials that feel all-encompassing. Verse 10 offers a response that transcends optimization or strategic maneuvering: when surrounded by forces that exceed human capacity to resist, the response is to invoke the name of the LORD and trust in divine judgment and deliverance. This is not passivity (the psalmist and later Israel did engage in battle and take practical steps) but rather a reorientation of confidence away from human strategy toward divine power. For modern Latter-day Saints, this means maintaining faith and covenant faithfulness even when all earthly indicators suggest defeat, trusting that the LORD's purposes will ultimately prevail. This is particularly relevant for those facing persecution for faith, economic hardship due to gospel principles, or family conflict due to Church membership—situations where 'all nations' seem arrayed against one's chosen path.

text_kjv: They compassed me about; yea, they compassed me about: but in the name of the LORD I will destroy them.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 11 repeats the structure of verse 10 but with significant intensification. The duplication 'They compassed me about; yea, they compassed me about' (Hebrew: savvuni gam sevavuni) emphasizes that this encirclement is not a momentary threat but an overwhelming, repeated, emphatic reality. The doubling in Hebrew is not merely stylistic; it is a rhetorical strategy that forces the hearer to acknowledge the seriousness of the situation. The enemies are not merely present; they are overwhelmingly, undeniably present. This intensification of the threat makes the response—'in the name of the LORD I will destroy them'—even more striking. The response does not escalate; it remains identical to verse 10. This is theologically significant: the psalmist's confidence in God does not increase with the threat; it remains stable and unshaken.

The repetition also serves a liturgical function. In temple worship and public prayer, repetition reinforces commitment and gives the assembly opportunity to join in affirming the truth. Verse 11 may have been sung as a refrain, with verses 10 and 11 forming a responsorial pattern where the first states the crisis and the second reiterates both the crisis and the divine response. This would make verse 11 not merely a logical repetition but a communal act of faith—the assembled people joining the psalmist in affirming that no matter how overwhelming the encirclement, the name of the LORD is sufficient.

The philosophical difference between verses 10 and 11 is subtle but important. Verse 10 might be interpreted as making a claim about a specific historical event or situation (nations did surround, and the LORD did destroy them). Verse 11, through its doubling and refrain-like quality, moves the statement toward timeless theological principle: whenever enemies surround, whenever the threat is overwhelming and repeated, the response is the same—trust in the LORD's name. This movement from historical narrative to universal principle is exactly what Psalm 118 accomplishes for the post-exilic community: it takes memory of past deliverance and transforms it into a template for present faith.

word_study.meaning: They surrounded me, they even surrounded me. The verb 'savvuni' (from sevav) appears twice, with 'gam' ('even' or 'also') intensifying the second occurrence. This construction emphasizes repetition and totality—not a single act of surrounding but repeated, comprehensive encirclement. The shift to 'they' personalizes the enemies as active agents, not mere circumstances.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering—'They surrounded me—yes, surrounded me on every side'—brings out the Hebrew doubling and its emphatic force. In covenant theology, this recalls God's surrounding protection of Israel: 'He found him in a desert land, and in the howling waste of the wilderness; he led him about, he instructed him, he kept him as the apple of his eye' (Deuteronomy 32:10). The reversal in Psalm 118 (enemies surrounding instead of God surrounding) heightens the drama and necessity of faith.

word_study.term_original: The TCR adds 'on every side' to render the nuance of gam sevavuni
word_study.meaning: The preposition 'gam' (also/even) combined with the repeated verb emphasizes that the encirclement is from all directions with no gap or escape. In siege terminology, this would mean that the enemies are not merely numerous but are positioned to prevent any break-out.
word_study.significance: For the psalmist's audience, this detail confirms hopelessness by worldly logic: the enemy has positioned forces comprehensively, blocking all escape routes. In such a situation, the only recourse is not military counter-attack but divine intervention. The verse's repeated emphasis on the completeness of the encirclement intensifies the miracle of the declaration of victory that follows.

cross_references.connection: Verse 11 is a deliberate repetition of verse 10, which itself suggests the unity and stability of the divine response: whether the crisis occurs once or repeatedly, whether the encirclement is sudden or persistent, the answer remains the same.

'He found him in a desert land, and in the howling waste of the wilderness; he led him about, he instructed him, he kept him as the apple of his eye.' This verse depicts God surrounding and protecting Israel, contrasting with Psalm 118:11 where enemies surround. The irony is that in Psalm 118, despite enemies surrounding, God's protection (invoked by His name) still prevails.

Paul writes, 'And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.' The principle echoes Psalm 118:11: weakness and being overwhelmed become the occasion for God's power to be displayed, not through escalation of human effort but through trust in divine sufficiency.

The Lord tells Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail: 'And all they who suffer persecution for my name, and endure in faith, though they are called to lay down their lives they shall receive an hundredfold, and shall dwell in my glory. But if they endure not, they shall obtain mercy.' The promise does not guarantee escape from persecution but guarantees that faith through persecution brings divine reward.

commentary.historical_context: The repetitive structure of verses 10–11 suggests liturgical use in temple worship, possibly as part of a festival celebration of God's deliverance. The Post-exilic community, lacking political independence and military power, would have regularly rehearsed experiences of being surrounded (literally by empires, metaphorically by spiritual opposition) and would have been gathered in the temple to affirm communal faith in divine protection. The Sukkot festival (Feast of Tabernacles) commemorated God's protection during the wilderness wandering and was celebrated with processional rites and communal recitation. Psalm 118 is explicitly associated with Hallel Psalms sung at Sukkot (Psalms 113–118) and Passover. The doubling of verses 10–11 would have resonated deeply with communities who lived in the reality of political encirclement but religious sanctuary—the temple was the one space where the surrounding empires' authority did not extend.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:12 records Ammon's trust: 'Behold, I say unto you, I do not boast in my own strength, nor in my own wisdom; but behold, my joy is full, yea, my heart is brim with joy, and I will rejoice in my God.' The principle of verse 11 is that joy and stability come not from military or strategic advantage but from invocation of God's name—which Ammon demonstrates even in the face of danger.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 109:22 teaches: 'And we ask thee, Holy Father, that thy servants may go forth from this house armed with thy power, and that thy name may be upon them, and thy glory be round about them, and thine angels have charge over them.' The name of God 'armed with power' and 'glory round about' them represents the fulfillment of Psalm 118:11's promise—that the name of the LORD becomes the armor and protection.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The repeated invocation of God's name in Psalm 118:11 parallels the temple liturgy where sacred names are invoked and covenants renewed. The temple endowment depicts the soul surrounded by opposition but protected through knowledge of God's name and sacred words. Verse 11, sung in the temple context, becomes not merely historical retrospective but present affirmation of protection through covenant and name.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's final words on the cross—'Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit' (Luke 23:46)—exemplify the principle of verse 11. Surrounded by enemies, abandoned by disciples, dying on the cross, Christ invokes the Father's name and trusts in the Father's care. His resurrection is the ultimate fulfillment of the promise that those who trust in God's name, even in complete encirclement, will be preserved. The refrain of verse 11—that the name of the LORD cuts off (destroys) the enemy—is fulfilled in Christ's victory over death and Satan.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, verse 11's repeated affirmation becomes particularly powerful in seasons of sustained opposition or trial. Unlike acute crises that resolve quickly, many covenant keepers face persistent, repeated opposition: chronic illness that returns, financial struggles that recur, workplace hostility that is ongoing, or family conflict that continues despite efforts at resolution. Verse 11 speaks directly to this experience—'they compassed me about, yea, they compassed me about.' The response is not to escalate one's own efforts or to despair at the persistence of opposition, but to renew one's invocation of God's name and commit more deeply to covenant trust. The doubled affirmation invites the hearer to echo it: 'Yes, the opposition is real, it is repeated, it is overwhelming—and in the name of the LORD I will overcome it.' This makes verse 11 a powerful scriptural anchor for those in long-term trials who need to renew their faith and commitment.

text_kjv: They compassed me about like bees; they are quenched as the fire of thorns: for in the name of the LORD I will destroy them.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 12 completes the cycle of verses 10–12 by adding vivid similes that characterize the nature of the enemies and make credible the declaration that they will be destroyed. The double simile—'like bees' and 'like fire of thorns'—is not merely poetic flourish; it makes a theological argument through metaphor. Bees are numerous, coordinated, aggressive, and their sting is painful and frightening; yet bees are fragile insects that can be driven off, drowned, or extinguished. Fire is fierce and consuming; yet thorn-fire burns with apparent fury but consumes the thorns quickly and completely, leaving ash and nothing remaining. The comparison suggests that the enemies, though numerous and fierce, are temporary and self-consuming.

The structure 'They compassed me about like bees; they are quenched as the fire of thorns' creates a profound theological inversion. In the first half, the enemies are 'like bees'—the comparison emphasizes threat and aggressiveness. But in the second half, they are not simply threatened; they are 'quenched' (Hebrew: doaku, from dak, to be extinguished or consumed)—the enemies themselves are consumed like thorn-fire. This is not a fight that the psalmist wins through superior strength; it is a self-consuming pattern where the enemies' own nature leads to their destruction. The fire of thorns burns hot and fierce but exhausts itself almost immediately because thorns are dry, brittle, and lack the substance to sustain flame. The metaphor suggests that the psalmist's enemies are similarly unsustainable—they may appear fierce, but their nature contains the seeds of their own destruction.

The closing refrain—'for in the name of the LORD I will destroy them'—reiterates the framework established in verses 10–11, but now the reader has been given the metaphors that make this declaration believable within the psalm's logic. The enemies are like bees (fierce but fragile) and like thorn-fire (hot but quickly extinguished). Because of this nature, and because the psalmist invokes the name of the LORD (whose power transcends any earthly force), the enemies will be cut off. This is not wish-thinking; it is theological realism grounded in the proper understanding of what makes a force enduring (divine power) versus temporary (human hatred, however organized and fierce).

word_study.meaning: Like bees, or more precisely, 'as bees.' The word devorim (דברים) can mean 'bees' (from davir, to buzz or hum) or 'words' (from dabar, to speak). In context, 'bees' is certain, though the ambiguity between 'bees' and 'words' might suggest that the enemies' aggression is as much through words and rhetoric as through action.
word_study.significance: Bees as a simile for enemies combines several associations: numerous (swarming), coordinated (organized in colonies), aggressive (stinging), and yet fragile (insects that can be overwhelmed by water, smoke, or cold). In biblical symbolism, bee imagery sometimes suggests judgment or plague (Deuteronomy 1:44—bees pursue the Amorites as God's instrument), making the comparison doubly suggestive that the enemies' swarming is itself under divine judgment.

word_study.meaning: They were extinguished, consumed, put out. The verb dak (דעך) means to be diminished, extinguished, or consumed. The Niphal form doaku emphasizes that the extinguishing happens passively (from the enemies' perspective) or is self-induced—the fire itself quenches.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering—'they blazed like a fire of thorns'—captures the active, fierce aspect before the verb 'quenched' describes the inevitable termination. The verb emphasizes that this destruction is not uncertain or remote but inevitable, like the certain extinction of a fire deprived of fuel.

word_study.meaning: Like fire of thorns, or fire consuming thorns. Thorn-fire is a vivid biblical image (Ecclesiastes 7:6—'For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool') that represents something fierce-seeming but short-lived and insubstantial. Thorns are dry, brittle, worthless plant material; when ignited, they burn with apparent fury but are quickly consumed, leaving nothing.
word_study.significance: The simile is culturally rooted: in the arid Near East, thorn-fire would have been a common, quickly-observed phenomenon. It serves as a universal symbol of something fierce but temporary, violent but ineffectual in any lasting sense. Ecclesiastes uses it to describe foolish laughter; Psalm 118 uses it to describe enemies—fierce in appearance but destined for quick consumption.

word_study.term_english: in the name of the LORD
word_study.meaning: In/by the name of Yahweh. As in verses 10–11, this phrase invokes God's revealed authority, power, and covenant identity. The name of God becomes the basis, the means, and the guarantee of the psalmist's response.
word_study.significance: The refrain 'in the name of the LORD I will destroy them' anchors all three verses (10–12) in the same source of power. No matter what simile is used (surrounded by nations, by enemies on every side, swarming like bees, burning like thorn-fire), the response is singular and unchanging: trust in God's name.

cross_references.connection: The Amorites pursue Israel, 'as bees do.' The simile appears in scripture as a metaphor for overwhelming, coordinated pursuit—which makes Psalm 118:12's comparison of enemies to bees a powerful inversion: though fierce, they will be consumed.

'For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool.' The thorn-fire simile appears here to denote something loud, apparent, but insubstantial—much like Psalm 118:12's depiction of enemies as fierce-seeming but self-consuming.

'And the light of Israel shall be for a fire, and his Holy One for a flame: and it shall burn and devour his thorns and his briars in one day.' The prophet reverses the simile: the LORD Himself becomes the fire that consumes thorn-briars, suggesting that enemies of Israel are like thorns to be consumed by God's fire.

'For while they be folden together as thorns, and while they are drunken as drunkards, they shall be devoured as stubble fully dry.' This judgment oracle uses the same logic as Psalm 118:12—that enemies grouped together like thorns are fuel for divine judgment, not sustainable opposition.

The Lord promises: 'And behold, this shall be given unto thee, that thou mayest overcome all the adversary, and to bring to light all things that are hid because of darkness—And to bring to pass thy covenants which I have made unto my people.' The name and authority of God, invoked through covenant, becomes the power to overcome enemies depicted in various metaphors.

commentary.historical_context: Psalm 118 emerges from a context where enemies are both metaphorically pervasive (opposition to God's people, to the psalmist, to right living) and sometimes literally military. The bee and thorn-fire similes would have been immediately intelligible to an agrarian, pastoral society where both insects and plant-fire posed genuine dangers. The images are not fantastical but grounded in observable reality: bees can indeed overwhelm and injure, and thorn-fire does indeed burn fiercely and briefly. The genius of the simile is to say that the enemies' real danger is of this character—temporary, consuming of themselves, lacking substance. This reframes the threat: rather than hopeless military inferiority, the situation is one where the enemy's nature contains inherent limitation. In a theological framework, this limitation becomes opportunity for faith: if enemies are inherently temporary and self-consuming, then trust in the eternal God becomes the only rational response.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Helaman 7:17–18 records Nephi's teaching: 'O ye people of these great cities which have fallen, and ye remnant of Joseph, behold, your great city shall be made desolate, that ye shall be thrown down, and there shall not be left one stone upon another; but there shall be thousands cast into the fire.' The pattern is similar to Psalm 118:12—fierce opposition that appears overwhelming but is ultimately consumed in judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:2 teaches: 'My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment. And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high; thou shalt triumph over all thy foes.' The principle of verse 12 is echoed: adversities are real but temporary and self-limiting; endurance results in exaltation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The endowment depicts opposition and temptation as fierce and pervasive, but also as subject to divine power when the correct name, sign, and token are invoked. Verse 12's bee and thorn-fire similes parallel the dramatization of opposition in the temple narrative—opposition is real but cannot ultimately prevail against those who know and invoke the name of God.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's crucifixion and the events leading to it present Him surrounded by enemies 'like bees'—the crowds who mock, the religious leaders who accuse, the Roman soldiers who crucify—each group acting with coordinated animosity. Yet Christ remains centered in trust in the Father, and the cross itself becomes the fire that consumes the enemies' power. Through the resurrection, the enemies' apparent victory turns to ash: Satan's kingdom is diminished, sin and death are overcome, and the powers arrayed against Christ are revealed as temporary and ultimately ineffectual. The bees and thorn-fire that surrounded Christ on the cross became the very instruments through which Christ's exaltation was secured.
