commentary.application: Modern Latter-day Saints face opposition that can feel overwhelming—cultural pressure against traditional values, hostile rhetoric in media and academia, family members who mock faith, colleagues who discriminate based on religious belief. Verse 12 invites a reframing of this opposition: however fierce and coordinated it appears, it contains inherent limitation. Trends that feel permanent are subject to cultural change; opponents who seem powerful are vulnerable to the consequences of their own choices; hostility fueled by deception contains the seeds of its own dissolution when truth prevails. The practical application is neither naivety (opposition is real and can cause real harm) nor despair (opposition is temporary and ultimately self-consuming). Rather, it is to maintain faith that God's name and power transcend all human opposition and that endurance through opposition becomes the occasion for one's own spiritual transformation and exaltation. The bee and thorn-fire similes grant permission to see opposition as fierce but finite, terrifying but temporary—which allows faith to persist even when opposition is real and pervasive.

text_kjv: Thou hast thrust sore at me that I might fall: but the LORD helped me.

commentary.narrative: This verse marks a sharp turn in Psalm 118. The psalmist has been celebrating victory, but now he pauses to recount the severity of the attack that preceded it. The enemy's intent was unambiguous: to push him down permanently, to cause a fall from which he would not rise. The Hebrew infinitive absolute (dachoh dechitani) intensifies the verb—this was not a casual shove but a determined, forceful assault meant to destroy. Yet in the very moment when physical collapse seemed inevitable, divine help arrived. The contrast between 'pushed hard—pushed to falling' and the simple declaration 'but the LORD helped me' is deliberately structured. The elaborate description of the attack makes the conciseness of God's aid all the more striking. The enemy's violence receives detailed attention; God's rescue, though utterly decisive, requires only four words in Hebrew. This rhetorical choice teaches that we need not dwell on the magnitude of our opposition—what matters is that the LORD's help is sufficient.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verse assumes a dangerous moment has passed. The psalmist is not describing an ongoing attack but a remembered crisis. By placing this recollection here, after verses celebrating victory in the gates and establishment in righteousness, the psalmist anchors his current confidence in a concrete historical moment when divine intervention proved real and immediate. For an ancient Israelite worshipper, this would resonate with collective memory of deliverance from Egypt, from enemies in the wilderness, from armies threatening Jerusalem. The personal 'I' in this verse speaks on behalf of the covenant community—every member of God's people has experienced this push toward destruction and this rescue.

word_study.meaning: The infinitive absolute dachoh intensifies the verbal root dachah ('to push, to shove, to drive away'). The doubling of the root with infinitive absolute creates an emphatic, forceful sense: 'pushing, you pushed me' or 'you thrust me hard.' The verb indicates violent physical force intended to overwhelm.
word_study.significance: In covenant theology, this language of being pushed toward destruction appears repeatedly when Israel faces enemies or internal sin. The intensity of the root word signals that the threat was real and existential, not merely theoretical. God does not minimize the danger His people face; He acknowledges it fully before revealing His rescue.

word_study.meaning: To help, to aid, to come alongside someone in need. The root conveys active support—one who helps is present and engaged. In covenant contexts, 'help' often means the full intervention of God's power on behalf of His people.
word_study.significance: The verb azar appears throughout the Psalms and the Standard Works as the signature word for divine assistance. It is not passive comfort but active intervention. When God helps, He changes the situation materially. This word carries the full weight of covenantal promise: 'I will be with thee' (D&C 6:34) is concretized as 'I helped you.'

word_study.meaning: The covenant name of God, appearing thousands of times throughout Hebrew scripture. The name itself derives from the verb 'to be' (hayah), suggesting God's eternal existence and presence.
word_study.significance: The psalmist deliberately uses the covenant name here rather than Elohim (God) or Adonai (Lord). This signals that the help comes not from a distant deity but from the God bound by covenant oath to His people. In Latter-day Saint theology, this name is associated with Jehovah, who became Jesus Christ in the meridian of time.

cross_references.connection: When Israel faces the Egyptian army at the Red Sea, Moses declares, 'Stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD.' This foundational deliverance mirrors the psalmist's experience: pushed toward destruction by enemies, rescued by God's mighty hand.

In the Kirtland Temple dedication prayer, the Lord promises, 'Thou hast given us a commandment that we should ask and receive...and we ask thee, Holy Father, that thy name may be kept holy.' The psalmist's cry for help and receipt of rescue exemplifies this pattern of petition and answer.

Alma testifies to his son Helaman: 'I have seen...the captivity and the release of Lehi in the wilderness, and the sending of the angels to minister unto them.' Divine help in the moment of greatest peril is a recurring pattern in Book of Mormon theology.

Nephi's declaration—'The Lord giveth no commandments unto the children of men, save he shall prepare a way for them'—captures the same principle: when God calls His people into difficulty, He does not abandon them to destruction but provides the means of deliverance.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern warfare and honor culture, being 'pushed' or 'shoved' was not merely a physical act but a public humiliation—a statement that one's opponent had superior strength and dominance. The enemy's intent in this verse is not only to defeat the psalmist but to establish public shame and permanent subordination. The language of being pushed 'to falling' suggests the psalmist is on the verge of permanent defeat, loss of status, and possibly death. In the context of Israel's history, such 'pushes' came from various enemies: Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Edom, neighboring peoples. But they also came from internal threats—the psalmist may be describing persecution from within Israel itself, perhaps enemies at the gates of Jerusalem or rivals at the sanctuary. The help of the LORD, by contrast, is not merely a lucky escape but a reversal of the entire power dynamic. Where the enemy pushed hard, God helps; where destruction loomed, rescue arrives.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 26:12, Ammon rejoices: 'My joy is full, yea, my heart is brim with joy, and I am filled with exceedingly great joy in the success of my brethren, who have been the means of bringing so many souls to repentance; and how blessed are they!' This passage mirrors the structure of Psalm 118:13—the recounting of past opposition followed by the declaration of God's help and the resulting joy. Alma 36 similarly recounts persecution and suffering followed by divine intervention and the ability to serve others.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 31:9 records: 'Contend against no church, save it be the church of the devil.' The recognition that opposition comes, and comes forcefully, is foundational to Restoration theology. Yet the covenant promise follows: 'Your Father knoweth that you have need of all things' (D&C 6:38). The pattern of the psalmist—pushed hard, helped by God—is woven throughout Doctrine and Covenants. See also D&C 121:7-9, where Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail recalls his afflictions and receives the assurance that God's help will not fail.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple worship, the pattern of being pushed toward destruction and rescued by God's hand is enacted symbolically. The endowment ceremony dramatizes the opposition of evil forces and the help of God's power to overcome them. The veil of the temple represents the membrane between the world's opposition and God's sanctuary—a place where one realizes that despite all opposition, the LORD has helped.

commentary.christological_typology: In the fullest sense, Psalm 118:13 prophetically describes Jesus Christ's experience. Christ was 'pushed' toward destruction by His enemies—the religious establishment, the political powers of Rome, and ultimately by the weight of all human sin. In Gethsemane, He faced the full force of opposition and the apparent certainty of death. Yet the Father 'helped' Him through resurrection and exaltation. The verb 'helped' (azar) points to the Father's intervention on behalf of the Son, a pattern that frames the entire Gospel narrative. Moreover, Christ becomes for all believers the source of help—those who are pushed by the world's opposition find their rescue in Him.
commentary.application: In modern covenant life, Psalm 118:13 offers clarifying perspective on trials. The verse does not deny that opposition is real or forceful—it acknowledges both fully. 'Thou hast thrust sore at me' is the psalmist's honest assessment, not an understatement. Yet the immediate turn—'but the LORD helped me'—teaches us not to fixate on the magnitude of opposition but to recognize where help comes from. When facing workplace persecution, family conflict, or internal doubt, the covenant member is invited to do what the psalmist did: name the push honestly, then declare confidently where rescue originates. The help may not come as dramatically as we hope, but it will come—sometimes through community, sometimes through sudden clarity, sometimes through the strength to endure. The key is recognizing that God's help is always active, always present, always sufficient.

text_kjv: The LORD is my strength and song, and is become my salvation.

commentary.narrative: Verse 14 is a direct quotation of Exodus 15:2, the ancient victory song sung by Israel after crossing the Red Sea. By embedding this line into Psalm 118, the psalmist claims that his personal deliverance is a re-enactment of the Exodus itself. Every survivor, every person rescued by God, participates in the cosmic pattern established when Israel passed through water to freedom. The psalmist does not merely say, 'God helped me.' He says, 'The God who was Israel's strength and song at the Red Sea is my strength and song now.' This is intertextual anchoring—placing a personal experience within the framework of Israel's greatest collective memory. The word 'song' (zimrat) carries a double resonance: it means both 'song' (something sung in celebration) and potentially 'strength' or 'protection' (from a related root meaning 'to be strong'). This ambiguity is likely intentional. God is both the strength that enables survival and the song that celebrates survival. He is the military power that defeats enemies and the joy that follows victory.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'is become my salvation' marks a shift from potential to realized, from promise to fulfillment. Vayehi li lishu'ah ('and He became for me salvation') uses the verb 'to be' in the perfect tense, indicating completed action. The salvation is not future or conditional but present and established. For the psalmist, this is not hope deferred but hope realized. The verse moves from characterizing God (what He is) to characterizing the psalmist's relationship to Him (what He has become for me). This is the movement from theology to testimony. Every member of the covenant community is invited to make this declaration: God is my strength (the power I need), my song (the joy I celebrate), and my salvation (the deliverance I have experienced).

word_study.meaning: My strength, my power, my might. From the root oz, meaning 'to be strong.' Ozzi is strength understood as the power to overcome, to endure, to accomplish what seems impossible. In military contexts, it refers to the power that wins battles; in personal contexts, it refers to the inner fortitude that persists through suffering.
word_study.significance: The Psalmist does not say God gives strength but that God is strength—He is the very source and substance of power. This echoes throughout Latter-day Saint covenant language: 'My Grace is sufficient for all men' (D&C 17:8). The strength available to the covenant member is not borrowed from some external store but flows directly from God's nature.

word_study.meaning: Song, music, or possibly strength/protection (the semantic range depends on which root is intended—zamar meaning 'to sing' or a related root meaning 'to protect'). The Covenant Rendering notes that this ambiguity may be intentional. The word carries connotations of celebration, of victory cries, of the sound that follows deliverance.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'strength and song' is a complete expression of God's rescue. He provides both the power needed for the battle and the joy that follows victory. In Jewish tradition, zimrat Yah ('the song of the LORD') became a title for divine praises. By using this exact phrase from Exodus 15, the psalmist claims that personal deliverance is never isolated—it is always a note in the larger symphony of God's redemptive history.

word_study.meaning: Deliverance, rescue, salvation. From the root yasha, meaning 'to save, to deliver, to set free.' Yeshu'ah encompasses physical rescue, spiritual restoration, and the reestablishment of right relationship with God. It is both a momentary rescue and an ongoing state of being saved.
word_study.significance: In Latter-day Saint theology, yeshu'ah points to Jesus (Yeshua in Aramaic), whose very name means salvation. The psalmist's personal experience of yeshu'ah from enemies is ultimately a type and shadow of the universal salvation offered through Christ. Every deliverance from sin, from despair, from opposition is a participation in the salvation that Christ accomplished.

cross_references.connection: The psalmist quotes this verse directly: 'The LORD is my strength and song, and is become my salvation.' The reference anchors the personal deliverance described in Psalm 118 within Israel's founding redemptive moment.

Isaiah uses the same phrase—'The LORD is my strength and my song'—in a context of restoration after exile, showing that this formula of praise becomes the recurring way Israel celebrates God's rescue across different historical periods.

The Book of Mormon quotes Isaiah 12:2: 'Behold, God is my salvation: I will trust, and not be afraid; for the Lord JEHOVAH is my strength and my song; he also has become my salvation.' This shows that the Restoration tradition preserves and affirms this pattern of praise.

The Lord declares to His people: 'Verily I say unto you...for I am the Lord your God, and the God of your fathers.' The personal claim of relationship ('my strength,' 'my salvation') is grounded in this covenant identity, where God is not abstract but personally bound to His people.

Ammon rejoices: 'And I do this that I may rejoice in the day when I shall see him in his glory.' Like the psalmist, Ammon moves from rehearsing deliverance to celebrating the God who accomplished it, combining testimony of salvation with joy.

commentary.historical_context: The Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:1-18) was likely one of the oldest liturgical pieces in Israel, preserved and recited across centuries. By the time Psalm 118 was composed (likely in the post-exilic period, though possible earlier), this song would have been ancient, venerable, and the foundational expression of Israelite faith. To quote it was to position oneself within continuity with all previous generations who had sung these words. The phrase 'strength and song' in ancient Near Eastern contexts evokes both military victory (strength) and the celebration that follows—feasting, music, poetry. When the psalmist claims, 'The LORD is my strength and song,' he is claiming not merely survival but victory, not merely escape but cause for celebration. In the context of Psalm 118, which celebrates entry into the gates of Jerusalem and establishment before all nations, this phrase takes on public and communal dimensions. The psalmist's personal salvation is celebrated as a sign that God's power is not diminished, that His covenant remains active, that His people can still trust in His strength.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon preserves the language of Psalm 118 and the Isaiah quotations that echo it, showing that latter-day saints understand themselves as participating in the same pattern of deliverance. Nephi's vision of Christ in 1 Nephi 11 shows that every deliverance from the world's opposition is ultimately wrought through Christ. The 'strength' that enables escape from Lehi's family's enemies, the 'song' that the righteous sing in the promised land—these are all reflections of the ultimate strength and song found in the Savior.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: In D&C 64:34, the Lord states: 'Wherefore, be not weary in well-doing, for ye are laying the foundation of a great work...Therefore, your potency shall not be diminished.' The psalmist's declaration of God's strength becomes a promise for latter-day saints enduring their own trials. The covenant God is the same God, possessing the same strength to save. D&C 84:88 adds: 'And whoso receiveth you receiveth me; and the same will feed you, and clothe you, and give you money...and shall be your physician and your counselor and your guide...and I will walk with you and talk with you.' This is the strength and song of the Lord made available to the covenant community.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple ceremony, the presentation of God as strength and song is central to the endowment's message. The participant experiences opposition (the fall in the garden, the deceits of Satan), but then receives instruction, covenants, and the assurance of God's protection and guidance. The language of praise—'Glory, honor, and immortality be to God the only wise and true God'—echoes the psalmist's celebration. The temple is where strength and song unite in the presence of God.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is, in the fullest sense, the strength and song of humanity. He is the strength that conquers sin, death, and the power of Satan. Every deliverance from evil finds its source in His atonement and resurrection. The 'song' that follows is the hymn of redemption, sung by all those who have been saved through Him. In Revelation 5, the redeemed sing a new song: 'Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood.' This song is the completion and fulfillment of Psalm 118:14. The personal salvation of the psalmist, and of every faithful member of the covenant community, participates in this larger Christological reality.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members can claim Psalm 118:14 as their own testimony. When facing uncertainty about whether God is truly present and active, the verse invites us to claim the same position as the ancient psalmist—to declare that God is not merely a historical figure from the Exodus but 'my strength' (available now), 'my song' (deserving of celebration now), and 'my salvation' (realized in my life now). This is not presumption but claim of covenant promise. In sacrament meetings, in family prayers, in moments of personal crisis, the declaration 'The LORD is my strength and song, and is become my salvation' is an act of covenant renewal. It says: I am joining Israel's ancient cry. I am joining all generations of the faithful. I am claiming the promise that God's strength is mine, God's joy is mine, and God's salvation is mine.

text_kjv: The voice of rejoicing and salvation is in the tabernacles of the righteous: the right hand of the LORD doeth valiantly.

commentary.narrative: Verse 15 shifts the focus from the psalmist's individual experience to the community's collective celebration. The 'voice of rejoicing and salvation' is not solitary; it fills 'the tabernacles of the righteous'—the dwellings where God's covenant people gather. The image is auditory and spatial: imagine entering an Israelite encampment (or the courtyards of Jerusalem's temple) and hearing the sound of celebration, the shouts of joy and testimony. The psalmist is not alone in his rescue; his deliverance has become the occasion for community-wide rejoicing. This is crucial to understanding Psalm 118 within its liturgical context. The psalm is likely sung by a pilgrimage or festival community, perhaps at the Feast of Tabernacles or another major celebration when Israel gathers at the sanctuary. What one person experiences becomes the basis for all God's people to celebrate, because the deliverance of any member of the covenant community is evidence of God's continuing faithfulness to the whole community.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'the right hand of the LORD doeth valiantly' appears to be a quotation—the psalmist marks it as something the righteous are actually saying within their tents. The verb 'does valiantly' (osah chayil, literally 'does might' or 'works with power') carries military connotations. It suggests not merely passive help but active, powerful intervention. The 'right hand' of God is mentioned three times in verses 15-16, creating an emphatic refrain. In Hebrew culture, the right hand is the hand of power, oath-taking, blessing, and action. To say God's right hand works with power is to affirm that God is not distant or indifferent but actively engaged in history, actively defending His people, actively asserting His will. The righteous in their tents are not merely celebrating a past deliverance; they are proclaiming a living reality: the LORD's power is actively at work on behalf of His covenant people.

word_study.meaning: Voice, sound, cry, noise. Qol can refer to human speech, animal sounds, thunder, wind—any audible phenomenon. In covenant contexts, it often refers to the voice of testimony, proclamation, or prayer that reaches God's ears.
word_study.significance: The psalmist emphasizes that what is happening in the tents of the righteous is not silent contemplation but vocal, public testimony. The salvation must be spoken, sung, proclaimed. This connects to the prophetic tradition where God's word (dabar) must be spoken into the world. The voice of the righteous community becomes a vehicle for God's testimony about His own faithfulness.

word_study.meaning: A shout of joy, a cry of jubilation, a ringing cry. The word connotes not quiet contentment but exuberant, public expression of delight. It is the sound made at celebrations, at victories, at the presence of the king.
word_study.significance: The psalmist chooses a word for joy that implies witness and publicity. This is not private happiness but communal exultation. It suggests that the salvation deserves to be celebrated boldly, without shame or restraint. In covenant contexts, such joyful shouting is appropriate and expected response to God's mighty works.

word_study.meaning: Tents, tabernacles, dwellings. Ohel (singular) originally referred to the nomadic tents of the patriarchal era, but it could also refer to the festival tents (sukkot) used during Tabernacles, or more broadly to any dwelling place of God's people.
word_study.significance: The choice of 'tents' rather than 'houses' or 'sanctuaries' may evoke the wilderness period or the festival context of Tabernacles, when Israel commemorated God's protection during the wilderness wandering. The tents of the righteous are portrayed as places where God's salvation is both recognized and celebrated—they are sacred spaces because they are inhabited by those in covenant with God.

word_study.meaning: The righteous, the just, those who are in right relationship with God. From the root tzedek (righteousness, justice). The righteous are not merely good people but those who are aligned with God's covenant, who have chosen to serve God and walk in His ways.
word_study.significance: The psalmist identifies those whose tents fill with the voice of salvation as 'the righteous'—implying that deliverance and salvation are experienced most fully by those who maintain covenant relationship with God. Righteousness and salvation are linked; they are not contradictory states but mutually reinforcing.

word_study.meaning: The right hand, the side of power and authority. In ancient Near Eastern culture, the right hand was the hand of action, blessing, military strength, and oaths. To place someone at one's right hand is to elevate them; for God to raise His right hand is to act in power.
word_study.significance: The emphasis on God's right hand throughout these verses invokes a cluster of associations: God's active power, His protective might, His ability to fulfill oaths. When Israel says 'the right hand of the LORD doeth valiantly,' they are claiming that God is not passive but actively fighting on their behalf, actively pursuing their enemies, actively establishing their deliverance.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'to do/work might' or 'to accomplish valor.' Chayil is military might, strength in warfare, power to overcome. Osah is simply 'to do' or 'to work.' Together, the phrase means God actively accomplishes mighty deeds, exerts power, conquers enemies.
word_study.significance: This is not passive presence but active intervention. God does not merely exist alongside His people; He acts on their behalf. The verb osah ('to do') appears throughout the Psalms in descriptions of God's mighty works (ma'aseh YHWH, 'the works of the LORD'). By using osah chayil, the psalmist affirms that God's character is revealed in action, in the mighty works He performs on behalf of His covenant people.

cross_references.connection: In the Song of the Sea, Israel proclaims: 'Thy right hand, O LORD, is become glorious in power: thy right hand, O LORD, hath dashed in pieces the enemy.' The same theme of God's right hand acting with power appears in this foundational victory song.

The very next verse repeats and expands this theme: 'The right hand of the LORD is exalted: the right hand of the LORD doeth valiantly.' The repetition creates a drumbeat emphasizing God's active power.

Nephi sees Christ and testifies: 'And I saw the Lamb of God going forth among the children of men...and I beheld that he was lifted up upon the cross and slain for the sins of the world.' The right hand of the LORD—Christ—does valiantly through the atonement.

The Lord declares: 'Hearken, O ye elders of my church...I am Jesus Christ, the Son of God. I came in the meridian of time unto my own, and my own received me not.' The voice of salvation and the mighty works of the Lord's right hand continue into the restoration.

Nephi teaches that by following Christ, we enter 'the narrow path which leads to eternal life; yea, the path which is prepared...and few there be that find it.' The righteous in their tents celebrate entry into this path, which is made possible by the Lord's mighty hand.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, the tabernacles or tents would likely refer either to the encampments of pilgrims gathering at a festival, or to the dwellings of Jerusalem, or both. When Psalm 118 is sung as a liturgical piece during the Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot), the reference to 'tabernacles of the righteous' has a double resonance: the sukkot (festival booths) where pilgrims dwell during the festival are literally tabernacles, and they house the righteous community celebrating God's protection. The 'voice of rejoicing and salvation' filling these spaces would be audible—pilgrims would hear singing, shouting, testimony from tent to tent. This creates a participatory, communal experience. The psalmist is not describing an imagined scenario but inviting hearers to recognize what is actually happening: across the encampment, from tent to tent, the sound of God's salvation is being proclaimed. In the context of ancient Near Eastern religious practice, such communal celebration was essential to covenant renewal. By gathering, by hearing the testimony of deliverance, by joining their voices in proclamation of God's mighty works, the community reaffirmed their corporate identity as God's people and their confidence in His continuing protection.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 5, Alma invites his people to gather and hear testimony: 'I see that ye are going about and serving the devil...Will ye persist in supposing that ye are better than your brethren?' Later in the same chapter: 'And now behold, I say unto you, my brethren, if ye have experienced a change of heart, and have felt to sing the song of redeeming love, I would ask, have ye spiritually been born of God?' The 'voice of rejoicing and salvation' in Psalm 118:15 finds its parallel in the 'song of redeeming love' sung by those who have experienced covenant conversion. The righteous community in their 'tabernacles' becomes the people gathered in the temple and in sacrament meetings, testifying of God's power.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: In D&C 43:15-16, the Lord declares: 'Harken to the voice of the Lord your God, while I speak unto you...for I am the God that have taken you for an house of Israel.' The voice of salvation filling the tabernacles of the righteous is God's promise made manifest through His people's testimony. D&C 133:56-57 teaches: 'And the glory of the Lord shall be there, and the terror of the Lord also shall be there, insomuch that the wicked will not come unto it, and it shall be called Zion. And it shall come to pass that the righteous shall be gathered out from among all nations, and shall come to Zion, singing songs of everlasting joy.' This describes the ultimate gathering of the righteous in their tabernacles, where the voice of rejoicing and salvation fills the place.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the modern 'tabernacle of the righteous.' In temple ceremonies, participants hear the voice of testimony and instruction about God's mighty works and His salvation. The temple ordinances are performed by the righteous and for the righteous, and they celebrate the power of the Lord's right hand extended through covenants. The voice of prayer, praise, and testimony that fills the temple grounds is the contemporary fulfillment of the voice of rejoicing and salvation described in Psalm 118:15.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the source and substance of the 'right hand of the LORD' that does valiantly. In Luke 22:69, Jesus tells the Sanhedrin: 'Hereafter shall the Son of man sit on the right hand of the power of God.' And in Acts 7:55, Stephen, filled with the Holy Ghost, looks into heaven and sees 'the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God.' The right hand of the LORD, which does mighty works in the Psalms, is ultimately revealed to be Christ Himself. Every mighty act of God on behalf of His people—from Egypt to Canaan, from exile to restoration—is ultimately an act of the right hand of God, which is Christ exalted. The voice of rejoicing and salvation filled the tents of the righteous at every crucial moment in salvation history, and reaches its crescendo in the proclamation of Christ's resurrection and atonement.
commentary.application: In modern covenant practice, Psalm 118:15 invites us to recognize and participate in the voice of rejoicing and salvation within our communities of faith. This is not optional or marginal; it is central to covenant identity. When we gather in sacrament meetings, family homes evenings, temple sessions, or informal testimonies with friends, we are filling the contemporary 'tabernacles of the righteous' with the voice of salvation. Each testimony of divine help, each song of praise, each teaching of God's mighty works is a note in the ongoing proclamation that 'the right hand of the LORD doeth valiantly.' The verse also invites us to listen—to hear the voice of salvation in others' testimonies, to recognize in their experiences evidence that God is actively at work, not historically but now. When a friend shares how they were protected from temptation, when a family member testifies of unexpected financial blessing, when a missionary describes a divine appointment, we are hearing the voice of rejoicing and salvation fill the tents of the righteous. To participate is to join our voice to this chorus, to sing and shout that God's power is real and active.

text_kjv: The right hand of the LORD is exalted: the right hand of the LORD doeth valiantly.

commentary.narrative: This verse repeats and expands the theme of verse 15, but with a crucial shift in emphasis. Where verse 15 quoted the righteous shouting about God's right hand doing valiantly, verse 16 adds a new descriptor: the right hand is 'exalted' (romemah). The image intensifies: picture a warrior who has won the battle and raises his sword-hand in triumph—not to strike again, but to demonstrate victory, to show that the enemy is defeated, to claim dominion over all who see the raised hand. The verb romemah ('is raised high, is exalted, is lifted up') suggests both the physical gesture of raising one's hand in victory and the spiritual elevation of God's power and status. By repeating the phrase 'the right hand of the LORD doeth valiantly,' the psalmist establishes a drumbeat rhythm. The repetition is not redundancy but emphasis—a proclamation that rings through the assembly. In Hebrew poetry, such repetition is a rhetorical technique that drives truth deep into the hearer's memory and heart. The message is: God's right hand is not hidden; it is displayed, exalted, lifted high for all to see. And its nature is to do valiantly—to accomplish mighty deeds, to defeat enemies, to establish righteousness.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verse also serves a structural function within Psalm 118. We are near the climax of the psalm. The individual has been rescued (verse 13), has claimed deliverance as his salvation (verse 14), and the community has joined to celebrate (verse 15). Now, in verse 16, the focus shifts to the cosmological level: God's right hand is exalted—not merely in one location or for one people, but in heaven itself, exalted above all creation. This is the movement from testimony to doxology, from telling what God did to proclaiming who God is. The psalmist is saying that the deliverance experienced in Jerusalem is a manifestation of a power that is universal and eternal—the right hand of the LORD that upholds the cosmos itself.

word_study.meaning: Is exalted, is raised up, is lifted high. From the root rum, meaning 'to be high, to be exalted, to be lifted up.' The verb conveys both physical raising and spiritual elevation—a high position, a state of honor and authority.
word_study.significance: The psalmist uses a verb associated with kingship and divine glory. When a hand is 'exalted' in the context of battle, it signals victory and dominion. In covenant theology, the exaltation of God's right hand affirms His supreme power and authority. Nothing can resist the exalted right hand of the LORD. This word echoes throughout the Psalms and the Restoration, where God's exaltation is the foundation of hope.

word_study.meaning: The right hand, the side of authority, power, blessing, and action. In ancient contexts, the right hand is consistently the hand of dominance and control.
word_study.significance: The triple (and soon quadruple, in verse 17) invocation of God's 'right hand' in close succession creates an almost incantatory effect. The psalmist is drilling this truth into consciousness: it is God's right hand—not the left, which is weaker; not a distant power, which is ineffectual; but the right hand of God, the hand of action and might. In Latter-day Saint discourse, God's 'right hand' can also evoke the concept of God's power and the priesthood which acts in that power.

word_study.meaning: To do mighty works, to act with strength, to accomplish powerful deeds. Chayil encompasses military prowess, wealth, strength, and the power to accomplish great things. Osah is simply the verb 'to do,' which in combination with chayil means God actively works might.
word_study.significance: By repeating osah chayil, the psalmist emphasizes that this is not merely a passive state (God's right hand is exalted) but an active, ongoing reality (God's right hand does valiantly). The exaltation of God's power is not historical (something that happened in the past) but continuous (something that is happening). This is central to covenant faith: God's mighty works are not confined to biblical history but continue into our own time and experience.

cross_references.connection: This verse directly echoes the Song of the Sea: 'Thy right hand, O LORD, is become glorious in power: thy right hand, O LORD, hath dashed in pieces the enemy.' The pattern of celebrating God's exalted right hand goes back to Israel's founding deliverance.

Another psalm declares: 'Thine hand shall find out all thine enemies: thy right hand shall find out those that hate thee.' The right hand of God is exalted not merely in abstract glory but in concrete opposition to God's enemies.

Israel testifies: 'For they got not the land in possession by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them: but thy right hand, and thine arm, and the light of thy countenance.' The right hand of God, not human strength, is the true source of all deliverance.

Ammon proclaims: 'And I do this that I may rejoice in the day when I shall see him in his glory.' The exalted right hand of the LORD is revealed in the exalted Christ, whose hand extends to save all who believe.

In the vision of the degrees of glory, John describes seeing Christ: 'And now, after the many testimonies which have been given of him, this is the testimony, last of all, which we give of him: That he lives!' Christ is the ultimate expression of the LORD's exalted right hand.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern culture, the exaltation of a king's hand or the hand of a deity signified dominion, victory, and authority. When an Assyrian king raised his hand in conquest, inscriptions would record it as a sign of universal power. Similarly, Egyptian pharaohs are depicted with raised hands in scenes of triumph. When the psalmist speaks of the LORD's right hand being exalted, he is claiming that God's power exceeds all earthly powers—it is higher, more enduring, more truly victorious. In the specific context of Psalm 118, which likely relates to a specific historical crisis (possible interpretations include the rededication of the temple after Maccabean victory, or a later military threat to Jerusalem), the verse affirms that whatever earthly enemy threatened Israel has been met by the exalted right hand of God. But the verse transcends the historical moment; it makes a claim about God's universal and eternal power. The raised hand of the LORD is not merely Israel's protection but the cosmic principle of God's supremacy.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 27:22, the Lord declares: 'And in that day the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people...and he shall set up a standard for the nations.' This is the exalted right hand of the LORD set to gather Israel in latter days. The raising of the hand of the LORD for a second time parallels the emphasis in Psalm 118:16 on the continuous, ongoing activity of God's exalted power.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: In D&C 29:2, the Lord declares: 'I am Jesus Christ, the Son of God. I came in the meridian of time unto my own, and my own received me not.' Yet verse 11-12 continue: 'And there shall be silence in heaven for the space of half an hour; and immediately after shall the curtain of heaven be unfolded...and the right hand of the LORD shall be upon them.' The exalted right hand of the LORD is explicitly identified as Christ's right hand, extended over the covenant people in the latter days.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple endowment, the presentation of God as exalted and powerful is central to the message. The participant is taught that God's hand is raised in blessing and protection, and that by entering into covenant with God, one comes under the shadow of that exalted right hand. The raising of the hand in temple worship (in certain ordinances and settings) mirrors the exaltation described in this verse—it is a gesture of power, of sealing, of divine authority.

commentary.christological_typology: In Ephesians 1:20, Paul describes the Father's power 'which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places.' The exalted right hand of the LORD is ultimately Christ Himself, exalted at the right hand of God the Father. Christ's exaltation is the culmination and revelation of God's right hand at work throughout history. In Hebrews 1:3, Christ is described as 'the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power.' Christ, exalted at God's right hand, upholds all things—He is the cosmic principle of God's power made personal, made incarnate, made present.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Psalm 118:16 offers a powerful corrective to any sense that God's power is diminished or that our challenges are beyond His reach. The verse invites us to look up, to raise our eyes to heaven, and to contemplate the exalted right hand of the LORD. This is not merely poetic fancy but a theological truth meant to shape how we understand our place in the cosmos. When facing opposition, opposition, illness, doubt, or despair, the psalmist invites us to affirm: 'The right hand of the LORD is exalted: the right hand of the LORD doeth valiantly.' This is not a claim that our difficulties will vanish but a recognition that our difficulties are met by a power infinitely greater than they are. The covenant member's response is to trust in that exalted power, to align himself or herself with its purposes, and to expect that God's right hand will accomplish mighty works on his or her behalf. In sacrament, in priesthood blessings, in temple ordinances, in prayer, the covenant member appeals to and claims the power of God's exalted right hand.

text_kjv: I shall not die, but live, and declare the works of the LORD.

commentary.narrative: Verse 17 is one of the most powerful and frequently quoted lines in the Psalms. The psalmist moves from celebrating God's exalted power (verses 15-16) to making a personal, absolute claim about his own destiny: 'I shall not die, but live.' The structure—'not death...but life'—is stark and definitive. This is not hope but conviction. The adversative ki ('but, rather, yet') creates a sharp contrast between two possible outcomes, and the psalmist declares which one has been determined. Scholars debate whether this refers to deliverance from literal death (the enemy sought to kill the psalmist, but he was rescued), deliverance from spiritual death (condemnation, shame, separation from God), or both. The most faithful reading honors both dimensions: the psalmist has been rescued from whatever threat to his life was present, and in being so rescued, he has been restored to full covenant life. The verb form 'I shall not die' (lo amut) is emphatic—it uses the imperfect tense to express both future intent and settled determination. This is not tentative or conditional but assured.
commentary.narrative_continued: The second half of the verse provides the purpose of this life: 'and declare the works of the LORD.' The survivor becomes a witness. This is crucial to understanding the verse not as mere personal rescue but as covenant participation. In ancient Israel, those who had experienced divine deliverance were obligated to testify about it. The testimony itself was seen as a sacred act, a way of making God's works known to all people. The verb 'declare' (sapper) means to recount, to tell, to speak, to repeat a narrative. It suggests formal testimony, not casual mention. The psalmist's life is spared not for his own comfort but so that he can testify. This links back to verse 16—if the right hand of the LORD does valiantly, then survivors must make that valiantly known through their testimony. The declaration of God's works is the public acknowledgment that God has acted, that He is powerful, that He is faithful to His covenant. For an Israelite hearing this psalm, it would have been clear: if you experience rescue, you are now obligated to speak about it, to bear witness before the community and before the nations.

word_study.meaning: I will not die, I shall not die. The imperfect tense form expresses both future action and present determination. Lo is the negative particle; amut is the first person singular imperfect of mut ('to die'). Together they express an absolute negation of death.
word_study.significance: The stark simplicity of this declaration—no hedging, no conditions, no ambiguity—is what gives the verse its force. In covenant theology, this is not arrogance but faith. The psalmist is not claiming personal immortality but claiming the covenant promise: God does not abandon those who serve Him. The negation of death is simultaneously an affirmation of life, of covenant belonging, of God's faithfulness.

word_study.meaning: And I will live. Ve is the conjunction 'and'; echyeh is the first person singular imperfect of chayah ('to live'). The verb suggests not merely biological existence but full, abundant life in covenant relationship.
word_study.significance: To 'live' in Hebrew covenant language means more than to exist. It means to fulfill one's purpose, to experience the blessings of covenant, to stand in right relationship with God. When the psalmist says 'I will live,' he means life in its fullness—life worthy of the name, life in communion with God and community.

word_study.meaning: I will declare, I will tell, I will recount. From the root saphar, which means 'to count, to recount, to narrate, to tell.' The verb is used for testimony, for the recitation of history, for the proclamation of God's mighty works. The Covenant Rendering translates it 'declare,' emphasizing its formal, public, authoritative character.
word_study.significance: The choice of this verb links the psalmist's survival to the task of testimony. To live is to declare; the declaration is not optional but constitutive of what it means to live as a member of God's covenant people. The prophetic tradition of speaking God's word (dabar) is here narrowed to the specific task of telling what God has done (ma'aseh YHWH, 'the works of the LORD'). Latter-day Saints understand this as the mission of the Church: to declare the works of God to all people.

word_study.meaning: Works, deeds, actions. From the root asah, 'to do, to make, to accomplish.' Ma'asei YHWH ('the works of the LORD') is a frequent phrase in the Psalms, referring to all that God has done in creation, history, and redemption.
word_study.significance: By using ma'asei (works), the psalmist affirms that God is not merely a principle or an abstraction but an agent who acts in history. God's character is revealed through His mighty works. To declare the works of the LORD is to show what kind of God He is—powerful, faithful, just, merciful. Every survivor's testimony adds to the accumulated evidence of God's character and faithfulness.

word_study.meaning: The LORD, a shortened form of YHWH (Yahweh). Yah is the covenant name of God, used frequently in prayers and psalms.
word_study.significance: The psalmist addresses his declaration specifically to Yah, the God bound by covenant. This is not testimony about a generic god but about the specific God of Israel who has made and kept covenant promises. In Latter-day Saint understanding, Yah is identified with Jehovah, the premortal Christ.

cross_references.connection: The psalmist declares: 'To hear the groaning of the prisoner; to loose those that are appointed to death.' Those delivered from death are specifically freed to declare God's works.

God declares: 'See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god with me: I kill, and I make alive; I wound, and I heal.' The power to determine death and life belongs to God alone; the psalmist's claim to live rests entirely on God's decision and power.

Alma proclaims: 'And now behold, I say unto you, my brethren, if ye have experienced a change of heart, and have felt to sing the song of redeeming love, I would ask, have ye spiritually been born of God?' Life in covenant terms means spiritual rebirth, and the evidence is the testimony (the singing, the declaring) of what God has done.

In the vision of the degrees of glory, the Lord declares: 'And now, after the many testimonies which have been given of him, this is the testimony, last of all, which we give of him: That he lives! For we saw him.' The declaration that Christ lives is the culmination of all testimony—it is the proclamation that death has been conquered and life has been restored.

Peter writes: 'But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light.' The declaration of God's works is the fundamental calling of the covenant community.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, the obligation to bear witness to God's mighty works was not merely encouraged; it was mandatory. When someone experienced divine deliverance, they were expected to testify before the community, to declare it before the congregation, to inscribe it in their household remembrance. This served multiple functions: it strengthened community faith, it multiplied the evidence of God's faithfulness, and it created accountability—by speaking what God had done, the survivor committed himself to living in alignment with that testimony. The phrase 'I shall not die, but live' would have resonated with the collective memory of Israel's founding deliverance at the Red Sea, where Israel crossed over while Egypt's armies drowned. Those who passed through the water were obligated to tell their children and grandchildren about what God had done. In the context of Psalm 118, which may relate to a specific historical crisis (whether military, personal, or spiritual), the verse claims that deliverance from that crisis enables and obligates the survivor to testify.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 26, Ammon recounts his missionary labors and declares: 'And I do this that I may rejoice in the day when I shall see him in his glory...because I shall have been an instrument in the hands of God in bringing so many souls to repentance.' Like the psalmist, Ammon's life has been spared for the purpose of declaring God's works. In fact, Alma's and Ammon's entire missionary work is an extended 'declaration of the works of the LORD.'
restoration_lens.dc_connections: In D&C 128:22-23, Joseph Smith teaches: 'Therefore we declare unto you the glad tidings of the restoration of all things which hath been spoken by the mouth of all the holy prophets since the world began.' The entire Restoration itself is framed as a declaration of God's works. The command to Joseph Smith and all members is explicit: 'Go ye therefore into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature' (D&C 68:8), which is essentially to declare the works of the LORD.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple ceremony, the participant who enters the covenant makes an implicit commitment to declare the works of the LORD. The instruction and ordinances themselves are forms of declaring God's character, His plan, His works in history, and His continuing authority. The temple is the place where God's works are most fully revealed and where members are called to become 'instruments in the hands of God' (Alma 26:3).

commentary.christological_typology: Psalm 118:17 is understood in Christian tradition as a prophecy of Christ's resurrection. Christ died but did not remain dead; He lived again—'I shall not die, but live.' And in His resurrection, Christ declared the works of the LORD most fully—through His own existence, He proclaimed God's power over death, God's faithfulness to covenant, God's redemptive plan for humanity. Every Christian who claims Psalm 118:17 is claiming participation in Christ's resurrection. In Romans 6:9, Paul writes: 'Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more. Death hath no more dominion over him.' This is the ultimate truth that the psalmist's words point toward. In Latter-day revelation, this typology is extended: all who are resurrected 'live' in the sense that Psalm 118:17 intends—they are restored to covenant relationship with God, and they are commissioned to declare His works throughout eternity.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Psalm 118:17 is both promise and calling. The promise: if you are in covenant with God, you will not be destroyed by opposition, by illness, by despair, by any enemy. God will preserve your life because your life has purpose within His plan. The calling: that purpose is to declare God's works. This is why testimonies are central to Latter-day Saint worship. When a member stands to share their experience of God's power, they are fulfilling the ancient obligation—they are declaring the works of the LORD. When a missionary serves, they declare God's works. When parents teach children about God's guidance in their lives, they declare His works. When a member faces illness and recovers, faces financial hardship and is relieved, faces doubt and finds faith, they are obligated to make that known—not for personal recognition but to strengthen faith in the covenant community. The verse invites us to live not for ourselves alone but as witnesses to the world that God lives, that He acts, that He is faithful. To live is to declare.

text_kjv: The LORD hath chastened me sore: but he hath not given me over unto death.

commentary.narrative: Verse 18 provides the final word on the nature of the adversity the psalmist has endured. It was not mere enemy attack, not chance misfortune, but divine discipline. The verb 'chastened' (yassor) has a specific resonance in covenant theology: it refers to the corrective discipline a father administers to his child, or that God administers to His covenant people. The psalmist acknowledges that the suffering he experienced came from God, that it had a purpose within the covenant relationship, and that it was meant to correct or refine him. Yet—and this is the crucial limitation—God disciplined but did not destroy. The contrast is sharp: 'chastened me sore...but he hath not given me over unto death.' The word 'sore' (emphasizing the infinitive absolute yassor yisserani, 'disciplining the LORD disciplined me') indicates that the discipline was real and severe. The psalmist is not minimizing his suffering or claiming it was gentle. Yet there was a boundary. God's discipline has limits; it does not cross over into destruction. This distinction is fundamental to covenant theology: God may punish sin, but His punishment is redemptive, not vindictive; it is meant to restore the covenant member, not to end the relationship.
commentary.narrative_continued: This verse also resolves a potential tension within the psalm. If the psalmist was pushed hard toward death by enemies (verse 13), why did he frame it as divine discipline? The answer is that in covenant theology, even enemies are ultimately instruments of God's will. The push that seemed to come from enemies is reframed as coming from God's hand for purposes of correction. This is not to deny the enemy's malice but to affirm that God's purposes transcend and ultimately control all events. For the psalmist, this realization transforms everything: what might have seemed like God abandoning him to his enemies is reframed as God's discipline, carried out through adverse circumstances but bounded by God's commitment not to destroy His covenant people. This perspective—that difficulties are often divine discipline rather than divine abandonment—is repeated throughout scripture and requires careful interpretation. The Latter-day Saint tradition is clear that not all adversity is punishment; much of it is testing, growth, or even preparation for greater service. But when adversity does come as a result of breaking covenant, the response is not despair but repentance and renewed commitment, trusting that God's discipline has limits.

word_study.meaning: To chastise, to discipline, to reprove, to correct. The root yasar refers to instruction through correction, the kind of discipline a father gives a child to guide him toward righteousness. It can be painful but is meant to be redemptive.
word_study.significance: The verb yassor appears throughout the Psalms and Proverbs, particularly in contexts of God's relationship with His covenant people. In Psalm 94:12, the psalmist blesses the one 'whom thou chastenest, O LORD, and teachest him out of thy law.' Discipline is understood as a form of teaching, a way of guiding the covenant member toward greater faithfulness. This is fundamentally different from punishment meant merely to inflict suffering. In Latter-day Saint theology, this distinction is preserved: the Lord chastens those He loves (D&C 95:1, 'I am the Lord thy God, and was angry with thee in mine anger when thou didst murmur against my law'), but the intent is always redemptive.

word_study.meaning: The construction uses the infinitive absolute (yassor) followed by the conjugated verb (yisserani) to intensify the action. This emphasizes the severity, the deliberateness, the intensity of the discipline. The doubling of the root creates an emphatic: 'disciplining, the LORD disciplined me,' or 'the LORD disciplined me severely.'
word_study.significance: This construction appears when the psalmist wants to convey not hesitant or light discipline but severe, undeniable discipline. Yet immediately after acknowledging this severity, the psalmist adds the crucial limit: 'but He did not give me over to death.' The acknowledgment of severity combined with the affirmation of God's restraint is what makes this verse theologically powerful. God can be both rigorous in correction and merciful in boundaries.

word_study.term_english: given over unto / handed over to
word_study.meaning: He gave me, he handed me over, he delivered me. From the root natan, 'to give, to place, to hand over.' The phrase 'not given me over unto death' means God did not hand the psalmist over to death's power, did not abandon him to destruction.
word_study.significance: The verb natan can be used both positively (God gave Israel the land) and negatively (God handed Israel over to enemies). In this context, 'not given me over unto death' is a negation of abandonment. It affirms that despite severe discipline, God maintained His covenant commitment and did not let the psalmist die. This is the crucial reassurance for anyone undergoing God's discipline: it may be severe, but it is not abandonment.

word_study.meaning: To death, unto death. Mavet is death understood not merely as biological cessation but as separation from God, as the ultimate consequence of covenant breaking. In Hebrew thought, death could be premature (death before one's time), violent death, or spiritual death (separation from God and covenant community).
word_study.significance: The psalmist's deliverance is not merely from premature physical death but from the spiritual death that would result from final rejection by God. To be 'given over to death' would mean God had abandoned the covenant relationship entirely. The psalmist affirms that God did not do this. This connects to Latter-day Saint theology of mercy and justice: judgment is real, but it is always balanced by mercy for the repentant, and even judgment does not sever the possibility of eventual redemption.

cross_references.connection: The wisdom tradition teaches: 'My son, despise not the chastening of the LORD; neither be weary of his correction: For whom the LORD loveth he correcteth; even as a father the son in whom he delighteth.' This is the classical formulation of the covenant principle that the psalmist applies to his own experience.

The New Testament applies this principle to the faithful: 'And ye have forgotten the exhortation which speaketh unto you as unto children, My son, despise not thou the chastening of the Lord...For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.' Discipline is evidence of covenant relationship, not abandonment.

The Lord reveals to the Church: 'I am the Lord thy God, and was angry with thee in mine anger when thou didst murmur against my law. Thou shouldst have been faithful; but thou wast not willing to do so.' Yet this is followed by opportunity for repentance and restoration, not destruction.

Alma teaches his son Corianton about God's justice and mercy: 'Now there is a law given, and a punishment affixed, and a repentance granted; which repentance, mercy claimeth; otherwise, justice claimeth the creature and executeth its law.' The mercy shown to the psalmist—sparing him from death despite discipline—is the operation of this divine principle.

Paul writes: 'But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world.' The purpose of divine discipline is not destruction but redemption and alignment with God's purpose.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern culture, the figure of a god or king disciplining his people or his subjects was a common motif. The Hittite treaties, for example, include clauses about the king's authority to discipline vassals for breach of covenant. However, these were often harsh and could result in complete destruction. The distinctive aspect of Israel's covenant theology is the idea of boundary: God will discipline, but He will not destroy. This reflects Israel's experience—throughout their history, Israel experienced exile, defeat, oppression, yet the covenant relationship was never completely severed. The northern kingdom fell to Assyria, the southern kingdom to Babylon, but there remained a 'remnant' (she'ar) who maintained covenant relationship and through whom God would restore His people. The psalmist's personal experience mirrors this national pattern: severe discipline, but not destruction. In the context of Psalm 118, the verse affirms that whatever crisis prompted the psalm—whether a military threat, a personal illness, or a spiritual trial—it came within the bounds of covenant discipline, not covenant rejection.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Helaman 12:2-3, the book records: 'And thus we see that except the Lord doth chasten his people with many afflictions...they will not remember him...Behold, we see that except the Lord doth chasten his people with many afflictions, yea, except he doth visit them with death and with terror, and with famine and with all manner of pestilence, they will not remember him.' Yet the purpose is always redemptive—the chastening is meant to bring the people back to covenant faithfulness. The Book of Mormon extensively develops this theme, showing that God's discipline is always bounded by His commitment to His covenant people.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: In D&C 121:43, the Lord teaches Joseph Smith about the proper use of authority: 'No power or influence can or ought to be maintained by virtue of the priesthood, only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned.' This principle applies to God's discipline as well—it should be corrective, not vindictive, bounded by love and the commitment to preserve and restore the covenant relationship. D&C 76:32-37 shows the limits of God's judgment: even those who suffer condemnation are not given over to death eternally but are assigned to degrees of glory appropriate to their choices.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple ceremony, the concept of God's discipline is implicit in the covenants and instruction. The participant is taught about opposition, sin, and the consequences of covenant breaking, but always within the framework of redemption. The temple teaches that God's house is a place of instruction and correction, where the covenant member can repent, make new commitments, and be assured of God's continued support despite past failings.

commentary.christological_typology: Psalm 118:18 can be understood as a type of Christ's experience in Gethsemane and at Calvary. Christ submitted to the Father's will and underwent suffering that appeared to be abandonment unto death—'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' Yet Christ did not remain in death. The Father did not ultimately give Christ over unto death but raised Him in resurrection. In this sense, Christ exemplifies the perfect submission to divine discipline and the perfect faith that God does not abandon even in the moment of greatest apparent desolation. For all members of the covenant community, this Christ-like pattern—submission to God's discipline, trust that it will not result in permanent destruction, and ultimate vindication and restoration—is the path of faithfulness.
commentary.application: Psalm 118:18 offers crucial wisdom for understanding adversity within a covenant framework. The verse does not claim that all adversity is punishment (wisdom literature makes clear that this is not always true), but it does affirm that when adversity comes as a result of sin or covenant breaking, it should be understood as discipline, not destruction. The proper response to such discipline is repentance and renewed commitment, not despair or doubt about God's faithfulness. For modern covenant members facing trials, the verse invites discernment: Is this trial a consequence of my covenant breaking? If so, let me repent and trust that God's discipline has limits. Or is this trial for other purposes—testing, growth, preparation? In either case, the fundamental promise holds: God does not give His covenant people over unto death. This does not mean physical suffering will not occur (the psalmist's very language shows he suffered severely), but it means that our ultimate destiny is not destruction but restoration and redemption. In times of hardship, sacrament meeting, family prayer, temple worship, or personal scripture study, the covenant member can claim this verse: Whatever I am enduring, it is not abandonment. God has not given me over unto death. Therefore, I will endure, repent where needed, and trust in God's faithfulness to complete the work of salvation in my life.

text_kjv: Open to me the gates of righteousness: I will go into them, and I will praise the LORD:

commentary.narrative: The psalmist's prayer has been heard and answered. Having escaped from the crisis described in earlier verses, he now approaches the Temple gates to enter and give public testimony. This verse marks a crucial transition: the private cry for help (verse 5) now becomes public thanksgiving. The request to 'open the gates of righteousness' is not merely a literal petition to Temple workers—it is a covenant statement. Only those who walk in righteousness can approach God's sanctuary, and the psalmist is affirming that he comes with a purified heart, ready to stand before the Lord and testify of His deliverance. The Hebrew word odeh (I will give thanks) is not passive gratitude muttered alone; it is declarative testimony—a public announcement of what God has done. In the Temple setting, this becomes a communal act: the individual's deliverance becomes the congregation's witness.

word_study.meaning: The gates belonging to the Temple through which the righteous enter. Tzedeq (righteousness) is not merely moral virtue but conformity to covenant relationship—right standing before God. The gates are called 'gates of righteousness' because they are entered only by those in proper covenant relationship.
word_study.significance: The designation 'gates of righteousness' sets a condition: not all gates are open to all people, but these specific gates belong to the righteous. This reflects Temple theology—access to God's house requires spiritual preparation and covenant fidelity.

word_study.meaning: From the root yodh-dalet-he, meaning to give thanks, praise, or confess. It carries the sense of public acknowledgment and testimony. When used in Temple contexts, odeh indicates a declarative act of gratitude offered before the community and God.
word_study.significance: The verb form indicates future intentional action: 'I will give thanks' is a commitment to public testimony. This is why the psalmist seeks entry to the Temple—not to pray privately but to testify publicly of God's salvation.

cross_references.connection: Enter His gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise—the same Temple gates are approached with gratitude and testimony as a foundation of worship.
Open the gates, that the righteous nation which keeps truth may enter—the gates of righteousness admit those aligned with God's covenant.
You are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation—the New Testament applies the idea of the righteous entering God's presence to the covenant community.
From the dedicatory prayer of the Kirtland Temple: that the righteous might enter and worship in the House of the Lord.

commentary.historical_context: The Temple gates mentioned here are literal architectural features of the Jerusalem Temple, but they also function symbolically in Israelite thought. In ancient Near Eastern practice, city and temple gates were not merely functional barriers but sacred thresholds. Gateways represented transitions from the profane to the sacred, from the wilderness to civilization, from separation to belonging. The gate itself might be guarded by priests or Levites who could examine the ritual purity of those seeking entry. Ancient inscriptions and reliefs show that important religious transitions frequently occurred at gates. The 'opening' of gates was sometimes a ceremonial act requiring authorization. By invoking the gates of the Temple, the psalmist invokes the full apparatus of covenant access—he is not simply entering a building but crossing into God's presence through proper channels.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:12—'Now when our hearts are exceedingly glad, we cry out with a mighty voice, singing the praises of our God'—the same impulse to public testimony after deliverance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 109:16 (Kirtland Temple dedication)—'We ask thee, Holy Father, to establish the people that shall worship, and honorably hold a name and standing in this glorious day, when thou art taking the kingdom to thyself'—the restored Temple as the space where the righteous gather to testify and worship.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Modern Temple covenants include the commitment to live righteously. The 'gates of righteousness' in ancient Temple theology become the literal gates of the restored Temple, which initiate members enter as they make covenants to walk in righteousness before God.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the righteousness that grants access to God's presence. In John 10:7-9, Jesus identifies Himself as the gate—'I am the door of the sheep.' The righteous who enter through the gates of righteousness prefigure those who enter eternal life through Christ, the ultimate expression of divine righteousness.
commentary.application: In modern covenant life, this verse invites members to examine their readiness to enter the House of the Lord—not physically alone, but spiritually. Before entering a Temple, the question posed is implicit: Are you righteous? Have you kept your covenants? Do you come with a pure heart to testify of God's deliverance in your life? The verse challenges each member to walk in righteousness not out of fear but out of joyful anticipation of standing before God with a clear conscience, ready to thank Him publicly for His salvation.

text_kjv: This gate of the LORD, into which the righteous shall enter.

commentary.narrative: A voice interrupts—likely a gatekeeper, priest, or Levite stationed at the Temple entrance. The psalmist's request to enter is affirmed and expanded. This verse constitutes a liturgical response, establishing a dialogue between the worshipper and the Temple establishment. The respondent identifies the gate as belonging to the Lord, not to human authority. This theological claim is crucial: the gates are not the property of the king, the high priest, or even the Temple staff. They belong to the Lord alone. Therefore, the condition of entry—'the righteous shall enter through it'—is not arbitrary human restriction but divine appointment. The gate operates according to God's standards, not human convenience or political favoritism. The response reassures the approaching psalmist that he meets the condition: if he is among the righteous, the gate will indeed open for him. This exchange demonstrates the liturgical practice of the Temple: entrance was not automatic but required verification of the worshipper's spiritual status.

word_study.meaning: The gate belonging to or dedicated to the Lord. The preposition la ('to, for, belonging to') establishes ownership. The gate is YHWH's gate—it functions under divine jurisdiction, not human administration.
word_study.significance: This is a declaration of sovereignty. The Temple gate, while physically guarded by humans, is ultimately subject to God's law and God's righteousness. Access through it cannot be negotiated, purchased, or politically arranged—it depends solely on meeting God's criterion of righteousness.

word_study.meaning: The righteous (those in right covenant relationship) will enter through it. The future tense indicates this is an established principle—entry through this gate always belongs to the righteous, not as privilege but as birthright of covenant.
word_study.significance: The condition is objective and verifiable. One either is among the righteous or is not. There is no middle ground, no negotiation. This reflects the covenantal theology of ancient Israel: righteousness is not a feeling or intention but a demonstrable alignment with God's law.

cross_references.connection: Who shall abide in thy tabernacle? He that walketh uprightly and worketh righteousness—the condition of entering God's dwelling is righteousness, just as verse 20 establishes.

Not everyone that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father—the New Testament applies the same criterion: not declaration but righteous action determines access to God's presence.
Ye should remember that ye are always indebted to your Father in Heaven—Book of Mormon teaching emphasizes that standing before God requires remembering one's covenant obligations.
The righteous shall be gathered to Zion and shall be holy—establishing that only those who walk in righteousness can enter and remain in sacred space.

commentary.historical_context: Temple gates in ancient Israel served both practical and symbolic functions. Archaeological evidence from comparable temples in the Levantine region shows that gates often had guardian chambers where priests or Levites could examine approaching worshippers. The practice of verifying eligibility for Temple entry is attested in biblical texts: Leviticus 15:31 warns that those in certain states of ritual impurity must not enter the Tabernacle. Psalm 15 functions as a checklist—a liturgical interrogation used at the gates to determine who may proceed. Some scholars suggest that certain gates had specific functions or admitted only specific groups (priests vs. laity, men vs. women, specific tribes). The 'Gate of Righteousness' may have been a particular gate through which pilgrims passed after purification. The respondent's voice in verse 20 likely represents the official Temple priesthood speaking with divine authority, clarifying that this gate's restrictions are not negotiable or politically motivated but grounded in covenant law.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 4:17-35—Nephi's personal testimony of walking in righteousness and feeling God's presence—illustrates the individual's verification of their own righteous standing before the Lord.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 27:1-2—'Behold, the mystery of godliness, how great it is. For behold, I am not at all angry with my servants who acknowledged their sins and repented'—Divine acceptance based on righteous alignment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple recommend interviews in the modern Church function similarly to the ancient gate-checking: a designated servant of God asks specific questions to verify that the person seeking entry is in good standing covenantally. The modern Temple recommend is the contemporary equivalent of being identified as 'righteous' and therefore permitted through the gate.

commentary.christological_typology: The righteous entering through the gate prefigures the redeemed entering eternal life. In Revelation 22:14, John states: 'Blessed are they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life, and may enter in through the gates into the city.' The risen Christ has already passed through all gates and now stands as the measure and mediator of all righteousness, determining who may enter.
commentary.application: This verse should prompt members to ask: What does it mean for me to be 'righteous' in a covenant sense? Righteousness is not self-assessed—it is measured against God's law and standards. A Temple recommend holder has essentially been verified as meeting the contemporary standard of righteous standing. But the verse goes deeper: it challenges members to examine whether their private actions match their public testimony. The gate stands as a reminder that integrity matters—you cannot enter falsely or with hidden sin. Living in alignment with your covenants is not merely personal virtue but the precondition for standing before God.

text_kjv: I will praise thee: for thou hast heard me, and art become my salvation.

commentary.narrative: Having crossed the threshold into the Temple, the psalmist now stands in God's presence and addresses Him directly. This verse marks the heart of the thanksgiving ceremony. The psalmist explicitly recalls the moment of distress—when he called out (verse 5) and the Lord answered. The phrase 'Thou hast heard me' is not merely passive audition; it is active response. God heard and acted. The statement 'Thou art become my salvation' reinforces a transformation: the Lord moved from being a distant power to being the active agent of deliverance in the psalmist's life. The verb 'became' (hayah) indicates a transition—God changed from potential savior to realized savior through concrete action. This verse echoes verse 14 ('The LORD is my strength and song, and is become my salvation'), creating structural reinforcement. The repetition is not redundant but liturgically intentional: by repeating the declaration, the psalmist embeds it deeper into the congregation's memory and into the Temple's worship tradition.
