The act of thanksgiving is thus not merely personal recollection but communal renewal of covenant confidence in God's power to save.

word_study.meaning: From the root yodh-dalet-he, here in the second person singular: 'I will thank/praise you specifically.' The Covenant Rendering translates this as 'I thank You,' emphasizing the directness of address to God Himself.
word_study.significance: The shift from verse 19 (public announcement before the gates) to verse 21 (direct address to God) shows the full arc of worship: first the worshipper announces intention to the community, then enters the sacred space, then addresses God directly. This movement from public to private (yet within a public liturgy) is essential to Hebrew worship practice.

word_study.meaning: From the root ayin-nun-he ('to answer, respond, hear and act upon'). The verb denotes not mere passive hearing but active response—God answered by doing something. In verse 5, the psalmist called out; here he confirms that the answer came.
word_study.significance: The verb anah is central to covenantal prayer theology: God is one who answers. To pray is to invoke this divine attribute. By using this verb, the psalmist places himself within the tradition of answered prayer found throughout Israel's history (Abraham, Moses, David, etc.).

word_study.meaning: The verb hayah ('to be, become') in the perfect tense indicates a completed transformation: 'You became my salvation.' Lishu'ah ('for salvation') uses the preposition le ('to, for'), making it 'You became for me my salvation'—salvation is realized not as abstract concept but as personal, concrete gift.
word_study.significance: Salvation (yeshu'ah) in this context is not theological abstraction but rescue from specific danger. The psalmist has moved from crisis to safety because God acted. Salvation is thus historical and personal: it happened to me, by God, in my circumstances.

cross_references.connection: When my father and mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up—the confidence expressed here that the Lord has become one's salvation rests on the prior confidence that God will not abandon.
Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD—Moses' declaration to Israel at the Red Sea establishes the foundational pattern that God's salvation is visible, temporal, and certain.
Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid—the prophet echoes this same confidence and calls for public thanksgiving for God's saving work.
The Book of Mormon describes the psalmist's experience: cry out in distress, receive the Lord's answer, and testify publicly in the Lord's house of His saving power.

commentary.historical_context: The act of thanksgiving (todah) was a formal sacrifice in ancient Israel, described in Leviticus 7:12-15. When a person survived a crisis or was delivered from peril, they would bring a todah offering to the Temple, accompanied by thanksgiving songs. These were not private ceremonies but communal worship acts. The worshipper would publicly recount the distress and deliverance, inviting the community to join in recognizing God's power. Psalm 118 itself may have been sung as part of such a todah ceremony. Archaeological evidence from the broader ancient Near East shows similar practices in other cultures—the formal public acknowledgment of deliverance by a god was a common religious obligation, serving both to honor the deity and to strengthen community trust in divine justice and power. The psalmist's testimony in verse 21 would have been heard by the gathered congregation, potentially inspiring their own confidence in divine responsiveness to prayer.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 1:14-15—Nephi's testimony that the Lord heard his prayers and showed him God's throne room and majesty—the direct address of God following crisis is Lehi's family pattern.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5—The Lord's promise that He will 'answer' those who call upon Him in faith—establishing the same anah principle that undergirds this psalm.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the Temple, members participate in recounting God's delivering mercies through covenant language. The modern endowment ceremony includes the worshipper's acknowledgment that the Lord has 'heard' and 'answered' through providing the way of salvation. Verse 21 anticipates this—standing in the sanctuary and thanking God for concrete deliverance.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate answer to human distress. In Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39), Jesus cries out to the Father in sorrow; in the Resurrection, the Father answers by raising Him from the dead. Christ 'becomes' salvation not just for Himself but for all humanity. His public testimony (verse 21) echoes the psalmist's—standing before the Temple of His body, He declares the Father's saving work.
commentary.application: Members should cultivate the habit of testifying explicitly that 'God has heard me and become my salvation.' In modern LDS practice, this takes form in fast and testimony meetings, in personal journals, in prayers, and in teaching. The verse invites you not to vaguely trust God but to point to specific instances when you cried out and God answered. This specificity deepens faith—both your own and that of those who hear you. When you can say, 'In this specific trial, God heard me and delivered me,' you are not speaking piously but bearing true witness grounded in experience.

text_kjv: The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.

commentary.narrative: This verse shifts suddenly from personal testimony to a universal principle. It is the most famous line in Psalm 118 and one of the most quoted verses in all of Scripture. The metaphor is architectural: during construction of a building, workers examine stones to determine fitness. Some stones fail inspection—they are deemed unsuitable, flawed, or ill-shaped for the project. The builders reject and discard them. Yet one particular stone—rejected and cast aside—becomes indispensable. It becomes the rosh pinnah, the cornerstone that determines the building's alignment, angle, and structural integrity. Two walls meet at the cornerstone; the entire edifice depends on it. What human judgment deemed worthless, divine wisdom made foundational. The reversal is complete and astonishing. In its original context, the 'stone' likely refers to Israel itself or its king—the nation or ruler that the surrounding powers (Assyria, Egypt, others) rejected and attempted to destroy, yet whom God chose as central to His purposes. The verse proclaims that rejection by the nations does not determine one's true value; God's selection does. This is a verse of cosmic encouragement to the marginalized, oppressed, or apparently failed—your worth is not determined by who dismisses you but by who chooses you. The New Testament authors recognized that this verse's deepest application is to Jesus Christ Himself, the one rejected by the religious establishment yet chosen by God as the foundation of salvation.

word_study.meaning: Literally a stone, rock. In biblical metaphor, 'stone' can represent stability, permanence, foundation, or (in this context) material for construction. The word appears throughout Scripture as a symbol of covenant (memorial stones, altar stones) and judgment (stoning).
word_study.significance: The choice of 'stone' rather than 'timber' or other materials emphasizes permanence and weight. A rejected stone cannot be 'forgotten' or easily replaced—it remains, rejected but present, until its true purpose is discovered.

word_study.meaning: From the root ma'as ('to refuse, reject, despise, find unfit'). The builders (bonim) examined the stone and rejected it as unsuitable. The verb is decisive—not uncertainty but deliberate dismissal.
word_study.significance: The builders represent human judgment, expertise, and authority. They are not incompetent—they are skilled professionals. Yet their judgment is overturned. The verse establishes that even expert human assessment can miss what matters most.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'head of the corner.' The rosh pinnah is the corner stone—the stone at the junction of two walls that determines their alignment and bears tremendous structural load. It is the most important stone in the building. The Covenant Rendering translates this as 'cornerstone,' capturing the architectural significance.
word_study.significance: In architecture, the cornerstone is selected with extreme care. It must be perfectly squared, absolutely level, precisely placed. Ironically, the builders rejected this stone, yet it is the one that should have been selected first and with greatest precision. The reversal is not random but purposeful—the one deemed unfit is actually the one most essential.

word_study.meaning: From hayah ('to be, become'). The perfect tense indicates completed action—the transformation is not hoped for or predicted but realized.
word_study.significance: This is not 'will become' but 'has become'—the reversal is already accomplished, established as fact. The verse proclaims what God has already done, not what He promises to do.

cross_references.connection: Jesus quotes this verse to the Pharisees, applying it to Himself—the one rejected by the religious establishment but chosen by God as the foundation of salvation.
The chief priests and scribes rejected Jesus, yet He became the cornerstone—a direct fulfillment of the psalm's reversal principle.
Jesus asks the leaders: 'What is this then that is written, The stone which the builders rejected...?' establishing the verse's application to His rejection and exaltation.
Peter declares: 'This is the stone which was set at nought of you builders, which is become the head of the corner'—applying the verse to Christ's Resurrection.
Peter connects believers to Christ the cornerstone: 'To whom coming, as unto a living stone...ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house.'
The Lord promises that those whom the world despises will become His foundation—the modern principle of divine reversal.

commentary.historical_context: Archaeologically, cornerstones from Levantine temples and public buildings (roughly contemporary with the Psalms period) show careful selection and precise shaping. A cornerstone that is even slightly off-square will cause cascading errors throughout the structure—walls will be crooked, doors won't hang properly, the building will be unstable. Therefore, master builders would have rejected any stone showing defects. The verse's irony is thus technically accurate: the builders' rejection of a flawed stone would have been professional and prudent. Yet in the psalm's metaphor, the rejected stone is declared to be, in fact, the masterpiece—perfectly suited for the corner precisely because of qualities only God recognizes. In the ancient Near Eastern context, rejection by powerful nations (represented by the 'builders') was a real threat to Israel's survival. The psalm offers theological reorientation: whether Egypt, Assyria, or other powers despise Israel, God has chosen Israel as His cornerstone in world history. The song would have been sung during crises when this affirmation was most needed.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 19:14—Nephi quotes this verse and applies it to Christ, establishing the Book of Mormon's recognition that the psalmist speaks of Jesus.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 113:2-4—The Lord identifies the 'stone' with His covenant people, assuring them that though rejected by the world, they are chosen as His foundation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In LDS Temple theology, Christ is the cornerstone—the foundation upon which all saving ordinances are built. Members, covenanting with Christ, participate in becoming part of His building—living stones in a spiritual house (1 Peter 2:5). The Temple itself is physically built with cornerstones; the dedication ceremonies emphasize Christ as the spiritual cornerstone upon which the Temple's saving work rests.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse is explicitly typological of Christ. The rejected stone is Jesus: rejected by the Sanhedrin (Matthew 26:3-4), despised by the crowds (Mark 15:29-32), crucified in shame (Luke 23:33), yet raised by God and exalted as the foundation of salvation. His 'rejection' is temporary; His exaltation is eternal. The stone metaphor appears throughout Christian tradition as a symbol of Christ's permanence, strength, and role as foundation. In Revelation 21:14, the New Jerusalem's foundation stones are inscribed with the names of the twelve apostles—yet Christ is the foundation beneath all of them.
commentary.application: This verse speaks directly to anyone who has experienced rejection, failure, or dismissal by authorities or institutions. If you have been rejected by a school, employer, family, religious community, or society—if you have been deemed 'unfit,' 'unsuitable,' 'not good enough'—this verse proclaims that human judgment does not determine your eternal value. God's assessment is different. The question is: Do you believe that? Can you trust that rejection by those who 'should know' is not the final word on who you are? The verse challenges you to ground your identity in God's choice, not in others' rejection. Moreover, the verse applies to your relationship with others: Are there 'rejected stones' in your community—people dismissed, marginalized, or written off? The verse invites you to reconsider them through God's eyes, asking whether those despised might carry hidden worth.

text_kjv: This is the LORD's doing; it is marvellous in our eyes.

commentary.narrative: The verse immediately follows the cornerstone declaration and provides its theological grounding: this reversal—the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone—is not accident, chance, or human cleverness. It is the Lord's doing. The psalmist's chorus (indicated by the shift to 'our eyes') affirms together that what they are witnessing exceeds human explanation. The word 'marvellous' (nifla't) comes from a root meaning 'to be extraordinary, beyond human capacity.' It describes something that cannot be understood through ordinary means or predicted through human foresight. A skilled builder might have eventually recognized a rejected stone's worth, but that discovery would take time and trial. What the Lord does is miraculous—it transcends normal processes. The corporate affirmation ('our eyes') is significant: the congregation is not asked to accept the psalmist's private experience on faith alone. They join in recognizing that something extraordinary has happened, something that requires divine explanation. This verse thus serves as a transition from the psalmist's personal testimony (verses 21-22) to a corporate acknowledgment that will lead to communal celebration (verse 24). The shift from 'I' to 'our' broadens the significance: the psalmist's individual deliverance becomes a revelation of God's nature that the whole community can witness and celebrate.

word_study.term_original: me-et YHWH hayetah zot (מֵאֵת יְהוָה הָיְתָה זֹּאת)
word_study.meaning: Literally 'from the LORD this has come about.' The preposition me-et ('from, from the hand of') attributes the action to God as its source and agent. The reversal is not an independent miracle but specifically God's work.
word_study.significance: By identifying the reversal as coming 'from YHWH,' the psalmist places it within Israel's covenantal theology. God is not merely a distant power but the active agent who orchestrates history and reverses human judgments according to His purposes.

word_study.meaning: From the root pala ('to be extraordinary, surpass, be beyond measure'). The adjective describes something that exceeds normal limits, is wondrous, beyond human explanation. When applied to God's acts, it indicates divine action that transcends natural processes or human capability.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering translates this as 'marvelous'—capturing both the sense of wonder and the implication of divine power. Nifla't appears throughout Scripture to describe God's mighty acts: the plagues in Egypt (Exodus 15:11), deliverance at the Red Sea, the provision of water in the wilderness. It is the language of theophany and divine intervention.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'in our eyes.' Eyes are the organs of sight and knowledge in biblical Hebrew. 'In our eyes' means 'as we see it,' 'to our perception,' 'in our judgment.' The corporate 'our' indicates the gathered congregation witnessing the reversal.
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes that this is not secret or hidden—it is visible, witnessed, testified to by many. The reversal is not a private mystical experience but a public recognition accessible to the community's collective observation.

cross_references.connection: Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law—both verses ask for perception of God's extraordinary work through understanding His purposes.
Behold, I make a covenant: before all thy people I will do marvels—the Lord regularly performs nifla't in the presence of witnesses to establish faith.
And one said to the man clothed in linen, How long shall it be to the end of these wonders?—the language of divine marvels applied to God's plan.
The Father's work and glory is to bring about the immortality and eternal life of man—the ultimate marvel of God's purposes.

commentary.historical_context: The use of corporate testimony ('our eyes') reflects the liturgical setting of the Psalms in the Temple. Many psalms appear to have been sung processionally by a priest or cantor, with the congregation joining in at certain points. The shift from singular to plural pronouns marks these moments of congregational participation. By affirming together that they see God's marvellous work, the community strengthens mutual faith and creates a shared theological narrative. In the ancient Near East, witness testimony was legally and religiously significant. When multiple people affirmed seeing something, it carried weight. Thus, the congregation's corporate 'our eyes have seen this' was not merely poetic but constituted valid testimony to the truth of God's intervention.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 4:9—'And behold, all that he requires of you is to keep his commandments; and he has promised you that if ye would keep his commandments ye should prosper in the land'—the congregation witnesses God's fulfilled promises.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:1-4—Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon's testimony: 'Hearing the voice of the Lord, they saw the Son of the Father'—modern witness to extraordinary divine revelation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the Temple endowment, the initiate witnesses God's marvellous work—the plan of salvation—unfold before their eyes. The endowment is designed as a guided witness to 'the work of our Father.' Members leave the Temple having, in a sense, 'seen' God's marvelous purposes revealed.

commentary.christological_typology: The resurrection of Christ is the ultimate 'marvel in our eyes.' The disciples witnessed something that no human power or foresight could have orchestrated—the reversal of death itself. The empty tomb, the risen Lord, the commission to take the gospel to all nations—these exceed all human explanation and establish Christ's divine sonship.
commentary.application: In your covenant life, take time to recognize the marvellous works of God that you have witnessed. Not just ancient miracles or scriptural accounts, but in your life: a needed answer to prayer, an unexpected provision, a relationship preserved despite odds, a personal weakness made into strength. When you can point to these and say, 'This was the Lord's doing; it is marvellous in my eyes,' you are joining the psalmist's chorus. Share these recognitions with others—not to boast but to strengthen collective faith. When others hear you testify that you have witnessed God's marvelous work, it encourages them to perceive His hand in their own lives. The verse invites you to develop the habit of spiritual perception—training your 'eyes' to see God's hand where others see only coincidence or luck.

text_kjv: This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.

commentary.narrative: The psalm reaches its culmination in a declaration of joy and celebration. 'This is the day' refers not to a generic, chronological day but to this specific day of reversal and vindication—the day on which the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone, the day the Lord has made, the day of deliverance. The phrase 'the day which the LORD hath made' attributes the day's creation and character to God's agency. God did not simply allow this day to occur; He made it. He orchestrated the circumstances, executed the reversal, and brought about the vindication. The response is unambiguous: rejoicing and gladness. The verbs 'nagilah' (let us exult, rejoice greatly) and 'nismechah' (let us be glad) are commands to the congregation, not passive suggestions. The people are called to join actively and enthusiastically in celebration. This is not grudging acceptance or quiet contentment but exuberant joy. The corporateness is complete now: from the individual's entrance at the gate (verse 19), to the individual's direct praise before God (verse 21), to the congregation's corporate acknowledgment (verse 23), to the final call for all to rejoice together (verse 24). Psalm 118 ends as it began—with praise and trust—but now enriched by the entire narrative of distress, deliverance, and vindication. The congregation exits the Temple with joy, having been renewed in faith that God makes days, orchestrates reversals, and invites His people into celebration of His work.

word_study.term_english: the day which the LORD hath made
word_study.term_original: zeh ha-yom asah YHWH (זֶה־הַיּוֹם עָשָׂה יְהוָה)
word_study.meaning: Literally 'this is the day the LORD has made.' Yom ('day') can mean a 24-hour period or, metaphorically, a decisive moment or season. Asah ('to make, to act, to bring about') indicates creative agency. God 'made' this day in the sense that He brought it about, orchestrated it, determined its character.
word_study.significance: This is one of the most beloved verses in the Bible, often sung at Easter and celebrations of resurrection. The attribution of the day's creation to God establishes that significant moments in history are not random or accidental but are crafted by divine intention.

word_study.meaning: From the root gimel-yodh-lamed ('to rejoice, exult, leap for joy'). The verb carries the sense of not merely being happy but actively expressing joy through celebration. In the jussive form (nagilah), it is a command or strong exhortation: 'Let us exult!'
word_study.significance: The word is strong and active. It is not contentment or satisfaction but exuberant celebration. This is appropriate to the magnitude of the reversal being celebrated—the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone, the crisis turned to vindication.

word_study.meaning: From the root samach ('to be glad, rejoice, be happy'). Often paired with giyl (to exult), these two verbs together express full emotional and active joy. Samach carries a sense of delight and contentment.
word_study.significance: While nagilah emphasizes active, exuberant celebration, samach emphasizes the internal state of gladness and delight. Together, they express both outer manifestation and inner emotion—you rejoice externally and are glad internally; your celebration is both authentic and expressed.

word_study.meaning: The preposition 'in' with the masculine singular suffix 'it,' referring to 'the day.' The rejoicing and gladness are in/during this day—the celebration is the appropriate response to the day the Lord has made.
word_study.significance: The 'day' becomes the container or context for joy. The day itself invites and occasions the celebration. To be in this day is to be in a space where rejoicing is not merely permitted but called for.

cross_references.connection: And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good—the first day God 'made' in Scripture was declared good; this day too is recognized as God's creation and as worthy of celebration.
Wisdom rejoices in God's work of creation—the proper response to God's making is rejoicing, as personified Wisdom demonstrates.
On the day of Resurrection, the disciples gather with joy: 'The Lord is risen indeed'—the ultimate 'day which the LORD hath made' is Resurrection Sunday.
These are they whose names are written in heaven, whose glory is that of the sun—the celestial kingdom is entered into through days the Lord has made for His purposes.
Men are, that they might have joy—the fundamental purpose of existence is to rejoice and be glad in the days God has ordained.

commentary.historical_context: In Jewish tradition, Psalm 118:24 has become one of the most-quoted verses in Passover liturgy and in celebration of the Exodus. The 'day' can refer to the day of the Exodus, when the Lord 'made' a day of deliverance for Israel. Similarly, in Christian tradition, it is sung on Easter (called 'the Day of Resurrection' or 'This is the Day the Lord Hath Made'). The verse's flexibility—allowing application to any day of God's intervention—explains its enduring use across centuries and cultures. In the Temple context of ancient Israel, the ceremony described in Psalm 118 would have culminated with the congregation's participation in a ritual meal or continuing celebration. The exhortation to rejoice was not merely emotional but was backed by actual festive practice—eating, drinking, music, and communal celebration.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 9:18—'O then, my beloved brethren, repent ye, and be born again, that ye may be saved'—the Book of Mormon calls all to rejoice in the day of deliverance that God has made.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 59:7—'And in nothing doth man offend God, or against none is his wrath kindled, save those who confess not his hand in all things, and obey not his commandments'—to rejoice in the day the Lord has made is to confess His hand.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The endowment ceremony concludes with the initiate stepping into the celestial room—a representation of God's presence—having witnessed and participated in the restoration of all things. This is a 'day which the LORD hath made,' and members exit into it rejoicing, having experienced the covenant restoration made possible through Christ.

commentary.christological_typology: Every Easter morning, Christians sing 'This is the day which the LORD hath made; let us rejoice and be glad in it' in celebration of Christ's Resurrection. The day of the Resurrection is the ultimate day the Lord has made—the day that reverses death itself, when the rejected and crucified Jesus becomes the cornerstone of all salvation. The entire New Testament's joy and confidence rests on this one day God orchestrated. For Latter-day Saints, the day of revelation (when the heavens are opened and truth is restored), the day of baptism and confirmation, and ultimately the day of resurrection all fit this pattern—days the Lord has made, in which we rejoice.
commentary.application: Begin the practice of recognizing and celebrating days that the Lord has made. Not just grand occasions but specific days of answered prayer, days of relief after anxiety, days when wisdom came suddenly, days of healing or reconciliation. Mark these days internally and, when appropriate, share them with loved ones or your community. The verse invites you to develop a posture of gratitude and celebration toward the Lord's creative and redemptive work in your life. Moreover, it invites you to call others to rejoice with you. Don't keep these days private—'we will rejoice and be glad' is plural. The act of celebrating together strengthens community and faith. Finally, the verse challenges your daily perspective: even ordinary days are 'made by the LORD.' Can you wake up with the attitude that this day, whatever it holds, is the Lord's creation and therefore worthy of gratitude? This shifts daily life from mere survival to active celebration of covenant belonging.

text_kjv: Save now, I beseech thee, O LORD: O LORD, I beseech thee, send now prosperity.

commentary.narrative:
Psalm 118:25 marks a pivot from narrative reflection to urgent, repeated petition. The psalmist has recounted deliverance, recognized God's hand, and processed his experience—but now he returns to the posture of need. The double invocation "Anna, YHWH" (O LORD, I beseech thee) signals escalating intensity. This is not casual prayer; it is the cry of one who has tasted both desperation and rescue, and who knows precisely whom to address. The parallelism of the two imperatives—hoshi'ah na (save us!) and hatzlichah na (grant success!)—creates rhythmic urgency, as though the petitioner cannot articulate the request once and move on. He must say it twice, in slightly different words, to capture the totality of his need: both immediate salvation from threat and the ongoing prosperity (success, progress) that follows deliverance.

The word 'Hosanna,' which would echo through the streets of Jerusalem on Palm Sunday when Jesus entered the city, originates directly from hoshi'ah na in this verse. The crowds who cried 'Hosanna' were not merely acclaiming Jesus with a joyful liturgical formula; they were crying out a plea for salvation embedded in their corporate memory and their weekly worship. The phrase had become both petition and praise—the cry that acknowledges both the need for rescue and the faith that deliverance is possible. The Covenant Rendering captures this dual force: "Please, LORD, save us! / Please, LORD, grant us success!" The repetition of 'please' (Anna) emphasizes the urgency of the moment and the intensity of the petitioner's longing.

word_study.meaning: To save, deliver, rescue; to bring to safety or wholeness. The root yasha carries the sense of liberation from immediate threat and the restoration of well-being. In the Qal imperative (as here), it is a direct command or earnest plea for intervention.
word_study.significance: This verb is foundational to the Hebrew concept of salvation—not merely personal spiritual redemption in the later Christian sense, but concrete, observable deliverance from enemies, siege, or death. The Greek transliteration of hoshi'ah na became 'Hosanna,' making this verse the etymological source of the word that would define the messiah's entry into Jerusalem.

word_study.meaning: A particle of urgent entreaty; 'please,' 'I pray you,' 'I beseech you.' It intensifies the following imperative and signals emotional weight. The double anna creates heightened supplication.
word_study.significance: Anna appears throughout the Psalms and Prophets as the voice of the vulnerable seeking divine attention. The doubled invocation in this verse—'anna YHWH ... anna YHWH'—is the voice of the remnant, the besieged, the one who has nowhere else to turn. In the liturgical setting of Sukkot (the Feast of Tabernacles, during which this psalm was likely sung), the anna cry was the worshiper's acknowledgment of total dependence on God's grace.

word_study.meaning: To cause to prosper, to grant success or progress; to make straight or smooth the way. The Hiphil form indicates causation—'cause to succeed.' Related to the noun tzlichah (prosperity, progress).
word_study.significance: Unlike hoshi'ah (which emphasizes rescue from danger), hatzlichah points to the positive outcome after deliverance—the flourishing that follows safety. Together, the two verbs frame salvation not as a single moment but as a process: first the rescue, then the restoration and advancement. This aligns with the covenant promise of both protection and blessing.

cross_references.connection: The crowds greeting Jesus at His triumphal entry cry 'Hosanna,' which is the direct Greek transliteration of hoshi'ah na from Psalm 118:25, applying this ancient plea for salvation to Jesus as the messiah.
The song of Moses after the Red Sea crossing uses similar language of salvation (yasha) and exaltation, creating a parallel between God's ancient rescue and the deliverance this psalm celebrates.
Isaiah's prophecy of future salvation echoes the prayer for success and deliverance found here, connecting the psalmist's petition to the messianic hope of restored Israel.
The dedicatory prayer of the Kirtland Temple uses language of salvation and divine blessing that mirrors the structure of petition followed by assurance found in this verse.

commentary.historical_context: Psalm 118:25 reflects the liturgical practice of the Second Temple period, particularly the Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot), when pilgrims would process around the altar with palm branches and recite prayers of supplication and praise. The doubled petition suggests a moment in the festival when the community acknowledged both corporate need and corporate trust. The request for 'success' (hatzlichah) in an agricultural society would have been understood as blessing on the harvest—a literal, tangible divine provision. The phrase hoshi'ah na became a fixed, recognized acclamation in Jewish worship, so that by the first century CE, when crowds shouted 'Hosanna!' at Jesus' entry, they were deploying a liturgically encoded plea that carried centuries of meaning: 'Save us! Deliver us! Make us successful!' The use of this specific phrase by the Gospel writers is not incidental; it signals that the crowd recognized in Jesus the fulfillment of the Psalmist's ancient hope.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon echoes this pattern of repeated, urgent petition for deliverance. In Alma 36:18, Alma cries out for salvation in language of desperation and faith, mirroring the psalmist's doubled anna prayer. The concept of being saved and granted success—deliverance and blessing—appears throughout Nephi's reflections on God's mercy (1 Nephi 1:20, 2 Nephi 4:20-25).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 50:36-37 uses parallel language of being saved and preserved, connecting individual petition to collective covenant keeping. The emphasis on asking for divine success appears in D&C 8:2-3, where Oliver Cowdery is instructed to ask for guidance and wisdom—a form of hatzlichah (success in spiritual understanding).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, the language of petition followed by blessing mirrors this verse's structure. The worshiper asks (in the garments of covenant) for deliverance from sin and opposition, and the ordinance structure affirms both salvation from darkness and blessing toward exaltation. The Sukkot festival, during which this psalm was sung, anticipated the millennial ingathering—a theme relevant to latter-day temple theology.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus' entry into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday, when crowds cry 'Hosanna!' (hoshi'ah na), transforms this verse's plea into an acclamation of the Savior. The psalmist's prayer for salvation becomes fulfilled in the person of Jesus—He is the answer to the anna cry, the one in whom all prior pleas for deliverance converge. The doubled petition in verse 25 finds its completion in the doubled work of Christ: His atoning sacrifice (the ultimate hoshi'ah—rescue from death and sin) and His resurrection and exaltation (the ultimate hatzlichah—grant success, transform defeat into victory).
commentary.application: For the modern reader, this verse invites a recalibration of how we pray. The psalmist does not merely ask once and move on; he repeats his plea, intensifying it with 'please.' In our private prayers and in our worship as a community, we are invited to bring our needs—both rescue and flourishing—before the Lord with the intensity and persistence of someone who has nowhere else to turn. The use of Hosanna in temple contexts (particularly Palm Sunday observances in Latter-day Saint practice) connects us to this same ancient cry. When we echo the plea 'Hosanna,' we are not engaging in historical recreation but joining our voice to the chorus of the faithful across centuries, acknowledging our dependence on divine deliverance and blessing.

text_kjv: Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the LORD: we have blessed you out of the house of the LORD.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 26 is a dramatic shift in voice and perspective. The psalmist's urgent plea (v. 25) is answered immediately—not by divine action, but by a priestly or liturgical response. The blessing formula "Barukh ha-ba beshem YHWH" (Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the LORD) appears to be spoken by priests or Levites standing at the Temple gates, addressing an arriving worshiper or dignitary. This is no longer individual supplication; it is corporate, official, liturgical affirmation. The person who has cried out 'Save us!' now receives the community's pronouncement of blessing. The second line—"We bless you from the house of the LORD"—grounds this blessing in the authority of the Temple itself. The blessing does not originate with the priests as private persons but flows from their official role as representatives of God's dwelling place.

The phrase beshem YHWH (in the name of the LORD) is crucial. It means 'by the authority of,' 'under the banner of,' 'as a representative of.' The one who comes in this name is acting with divine authorization. In the Gospels, when the crowds cry out Psalm 118:26 to Jesus—'Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord'—they are explicitly recognizing Him as one who comes with God's authority, who is not a private person but an official representative of the divine will. The liturgical setting of verse 26, with its movement from petition to blessing, from individual need to corporate affirmation, creates the theological framework within which the messiah's entry is understood: He is the one for whom all previous prayers and processions have waited.

word_study.meaning: Blessed, praised, honored; from the root meaning 'to kneel' or 'to bend the knee.' The adjective form indicates a state of being blessed or favored. In the Qal participle, it can refer to someone as the recipient of blessing or as someone whose character is worthy of blessing.
word_study.significance: Barukh is not merely a sentiment of well-wishing but a pronouncement of favor, a declaration that God's blessing rests upon the person or thing addressed. In the Temple liturgy, when priests pronounce barukh upon an arriving worshiper, they are not offering an opinion but speaking a blessing into effect—an utterance that carries the weight of priestly authority and divine association.

word_study.meaning: The one who comes, the coming one; the Qal participle of bo ('to come'). Used with the definite article (ha-), it suggests a specific, anticipated figure rather than just any arrivals.
word_study.significance: The use of the definite article 'the coming one' rather than 'a coming one' suggests that by the time this psalm was being sung in the Second Temple period, there was a recognized, anticipated figure associated with this phrase. The Gospels understand Jesus as the fulfillment of this expectation—He is 'the one who comes' (ho erchomenos in Greek, John 1:15, 1:27; Matthew 11:3).

word_study.term_english: In the name of the LORD (beshem YHWH)
word_study.meaning: In the name of, by the authority of, under the designation of, on behalf of. The preposition be- ('in') joined with shem ('name') creates a formula of authorization and representation.
word_study.significance: To come beshem YHWH is not merely to invoke God's name but to come with His authority, as His representative, bearing His mandate. In the New Testament, Jesus teaches His disciples to do all things in His name (John 14:13-14), creating a parallel: just as the psalmist's figure comes in God's name, believers are to act in Christ's name. This phrase became crucial for messiah-identification in Jewish expectation.

word_study.meaning: The Temple, the dwelling place of God, the nexus of divine presence and earthly worship. Beit ('house') in this context refers not to a private residence but to the sacred sanctuary.
word_study.significance: The blessing flows 'from the house of the LORD'—its source is the Temple, the place where heaven and earth intersect, where God's presence dwells. The blessing pronounced upon the arriving worshiper carries the weight of the sacred space itself. In Christian interpretation, the 'house of the LORD' becomes typological of Christ as the true Temple—the one in whom God's presence dwelt fully (John 1:14, 2:19-21).

cross_references.connection: The crowds greet Jesus with the exact words of Psalm 118:26, 'Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord,' identifying Him as the anticipated arrival figure of the psalm.

Mark's version of the triumphal entry explicitly links Psalm 118:26 to Jesus and adds 'Blessed is the kingdom of our father David that cometh,' showing Jewish expectation of a davidic messiah arriving in God's name.
Luke preserves the blessing formula with reference to 'peace in heaven,' expanding the psalm's blessing to cosmic scope—the arrival of the blessed one restores peace between earth and heaven.
John's account of the palm processional directly quotes Psalm 118:25-26, making explicit that the crowd understood Jesus' entry as the fulfillment of this specific psalm's eschatological hope.

The Aaronic priestly blessing uses parallel structure and invokes God's name over the blessed; Psalm 118:26 echoes this priestly authority, with Temple priests blessing the arriving worshiper in God's name.

When David brings the ark into Jerusalem, he pronounces blessings on the people in God's name, creating a precedent for the king or official figure acting in God's authority before the gathering community.

commentary.historical_context: In the liturgical context of the Second Temple, Psalm 118:26 appears to have been spoken responsively—the arriving pilgrim or dignitary (perhaps the king at festival time, or a high priest) would cry 'Save us!' (v. 25), and the Levitical choir or priestly guardians at the Temple gates would respond with the blessing formula. This call-and-response structure is preserved in the Gospel accounts, where the crowds cry 'Hosanna!' and then, in the parallel tradition, voice the blessing 'Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord.' The Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles) context is crucial: during this autumn festival, pilgrims would process to the Temple with palm branches (lulavim) and perform circumambulations (hakkafot) around the altar, reciting psalms. The blessing of verse 26 would have been spoken by the Temple authorities to recognize and honor the arriving worshippers. By Jesus' time, the eschatological weight of this psalm was fully recognized—the 'coming one' was understood as the messiah. The Gospels, by having the crowds quote Psalm 118:26 to Jesus, place Him directly into the framework of this expectation, identifying Him as the one in whom all previous arrivals and blessings converge.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The structure of blessing and authorization appears in Alma 5:48-52, where Alma blesses the people in God's name, acting as an authorized representative of divine will. The language of coming 'in the name of the Lord' resonates with Alma's mission language in Alma 17:9-11, where the missionaries are sent to teach and bless in God's authority. The Book of Mormon's emphasis on prophetic authority—speaking and acting beshem YHWH (in the name of the Lord)—reflects this psalm's theology of authorized representation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:30 identifies the Church as 'the only true and living church' upon the earth, establishing Christ as its head and setting the framework for all authorized blessings flowing from His name. D&C 21:4-5 promises that the Church president, acting in the Lord's stead, will receive His word and speak in His name—a direct parallel to the authorized blessing of Psalm 118:26. The entire structure of priesthood authority in D&C 27:12-13, 50:24 rests on the principle of acting beshem YHWH (in the Lord's name).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In Latter-day Saint temple practice, the patriarch and temple officiators pronounce blessings in the name of the Lord upon the covenant-makers, echoing this verse's structure. The movement from petition (v. 25) to blessing (v. 26) reflects the temple endowment's progression from the worshiper's supplication to the divine blessing of exaltation. Christ is understood as the ultimate 'one who comes in the name of the LORD'—the great high priest whose authority and blessing are foundational to all temple ordinances.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 26 contains one of the clearest typological prophecies of Christ in the Psalms. The 'one who comes in the name of the LORD' is fulfilled in Jesus' entry into Jerusalem, as all four Gospels affirm by quoting or alluding to this verse. Jesus is the anticipated figure, the messianic arrival, the one who comes with God's full authority and blessing. The priestly blessing pronounced upon Him becomes, in the Christian understanding, the consecration of the sacrificial High Priest. The movement from verse 25 (urgent petition for salvation) to verse 26 (blessing of the coming deliverer) prefigures the pattern of the Gospels: the people cry for deliverance, and Jesus arrives as the answer. His entry is not merely a procession but a coronation—the formal, liturgical recognition that He comes beshem YHWH, bearing God's mandate and blessing.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse invites reflection on the nature of authorized blessing in the Church. Just as the Temple priests blessed the arriving worshiper in verse 26 with the authority of the sacred space, modern priesthood holders bless the Saints in Christ's name, carrying forward the same tradition of authorized, effectual blessing. When we participate in patriarchal blessings, parental blessings, or priestly blessings over the sick, we are standing in the line of the priests of Psalm 118, pronouncing favor 'in the name of the Lord.' Additionally, this verse challenges us to recognize and honor those who come 'in the Lord's name'—prophets, missionaries, and all who are sent with His authority. The blessing is not theirs to give of themselves but belongs to God alone; they are merely the conduits. As we grow in our faith, we are invited to increasingly understand ourselves as those who 'come in the name of the Lord'—to carry His authority, speak His word, and bless in His power.

text_kjv: God is the LORD, which hath shewed us light: bind the sacrifice with cords, even unto the horns of the altar.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 27 transitions from the priestly blessing (v. 26) to specific cultic action—the preparation of the sacrifice within the Temple. The opening declaration "El YHWH vayyaer lanu" (The LORD is God, and He has shone upon us) echoes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:25 ('the LORD make His face shine upon you') and frames the entire liturgical moment in terms of divine illumination and favor. This is not merely poetic language; the 'light' that YHWH shows is the visible sign of His presence—the glory, the approval, the revelation that has come upon the worshiper and the community. With this cosmic framework established, the psalmist then gives a detailed instruction: the festival offering is to be bound with branches or cords up to the horns of the altar.

The practical detail of verse 27b is more significant than it might first appear. The 'horns of the altar' were the four projecting corners of the sacrificial altar—places of sanctity to which those seeking refuge could cling (see 1 Kings 1:50). To bind the sacrifice 'up to the horns' is to establish a continuity between the offering and the most sacred parts of the altar itself, maximizing the offering's contact with the holy space. The verb 'bind' (asru) can mean to bind with cords or to bundle together with branches (avotim). In the Sukkot context, this likely refers to binding the lulavim (palm and willow branches) as part of the festival ritual, though the instruction may also refer to the preparation of actual sacrificial offerings. The combination of cosmic declaration (v. 27a) and concrete ritual action (v. 27b) creates a unified theology: the unseen work of God (His light shining upon us) becomes visible and tangible through the community's faithful enactment of the sacrificial system.

word_study.meaning: A declaration of identity: El (the strong one, the divine being) is identified as YHWH (the covenant name of Israel's God). This is not two separate entities but a clarification and affirmation of singular divine identity.
word_study.significance: The pairing of El (used more broadly in ancient Near Eastern contexts for divinity generally) with YHWH (Israel's specific covenant name) creates a statement of both universal and particular significance: the one true God, El, is the God of Israel's covenant, YHWH. This declaration appears in a few psalms and affirms monotheistic conviction amid the religious pluralism of the ancient world.

word_study.meaning: And He shone upon us, He gave light to us. The Hiphil form of 'or ('light') indicates causative action—the Lord causes light to shine. The preposition le- ('to') signals the passive recipients: to us, upon us.
word_study.significance: Light in biblical theology is the sign of God's presence, favor, and revelation. The priestly blessing of Numbers 6:25—'The LORD make His face to shine (ya'er) upon you'—uses the same verb. Here, the psalmist affirms that this blessing has already been realized: the light has shone, the divine favor is visible. This moves the community from petition to affirmation—from 'please save us' (v. 25) to 'God has given us light' (v. 27).

word_study.meaning: Bind, tie, secure. The Qal imperative form is a direct command. The object of binding is the sacrifice or festival offering.
word_study.significance: The binding is not merely practical preparation but a ritual action that connects the earthly offering to the heavenly reality. By binding the sacrifice securely, even up to the horns of the altar, the worshiper is establishing a channel of communication and offering from earth to God's dwelling place. The verb appears in similar ritual contexts (Numbers 30:2 regarding vows; Proverbs 26:8 regarding the fool).

word_study.meaning: A festival, a festive gathering, or the offering associated with the festival. The root suggests movement in a circle, dancing, procession. In this context, it refers to the Sukkot festival and its associated offerings.
word_study.significance: The chag is not a burden imposed by law but a joyful occasion, a movement of the community in worship. The binding of the chag with branches or cords is a way of unifying the community's joyful offering with the altar's sanctity, making the entire festival an offering to God.

word_study.meaning: The four projecting corners of the sacrificial altar, which rose upward from each corner. These were places of particular sanctity, to which refugees could cling for protection.
word_study.significance: The horns of the altar were places of refuge and sanctuary in ancient Israel (1 Samuel 2:28, 1 Kings 1:50, 2:28). To bind the offering 'up to the horns' creates a direct connection between the community's gift and the most sacred parts of the sacrificial space, suggesting that the offering rises upward to the highest point of holiness.

cross_references.connection: The priestly blessing 'the LORD make His face to shine upon you' uses the same verb (ya'er) as Psalm 118:27, establishing continuity between the priestly blessing invoked and the light that has shone upon the community.

The instructions for Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles) include binding branches (lulavim) and performing sacrifices, providing the cultic context for verse 27's command to bind the festival offering with branches.

Adonijah seeks refuge by grasping the horns of the altar, illustrating that the altar's horns were recognized as places of sanctuary and divine protection, illuminating the significance of binding the offering up to them.

The menorah in the Tabernacle provided light and illuminated the sanctuary; Psalm 118:27's imagery of light shining connects the divine glory revealed through light with God's presence in the holy place.

The familiar declaration 'The LORD is my light and my salvation' echoes the cosmic affirmation of Psalm 118:27a, establishing light as the consistent biblical symbol of divine presence and deliverance.

commentary.historical_context: Psalm 118:27 is set firmly within the Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles) liturgy. This autumn festival was one of Israel's three pilgrimage feasts, observed in the seventh month (September/October), and it included the binding of palm and willow branches (lulavim and aravim) as a central ritual element. The command to 'bind the festival offering with branches up to the horns of the altar' reflects the actual cultic practices of Second Temple Judaism. The priest or Levite would give specific instructions to the gathered pilgrims regarding how the offerings were to be prepared and presented. The opening declaration 'El YHWH vayyaer lanu' ('The LORD is God, and He has shone upon us') places the ritual action within a theological framework: the visible, concrete acts of worship are expressions of and responses to the invisible, cosmic reality of God's favor and presence. The 'light' that YHWH shows may also allude to the Festival of Lights (understood by some to be an ancient aspect of Sukkot, though more famously associated with Hanukkah), when the Temple was illuminated and the community celebrated by lamplight. The instruction to bind the offering up to the altar's horns ensures maximum contact between the community's gift and the holiest part of the sacrificial apparatus, maximizing the offering's efficacy.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The imagery of binding offerings appears in the Book of Mormon in connection with covenant-keeping and the law of sacrifice. Nephi's emphasis on offering a broken heart and contrite spirit (2 Nephi 2:7) stands in contrast to the physical binding of sacrifices but illustrates the principle that all offerings must be bound—connected—to genuine internal devotion. The Atonement of Christ replaces the physical offerings of the temple, but the principle of binding ourselves through covenant to God's altar remains central (Alma 5:26-27).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 59:9-13 instructs the Saints to remember the sabbath and to keep the Lord's commandments, creating a parallel to the binding of offerings in verse 27—our whole selves, our time, our energy, are to be bound (dedicated, consecrated) to God's service. The law of sacrifice in D&C 97:8-9 teaches that the Church must be sanctified through the shedding of blood (ultimately Christ's) and through the devoted offering of our hearts, a spiritual parallel to the binding of sacrifices in the temple.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The binding of the sacrifice in verse 27 prefigures the temple endowment's emphasis on covenant binding. Just as the offering is bound up to the horns of the altar, the covenant-maker is bound through the ordinances to God's purposes. The 'horns of the altar' become metaphorically the highest point of exaltation, and the covenant-maker seeks to ascend toward it through faithful participation in the ordinances. The movement from petition (v. 25) through blessing (v. 26) to offering and binding (v. 27) mirrors the temple's progression toward covenant and consecration.

commentary.christological_typology: The binding of the sacrifice up to the horns of the altar points toward Christ's offering on the cross. In the Christian reading of the Psalms, every sacrificial binding in the Temple is a type of Christ's self-offering. The Epistle to the Hebrews (particularly Hebrews 9-10) establishes that Christ is the final, perfect offering, and that all prior temple sacrifices pointed forward to His sacrifice. The 'light' that shines in verse 27a is also Christ—'the light of the world' (John 8:12, 9:5). Thus, verse 27 simultaneously affirms the cosmic revelation of God's favor (through Christ as light) and the community's participation in the redemptive work through the binding of offerings (pointing to Christ's binding upon the altar of the cross).
commentary.application: Verse 27 calls modern readers to understand worship as both cosmic affirmation and concrete action. We cannot merely declare theologically that 'God is the Lord and has given us light' without then binding our actual lives, time, and resources to His service. The verse moves from declaration to command: having affirmed God's favor (light shining upon us), we are obliged to respond through dedicated action. In the context of covenant membership, this means bringing our whole selves—our talents, our resources, our families—and binding them to God's altar through participation in the temple, through service in His kingdom, through the keeping of commandments. The image of binding the offering 'up to the horns of the altar' suggests that our service, our offerings, our devotion are not isolated acts but are part of a unified ascent toward holiness and sanctity. We offer not merely portions of ourselves but seek to align our entire lives with God's purposes.

text_kjv: Thou art my God, and I will praise thee: thou art my God, I will exalt thee.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 28 marks a fundamental shift from communal action back to intimate personal address. After the corporate liturgy of verses 25-27—the community's petition, the priestly blessing, the bound offerings at the altar—the psalmist now speaks as an individual, in direct conversation with God: "Eli attah" (You are my God). The repetition is striking: 'You are my God' appears twice in this single verse, and the doubled affirmation creates an intensity of personal devotion. This is not the distant monotheistic declaration of verse 27a ('El YHWH'), but the intimate covenantal confession of an individual who has experienced God's hand directly. The shift from 'our' (v. 25-27) to 'my' (v. 28) is theologically significant: the psalm moves from corporate petition to personal testimony, from ritual obligation to heartfelt gratitude.

The two verbs that follow—'I will praise thee' (ve-odekka) and 'I will exalt thee' (aromemekka)—are not merely repetitive expressions of thanksgiving but complementary acts. To praise (hodah, from which odekka derives) is to acknowledge, to confess, to publicly recognize. To exalt (romam) is to lift up, to magnify, to raise to prominence. Together, they encompass both the internal recognition of God's greatness and the external proclamation of it. The psalmist is not content with quiet gratitude; he will make known what God has done. This verse is the turning point where the psalm becomes personal testimony—the place where the individual reader or worshiper says, 'This psalm is about me. This God who delivered Israel and blessed the arriving pilgrims is MY God, and I am committing myself to praise and exalt Him.' The doubled assertion 'Thou art my God' creates a personal covenant statement, a moment of individual rededication within the larger liturgical frame.

word_study.meaning: You are my God. Eli is the possessive 'my God' (elohim with first person singular possessive suffix); attah is the second person singular 'you' (emphatic). Together: 'You specifically, you alone, are the one I recognize as divine.'
word_study.significance: This is not an abstract theological statement but a personal covenant claim. The doubling of this phrase in verse 28 (appearing once more as 'my God' in the second line) is a personal parallel to the great covenantal affirmations of Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4, 'The LORD is our God'). Here, an individual speaks: This God is mine. I belong to Him, and He is my God. In the context of the broader psalm's narrative of deliverance, this is the response of someone who has experienced God's saving work directly.

word_study.meaning: And I will praise you, I will thank you, I will confess you. The verb hodah primarily means 'to acknowledge' or 'to confess,' and in the context of worship, it means to publicly recognize and celebrate.
word_study.significance: Praise in Hebrew is not merely emotional expression but active acknowledgment and public declaration. To odekka is to confess God's greatness before others, to make His mighty acts known. The commitment 'I will praise you' is a vow to become a witness, a testimony-bearer to God's faithfulness. The future tense (I will praise) indicates this is not a momentary emotion but a sustained commitment.

word_study.meaning: I will exalt you, I will lift you up, I will magnify you. From the root romam, meaning 'to be high' or 'to lift up.' The Piel form (as here) indicates causative intensity: I will make you high, I will cause you to be elevated in honor.
word_study.significance: To exalt God is not to elevate His objective status (which cannot be changed) but to elevate Him in the estimation and proclamation of the community and the worshiper. The commitment 'I will exalt you' is a vow of advocacy and honor-giving. This verb appears in hymns of thanksgiving throughout the Psalms and indicates active promotion of God's reputation and fame. It carries the sense that the psalmist will not merely think well of God privately but will be an active agent in raising His profile and spreading word of His greatness.

cross_references.connection: A similar structure and commitment: 'O magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together,' showing the pattern of moving from personal experience to public exaltation of God.
David declares 'Thou art my God' and commits to praise, bless, and magnify God's name forever—a sustained, personal testimony paralleling verse 28's intimate affirmation.
The Shema affirms the LORD as God and commands love for Him with all one's being; Psalm 118:28 echoes this covenantal confession with personal intensity.
The command 'Be still, and know that I am God' precedes the exaltation of God's name; verse 28's commitment to exalt God flows from the foundational knowledge of His identity.

Nephi's personal testimony of faith—'And I, Nephi, being exceedingly young...did cry unto the Lord; and behold he did visit me'—demonstrates the Book of Mormon parallel to the personal covenant claim of verse 28.

commentary.historical_context: Verse 28 reflects the personal piety that characterized post-exilic Judaism and would have been especially resonant in the context of Sukkot pilgrimage. While the festival was a corporate occasion with prescribed rituals, it was also a time for personal spiritual renewal and individual testimony. As pilgrims arrived at the Temple, they would have been invited to offer their own prayers and confessions alongside the communal liturgy. The doubling of 'You are my God' may reflect the practice of personal testimony-giving within the festival context—a moment when an individual would step forward (metaphorically, even if not physically) and make a personal affirmation before God and the gathered community. The commitment 'I will praise you' and 'I will exalt you' is a vow taken, presumably before witnesses (at the Temple), to become a living testimony to God's faithfulness. Such personal covenants would have been understood as binding—the individual is pledging that his future life will be devoted to the proclamation of God's greatness.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of personal testimony followed by commitment to exaltation appears throughout the Book of Mormon. Alma the Younger's conversion experience (Alma 36) leads him to declare that he will teach and testify of God's greatness. Nephi's personal covenant claims—'I know that the Lord loves me' (2 Nephi 4:20)—parallel the intimate 'You are my God' of verse 28. The Book of Mormon emphasizes repeatedly that individual conversion must lead to public testimony and active participation in God's work.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 84:88 promises the Saints that those who diligently seek the Lord will receive His Spirit and power to accomplish His purposes. The commitment 'I will praise thee, I will exalt thee' aligns with the covenant promise in D&C 42:61 that the Lord will give power to those who keep His commandments. D&C 50:43 teaches that the faithful 'shall be a light unto the world'—a way of exalting God and making His greatness known through their own sanctified lives.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The personal affirmation 'Thou art my God' is renewed in temple covenants, where the individual makes binding commitments to serve God. The vow to praise and exalt God becomes part of the temple covenant's promise to dedicate oneself to God's service. The movement from communal ritual (verses 25-27) to personal covenant (verse 28) mirrors the temple's structure: while the temple is a community of the covenant, the ordinances are ultimately received by and binding upon individuals. Each person standing in the temple must make the personal claim: 'Thou art my God.'

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 28's personal claim 'You are my God' is the voice of anyone who has experienced God's saving work—but in the context of Jesus' triumphal entry (to which this psalm directly points), it becomes His voice as well. Jesus, in His humanity, makes the ultimate personal claim upon God the Father: 'My God, my God' (quoting Psalm 22:1 in Matthew 27:46). The commitment to praise and exalt God characterizes Jesus' entire earthly mission—He came to glorify the Father (John 17:4) and to make God's name known (John 17:6, 26). For those who follow Christ, verse 28 becomes a way of participating in His work: as we exalt and praise God, we join Christ in His mission of revelation and glorification.
commentary.application: For the modern reader, verse 28 is an invitation to move from passive participation in Church community to active personal testimony. It is one thing to sing hymns, attend services, or participate in the collective practices of the faith community (verses 25-27). It is another to stand and declare, 'You are my God.' This verse challenges each individual to ask: Do I truly own my testimony? Can I say with conviction, 'Thou art my God'? And beyond mere affirmation, can I commit to praise and exalt Him—to be an active advocate for His truth, a living witness to His faithfulness in my life? The doubled assertion invites deliberation: the first 'You are my God' is affirmation; the second, reinforcement. It is as though the psalmist pauses and restates the commitment, emphasizing its seriousness. In our own lives, this calls us to seasons of spiritual renewal where we recommit ourselves, not out of obligation but out of genuine gratitude for God's hand in our lives. It also invites us to move from private faith to public testimony—to speak openly of what God has done in our own story, to exalt His name among our families and communities.

text_kjv: O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever.

commentary.narrative:
Psalm 118 ends where it essentially began (cf. v. 1), creating a perfect frame: the psalm opens with "Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His steadfast love endures forever" (v. 1) and closes with the identical refrain in verse 29. This is not mere repetition but structural completion—the entire narrative arc of the psalm, from initial exhortation through the account of distress and deliverance, through liturgical action and personal testimony, returns to the foundational affirmation from which it all flows. Everything the psalmist has recounted—the siege, the rejected stone, the gates flung open, the pilgrimage and blessing, the binding of offerings, the personal claim 'You are my God'—all of it finds its ultimate explanation in the single theological reality: God is good, and His mercy (steadfast love, covenantal faithfulness—chasdo in Hebrew) endures eternally.

The choice to return to this refrain rather than to conclude with verse 28's personal testimony is theologically profound. Verse 28 was the 'I' voice—'I will praise you, I will exalt you.' But verse 29 returns to the communal 'we' voice: 'O give thanks unto the LORD.' This is an invitation, even a command, to join the chorus of thanksgiving. The psalmist is not merely expressing his own gratitude but calling the entire community—readers throughout the ages—to enter into the same grateful proclamation. The phrase 'His mercy endureth for ever' (le'olam chasdo) is not hyperbole but theological conviction rooted in Israel's history. God's covenantal love has been demonstrated across generations: the ancestors experienced it, the present generation experiences it, and future generations will experience it. This is why thanksgiving is not a momentary emotion but a perpetual posture. The refrain frames all of human existence within the mercy of God—nothing that has happened to the psalmist has broken God's love, and nothing that will happen in the future can exhaust it. Thus the psalm ends not with a question mark or an exclamation of wonder, but with a period—a settled, assured affirmation that the word has been spoken, the truth has been proclaimed, and the community is called to take up and repeat it forever.

cross_references.connection: Verse 29 repeats the refrain that opens the psalm, creating an envelope structure where the entire narrative and testimony of the psalm rests within the foundational affirmation of God's goodness and eternal mercy.

God's self-revelation to Moses includes 'The LORD, the LORD, God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness' (using the same word chesed)—this is the theological tradition verse 29 invokes and affirms.

Another closing affirmation: 'For the LORD is good; his mercy is everlasting; and his truth endureth to all generations'—using nearly identical theological language to establish God's eternal goodness as foundational to all worship.

An extended meditation on God's mercy (chesed) that describes it as 'tender' and 'abundant,' offering comfort that even when our sins are great, God's mercy surpasses them—the comfort underlying verse 29's confidence.

An entire psalm structured on the refrain 'His steadfast love (chasdo) endures for ever,' with the phrase repeated after each line of salvation history, showing how verse 29's affirmation was the central liturgical conviction of post-exilic Israel.

Nephi quotes Isaiah and affirms that God's mercy endures forever to those who have faith in Christ and keep His commandments, extending the Psalm's affirmation into a Book of Mormon context of covenant keeping.
Ammon declares 'Let us thank the Lord our God' and affirms His mercy, using the same structure of thanksgiving and affirmation of God's eternal steadfast love found in verse 29.

commentary.application: Verse 29 serves as both conclusion and renewed beginning. In our personal faith journeys, we return again and again to this foundational affirmation: 'The Lord is good. His mercy endures forever.' When we face seasons of doubt or difficulty, this refrain becomes our anchor. It is not a naive denial of hardship but a conviction rooted in God's actual character and demonstrated faithfulness. The verse invites us to become people whose lives are framed by gratitude—not as a feeling dependent on circumstances, but as a posture rooted in the unchanging reality that God is good. Additionally, the communal call 'O give thanks unto the LORD' reminds us that gratitude is not a solitary practice but a communal one. We are invited to join our voices with countless others—across centuries, across traditions—in affirming that God's mercy has no end. In practical terms, this might mean: speaking gratitude aloud in our families and communities, teaching our children to recognize God's hand in their lives, and building our faith on the bedrock conviction that whatever comes, God is good, and His steadfast love endures forever. This is the note on which the entire psalm—and this week's reading of the Psalms—concludes: not with questions but with settled certainty, not with doubt but with gratitude, not with anxiety about the future but with confidence in God's eternal faithfulness.
commentary.christological_typology: While verse 29 does not explicitly mention the Messiah, it provides the theological foundation for understanding Christ's entire work. The goodness and mercy of God—affirmations that close Psalm 118—find their fullest expression in Christ's atoning sacrifice. The Apostle Paul writes in Romans 5:8, 'God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us'—the ultimate expression of God's chesed (steadfast love). In the context of Psalm 118's journey from petition (v. 25) through the blessing of the one who comes in God's name (v. 26) to the final affirmation of God's eternal goodness (v. 29), Christ is the answer to every stage: He is the salvation cried for, the blessed one arriving with divine authority, and the ultimate proof that God's mercy is indeed forever—because in His resurrection, He conquered even death itself.

word_study.meaning: Give thanks, acknowledge, confess. The Qal imperative plural form, addressing a community. The root hodah carries the sense of 'to acknowledge' or 'to recognize the truth of.'
word_study.significance: Thanksgiving in Hebrew is not merely emotional gratitude but active recognition and proclamation of what is true about God. To give thanks (hodu) is to acknowledge God's greatness, His faithfulness, His goodness as objective reality—not as opinion but as fact. The imperative form makes this a command to the community: thanksgiving is not optional but obligatory for those who have experienced God's mercy. This is why verse 29 can close the psalm as a universal call—the thanksgiving is not contextual to the psalmist's particular story but is the appropriate and necessary response of any who recognize God's goodness.

word_study.meaning: Good, pleasant, favorable; describing what is beneficial, what brings well-being. Can refer to both moral goodness and practical goodness—what is genuinely good for human flourishing.
word_study.significance: To declare 'The LORD is good' (YHWH ki tov) is to affirm that God's character, His actions, and His intentions toward His creation are fundamentally beneficent. This is the answer to the problem of evil and suffering posed by the psalm's narrative: even in the midst of distress and siege, God is good—His intentions toward His covenant people are never malicious, always ultimately redemptive. The repeated affirmation of God's goodness in verses 1 and 29 brackets the entire psalm with this conviction.

word_study.meaning: His steadfast love, His mercy, His covenantal faithfulness. The noun chesed is one of the richest words in biblical Hebrew, encompassing loyalty, reliability, grace, and covenantal love. The -o suffix indicates 'His' (God's chesed). The Covenant Rendering translates this as 'faithful love,' capturing both the emotionality and the steadiness of the concept.
word_study.significance: Chesed is not sentimental; it is covenantal obligation met with consistency and generosity. When God's chesed is said to 'endure forever' (le'olam), the claim is that His commitment to His covenant people is not episodic but eternal, not conditional but given freely, not based on the people's merit but on His own character. This is the theological foundation of Israel's existence: God loved them into being as a people (Exodus 20:2-4), and that love does not waver with their faithlessness. The psalmist can affirm that even in distress and siege, God's chesed continues to operate.

word_study.meaning: For ever, for all time, perpetually. The preposition le ('for,' 'unto') combined with olam ('eternity,' 'the age,' 'time without end'). This is not merely quantitative but qualitative—it speaks of a love that transcends and encompasses all moments.
word_study.significance: The affirmation that God's mercy 'endures for ever' (le'olam) creates a temporal envelope around all human experience. Past, present, and future are all enclosed within God's faithful love. For the individual reader, this means that whatever has happened or will happen is held within the constancy of God's steadfast love. For the community, it means that God's commitment transcends generations—what God did for the ancestors, He does for the present generation, and what He does now, He will do for those yet to come. This is why the psalm returns to this refrain: it is the unchanging, all-encompassing truth that makes sense of everything else.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon returns repeatedly to this same refrain-like affirmation. Lehi's blessing to his sons (2 Nephi 1:15) emphasizes God's mercy; Alma's testimony (Alma 36:24-26) affirms that God's love and mercy exceed all understanding and endure forever. The repeated Book of Mormon theme that God's covenantal love is constant and never-failing (mosiah 24:12-14) directly parallels verse 29's affirmation that 'His mercy endureth for ever.' The Book of Mormon also adds the christological dimension: it is through Christ's atonement that God's mercy becomes operative and available to all who believe (Alma 42:15-17).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:39 declares that 'the same sociality which exists among us here will exist among us there,' suggesting that God's faithful love extends beyond mortal life into eternity. D&C 101:16 uses the phrase 'his goodness shall not fail,' affirming that God's tov (goodness) and chesed (steadfast love) are the governing realities of existence. The oath and covenant of the priesthood (D&C 84:33-39) describes God's promise to the faithful in terms that echo verse 29's affirmation—God's mercies are sure and His word is sure.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment moves the individual through a progression toward the presence of God, ending in the celestial room—which represents the very presence of divine love and mercy. Verse 29's affirmation 'His mercy endureth for ever' is realized in the temple as the worshiper is sealed and promised that 'all that my Father hath shall be yours' (D&C 84:38)—the ultimate realization of living eternally in God's covenantal love. The temple liturgy itself frequently returns to affirmations of God's goodness and the constancy of His commitment to the faithful.

commentary.historical_context: Verse 29's return to the opening refrain would have been familiar to worshippers at the Second Temple, as Psalm 136 (also known as the Egyptian Hallel, recited during Passover) employed the identical refrain throughout, making this pattern of repeated affirmation of God's eternal chesed a recognizable liturgical structure. The closing of Psalm 118 with this refrain would signal to the gathered community that the psalm was ending and that the fundamental truth had been proclaimed and reaffirmed. In the Sukkot context, this closing affirmation would be particularly poignant: the autumn festival was the time for giving thanks for the harvest, and it also commemorated the wilderness wandering, when God's chesed was the sole provision and protection of the people.
