text_kjv: Thou art near, O LORD; and all thy commandments are truth.

commentary.narrative:
After the preceding verse's lament about the wicked drawing near (v. 150), the psalmist pivots to an affirmation of God's proximity. This is not a claim about God's omnipresence in an abstract theological sense, but a relational reality: in the moment of distress, when the psalmist is surrounded by enemies, God is closer than they are. The structure mirrors the threat—just as enemies approach, so too does the LORD draw near. This nearness is not passive observation; it is the psalmist's refuge and vindication.

The second half of the verse establishes the foundation for trust: God's commandments are truth (emet). In Hebrew thought, emet is not merely theoretical correctness but reliable, trustworthy reality—something you can build your life upon. Every command God has given is rooted in what is ultimately real and dependable. This moves the psalm beyond emotional comfort into theological bedrock. The commandments are not arbitrary rules but windows into God's character and the structure of reality itself.

word_study.meaning: Near, close, at hand; indicates proximity in space or time, and relationally conveys intimacy and availability. In covenant contexts, qarov suggests God's active presence and responsiveness to the covenant partner.
word_study.significance: The psalmist does not ask God to become near but affirms that God already is near. This is an act of faith—a recognition of covenant reality even in the midst of pressure from adversaries. Against the nearness of external threats, the nearness of God is the greater reality.

word_study.meaning: Truth, reliability, faithfulness, that which is firm and enduring. Unlike abstract truth-as-proposition, emet in biblical Hebrew refers to dependable reality—what you can trust and build upon.
word_study.significance: God's commandments are not merely correct doctrines but reliable promises and patterns. To say they are emet is to say they align with reality and will not fail. This is why the psalmist can rest in them even under pressure.

cross_references.connection: The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart—affirming God's nearness to the afflicted, paralleling this verse's claim of divine proximity in distress.
What nation hath God so nigh unto them—Moses reminds Israel that God's nearness is their unique covenant privilege and distinguishes them among all peoples.
If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him—the New Testament echo of God's nearness as contingent upon covenant faithfulness and reception.
Thy word is true from the beginning—another affirmation in this psalm that God's word (commandments) is rooted in emet, truth that has always existed.

commentary.historical_context: The Psalms reflect a world in which the vulnerable (the righteous, the afflicted, those in covenant with God) face concrete threats from the powerful and ungodly. The claim that God is 'near' would have resonated in communal worship as an assertion that despite the psalmist's isolation or danger, covenant relationship with the invisible God is more real than the visible threats. In ancient Near Eastern contexts, the gods were often invoked to be present at crucial moments; Israel's distinctive claim was that their God was already present, already committed, already near.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:3 describes Alma's nearness to spiritual and physical destruction, yet recalls being 'brought to repentance by my Savior'—the nearness of salvation answering the nearness of despair, echoing this psalm's structure of threat-and-refuge.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 6:36 states 'I will go before thy face. I will be on thy right hand and on thy left.' This Restoration clarification of divine nearness—not just spiritual presence but active agency—expands the psalmist's affirmation into covenantal promise of literal divine companionship.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is understood in Latter-day Saint theology as the place of God's nearness, where covenants are made and renewed. This verse's affirmation that 'thou art near' prefigures the temple as a location where the normally invisible nearness of God becomes palpable and sacramentally real.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is God's ultimate nearness to humanity. The promise 'Thou art near, O LORD' finds its fullest expression in the Incarnation: God drawing so close that He dwells in human flesh. The commandments being 'truth' points to Christ as 'the way, the truth, and the life' (John 14:6)—the living embodiment of God's emet, God's reliable and trustworthy character made personal.
commentary.application: In moments when opposition or doubt presses in, this verse invites a reorientation: What is actually nearest to you? The threat or the LORD? The psalmist models faith not as denying the threat but as asserting a higher proximity—God is closer. In modern covenant life, this means cultivating awareness of God's nearness through obedience to His word, which is demonstrated reliable (emet) by our lived experience. When we keep the commandments and find them to bring peace, we prove their truth-character and deepen our sense of God's presence.

text_kjv: Concerning thy testimonies, I have known of old that thou hast founded them for ever.

commentary.narrative:
The psalmist now grounds his confidence in the historical reliability of God's testimonies (edot). The phrase 'known of old' (qedem) is crucial: this is not recent discovery or novelty, but ancient knowledge carried through generations. The psalmist has learned—likely through tradition, community teaching, and personal experience—that God's testimonies have an unshakable foundation. The verb yasad ('to found, to establish') carries architectural weight: these are not fragile, temporary rules subject to fashion or revision, but structural pillars on which the cosmos and covenant are built.

This verse directly counters spiritual amnesia. In the pressure of persecution or temptation, believers are tempted to doubt whether God's law is truly reliable or merely a construct of the moment. The psalmist refuses this doubt by anchoring himself in the antiquity and permanence of God's word. What has been true for ages remains true today. The word 'forever' (le'olam) suggests both temporal endlessness and the sense of 'the age'—God's word is woven into the fabric of reality itself.

word_study.meaning: Long ago, ancient time, what is before or prior. Can refer to temporal distance or to what is foundational and primary. Often implies inherited or primordial knowledge.
word_study.significance: The psalmist's confidence is not in fresh insight but in the tested testimony of ages. This is the kind of knowledge that comes through lived tradition and communal inheritance—the law proven reliable by generations.

word_study.meaning: To found, to establish, to lay a foundation; to set in place something permanent and structural. Often used of founding cities, temples, or cosmic order.
word_study.significance: God's testimonies are not provisional or contingent. They are founded—set as bedrock upon which everything else rests. This verb elevates the law from rules to cosmic order.

word_study.meaning: For eternity, forever, for the age; can refer to temporal infinity or to the enduring order of creation. In covenant language, suggests what is established and unbreakable.
word_study.significance: God's testimonies are not subject to revision, reinterpretation by human whim, or historical supersession. They endure as long as creation endures.

cross_references.connection: Thy throne is established of old—God's foundational (yasad) authority is prior to all things, paralleling the psalmist's claim that God's testimonies are founded eternally.
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever—reinforces the permanence and reliability of God's word against all temporal flux.
I am the LORD, I change not—God's immutability grounds the reliability of His testimonies; if God does not change, His law does not change.
Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever—Christ embodies the eternal consistency of God's character and word that the psalmist trusts.
For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven—another verse in this psalm affirming the eternal, heavenly foundation of God's law beyond human alteration.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, wisdom was often depicted as primordial and foundational—something antecedent to creation or at least to human institutions. Israel's claim that God's law was 'founded of old' placed the Torah in this mythological register: it was not a human invention or a recent legal code, but part of the cosmic order. This would have resonated powerfully in a culture where laws could be changed by kings or superseded by stronger powers. Israel's law, by contrast, was grounded in divine, unchanging reality. The phrase 'I have known of old' also reflects the role of elders and tradition-bearers in Israelite community, who transmitted tested wisdom across generations.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 32:21 describes faith as 'an experiment upon the word'—suggesting that like the psalmist, believers test and know through time that God's word is reliable (emet, founded forever). The Nephites' long history of receiving testimony and revelation demonstrates this pattern of qedem, ancient knowledge proven reliable.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 35:1 declares 'Hear the word of the Lord, for there is none else that will speak it'—the Restoration affirms that God's word is singular and founded, not subject to competing authorities or revision by human preference.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment sequence was revealed in this dispensation but grounded in 'ancient' truths—Adam and Eve, the Garden, the covenant. This mirrors the psalmist's insight: the deepest truths are the oldest, and they are founded forever in God's eternal purposes.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ as the 'Word' (John 1:1) is literally the embodiment of what is 'founded of old.' He is the Logos through which all things were made and sustained—the ultimate yasad, the foundation upon which all being rests. His testimony, once given, stands forever because it is grounded in His divine nature, not in human opinion or historical fashion.
commentary.application: Modern believers often feel pressure to accommodate God's word to contemporary values or to assume that ancient truths are somehow outdated. This verse invites resistance to that pressure. The psalmist's affirmation—'I have known of old'—suggests that wisdom from the past, especially God's law, deserves trust precisely because it has been proven reliable across time and circumstance. In personal covenant life, this means returning to foundational principles when confused or tempted: the law of the harvest (you reap what you sow), the law of sacrifice, the law of chastity. These are not ancient relics but eternal structures. Trusting them is trusting what has been founded forever.

text_kjv: Consider mine affliction, and deliver me: for I do not forget thy law.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 153 opens the Resh stanza (vv. 153–160), the final section of Psalm 119, where each verse begins with the Hebrew letter resh. The stanza begins with direct petition: 'See my suffering and rescue me.' The verb re'eh ('see') is not passive observation but active acknowledgment—a plea for God to look upon the psalmist's condition and recognize it. The word onyi ('affliction, suffering, humiliation') encompasses both external circumstance and the psychological devastation that accompanies it. The psalmist is not merely in difficulty but is diminished, brought low.

Yet even in this plea, the psalmist adds a reason: 'for I have not forgotten thy law.' This is striking—the statement is not 'because I have been faithful' but 'because I remember your instruction.' It is the very act of remembering, of holding fast to Torah in the midst of suffering, that constitutes the psalmist's claim on God. Memory becomes a form of loyalty. The law is not abandoned despite the pain; it is clung to all the more. This recalls the logic of covenant: the psalmist's faithfulness, expressed as non-forgetfulness, creates standing before God to petition for rescue.

word_study.meaning: To see, to look, to perceive, to regard. In petition contexts, suggests not merely visual observation but active recognition and response. To 'see' someone's suffering is to acknowledge it and be moved to act.
word_study.significance: The psalmist is not hidden from God; God is asked to acknowledge and respond to what God already perceives. This is covenant language—calling God to fulfill the relational obligation of seeing and caring for the covenant partner.

word_study.meaning: Affliction, suffering, humiliation, oppression. Can denote both external hardship and the internal experience of being brought low, diminished, or treated with contempt.
word_study.significance: The psalmist names the specific form of suffering—not mere physical pain but the diminishment of dignity and status. This is the suffering of the righteous who are persecuted or oppressed.

word_study.meaning: To draw out, to pull out, to rescue, to deliver. Implies extraction from a difficult or dangerous situation, as one might pull someone from a pit or from an enemy's grasp.
word_study.significance: Rescue is not a gentle lift but an active extraction. The psalmist envisions God as one who grasps and pulls the sufferer out of the situation threatening to destroy them.

word_study.meaning: To forget, to lose memory of, to neglect. In covenant contexts, forgetting God's law is a form of infidelity, while remembering is an act of faithfulness.
word_study.significance: The psalmist's statement—'I have not forgotten'—is a claim of covenant loyalty. Despite suffering, the psalmist has maintained the memory and practice of Torah.

cross_references.connection: I am small and despised—similar language of humiliation and diminishment earlier in this psalm, showing the ongoing theme of the psalmist's affliction.
Thou shalt love the LORD thy God...and these words, which I command thee, shall be in thine heart—the covenant obligation to remember and hold God's law close, which the psalmist claims to fulfill.

Remembering mine affliction and my misery, the wormwood and the gall...this I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope—mirrors the psalmist's experience of suffering coupled with the resolve to remember God's word as source of hope.
But I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me—expresses the same petition that God would look upon and rescue the afflicted and faithful.

commentary.historical_context: The Resh stanza (final stanza of Psalm 119) was likely composed to address believers in acute distress—possibly persecution, exile, or internal community pressure. The repeated theme is that faithfulness to the law remains the psalmist's anchor even when external circumstances deteriorate. In ancient Israel, suffering could be interpreted as divine abandonment or curse; this psalm reframes it: the suffering psalmist who clings to Torah is actually demonstrating the deepest loyalty and has grounds to petition God for vindication. This reflects a theology in which covenant faithfulness is not contingent on comfort but is demonstrated precisely in the midst of hardship.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:27 records Alma's cry: 'O that I could shout from the housetops, saying: Repent ye, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.' Alma's affliction (persecution, burden of souls) is not a sign of God's absence but of deep engagement with God's purposes. Similarly, the psalmist's suffering is consistent with covenant loyalty.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:7-9 promises that even in tribulation, the faithful one will be 'exalted hereafter'—God sees the affliction (re'eh) of the covenant partner and will deliver them according to His timing and purposes.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony includes the theme of trials and testing; the faithful are taught that memory of covenants is the means by which one is sustained through difficulty. The psalmist's refusal to forget the law mirrors the endowment participant's covenant to remember divine instructions in all circumstances.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's suffering in Gethsemane and on the cross is the ultimate fulfillment of the righteous sufferer who cries out to God: 'See my affliction and deliver me.' Yet unlike the psalmist, Christ's suffering is redemptive—His cry is not only for personal vindication but for the salvation of all who will remember and keep His word. Christ's petition in the garden ('if it be possible, let this cup pass from me') is followed by submission to divine will, modeling the deeper truth of the psalmist's cry.
commentary.application: This verse speaks to modern believers who experience suffering while maintaining their faith. The psalmist models the position: name the affliction honestly, cry out to God, and simultaneously assert your faithfulness. You are not required to spiritualize away the pain or pretend it is not real. Instead, you hold both truths: the suffering is real AND your covenant loyalty is not contingent on comfort. In practical terms, this means: When distressed, review your covenants and law-keeping. This is not self-justification but reorientation—remembering that the gospel works, that God's commandments have proven reliable, that fidelity itself becomes a form of power and a basis for asking God's intervention.

text_kjv: Plead my cause, and deliver me: quicken me according to thy word.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 154 intensifies the legal language introduced in the previous verse. The psalmist now invokes God as a legal advocate: 'Plead my case and redeem me.' The word riv ('contend, plead a case') appears twice—riv rivi—creating an emphatic petition: 'Plead, plead my case!' This is the language of a courtroom or a covenant dispute. The psalmist does not argue their own case but calls upon God to serve as counsel and advocate. This reflects a deep theology: the ultimate arbiter of justice is God, and the psalmist's vindication depends not on human legal systems but on God taking up their cause.

The verb ga'al ('redeem, act as kinsman-redeemer') adds another layer. In ancient Israel, a ga'al was a family member with the legal and financial means to restore a relative who had fallen into debt-slavery or hardship. By invoking ga'al, the psalmist claims a kinship relationship with God and asks God to exercise the rights and responsibilities of a redeemer. Finally, 'revive me according to your promise' echoes the theme of v. 153 but adds theological precision: the revival sought is not mere physical survival but spiritual re-quickening, restoration to covenantal life, according to God's stated word (imrah, 'promise, utterance').

word_study.meaning: To contend, to plead a case, to dispute, to engage in legal proceedings. The doubled form (riv rivi) emphasizes the urgency and centrality of the petition.
word_study.significance: The psalmist positions God as a legal advocate or judge who will argue for the psalmist's vindication against false accusers. This moves the relationship beyond personal piety into the sphere of justice and vindication.

word_study.meaning: To redeem, to act as kinsman-redeemer, to restore, to recover. In Torah law, the ga'al had legal obligation to buy back a relative's property or buy a relative out of slavery. Implies both power and relational obligation.
word_study.significance: By using ga'al, the psalmist asserts that God has both the power to rescue and the relational commitment to do so—God is not merely a judge but a family redeemer with skin in the game.

word_study.meaning: To make alive, to revive, to preserve life, to restore. Can be physical but often carries spiritual meaning—restoration to covenant relationship and vitality.
word_study.significance: To be revived according to God's word is to be restored not just to physical existence but to spiritual aliveness, to full participation in covenant relationship.

word_study.meaning: Word, utterance, promise, saying. Refers to God's spoken or revealed word, especially in the form of command or assurance.
word_study.significance: Revival is calibrated to God's revealed word—not according to human desire or emergency, but according to God's stated purposes and timing.

cross_references.connection: My soul cleaveth unto the dust: quicken thou me according to thy word—the same request for revival according to God's word appears earlier in this psalm, showing the persistent theme.
Boaz recognizes himself as a kinsman-redeemer (ga'al) and enacts that role—illustrating the legal and relational meaning of the term the psalmist invokes of God.
I have redeemed (ga'al) thee, I have called thee by thy name—God's redemptive action toward Israel parallels the psalmist's petition that God redeem them as kinsman-redeemer.
Judge me, O LORD; for I have walked in mine integrity—another petition that God serve as judge and advocate, vindicating the righteous.
Literal modern revelation: 'May thy people, upon whom thou hast bestowed such tokens and signs, be preserved'—the pattern of God as redeemer and preserver continues in Restoration theology.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, the legal system relied heavily on witnesses, oath-taking, and the role of elders as judges. However, access to justice was not always guaranteed to the poor or the persecuted. The psalms frequently invoke God as the ultimate judge and advocate precisely because human legal systems could be corrupted or inaccessible. The concept of ga'al (kinsman-redeemer) comes from family law—the obligation of a relative to rescue a family member in distress. By extending this to God, the psalmist claims that God's relationship to Israel is familial, not merely formal, and that God therefore has binding obligation to intervene.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Jacob 5, the allegory of the olive tree, depicts God as actively laboring to redeem and restore the vineyard (covenant people). God serves as the ultimate husbandman and redeemer, working to restore what has been corrupted, paralleling the psalmist's trust that God will ga'al them.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:69 describes God's role as one who 'shall redeem all the works of his hands'—confirming that God's nature is redemptive and that all who covenant with Him are objects of that redemptive intent.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony depicts God offering covenants of redemption and divine assistance—God becomes the advocate and redeemer of those who enter the covenant. The psalmist's petition mirrors the temple participant's invocation of God's redemptive power.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate kinsman-redeemer (ga'al) and legal advocate. He 'pleads our cause' before the Father (1 John 2:1), serves as our advocate and mediator. His redemption is legal and familial—He is the Son of God and the brother of all humanity, with power and obligation to rescue. His resurrection demonstrates His power to 'revive' not just individuals but all of humanity according to the Father's word.
commentary.application: This verse invites trust that you need not defend yourself alone. In moments when you feel accused, misunderstood, or facing injustice, the psalmist models the practice of bringing your case to God and asking God to be your advocate. This is not passivity but active faith—you state your case to God with honesty, then release the outcome to God's judgment. In covenant practice, this might mean: In workplace conflicts, relationship disputes, or spiritual struggles where you feel falsely accused, take it to God in prayer. State clearly what you believe is true, ask God to vindicate your cause and to revive you according to His word, then wait for God's timing and judgment rather than defending yourself through human means or seeking worldly vindication.

text_kjv: Salvation is far from the wicked: for they seek not thy statutes.

commentary.narrative:
This verse shifts from the psalmist's personal petition to a statement about the fundamental divide between those who seek God and those who do not. The word 'far' (rachok) is key: salvation is not merely withheld from the wicked; it is remote, inaccessible to them. This is not arbitrary punishment but the natural consequence of their refusal. The verse then provides the cause: 'they do not seek your statutes.' The logic is causal and relational: to reject seeking God's decrees is to cut oneself off from the source of salvation.

This verse introduces a theological principle that underlies the entire psalm: the structure of the universe is such that seeking God's word leads to life, while rejecting it leads to alienation from salvation. The wicked are not punished by God arbitrarily; they are separated from salvation by their own choice not to seek it. The Hebrew verb darash ('seek') implies not a casual glance but active pursuit, study, and commitment. Those who do not darash the statutes (huqqim) are those who are not in covenant pursuit of God's way. This verse also provides comfort to the persecuted psalmist: the very people afflicting the psalmist are cut off from salvation by their own refusal to seek God's word. Their temporary power means nothing; they are already excluded from the deepest good.

word_study.meaning: Far, distant, remote; can be spatial or relational. Indicates separation and separation that is profound or insurmountable.
word_study.significance: Salvation is not temporarily withheld from the wicked but is fundamentally distant and inaccessible. The separation is not incidental but structural.

word_study.meaning: Wicked, ungodly, those who act with moral disorder or defiance. In psalmic usage, often refers to those who oppose God's law and persecute the righteous.
word_study.significance: The 'wicked' are not merely those who make mistakes but those characterized by active refusal of God's way. They are defined by their opposition.

word_study.meaning: To seek, to search, to investigate, to inquire, to pursue. Implies active, sustained effort to find something of value.
word_study.significance: Seeking God's statutes is not a passive reception but active pursuit. Those who do not darash God's word are those who have not made the effort to learn and follow.

word_study.meaning: Statutes, decrees, ordinances; fixed, unchanging laws. Emphasize the binding and perpetual character of God's commands.
word_study.significance: The statutes are not suggestions or opinions but fixed decrees. To refuse to seek them is to refuse the ordered structure God has established.

cross_references.connection: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly...but his delight is in the law of the LORD—contrasts the blessed (who seek) with the wicked (who do not seek), paralleling this verse's structure.
There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death—those who do not seek God's statutes follow their own way, which leads away from salvation.
Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find—the principle that seeking produces finding, mirrored negatively: those who do not seek God find neither salvation nor truth.
Blessed are they that keep his testimonies, and that seek him with the whole heart—the blessed are those who actively seek (darash) God's word, the inverse of v. 155's wicked who do not seek.

commentary.historical_context: This verse reflects the ancient Near Eastern understanding of retribution theology: the cosmic order is structured such that following divine law brings blessing while rejecting it brings curse. In Israel's covenant framework, this principle operated both individually and nationally. The psalmist articulates this not as a complaint but as theological assurance: the persecutors may have temporary power, but they are already separated from the ultimate good—salvation—by their own refusal to seek God's way. This would have provided comfort to persecuted believers: your enemies cut themselves off from salvation by their own choice. Their opposition to you is therefore self-destructive.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 41:8 teaches that 'wickedness never was happiness'—the wicked are intrinsically separated from the good by their own moral choices. The Book of Mormon repeatedly shows that those who reject the word of God (refuse to darash) cut themselves off from salvation, even when righteous people offer it to them.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:33 warns that those who reject God's word will 'be cut off from among my people'—salvation is literally and relationaly inaccessible to those who refuse God's statutes.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that only those who make and keep covenants receive exaltation—salvation is contingent on covenant seeking and faithfulness. Those who do not seek (darash) God's ordinances are excluded from the deepest salvific blessings.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is both the source of salvation and its gatekeeper. 'I am the way, the truth, and the life' (John 14:6) means that to reject seeking Christ is to cut oneself off from salvation. Christ's call to 'seek and ye shall find' (Matthew 7:7) is the invitation to pursue Him as the living embodiment of God's word (statutes). The separation of the wicked from salvation is ultimately separation from Christ.
commentary.application: This verse offers perspective during persecution or when facing opposition. Rather than focusing on the power of those who oppose the gospel, you can recognize that they are already cutting themselves off from the greatest good by refusing to seek God's word. This should inspire compassion—they are choosing separation from salvation—and confidence in the long view: those who seek God's statutes find salvation, while those who refuse to seek find themselves increasingly distant from it. In practical terms: Don't be intimidated by those who oppose the faith; recognize that their opposition is self-sabotaging. Instead, invest your energy in seeking (darash) God's word—study scriptures deeply, keep the commandments as stated ordinances (huqqim), and trust that this active pursuit connects you to salvation while separation from it is the fate of those who choose not to seek.

text_kjv: Great are thy tender mercies, O LORD: quicken me according to thy judgments.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 156 concludes the Resh stanza (vv. 153–160) and carries profound theological weight. The psalmist opens with an absolute affirmation: 'Your mercies are great, O LORD.' The word rachamim ('mercies, compassions') refers to God's tender, womb-like compassion—from the root rechem ('womb'). This is not abstract mercy but the visceral, protective compassion of a parent for an offspring. The adjective rabbim ('many, great, abundant') emphasizes both the quantity and the quality of this mercy; it is overwhelming in its sufficiency.

What is remarkable is the context: this affirmation comes after petitions for rescue, assertions that God is near while enemies press close, and the declaration that the wicked cut themselves off from salvation. In other words, the psalmist has faced the worst case—persecution, suffering, exposure to evil—and has not lost faith in God's mercies. This is not naive optimism but tested conviction. The final petition—'revive me according to your judgments'—circles back to the language of v. 154 but adds specificity: the revival sought is not according to the psalmist's preference or timing but according to God's judgments (mishpatim). God's judgments are just and measure-giving; they determine not only what is right but the proper response and remedy. To be revived according to God's judgments is to be restored by God's wisdom and justice, not by human sentiment or the psalmist's emergency.

word_study.meaning: Mercies, compassions, pity; from the root rechem ('womb'). Refers to deep, visceral compassion—the tender care a parent has for a child. Emphasizes emotional and relational engagement, not abstract justice.
word_study.significance: God's response to the psalmist is not duty-bound obligation but deep, maternal compassion. This is the love of the parent who protects the vulnerable. The metaphor suggests that God's mercy is primary and abundant.

word_study.meaning: Many, much, great, abundant; emphasizes quantity, quality, and sufficiency. Suggests that what is great is more than adequate for the need.
word_study.significance: God's mercies are not rationed or barely sufficient; they are abundant and overflowing, more than adequate for any suffering or need.

word_study.meaning: Judgments, ordinances, regulations, decisions. Refers to God's wise determinations about what is right and how situations should be remedied.
word_study.significance: To be revived according to God's judgments is to be restored according to God's righteous wisdom, not according to human preference or emergency. God's judgments measure out justice and restoration.

cross_references.connection: All the paths of the LORD are mercy and truth—God's ways (including His judgments) are fundamentally rooted in mercy and reliability, so being revived according to them is secure.

It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed...his compassions fail not; they are new every morning—affirms that God's rachamim (mercies) are the reason the persecuted survive, mirroring the psalmist's reliance.

I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice—Paul grounds the call to covenant obedience in the foundation of God's rachamim, echoing the psalmist's logic.
Let, I pray thee, thy merciful kindness be for my comfort—another petition in this psalm that God's rachamim sustain and comfort the afflicted.

And this is the gospel which I have given unto you...that by it ye might be judged—Restoration theology affirms that God's judgments operate through divine word and measure out both justice and mercy.

commentary.historical_context: This verse concludes a stanza in which the psalmist has repeatedly asked God to 'see,' 'rescue,' 'plead the cause,' 'redeem,' and 'revive.' These are not passive requests but active invocations of God's covenant power. The affirmation that God's mercies are great responds to ancient Near Eastern anxieties about divine absence or indifference. In that world, gods could be distant, capricious, or indifferent to human suffering. Israel's distinctive claim was that their God is fundamentally compassionate (rachamim)—moved by the suffering of the covenant partner and actively engaged in rescue. The closing affirmation that revival will come 'according to thy judgments' places trust in God's wisdom and timing rather than human demand. This reflects mature faith: not the faith that demands immediate answers but the faith that trusts God's judgment even when relief is delayed.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 3:7 describes Christ's willingness to suffer 'according to the flesh that he might take upon him the sins of his people...that he might bring his people unto salvation'—God's judgments determine the necessity of suffering and the means of redemption, just as the psalmist trusts revival to come according to God's judgments.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:12-13 describes God's word as the law by which all things are governed and judged—'All things are by him, and of him, are governed by his incomparable power.' The psalmist's trust in being revived according to God's judgments aligns with the Restoration understanding of divine governance.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony culminates in the participant receiving blessings according to their faithfulness—not according to their desires but according to God's wise judgment about what each person needs for salvation and exaltation. This is the living enactment of the psalmist's principle.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ embodies both the mercies (rachamim) and the judgments (mishpatim) of God. His compassion for the suffering is limitless—He wept at Lazarus' tomb, healed the sick, forgave the adulterous woman. Yet His judgments are also just—He will judge all people and determine their eternal state according to righteousness. Being revived according to God's judgments in Christ means being saved by a Savior who judges justly but tempers justice with infinite mercy. The resurrection is the ultimate revivification according to God's judgments: all will be restored to life, but according to their deeds.
commentary.application: This verse is the capstone of the Resh stanza: after naming affliction, pleading for rescue, asserting loyalty to God's law, invoking God as advocate, and recognizing the separation of the wicked from salvation, the psalmist returns to fundamental trust. The mercies of God are great. This means: Even if your immediate situation does not improve, the foundation of your life is God's compassion. Even if God's timing is not your timing, God's judgments are wise and will bring the right kind of revival at the right time. In modern covenant life, this means: When you feel desperate for relief or change, anchor yourself in this dual truth: God's mercies are abundant and real, AND God's judgments about how and when to revive you are wise and just. This may require patience, but it prevents you from either despairing (losing faith in the mercies) or demanding (refusing to trust the judgments). Instead, you can pray with intensity while also releasing the outcome to God's wisdom.

text_kjv: I hate and abhor lying: but thy law do I love.

commentary.narrative: This verse opens the final stanza (א-Aleph) of Psalm 119 with a stark antithesis: two verbs of revulsion against one verb of love. The psalmist does not merely dislike falsehood; he hates it with double intensity—using both śānē'tî ("I hate") and va'ata'ēvāh ("I abhor/detest"). This is visceral language, expressing moral recoil at deception. Yet this doubled revulsion toward lying exists in direct proportion to his simple, unqualified love for Torah. The structure of the verse is psychologically astute: the psalmist's horror at falsehood and his devotion to God's instruction are not separate emotions but aspects of the same moral orientation. To love truth is to abhor its opposite. In the context of Psalm 119's narrative arc—where the psalmist has endured opposition, mockery, and persecution—this confession becomes an act of moral defiance. He will not be corrupted by the deceptions of his enemies nor compromised by the seductive logic of those who reject God's law.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verse also articulates a principle central to covenantal faithfulness: integrity of speech and integrity of heart cannot be separated. The psalmist's hatred of lying is not merely an ethical preference but a spiritual discipline. He understands that falsehood fractures the relationship between God and His people. This becomes particularly significant in a psalm that repeatedly positions God's Word as the standard by which all truth is measured. When the psalmist says "thy law do I love," he is expressing that Torah is not a burden imposed externally but a delight embraced internally—the antidote to the poisoning that falsehood introduces into the soul.

word_study.meaning: śânē' (to hate, to reject, to regard with hostility) is a strong verb denoting personal aversion; ta'ab (to abhor, to detest, to regard as abominable) intensifies this with a sense of moral revulsion and physical disgust. Together they create a doubling effect of moral recoil.
word_study.significance: The stacking of two verbs rather than one emphasizes that the psalmist's opposition to falsehood is not mild or theoretical but existential. In Hebrew thought, using two verbs where one would suffice signals intensity and emotional weight. This reflects the covenant principle that God's people must embody His character—and God abhors deception (Prov. 6:16-19).

word_study.meaning: Instruction, teaching, law—derived from the verb yārah (to throw, to direct, to guide). Tôrāh is not merely a legal code but the revealed guidance and direction that God provides to His covenant people.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering uses 'instruction' rather than 'law' to capture the pedagogical and relational dimension of Torah. The psalmist loves it not as an external constraint but as divine wisdom that orients and shapes life. This aligns with the Latter-day Saint understanding of God's word as a lamp unto our feet (D&C 11:4).

word_study.meaning: To love, to choose, to hold dear—a verb expressing deep affection, loyalty, and commitment. Distinct from mere preference, āhab describes covenant love.
word_study.significance: The simplicity of this single verb—placed against the doubled verbs of hate—conveys an intimate, unqualified devotion. The psalmist's love for Torah is personal and whole-hearted, mirroring the love that God commands Israel to give Him (Deuteronomy 6:5).

cross_references.connection: The command to love the LORD with all your heart echoes throughout Psalm 119; here, that love is extended to God's law as the expression of His will. The psalmist models the complete devotion that Moses commanded.

The list of seven things God hates, with 'a lying tongue' and 'he that soweth discord' at the forefront, explains why the psalmist's hatred of falsehood reflects God's own character. Loving truth means aligning with God's moral order.

Earlier in this same psalm, the psalmist declares 'Through thy precepts I get understanding: therefore I hate every false way'—establishing that hatred of falsehood flows naturally from embracing God's instruction.

Laman and Lemuel struggle with God's commandments, while Nephi declares 'I will go and do the things which the Lord hath commanded'; the psalmist's love of Torah reflects the Nephite ideal of willing obedience.
The revelation describes God's word as 'a lamp unto thy feet, and a light unto thy path'—precisely the role Torah plays for the psalmist: not a burden but a guide that illuminates the way.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the concept of divine instruction (tôrāh) was understood as a gift from the gods to establish order (ma'at in Egyptian thought, ḫubur in Akkadian thought). The psalmist's confession of love for God's law would have been audacious in a polytheistic context—claiming that a single God's instruction is sufficient and supremely valuable. The explicit rejection of falsehood also echoes the covenant renewal ceremonies of Israel, where people affirmed their commitment to God's word while renouncing false gods and false practices. In Deuteronomic thought (which influenced the composition of many psalms), loving God's law was the sign of covenant loyalty.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 32 compares the word of God to a seed that grows within the heart—the psalmist's love for Torah produces this same organic, internal growth. Also, 2 Nephi 31:20 emphasizes that the righteous 'endure to the end' by following God's word, paralleling the psalmist's steadfast devotion despite opposition.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 19:26-27 instructs that 'I have sent my everlasting covenant into the world' and that those who receive it 'shall gain all things.' The psalmist's love of Torah prefigures the Restoration understanding that God's word is an eternal covenant, not a temporary instruction.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The psalmist's love of God's testimonies and precepts reflects the temple principle of covenant-making—the willingness to enter into binding relationship with God and internalize His law. This love is enacted in the temple through the making and keeping of sacred covenants.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the fullness of the Law (D&C 45:5, referencing Romans 10:4). The psalmist's hatred of falsehood and love of truth prefigures Christ, who declares 'I am the way, the truth, and the life' (John 14:6). Jesus embodies perfect alignment with God's instruction—He never deviated from the path His Father set before Him. The psalmist's dual emotional stance (hatred of lies, love of truth) finds its ultimate expression in Christ's incarnational witness to truth.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse asks: What do you hate? What do you love? The psalmist's doubled revulsion at falsehood challenges us to examine whether we are truly repulsed by deception—in ourselves, in our media consumption, in our choices. Do we lie in little ways? Do we tolerate falsehood when it serves our purposes? Conversely, the simplicity of 'thy law do I love' invites us to consider whether we genuinely love God's word or merely respect it intellectually. Real love for the scriptures changes how we read them, how we live them, and how we teach them to our families. In an age of information overload and competing narratives, the psalmist's stance offers clarity: cultivate a hatred of falsehood sharp enough to wound you morally when you encounter it (or practice it), and cultivate a love for God's instruction deep enough to be your primary emotional and spiritual reality.

text_kjv: Seven times a day do I praise thee because of thy righteous judgments.

commentary.narrative: The number seven in Hebrew thought often signifies completeness, fullness, or a divinely ordered totality—not necessarily a literal count but a theological statement about the comprehensiveness of the psalmist's devotion. Seven times a day means praise that covers the whole day, from beginning to end, in every circumstance. This verse shifts from the previous moral stance (hating falsehood) to a rhythmic practice (praising God). The psalmist commits to a structured, repeated discipline of praise that is not dependent on his emotions or circumstances but ordered by a principle—that God's righteous judgments deserve continuous, systematic acknowledgment. The phrase "because of thy righteous judgments" (עַל מִשְׁפְּטֵי צִדְקֶךָ) is crucial: the psalmist praises not in spite of God's judgments but because of them. Even when God's judgments are hard, mysterious, or costly to the psalmist (as much of Psalm 119 suggests), he affirms their righteousness. This is not naive optimism but theological conviction rooted in the psalm's earlier declarations about God's character.
commentary.narrative_continued: In the context of a psalm composed by someone suffering affliction and opposition (as Psalm 119 repeatedly attests), this confession of seven-times-daily praise is radical. It means the psalmist does not make his praise contingent on his circumstances. The structure of praise—repeating it seven times daily—resembles the discipline of Jewish prayer practice (which developed into the system of daily services in later rabbinical Judaism, though we should not assume such a formal system existed at the psalm's composition). The psalmist is arguing that regular, rhythmic engagement with God's righteous judgments actually transforms one's entire day, fragmenting it into moments of recognition and acknowledgment. This transforms suffering from meaningless pain into an arena where God's character is continuously revealed and vindicated.

word_study.meaning: The number seven; in Hebrew cosmology, associated with completion, wholeness, and divine order (seven days of creation, seven years in sabbatical cycles, seven times seven in jubilee calculations). In some contexts, 'seven times' means 'repeatedly' or 'continually' rather than literally seven instances.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering and the translator notes suggest that 'seven times' may be read both literally (a structured daily practice) and theologically (praise that encompasses totality). This flexibility honors the Hebrew poetic tradition where numbers often carry symbolic weight. For a Latter-day Saint reader, seven also resonates with temple symbolism and the principle of covenantal order.

word_study.meaning: To praise, to sing praise, to celebrate publicly. From hallal (to shine, to be bright, to boast)—praise that makes something shine or become prominent. The reflexive form suggests that the subject makes himself a vessel of praise.
word_study.significance: Praise is not passive appreciation but active, public testimony. The psalmist does not merely feel grateful; he gives voice to that gratitude in a way that declares God's character.

word_study.meaning: Mishpat (judgment, decree, ordinance, justice) paired with tsedaqah (righteousness, justice, vindication). God's mishpetim are tsedaqim—they are inherently just, aligned with the moral order, and ultimately vindicate God's character.
word_study.significance: The psalmist does not praise God's power in isolation but specifically his righteous character as expressed in judgment. This matters because it means the psalmist's praise is rooted not in fear of an arbitrary power but in confidence that God acts justly. This is covenant language—the psalmist trusts that God's judgments serve the covenant relationship.

cross_references.connection: 'I will praise thee with uprightness of heart, when I shall have learned thy righteous judgments'—establishing that learning God's justice and praising Him are inseparable acts throughout the psalm.

Daniel prayed 'three times a day' despite the king's decree, modeling the principle that regular, structured prayer and praise transcend circumstantial opposition—similar to the psalmist's seven-times-daily practice.

Paul commands 'Rejoice in the Lord alway...In every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God'—the New Testament crystallization of the psalmist's principle that praise and petition should structure every day.

The revelation commands that 'in nothing doth man offend God...but those who confess his name before the world'—relating to how the psalmist's public praise of God's righteous judgments constitutes a form of confession and covenant loyalty.

Ammon declares 'I glory in my Jesus' and repeatedly affirms God's goodness despite hardship, reflecting the same pattern of praise rooted in confidence in divine righteousness regardless of circumstance.

commentary.historical_context: The Deuteronomic tradition emphasized that Israel's proper response to God's law was not merely obedience but joyful celebration. The festival system (Passover, Shavuot, Sukkot) were structured as occasions for communal praise and testimony. The structure of 'seven times a day' may reflect an idealized liturgical practice—perhaps connected to the times of prayer that would later develop in Jewish tradition (though we should be cautious about reading later rabbinic practice back into the psalmist's era). In any case, the verse reflects a theology in which encountering God's word should generate repeated, habitual praise throughout the day. This contrasts with a merely transactional view of religion in which one fulfills obligations and moves on; instead, the psalmist envisions a life saturated with the acknowledgment of God's character.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 4:15-35 records Nephi's personal prayer and meditation, in which he repeatedly affirms God's goodness despite his sufferings. Like the psalmist, Nephi structures his spiritual life around regular acknowledgment of God's character. Also, Alma 34:26-27 teaches that one should 'pour out thy soul' to God 'in thy closets, and thy secret places, and in thy wilderness'—suggesting that the righteous make prayer and praise a regular, structured part of their entire day.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 109:16 records the Kirtland Temple dedication prayer: 'That all people may know and feel thy power'—the psalmist's seven-times-daily praise is a personal enactment of this principle, allowing him to feel and demonstrate God's righteous power. D&C 88:63 teaches 'Draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you'—the structured practice of regular praise is how the psalmist draws near to God throughout the day.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is a place of continuous praise and worship—even when the building is closed, its purpose is to host endless cycles of ordinances and prayers. The psalmist's seven-times-daily praise mirrors this principle of continuous, structured worship. In Latter-day Saint theology, the temple embodies the righteousness that the psalmist celebrates—God's judgment made manifest in sacred space and covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ practiced continual prayer and praise despite His suffering and approaching crucifixion (Luke 22:41-44). He exemplified the principle that praise and submission to God's righteous judgments transcend circumstance. The Book of Mormon records that Christ's resurrection validated His submission to the Father's judgment (Alma 34:15), and in the Restoration, we understand that Christ's entire life was characterized by praise of His Father's righteousness—'not my will, but thine, be done' (Luke 22:42).
commentary.application: This verse invites a discipline: What if you structured your day around seven moments of praise? Not seven formal prayers necessarily, but seven moments—morning, midday transitions, evening—where you pause to acknowledge God's righteous character. In our age of fragmentation and complaint, this practice becomes countercultural. It does not require that your circumstances change; it requires that you change your attentional focus. Consider: Do I praise God only when things go well, or do I maintain rhythmic acknowledgment of His justice even when His judgments are hard to understand? The psalmist suggests that the latter is possible, and that it transforms the whole day. Try it: mark seven moments today when you will pause to affirm one thing God has done that you recognize as righteous, even if other things remain mysterious. This small discipline accumulates into the 'great peace' described in the next verse.

text_kjv: Great peace have they which love thy law: and nothing shall offend them.

commentary.narrative: Verse 165 is the spiritual culmination of the entire Aleph stanza and one of the most profound statements in all of scripture about the relationship between covenantal fidelity and inner peace. The Hebrew shalom rav (שָׁלוֹם רָב) does not mean the absence of conflict—as the entire Psalm 119 makes abundantly clear, the psalmist faces actual persecution, lies spoken against him, and genuine suffering. Instead, shalom rav describes a comprehensive wholeness, a deep stability, a sense of rightness and integration that comes from knowing one's life is aligned with ultimate reality (God's law). This peace is not circumstantial but existential—it is the peace of someone whose foundation is unmoved even when the surface of life is turbulent. The second clause—"nothing shall offend them" (ve'ein lamo mikhshol)—is equally significant. The word mikhshol (stumbling block) refers not to minor irritations but to fundamental disorientation. A person without God's law stumbles; they don't know which way leads forward. A person who loves Torah doesn't have stumbling blocks because their path is lit.
commentary.narrative_continued: The timing of this verse is remarkable: it comes immediately after the psalmist has just declared his commitment to hate falsehood (v. 163), love God's law (v. 163), and practice seven-times-daily praise (v. 164). In other words, the peace described here is not a gift given to passive believers but a reality that emerges from active moral alignment, continuous discipline, and the practice of praise. This peace is promised not to everyone but specifically to "they which love thy law"—those who have deliberately oriented their entire lives around God's instruction. The psalmist is not making a conditional promise ("if you love God's law, then you will never suffer") but rather a promise about the quality of one's internal state ("if you love God's law, then even in suffering, you will have peace and clarity"). This aligns perfectly with later New Testament teaching: 'And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and your minds through Christ Jesus' (Philippians 4:7).

word_study.meaning: Shalom (from shalem, 'to be complete, whole, at peace') means much more than the absence of war; it describes completeness, wholeness, harmony, well-being, flourishing. Rav means 'great, abundant, much.' Together, shalom rav is overwhelming, abundant peace—peace that overflows and fills the person.
word_study.significance: As The Covenant Rendering notes, shalom is one of the richest words in Hebrew theology. It reflects the Hebrew cosmological understanding that reality is fundamentally integrated and harmonious when aligned with God's order—shalom is what it feels like to be in sync with that order. This is not mere happiness or positive emotion but the deep rightness of being whole.

word_study.meaning: Those who love, those who are devoted to—the plural participle form emphasizing a class or group characterized by this devotion. Not a momentary feeling but an ongoing, constitutive relationship.
word_study.significance: The psalmist identifies a specific category of people—not everyone, but those who actively love God's law—and promises that this group will experience shalom. This is both encouraging and demanding: peace is available but requires orientation toward Torah.

word_study.term_english: nothing causes them to stumble (ve'ein lamo mikhshol)
word_study.meaning: Mikhshol (from kashal, 'to stumble, to fall, to be ruined') literally means a stumbling block—an obstacle that causes one to fall. The phrase 'there is no stumbling block for them' means they are not fundamentally lost or disoriented.
word_study.significance: This directly addresses the anxiety of the person seeking wisdom: Will I know the right path? Will I lose my way? The promise is that those who love God's law will not have their footing fundamentally knocked out from under them. They may face trials, but they won't be lost.

cross_references.connection: 'Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee'—Isaiah articulates the same principle as the psalmist: peace comes from fixing one's mind on God rather than on circumstances.

'And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and your minds through Christ Jesus'—Paul applies the psalmist's principle through the lens of Christ, promising that active pursuit of righteousness generates supernatural peace.

'Happy is the man that findeth wisdom...Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace'—Wisdom literature echoes the psalmist's teaching that alignment with God's truth (law/wisdom) produces peace and a clear path.

'Wherefore, I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another; for he that forgiveth his brother the most shall be the greatest among you'—the Restoration emphasizes that peace comes through alignment with God's principles, which the psalmist models.
Alma teaches that the word of God 'swelleth up' the soul and produces 'enlightening of the mind'—describing the same peace and clarity that the psalmist attributes to loving God's law.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern thought, the concept parallel to shalom was Egyptian ma'at (order, justice, truth) and Mesopotamian concepts of divine orderliness. A person who lived according to divine order was understood to be in harmony with the cosmos itself. The psalmist's claim that those who love God's law experience shalom rav reflects this broader ancient understanding that morality and well-being are not separate domains—they are integrated. To act justly and to love truth is to align oneself with the fundamental structure of reality. Moreover, the concept of stumbling blocks (mikhshol) draws on ancient Near Eastern imagery of journeys, warfare, and navigation—a person without guidance quite literally didn't know which way to go in an age without maps or clear roads. God's law provides the equivalent of a lamp in darkness (as Psalm 119:105 says).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 32 describes the growth of faith in the heart as producing "swelling motions" and "enlarge[ment]"—describing the same kind of peace and wholeness that the psalmist attributes to loving God's law. Also, 2 Nephi 2:25 teaches that 'men are, that they might have joy'—the psalmist's shalom is the experiencing of that joy through covenantal alignment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 6:23 and similar revelations repeatedly promise that those who follow God's word will have peace: 'Verily, verily, I say unto you, as I said unto my disciples, where two or three are gathered together in my name, as touching one thing and agree as touching that one thing which they shall ask, it shall be done for them'—the principle is that alignment with God's will produces the peace of answered prayer.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is understood as a place of peace precisely because it embodies perfect alignment with God's law and covenant. The endowment ceremony walks the participant through the covenantal path and ends in the celestial room—a space of peace and wholeness. The psalmist describes an interiorized version of this: carrying the temple principle—alignment with God's law—into one's entire life produces the peace of wholeness.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the embodiment of shalom—He is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). His entire life exemplified perfect alignment with God's law, and He repeatedly promised peace to His disciples: 'Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you' (John 14:27). The psalmist's promise that those who love God's law will experience great peace finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ, who is the Law made flesh and who offers peace not as the world gives (circumstantially) but as a transformation of the soul.
commentary.application: Test this promise in your own life: When you are experiencing genuine peace—not happiness (which can be circumstantial) but deep, abiding peace—what has produced it? Often it is moments when you feel your life is aligned with something larger and truer than yourself, when you're living according to principle rather than impulse, when you've oriented yourself around God's word rather than around what others think. Conversely, when you experience the opposite—anxiety, being lost, a sense of fundamental disorientation—where has that come from? The psalmist suggests that the antidote is not to fix your circumstances but to deepen your love for God's law. This doesn't mean circumstances won't be hard; it means you will experience a peace beneath the hardship. In our contemporary context, where anxiety and depression are epidemic, this verse suggests that part of the cure is not merely therapy or medication (which may have their place) but reorientation around ultimate meaning—which, for Latter-day Saints, means deeper engagement with scripture and covenant. Try this: when you feel anxiety rising, instead of immediately trying to solve the problem, pause and ask yourself: Am I currently oriented toward God's law? Is my mind fixed on His principles? Often, the answer will reveal that you've drifted into focusing on the obstacle rather than on the path. Reset your orientation—read a relevant scripture, offer a prayer of alignment—and notice how the quality of your inner state shifts.

text_kjv: LORD, I have hoped for thy salvation, and done thy commandments.

commentary.narrative: This verse introduces a new element into the psalmist's testimony: hope (śiberti, from the verb sābar, 'to wait, to expect, to hope'). The psalmist is not waiting passively for God to act; instead, the verse shows that hope and obedience are simultaneous and mutually reinforcing. "I have hoped for thy salvation, and done thy commandments"—these are not sequential (first hope, then obey) but concurrent. The psalmist's hope is not naive optimism but is grounded in active obedience. This reflects a deeper Hebrew understanding of hope that differs from English intuition: in English, hope often feels passive ('I hope things will get better'), whereas in Hebrew, sābar frequently implies an active waiting that includes continued faithfulness. The grammatical structure is also significant. The psalmist addresses God directly—"LORD" (yhwh, יהוה)—personalizing the relationship. He is not theorizing about salvation in the abstract but declaring his own particular stance toward God in his particular circumstances.
commentary.narrative_continued: The reference to God's salvation (yeshū'ātekha) invokes deliverance, rescue, and restoration. In the context of Psalm 119, where the psalmist faces opposition, lies, and affliction, salvation means God's vindication of the righteous and judgment against the wicked. But the crucial point is this: the psalmist's hope in that salvation does not paralyze him or excuse him from obedience. Instead, it empowers him to "do thy commandments." This anticipates a New Testament principle: faith without works is dead (James 2:26). The psalmist demonstrates that hope and obedience are the two sides of a single coin—they cannot be separated. A person who truly hopes in God's salvation will inevitably be motivated to keep His commandments; conversely, a person keeping God's commandments is expressing confidence that His salvation is real and will come.

word_study.meaning: From sābar (to wait, to look forward to, to expect, to hope). The verb often implies a hopeful expectation that involves continued faithfulness and endurance, not mere wishful thinking.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering chooses 'hope' rather than a more passive term, emphasizing that this is active trust. In Hebrew wisdom literature, hope is often paired with waiting and endurance; it's a virtue that sustains the righteous through difficulty.

word_study.meaning: From yāsha' (to save, to deliver, to rescue, to make safe). Salvation in Hebrew is not merely spiritual salvation but comprehensive deliverance and vindication—God acting to rescue and restore His people.
word_study.significance: For the psalmist, hoping in God's salvation means trusting that God will ultimately act to vindicate the righteous and judge the wicked. This is not abstract theology but concrete trust that God will intervene in history.

word_study.meaning: From 'āsāh (to do, to make, to act, to accomplish). The simple past form emphasizes completed action—not 'I am trying to do' but 'I have done.'
word_study.significance: The psalmist's claim is bold: despite persecution and opposition, he has kept God's commandments. This is not boasting but testimony—evidence that his hope is not in his own strength but in God's character, which motivates obedience.

word_study.meaning: From mitzvāh (commandment, directive, instruction). These are God's specific directives—not abstract principles but concrete commands that require action.
word_study.significance: The plural form emphasizes the totality of God's will; the psalmist is not selectively obeying but committing to the whole body of God's commandments.

cross_references.connection: 'I cried with my whole heart; hear me, O LORD: I will keep thy statutes'—earlier in Psalm 119, the psalmist models the same combination of petition (crying out) and commitment to obedience.
'For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also'—the New Testament explicates the principle the psalmist embodies: hope/faith and obedience are inseparable.
'Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen'—the psalmist's hope is this kind of substantive, activating faith that expresses itself in obedience.

'I will go and do the things which the Lord hath commanded, for I know that the Lord giveth no commandments unto the children of men save he shall prepare a way for them that they may accomplish the thing which he commandeth them'—Nephi exemplifies the psalmist's principle: obedience is empowered by confidence in God's salvation/deliverance.

'And I, the Lord, am bound when ye do what I say; but when ye do not what I say, ye have no promise'—the revelation emphasizes that hope in God's promises and obedience to His commandments are bound together.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Israelite covenant tradition, hope (tiqwāh or related concepts) was always tied to the covenant relationship. To hope in God's salvation was to trust that He would keep His covenant promises—promises made to Abraham and reinforced through Moses and the prophets. The psalmist's dual affirmation of hope and obedience would have resonated with Deuteronomic theology (influential in shaping the Psalter), which emphasized that covenant blessing flows from covenant fidelity. The historical context of Psalm 119 suggests a time when God's people faced opposition—possibly exile, persecution, or foreign domination—when hope and obedience were most tested. In such a context, the psalmist's testimony is powerful: "Even now, when salvation seems distant and opposition is present, I continue to hope in God and obey His commandments."

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 31:20 teaches: 'Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life'—the psalmist's twin commitment to hope and obedience is exactly what Nephi describes as the path to eternal life.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 58:26-29 teaches that those who keep God's commandments shall have forgiveness and blessing: 'For all who will have a blessing at my hands shall abide the law which was appointed for that blessing'—tying God's salvation/blessing directly to obedience, just as the psalmist does.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenants structure the participant's journey as a progression in understanding and commitment—exactly mirroring the psalmist's combination of hope and obedience. One makes covenants (expressing obedience) while moving toward the celestial room (expressing hope in exaltation). The endowment ceremony teaches that participation in God's salvation (exaltation) flows from covenantal obedience.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ perfectly embodies the integration of hope and obedience. He declares 'I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me' (John 6:38), expressing absolute obedience grounded in hope in the Father's plan. His entire redemptive mission was animated by faith in God's salvation—faith that sustained Him through suffering and sustained His disciples through their doubt. The psalmist's promise that God's salvation will come is ultimately fulfilled in Christ's resurrection and glorification.
commentary.application: This verse challenges a common modern assumption that hope is passive—something we do when we're waiting for others to fix things. The psalmist and the gospel both teach active hope: genuine trust in God's salvation is inseparable from immediate obedience to His commandments. Where in your life are you hoping passively rather than actively? Are you hoping God will make you healthier while ignoring His commandments about physical care? Hoping He'll bless your marriage while neglecting to work on honesty and kindness? Hoping He'll prosper you while avoiding honest work? The psalmist's formula is simple and demanding: hope in His salvation, and do His commandments, right now, in this moment. This is how you test whether your hope is real. Additionally, consider the reverse: What commandments is God asking you to keep right now? Your willingness to obey them, despite the difficulty or the uncertainty of outcome, is your most powerful way of expressing hope in His salvation. That obedience is not payment for His blessing; rather, obedience is the way your hope becomes visible and real.

text_kjv: My soul hath kept thy testimonies; and I love them exceedingly.

commentary.narrative: Verse 167 moves from the psalmist's external actions (doing commandments) to the interior disposition of his soul (nephesh—his deepest self, his vital essence). "My soul hath kept thy testimonies" uses the past tense to emphasize that this is not merely aspirational but an accomplished reality. The psalmist's deepest self, his most intimate consciousness, has been devoted to preserving and protecting God's testimonies (eduyot—records of God's acts, covenants, and truth). The testimonies are not burdensome obligations but treasures to be kept and guarded. The second clause—"and I love them exceedingly" (me'od—'greatly, intensely, exceedingly')—emphasizes that this is not mere dutiful compliance but passionate devotion. The psalmist's soul does not merely obey God's testimonies; it loves them with intensity. This is the deepest level of spiritual maturity the psalm has described: the transformation of the will so that one delights in God's law not because one must but because one genuinely loves it.
commentary.narrative_continued: The progression through these final verses is striking. In verse 163, the psalmist hates falsehood and loves the law. In verse 164, he practices daily praise. In verse 165, he experiences the resulting peace. In verse 166, he combines hope with obedience. Now in verse 167, he testifies that his soul—his deepest self—has internalized these commitments so thoroughly that he loves God's testimonies not from duty but from the heart. This represents the fulfillment of what Moses commanded: 'Thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul' (Deuteronomy 6:5). The psalmist has not merely learned God's law intellectually or kept it behaviorally; he has allowed it to transform his soul so that what he once obeyed from duty has become the object of his love.

word_study.meaning: Soul, self, life-force, consciousness, appetite, desire. In Hebrew thought, nephesh is not merely the spiritual component (as opposed to body) but the whole integrated being—what makes a person alive and conscious.
word_study.significance: When the psalmist says 'My soul hath kept thy testimonies,' he is claiming that his deepest, most vital self is devoted to God's testimonies. This is not a superficial or external obedience but a transformation of the core self.

word_study.meaning: From shāmar (to keep, to guard, to protect, to watch over, to preserve). The verb suggests not just following rules but actively preserving and protecting something precious.
word_study.significance: The psalmist's soul doesn't merely obey God's testimonies; it guards and protects them as something treasured. This echoes the command to 'keep thy heart with all diligence' (Proverbs 4:23).

word_study.meaning: From 'ēd (witness, testimony). The plural eduyot refers to God's testimonies—records of His acts, His covenant, His truth that bear witness to His character.
word_study.significance: Throughout Psalm 119, eduyot and other terms for God's word (Torah, mitzvot, piqqudim, mishpatim) are used almost interchangeably, emphasizing that all of God's revealed word is testimony to His character and purposes.

word_study.meaning: Me'od means greatly, intensely, exceedingly—it amplifies the verb 'love' to emphasize passionate, overwhelming affection.
word_study.significance: The psalmist does not merely love God's testimonies adequately or appropriately; he loves them with superlative intensity. This is not restrained emotion but exuberant devotion.

cross_references.connection: 'And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might'—the psalmist's love of God's testimonies is the outworking of this foundational command.
'But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night'—the righteous person's passionate love for God's law is the psalmist's exemplar.
'Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life'—the psalmist's testimony that his soul keeps God's testimonies is the fulfillment of this Proverb.
'And now I, Nephi, write more of the words of Isaiah, for my soul delighteth in his words'—Nephi expresses the same passionate love for God's word that the psalmist describes.

'And now, verily I say unto thee, put your trust in that Spirit which leadeth to do good'—the revelation emphasizes that one's soul (one's deepest self) should be devoted to following God's spirit and His truth.

commentary.historical_context: In Deuteronomic and prophetic theology, the keeping of testimonies involved not merely individual obedience but the preservation of God's covenantal memory within Israel's collective consciousness. When the psalmist speaks of his soul keeping God's testimonies, he is participating in Israel's larger calling to preserve and transmit God's truth across generations. The testimonies that the psalmist keeps are the accumulated revelation of God—the covenant with Abraham, the law given at Sinai, the prophetic warnings and promises. To love these testimonies exceedingly was to refuse the spiritual amnesia that plagued Israel in times of unfaithfulness.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 32 teaches that the word becomes 'delicious' and produces growth and expansion in the soul—exactly the kind of deep love for God's word that the psalmist describes. Also, 1 Nephi 1:1 records that Nephi 'was born of goodly parents' and 'was taught somewhat in all the learning of my father,' indicating that the family's love for God's word (their testimonies) shaped his soul from childhood.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 6:20 teaches: 'Yea, behold, I will tell you in your mind and in your heart, by the Holy Ghost, which shall come upon you and which shall dwell in your heart'—this describes the interior transformation that the psalmist testifies to: the soul's alignment with God's truth.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment is designed to inscribe God's testimonies upon the soul—to move beyond intellectual understanding to a transformation of one's deepest self. The endowment participant, like the psalmist, enters with knowledge but hopefully exits having experienced a change in soul-love for God's covenants.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's love for God the Father's testimonies and purposes was absolutely exceeding—it consumed His entire being. 'I must be about my Father's business' (Luke 2:49) and 'Not my will, but thine, be done' (Luke 22:42) express the same soul-level devotion that the psalmist describes. Moreover, Christ is the embodiment of all God's testimonies—He is the living testimony of God's truth, justice, and love.
commentary.application: The trajectory of these final verses is significant: from doing commandments (v. 166) to the soul's love (v. 167). This suggests that spiritual maturity involves a transformation of desire. Ask yourself: Do I keep God's commandments from external pressure or internal love?
