word_study.significance: The repetition of this word throughout Psalm 136 (26 times in 26 verses) emphasizes that every act of power and judgment enumerated is, fundamentally, an expression of God's chesed. This reframes the Exodus—which could be read as judgment on Egypt—as mercy toward Israel. God's faithfulness endures not because Israel deserves it, but because God has bound Himself to them in covenant.

cross_references.connection: The actual account of God dividing the sea: 'And Moses stretched out his hand over the sea; and the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night, and made the sea dry land.' This is the historical event to which Psalm 136:13 testifies.

The Song of the Sea, Israel's immediate response to the splitting of the waters: 'I will sing unto the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously: the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea.' The psalmist recalls the same event with the same tone of triumphant gratitude.
The parallel psalm immediately preceding Psalm 136 in the psalter, which also recounts the Exodus and the splitting of the sea. Psalm 136 expands and emphasizes the refrain of God's enduring mercy.

Another recitation of the Exodus in the context of covenant remembrance: 'And thou didst divide the sea before them, so that they went through the midst of the sea on the dry land.' The splitting of the sea is a recurring touchstone in Israel's historical faith.

Paul typologically reads the sea-crossing as a prefigurement of Christian baptism and covenant entry: 'Moreover, brethren, I would not that ye should be ignorant, how that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea.' The sea becomes a type of passage into covenant.

commentary.historical_context: The Sea of Reeds crossing would have occurred in the Late Bronze Age (c. 13th century BCE), likely in the Nile Delta region where marshes, papyrus reeds, and seasonal flooding created conditions that could be dramatically altered by wind and tide. Ancient Near Eastern accounts describe similar deliverance stories—Ugaritic, Hittite, and Egyptian texts contain motifs of god-mediated crossing and the defeat of enemies in waters. What distinguishes the biblical account is not merely the divine action but its purpose: God does not split the waters for national glory alone, but for covenant purposes. The 'mighty acts of the Lord' in ancient Near Eastern rhetoric typically celebrate royal or divine power; the biblical psalmist frames this as an act of steadfast love (chesed) toward a liberated people.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Lehi's flight from Jerusalem parallels Israel's exodus from Egypt in structure and typology. Both involve God's deliverance of a covenant people through wilderness, both are marked by divine guidance (pillar of fire for Israel; Liahona for Lehi's family). Nephi explicitly draws this connection: 'And he said unto me: These last records, which thou hast seen among the Nephites, shall make known to all kindreds, tongues, and nations, that these things are true' (1 Nephi 19:21). The exodus pattern becomes the template for all covenant deliverance in Restoration theology.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The splitting of the sea presages the parting of the veil and the opening of celestial glory in latter-day revelation. D&C 88:68 speaks of God's power in opening ways: 'Draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you; seek me diligently and ye shall find me.' The miraculous opening of pathways—whether waters, mountains, or the heavens themselves—becomes a symbol of God's responsive grace to those who covenant with Him.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The crossing of the Sea of Reeds on dry land mirrors the passage through the waters of baptism as a form of covenant entry. In the temple, the progression from the world, through waters of baptism (represented in temple fonts), into the covenant path, parallels Israel's passage from Egypt through the sea into the wilderness of covenant formation. Both involve death to the old state and resurrection into a new covenant identity.

commentary.christological_typology: The splitting of the Sea of Reeds prefigures Christ's passage through death and resurrection. As Israel passed through the sea on dry land—alive, preserved, passing through what should have been death—Christ passes through death and emerges to resurrection, opening a way for His people to follow. The Apostle Paul develops this typology directly in 1 Corinthians 10:1-2, linking the sea-crossing to baptism into Christ. The miraculous opening of the waters becomes a figure of the 'narrow way' Christ opens through death into life eternal.
commentary.application: In modern covenant life, Psalm 136:13 invites us to remember our own 'exodus moments'—the times when God has divided the obstacles before us, opened ways that seemed impossible, and delivered us from bondage (whether literal or spiritual). The refrain 'for his mercy endureth for ever' is not abstract; it connects every personal deliverance to God's faithfulness. When we face our own 'Red Seas'—overwhelming challenges that seem to block our forward movement in discipleship—we are invited to recall that the God who split the sea has not lost power. The psalmist's repeated testimony teaches us to cultivate a habit of recognizing and naming God's steadfast love in our histories. Do we rehearse our own exodus narratives? Do we see our conversions, our healings, our rescues from sin as moments of God's chesed? This verse calls us to that recollection and gratitude.

text_kjv: And made Israel to pass through the midst of it: for his mercy endureth for ever:

commentary.narrative: Psalm 136:14 shifts from the splitting of the waters to the actual passage—from the miracle itself to its purpose. God did not split the sea merely to display power; He split it so that Israel could pass through. This verse emphasizes divine agency and intention: 'He made Israel pass through'—the people did not swim, did not wade, did not find a natural ford. God caused them to cross. The hiphil verb he'evir ('He caused to pass through') places the entire action under God's control. Israel's role was to trust and obey; God's role was to accomplish the passage.
commentary.narrative_continued: The prepositional phrase 'through the midst of it' (be-tokho) evokes a specific, almost visceral image: Israel walking in the center of the divided sea, surrounded by walls of water on both sides. This positioning is crucial to understanding the miracle. Israel was not escaping along the periphery or finding a natural shallow crossing; they were moving through the heart of the sea itself, dependent entirely on God's power to hold back the waters. The Covenant Rendering captures this by emphasizing 'the middle of it'—the heart, the most vulnerable place, made safe only by divine action. Every step was an act of faith because every step was surrounded by the evidence of God's immediate presence and power.

word_study.meaning: To cause to pass through, to bring across. The hiphil form emphasizes causative action—God is the agent who brings about the passage. Not 'Israel passed' but 'God caused Israel to pass.'
word_study.significance: This grammatical form is theologically significant. It removes any ambiguity about the source of the deliverance. Israel did not accomplish this through human resourcefulness, courage, or swimming ability. God's action is total and intentional. In Restoration theology, this emphasizes God's role as the active agent in salvation—we are 'saved by grace, not of ourselves.'

word_study.meaning: The middle, the interior, the central part. From the root meaning 'to be in the middle.' This term emphasizes position within a larger space.
word_study.significance: By placing Israel 'in the midst' of the sea, the psalmist stresses the completeness of the miracle and the absolute dependence of the people on God. They were not on the edges, where one might imagine natural causes at work; they were in the heart of the sea itself, where only divine power could explain their safety.

cross_references.connection: The moment when the waters return upon the Egyptians: 'And the LORD said unto Moses, Stretch out thine hand over the sea, that the waters may come again upon the Egyptians, upon their chariots, and upon their horsemen.' Verse 14 alludes to the successful passage that verses 14-29 describe.

A second crossing of waters (the Jordan) that echoes the Sea of Reeds: 'That the waters which came down from above stood and rose up upon an heap very far from the city Adam...and all Israel passed over on dry ground.' The pattern of miraculous passage is repeated in Joshua.

God's power over waters as a sign of salvation: 'Thus saith the LORD, which maketh a way in the sea, and a path in the mighty waters; Which bringeth forth the chariot and horse, the army and the power; they shall lie down together, they shall not rise: they are extinct, they are quenched as tow.' The same motif in prophetic form.

Alma the Younger's recollection of deliverance through the wilderness: 'And now behold, I say unto you that neither have the children of men ceased to dwindle in unbelief from that day forward even until now.' The wilderness passage as a place of God's guidance toward covenant formation.

Christ as the agent of salvation: 'And verily I say unto you, that it is my will that thou shouldst hasten in the work of translation...for thou hast been faithful over a few things; behold, I will make thee ruler over many things.' The language of God 'causing' passage into greater covenant responsibilities.

commentary.historical_context: The mechanism of the sea-crossing has been debated by scholars for centuries. Some propose wind-driven tidal movements in the Nile Delta that could lower water levels; others point to tsunamis or underwater earthquakes. However, from the ancient Israelite perspective, such discussions would have missed the point. The miracle was not whether a natural explanation existed but that God caused Israel to cross at precisely the right moment, in precisely the right way, for their deliverance and Egypt's judgment. Ancient Near Eastern literature (Ugaritic texts, Egyptian accounts) does not typically emphasize human passage through divine power in the same way; the Israelite account makes God's intentional action toward a specific people central. This reflects the covenantal theology unique to Israel—God's acts are not impersonal displays of cosmic power but personal acts of loyalty to His chosen people.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Lehi's journey through the wilderness is guided by the Liahona, a device that works according to faith—'if ye will have faith ye shall prosper' (Alma 37:40). The Liahona guides the family through the midst of the wilderness much as God guided Israel through the midst of the sea. Both require faith, both place the covenant people in the heart of danger, both result in the formation of a new covenant community.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 82:14 speaks of God's role in covenant deliverance: 'I, the Lord, am bound when ye do what I say; but when ye do not what I say, ye have no promise.' The principle underlying verse 14 is covenant reciprocity—God causes passage for those in covenant with Him. He makes a way through otherwise impassable terrain or water.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The passage through waters in the temple, specifically the baptismal font and the passing through successive veils, mirrors Israel's passage through the midst of the sea. Each passage represents movement from one state of covenantal understanding to another, made possible only through God's power and direction.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's passage through death and out the other side (resurrection) is the supreme 'causing to pass through.' As Paul writes, 'But every man in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ's at his coming' (1 Corinthians 15:23). Christ passes through death first, opening the way for all who are 'in Him' to follow. The passage through the midst of waters becomes a type of the narrow way through death that leads to life.
commentary.application: For modern members of the covenant, verse 14 teaches that we are not self-directed in our journey. We do not 'make it through' by our own strength or wisdom. God is actively 'causing us to pass through' the midst of our trials. This reframes difficulty: we are not abandoned in the desert or drowning in our challenges; we are in 'the midst' because that is where God has deliberately placed us to form us into a covenant people. We are invited to locate ourselves in the center of God's attention and care, not on the margins. When we walk through family conflict, financial hardship, loss of faith, or any wilderness, we can ask: Is God causing me to pass through this? What covenant work is being accomplished in the midst of my trial? This verse calls us from passivity to active trust—to move forward not because we understand the way, but because we trust the One who causes the passage.

text_kjv: But overthrew Pharaoh and his host in the Red sea: for his mercy endureth for ever.

commentary.narrative: Psalm 136:15 completes the thought of the exodus narrative by describing the judgment that befell Egypt's army. Where verses 13-14 emphasized God's deliverance of Israel, verse 15 emphasizes the simultaneous destruction of the opposing force. The verb ni'er ('to shake off, to shake out') in The Covenant Rendering is startlingly dismissive—God did not engage in a prolonged battle with Pharaoh's army; He shook them off as one shakes crumbs from a cloth or insects from one's garment. This linguistic choice reduces the military might of Egypt, one of the ancient world's great powers, to something utterly insignificant before God's power. Pharaoh, who ruled the most advanced civilization of the era and who had enslaved millions, is treated as something to be brushed away.
commentary.narrative_continued: Crucially, the psalmist maintains the refrain: 'for his mercy endureth for ever.' This is theologically audacious. The destruction of Pharaoh's army could be read as raw judgment, divine violence, retribution. Yet the psalmist frames it as an expression of God's chesed—His steadfast love toward His covenant people. This is possible because, from Israel's perspective, the destruction of Pharaoh's army was the necessary precondition for their freedom. Pharaoh had not agreed to release the slaves; he had hardened his heart repeatedly. God's judgment upon Egypt was inseparable from God's mercy toward Israel. The drowning of the Egyptian army was the dark side of Israel's salvation—but salvation nonetheless. This helps explain why this verse, like all 26 verses of Psalm 136, ends with the affirmation of God's enduring mercy.

word_study.meaning: To shake, to shake off, to shake out; to shake loose. The verb conveys the action of shaking something free from one's self or from a surface, as one shakes crumbs from cloth or bugs from one's robe. The root carries a sense of dismissal and lack of effort.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'shook off' better captures the contemptuous ease implied by the Hebrew. The KJV's 'overthrew' suggests a struggle, a battle; ni'er suggests no struggle at all. God's gesture is as casual as shaking off dust. This carries theological weight: the mighty Egyptian military, which should be formidable, is treated as negligible before God's power. The verb appears in Nehemiah 5:13, where Nehemiah shakes out his robe as a sign of judgment and separation—a dismissive gesture. God's handling of Pharaoh's army is similarly dismissive.

word_study.meaning: Army, military force, mighty men, strength. The word can also mean wealth or resources. In military contexts, it refers to the full complement of warriors available to a ruler.
word_study.significance: Pharaoh's 'host' (chayil) represents organized, trained, experienced military power. That this formidable force is 'shaken off' emphasizes not the strength of the enemy but the absolute superiority of God's power. Egypt's chayil, impressive by human standards, is nothing before the God of Israel.

word_study.meaning: Steadfast love, covenant loyalty, mercy. The term fundamentally denotes relational commitment within a covenant bond.
word_study.significance: The maintenance of this refrain even in verse 15—which describes judgment and death—is the key to the psalm's theology. God's chesed is not soft sentimentality; it is fierce, protective, jealous love for His covenant people. The destruction of those who oppose His people is an expression of His loyalty to those He has chosen.

cross_references.connection: The actual return of the waters upon the Egyptian army: 'And Moses stretched forth his hand over the sea, and the sea returned to his strength when the morning appeared; and the Egyptians fled against it; and the LORD overthrew the Egyptians in the midst of the sea.' The psalmist recalls the historical event.

The Song of the Sea celebrates the same destruction: 'Pharaoh's chariots and his host hath he cast into the sea: his chosen captains also are drowned in the Red sea. The depths have covered them: they sank into the bottom as a stone.' Israel's immediate response to the event.

The parallel account in the preceding psalm: 'Who smote the firstborn of Egypt, both of man and beast. Who sent tokens and wonders into the midst of thee, O Egypt, upon Pharaoh, and upon all his servants.' Psalm 136 expands on this account.

The same verb ni'er ('shake off') used as a sign of judgment: 'Thus said I, So God shake out every man from his house, and from his labour, that performeth not this promise, even thus be he shaken out, and emptied.' The dismissive gesture of judgment.

The heavenly song recalls the crossing of the sea as a type of salvation: 'And I saw as it were a sea of glass mingled with fire: and them that had gotten the victory over the beast...sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb.' The exodus becomes a pattern for all God's saving acts.

commentary.historical_context: Pharaoh ruled the 19th Dynasty of Egypt (likely Ramesses II, though scholarly consensus on exact dating remains debated). The Egyptian military was indeed formidable—chariot armies, professional soldiers, advanced weaponry. From an Egyptian perspective, the 'host' represented substantial military investment and national power. Yet from the Israelite perspective, this power meant nothing before God's will. The account in Exodus does not describe a military conflict but a reversal—the sea that was divided for Israel becomes the instrument of judgment for Egypt. This reflects ancient Near Eastern theology, where a god's ability to control cosmic forces (waters, sky, earth) was the highest expression of divine power. However, the biblical account makes this power purposive: it serves the liberation and formation of a covenant people. The destruction is not an end in itself but a means to covenant establishment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Lehi's warnings to Jerusalem precede a judgment—'many shall perish in the flesh, and shall be lost because of the hardness of their hearts' (1 Nephi 17:35). Those who resist God's covenant purposes experience judgment; those who accept them experience deliverance. The pattern of Exodus (judgment on the resistant, deliverance for the faithful) is repeated in Book of Mormon history.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:31-37 describes the fate of those who reject God's covenant: 'And again we saw the glory of the telestial...which surpasseth all understanding.' By contrast, D&C 76:50-70 describes the celestial kingdom for the faithful. Judgment and mercy are two sides of the same divine action—mercy toward the faithful, judgment toward the resistant.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The destruction of Pharaoh's host represents the symbolic 'overthrow' of worldly powers that oppose the covenant. In the temple, the journey of the individual through the endowment includes the representation of the defeat of those forces that would prevent exaltation.

commentary.christological_typology: Pharaoh represents the power of sin and Satan—the enslaver whose claims on God's people are absolute and irresistible from a human standpoint. Pharaoh's destruction parallels Satan's defeat through Christ's sacrifice. As Paul writes, 'Having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it' (Colossians 2:15). Christ 'shakes off' the claims of sin and death through His resurrection, much as God shakes off Pharaoh's army. The pattern of exodus (liberation through a champion figure; defeat of the enslaver; passage into covenant) is repeated in Christ.
commentary.application: Psalm 136:15 teaches that God's love is not passive or permissive. Chesed is not mere tolerance of evil; it is active opposition to whatever threatens the covenant people. For modern believers, this verse invites us to trust God's power against obstacles and adversaries. We live in a world of competing loyalties and forces that would enslave us to sin, addiction, despair, or rebellion. We are invited to believe that these 'Pharaohs' have no ultimate power. God can 'shake them off' with an ease that makes their apparent might irrelevant. This verse also invites us to contemplate the price of liberation—it is not costless. Pharaoh's destruction was necessary for Israel's freedom. The cross of Christ was necessary for humanity's redemption. We cannot always avoid conflict with opposing forces; what we can do is trust the One who has already demonstrated His power to overcome. Do we believe that the obstacles we face are ultimately negligible before God's power? Do we see God's opposition to evil as an expression of His love for us?

text_kjv: To him which led his people through the wilderness: for his mercy endureth for ever.

commentary.narrative: Psalm 136:16 shifts from the miraculous act of deliverance (the splitting of the sea) to the sustained work of formation (the wilderness journey). The participle molikhi ('the one leading') in The Covenant Rendering denotes ongoing action rather than a completed event. This is not a single miracle but a forty-year process of divine guidance and covenant formation. The wilderness (midbar) was not merely a transit zone between Egypt and Canaan; it was the crucible in which Israel became a covenant people. It was in the wilderness that Israel received the Torah at Mount Sinai, experienced the repeated failures and failures of faith, witnessed God's judgment and God's patience, learned obedience, and was formed into a unified people under God's law. The wilderness was where Israel's identity was forged.
commentary.narrative_continued: The psalmist's inclusion of this verse is theologically significant. One might expect the exodus narrative to jump directly from the crossing of the sea to the conquest of Canaan—from deliverance to possession. Instead, the psalm insists on the wilderness. This emphasizes that God's mercy is not a single act but an extended commitment. God did not merely free Israel; He stayed with them through the barren places, sustained them with manna and water, guided them with a pillar of fire by night and a cloud by day, gave them the covenant and the law, and brought them to the edge of the Promised Land. The wilderness, with all its hardships, is itself presented as an expression of God's chesed—of His faithfulness to the covenant even when the people faltered.

word_study.meaning: The participle form of halakh ('to go, to walk, to lead'). The participle denotes continuous or habitual action. Molikhi = 'the one leading,' with the sense of ongoing, repeated action.
word_study.significance: The participle emphasizes that God's leading was not a one-time event but a sustained, continuous guidance. For forty years, God led. This speaks to God's patience and commitment—He did not abandon Israel in the wilderness despite their repeated murmurings and failures. The English past tense 'led' can obscure this sense of sustained action captured by the Hebrew participle.

word_study.meaning: People, nation, folk. The term denotes a community bound together by common identity, covenant, or allegiance. It is often used in the context of God's covenanted people.
word_study.significance: By the time of the wilderness journey, Israel is referred to as God's 'am (people)—a corporate identity defined by relationship to God. This is a shift from the individual households enslaved in Egypt. The wilderness experience creates not merely freed individuals but a covenanted people with shared law, shared history, and shared destiny.

word_study.meaning: Wilderness, desert, uncultivated land. The term encompasses arid regions, but also the liminal space between civilization and habitation. The midbar is the place of encounter with God, testing, and formation.
word_study.significance: In biblical theology, the wilderness is not merely a geographical location but a spiritual state—a place of dependence on God, exposure, vulnerability, and testing. It is where the old (slavery) dies and the new (covenant identity) is born. The wilderness is also where Israel encounters God's law, miracles, and guidance most directly. For Latter-day Saints, the wilderness becomes a type of spiritual testing and formation in covenant.

cross_references.connection: The daily guidance of Israel in the wilderness: 'And when the cloud was taken up from over the tabernacle, the children of Israel went onward in all their journeys: But if the cloud were not taken up, then they journeyed not till the day that it was taken up.' God's presence was the constant guide.

The consequence of Israel's faithlessness in the wilderness: 'But as for you, your carcases, they shall fall in this wilderness...And your children shall wander in the wilderness forty years, and bear your whoredoms, until your carcases be wasted in the wilderness.' The wilderness as a place of testing and judgment as well as mercy.

Moses' recollection of God's wilderness provision: 'For the LORD thy God hath blessed thee in all the works of thy hand: he knoweth thy walking through this great wilderness.' Explicit acknowledgment of God's sustained presence.

Alma the Younger's teaching about the Liahona as a type of God's guidance: 'And thus we see that by small means the Lord can bring about great things...And by very small means we do bring to pass great things.' The wilderness journey as a pattern of God's guidance through 'small means' applied to covenant people.

The wilderness as the context of covenant-making: 'Therefore, verily I say unto you, that my law of the priesthood is of full force when ye are out of the world; And the power thereof is in you, wheresoever ye are.' The wilderness journey culminates in the law being given.

commentary.historical_context: The forty-year wilderness journey (traditionally dated to c. 1400-1360 BCE or 1290-1250 BCE depending on the Exodus date) would have traversed the Sinai Peninsula and surrounding regions. The route described in Numbers involves extensive time at Mount Sinai (where the law was given), then northward through the Transjordan. Archaeological surveys have found sparse evidence of a large population traversing the Sinai during this period, which has led scholars to propose smaller populations, different routes, or later legendary elaboration. However, from the ancient Israelite perspective, what mattered was not the archaeological footprint but the theological significance: the wilderness was where God formed Israel as a people under His law. The cultural context of ancient Near Eastern nomadic societies shows that wilderness journeys were common, often as part of migration or displacement; what is unique to Israel's account is that the wilderness journey is framed as part of God's active plan to form a covenant people.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's journey through the wilderness (1 Nephi 16-17) parallels Israel's wilderness formation. The Liahona guides Lehi's family through the desert as the cloud and pillar of fire guided Israel. Both groups are tested in the wilderness; both are provided for miraculously; both are being prepared for covenant possession. Nephi explicitly connects these: 'And I said: Father, whither shall I go?... And he said: Arise, and go up into the ship... And it came to pass that as I spake these words... I beheld that the Lord had spared them all in the wilderness' (1 Nephi 18:8,19).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 105:10-11 discusses the wilderness as a place of preparation: 'I have prepared all things for my people; but the children of men turn their hearts away from me, because they are blinded by the craftiness of men.' The wilderness remains God's place of testing and forming the faithful. D&C 86:5 speaks of the 'field' as the world where the faithful are tried: 'Therefore, let the wheat and the tares grow together until the harvest is fully ripe; therefore, I, the Lord, do not will that he should lose his life.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The wilderness journey represents the outer courtyard of the temple—the place of wandering, testing, and preparation before entering the sanctuary proper (Canaan, the temple, the inner sanctum of God's presence). The forty years in the wilderness prefigure the seven years of temple construction (symbolic of the complete formation necessary). The manna from heaven and water from the rock are types of the sacrament—spiritual nourishment provided by God in the wilderness.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's forty-day wilderness sojourn (Matthew 4:1-11; Luke 4:1-13) parallels Israel's forty-year wilderness journey. Both involve testing, both involve Satan's temptations (Israel tempted to abandon faith in God; Jesus tempted to abandon His mission), both involve God's provision. Christ emerges from the wilderness empowered to begin His earthly ministry; Israel emerges from the wilderness ready to possess the Promised Land. The wilderness becomes a type of spiritual formation necessary before entering into one's inheritance.
commentary.application: Psalm 136:16 invites modern covenant members to reframe their own wilderness seasons. Not all seasons of life are seasons of abundance, clarity, and comfort. Many are seasons of testing, uncertainty, wandering, and waiting. Yet the psalmist insists that God is leading even in these seasons. The wilderness is not a punishment or an abandonment; it is a place of formation. When we face extended seasons of difficulty, illness, grief, doubt, or struggle, we are invited to ask: What is God forming in me through this wilderness? How is He leading me toward covenant maturity? The wilderness teaches dependence—manna teaches us we cannot sustain ourselves; water from the rock teaches us that provision comes from God alone; the pillar of fire teaches us that God's presence is constant even in darkness. Do we experience wilderness seasons as expressions of God's chesed, or do we resist them as interruptions to our plans? This verse calls us to a deeper trust in God's guidance, even through terrain we do not choose.

text_kjv: To him which smote great kings: for his mercy endureth for ever:

commentary.narrative: Psalm 136:17 marks a transition in the psalm's historical narrative. The focus shifts from the exodus and wilderness (vv. 10-16) to the conquest of Canaan. The phrase 'great kings' (melakhim gedolim) refers specifically to the kings whom Joshua defeated as Israel entered the Promised Land. The refrain shifts slightly from 'divided' and 'led' (actions completed long ago) to 'smote' (a completed past action that extended over time). The conquest was not instantaneous; it involved years of warfare, conflict, and the defeat of multiple Canaanite kingdoms. The psalmist presents this conquest as yet another expression of God's chesed—His faithfulness to the covenant promise to Abraham that his descendants would possess the land.
commentary.narrative_continued: The compression of the conquest into the phrase 'great kings' is significant. Entire narratives of battle, strategy, faith, and struggle are reduced to a single affirmation of God's power. The 'greatness' of the kings emphasizes the magnitude of God's gift—Israel's inheritance was won not from petty chieftains but from established regional powers. That God defeated them is presented as evidence of God's superior power and His commitment to Israel. Yet even here, in an account of warfare and conquest, the psalmist maintains: 'for his mercy endureth for ever.' This raises the theological question: How can the conquest, which involved the dispossession and death of the Canaanite peoples, be an expression of God's mercy? The answer, from Israel's perspective, is that God's mercy is covenantal—it is faithfulness toward His chosen people, even if that faithfulness has consequences for those outside the covenant.

word_study.meaning: To strike, to hit, to smite. The verb conveys the action of violent contact—whether with a weapon, a hand, or a force. In the context of warfare, it means to defeat in battle.
word_study.significance: The verb is concrete and physical. God did not merely 'overcome' the kings in a passive sense; He actively struck them down. This emphasizes divine agency in warfare. In Psalms and in historical accounts of Israel's wars, God is presented as the active agent in victory—it is God who strikes down the enemy, not merely Israel's military strength.

word_study.meaning: Great, mighty, large kings. Melakhim = kings; gedolim = great, large, mighty, powerful. The term 'great' can refer to political power, military might, or size of realm.
word_study.significance: The specification that these were 'great kings' makes the victory more impressive. These were not minor rulers or tribal chieftains but established monarchs with resources and power. Defeating such figures demonstrates the extent of God's power and the likelihood of the success of Israel's claim to the land. The 'greatness' of the kings becomes a foil for the 'greatness' of God's power.

cross_references.connection: Joshua's defeat of the Canaanite kings: 'And it came to pass, when they brought out those kings unto Joshua, that Joshua called for all the men of Israel, and said unto the captains of the men of war which went with him, Come near, put your feet upon the necks of these kings.' The specific moment of victory over the kings.

A detailed list of the kings defeated in the conquest: 'Now these are the kings of the land, which Joshua and the children of Israel smote on this side Jordan on the west.' This provides the historical detail behind verse 17's compressed summary.

The parallel psalm's account of the conquest: 'Who smote many nations, and slew mighty kings; Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan.' Psalm 136 echoes and expands this account.

The command to defeat the Canaanite kings: 'When the LORD thy God shall bring thee into the land whither thou goest to possess it, and hath cast out many nations before thee, the Hittites, and the Girgashites, and the Amorites...thou shalt smite them, and utterly destroy them.' The conquest is presented as a commanded action.

Lehi's prophecy of the Nephites' future strength: 'And inasmuch as ye shall keep my commandments, ye shall prosper, and shall be led to a land of promise...And if it so be that ye keep the commandments of my Father, ye shall prosper in the land.' The pattern of covenant obedience leading to conquest and possession.

commentary.historical_context: The conquest of Canaan, traditionally dated to the late 13th century BCE (c. 1200 BCE), involved the defeat of multiple Canaanite city-states. The 'great kings' specifically referenced in Joshua 12 include rulers of Beth-el, Jericho, Ai, Jerusalem, Hebron, and numerous others. Archaeological evidence from this period shows destruction layers in multiple Canaanite cities, though scholarly debate continues regarding which destructions correspond to Israelite military action versus other causes (earthquakes, conflicts between Canaanite powers, etc.). From the Israelite perspective, what mattered was that God had enabled victory over established rulers and secured the land promised to Abraham. The historical fact of conquest was less theologically significant than the theological claim that God was the agent of victory.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Lehi's family encounters opposition from the Lamanites, who become a 'great power' opposing the Nephite possession of the land. The pattern of conquest and victory appears in the Book of Mormon, with God enabling military success for the righteous: 'And it came to pass that the Lord did prosper them, insomuch that they did slay the Lamanites with a great slaughter' (Alma 2:28). The same theological pattern—God defeats enemies of the covenant people—recurs.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 98:23-24 speaks of God's command to defeat enemies: 'Behold, I say unto you, my friends, fear them not. Those who charge you an interest...take not their lives; Neither shall you fight them...But if they come upon you to destroy you, then ye are justified in your own eyes to defend yourselves.' The principle of divinely sanctioned victory over those who oppose the covenant.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The defeat of the kings represents the 'overthrow of opposition' to the covenant journey. In the temple, the journey involves the defeat of opposing powers (represented symbolically) to reach the highest degree of glory. The conquest becomes a type of the inner spiritual conquest necessary to 'enter in at the strait gate.'

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's conquest of sin and Satan parallels Israel's conquest of Canaan. The 'great kings' who oppose Israel's possession of the land represent the forces of sin, death, and Satan that oppose Christ's victory and the redemption of humanity. As the Letter to the Hebrews presents it, Christ is the 'captain of our salvation' who leads us into 'the land of promise.' The conquest becomes a type of spiritual victory—the defeat of powers that oppose salvation.
commentary.application: Psalm 136:17 speaks to the modern understanding of spiritual warfare and opposition. The 'great kings' opposing Israel's inheritance can be understood as the powers—whether literal adversaries, internal struggles, or spiritual opposition—that stand between us and our covenant promises. The verse affirms that God is sufficient to defeat such opposition. For modern members, this raises important questions: What are the 'great kings' that oppose my possession of my spiritual inheritance? Am I trying to defeat them through my own strength, or am I trusting God to 'smite' them? The verse also cautions against underestimating opposition—the kings are called 'great' precisely because they are real threats. We should not assume our journey is smooth or costless. But we are also invited to trust that God's power exceeds whatever opposition we face. Have we seen God defeat 'great kings' in our own lives? Are we tempted to fear the magnitude of current opposition and forget God's pattern of victory?

text_kjv: And slew famous kings: for his mercy endureth for ever:

commentary.narrative: Psalm 136:18 continues the conquest narrative with a slight variation in terminology. Where verse 17 spoke of 'great kings' (melakhim gedolim), verse 18 refers to 'mighty kings' or 'famous kings' (melakhim addirim). The Covenant Rendering's 'mighty kings' captures the sense of addirim—rulers who are not merely numerous or politically established but who possess personal power, majesty, and renown. The verb yag-harg ('slew, killed') is more violent than the 'smote' of verse 17, emphasizing the finality and totality of the defeat. These kings were not merely defeated; they were killed. The conquest resulted in death—the death of the opposing rulers and, by extension, the dispossession of the populations they ruled.
commentary.narrative_continued: The parallelism between verses 17 and 18 is intentional. Together, they emphasize the completeness of the conquest: the great (in political power) and the mighty (in personal or military prowess) were all defeated. No one who opposed Israel's inheritance escaped judgment. Yet the refrain persists: 'for his mercy endureth for ever.' This is the theological audacity of Psalm 136. The killing of kings, the conquest of cities, the dispossession of peoples—all are subsumed under the category of God's enduring mercy toward the covenanted people. This requires a particular theological framework: God's covenant with Abraham included the land promise; that promise could not be fulfilled without the removal of the current inhabitants; therefore, the removal—however violent—is presented as part of God's faithfulness to His covenant. Modern readers, aware of the complexities of conquest narratives and the suffering they caused, must grapple with this theological claim rather than dismiss it.

word_study.meaning: To kill, to slay, to put to death. The verb is used in contexts of violent death, whether in warfare, execution, or murder. It emphasizes the finality and completeness of death.
word_study.significance: The shift from 'smote' (makke, which can mean to strike with force but is often paired with military action) to 'slew' (harag, which emphasizes the result—death—of the striking) underscores the finality of the conquest. The kings were not merely defeated; they ceased to exist as powers opposing Israel. This is a harder statement than verse 17, acknowledging the violent reality of conquest without euphemism.

word_study.meaning: Mighty, powerful, majestic, famous, splendid, glorious. The term can describe personal power (strength, might) or social power (majesty, renown). The plural addirim indicates multiple such rulers.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'mighty kings' preserves the sense of personal potency and majesty. These were not petty rulers but monarchs whose power was undeniable. That God 'slew' such figures emphasizes the extent of divine power—not merely overwhelming political structures but removing individually powerful figures. The raising of addirim (the mighty) and their defeat becomes a testimony to God's supremacy over all forms of earthly power and majesty.

word_study.meaning: Steadfast love, covenant loyalty, enduring mercy.
word_study.significance: By the 18th verse of a 26-verse poem where this refrain appears in every verse, the reader has encountered chesed 18 times. The repetition is not accidental; it is the theological point of the entire psalm. God's acts—including acts of violence and conquest—are all framed as expressions of His covenant faithfulness. This forces the reader to reconsider what chesed means in the context of divine action toward multiple peoples. The psalm does not present God's mercy as indiscriminate or universal, but as covenantal—mercy toward the elect people, even when that mercy requires hardship for others.

cross_references.connection: The specific defeat of Sihon and Og, the Transjordanian kings: 'And Israel smote him with the edge of the sword, and possessed his land from Arnon unto Jabbok, even unto the children of Ammon.' These 'mighty kings' are the historical examples of verse 18.

Joshua's defeat of the northern Canaanite coalition: 'And when Jabin king of Hazor had heard those things, he sent to Jobab king of Madon, and to the king of Shimron...and they went out, they and all their hosts with them...and the LORD said unto Joshua, Be not afraid because of them.' The conquest of mighty kings continues.

The immediate parallel: 'Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan; And gave their land for an heritage, even an heritage unto Israel his people.' Psalm 136 echoes and expands this account.

The principle of divine judgment on the mighty: 'And Samuel said, As thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women.' The judgment of kings continues throughout Israel's history.

A typological fulfillment in the eschaton: 'And the ten horns which thou sawest are ten kings...These shall make war with the Lamb: and the Lamb shall overcome them: for he is Lord of lords, and King of kings.' Christ overcomes the kings of the earth in the final age.

commentary.historical_context: The historical identities of the 'mighty kings' most directly referenced in Psalm 135-136 are Sihon of the Amorites and Og of Bashan, rulers of the Transjordanian regions east of the Jordan River. Sihon controlled territory from the Arnon River to the Jabbok River; Og ruled the mountainous region of Bashan. Both were defeated by Israel under Moses and Joshua. Archaeological evidence from the Iron Age (c. 1200-1000 BCE) shows destruction layers in multiple Canaanite cities, though the specific attribution of these destructions to Israelite conquest remains debated among scholars. The historical reality of some form of Israelite military expansion is accepted, though the scale, timing, and nature of the 'conquest' continue to generate scholarly discussion. From the theological perspective of the psalm, the specific historical details matter less than the fact that God enabled Israel to possess the land.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Nephites encounter 'mighty' enemies throughout their history—the Lamanites, the Gadiantons—and experience both victories and defeats depending on their righteousness. Alma 2:27-28 describes a mighty Nephite victory: 'And it came to pass that the Lord did prosper them, insomuch that they did slay the Lamanites with a great slaughter.' The pattern of divine-enabled victory over mighty opponents recurs in the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:1-6 addresses the suffering of Joseph Smith and the Saints, inviting them to trust in God's ultimate judgment of the 'mighty' who oppose the covenant: 'O God, where art thou? And where is the pavilion of thy hiding place?...How long shall thy hand be stayed? How long wilt thou suffer the wicked to triumph?' The tension between present suffering and ultimate divine vindication mirrors the conquest theme.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The overthrow of the 'mighty kings' represents the spiritual overthrow of the adversary's forces that oppose the covenant journey. In the temple, the individual's progression involves symbolic victory over opposition, moving from outer to inner sanctums as Israel moved from wilderness to possession of the land.

commentary.christological_typology: The defeat of the 'mighty kings' prefigures Christ's ultimate triumph over the powers that oppose His kingdom. As Colossians 2:15 states, Christ 'spoiled principalities and powers, making a shew of them openly, triumphing over them.' The mighty rulers of Canaan become types of the spiritual powers—Satan, death, sin—that Christ defeats. Christ's victory is more ultimate and comprehensive than Joshua's earthly conquest; it extends into the spiritual realm and encompasses all of human history.
commentary.application: Psalm 136:18 presents a difficult theological question for modern readers: How do we understand God's faithfulness in contexts where that faithfulness to one people results in harm to another? This is not a question the psalmist addresses directly; the psalm assumes that God's covenantal mercy toward Israel overrides concern for the Canaanite powers. Modern Latter-day Saints must grapple with this honestly. We can acknowledge that (1) the conquest narratives are real historical accounts with real human consequences; (2) we do not fully understand all God's purposes in ancient history; (3) God's stated covenant is with Israel, and that covenant included the land promise; (4) we should be cautious about assuming our own moral judgments override divine commands and purposes we do not fully comprehend. Yet we can also recognize that God's ultimate purposes extend beyond Israel to all humanity, and that Christ's sacrifice aims at the redemption of all people. The verse invites us to trust God's justice and mercy even when we cannot fully comprehend His historical actions, while maintaining our own commitment to justice and mercy toward all people in the present.

text_kjv: Sihon king of the Amorites: for his mercy endureth for ever:

commentary.narrative: Psalm 136 is a liturgical recitation of God's mighty acts throughout Israel's history, structured as a call-and-response hymn where the congregation echoes 'for his mercy endureth for ever' after each statement. Verse 19 zooms into a specific conquest narrative: Sihon, king of the Amorites. This is not a random historical reference. Sihon's defeat (Numbers 21:21-31) was a watershed moment—the first major military victory after Israel's wilderness wandering, the first breach of the Jordan River region, and the gateway to the promised land itself. By naming Sihon, the psalmist is invoking the memory of a defining moment when God proved He would fight for His people.

word_study.meaning: The name likely derives from an Amorite royal lineage, not a common Hebrew word. Sihon was a historical Amorite king whose territory lay between the Arnon and Jabbok rivers in Transjordan.
word_study.significance: The psalmist names a specific historical enemy—not just 'the Amorites' but Sihon by name. This personalizes the victory and grounds the liturgy in concrete history. Ancient Near Eastern victory hymns regularly named defeated enemies to glorify the victor's power.

word_study.meaning: A title of political authority. The Amorites were West Semitic peoples who occupied much of the Levant in the pre-Israelite and early Israelite periods. The Amorites in biblical memory represent the indigenous inhabitants of Canaan whom Israel displaced.
word_study.significance: By calling Sihon 'king,' the psalm acknowledges that Israel faced organized, legitimate political opposition—not chaos or lawlessness. Yet Yahweh defeated this established power, making the victory a theological statement: no human kingdom stands against God's purposes.

word_study.meaning: A covenant term denoting loyal love, steadfast kindness, mercy. Chesed is not abstract sentiment but covenantal action—the binding commitment a lord makes to his servants, a king to his subjects. The Covenant Rendering renders this 'faithful love' to capture the relational and obligatory quality.
word_study.significance: The refrain 'for His faithful love endures forever' appears 26 times in Psalm 136, once after each divine action. This relentless repetition teaches that every conquest, every deliverance, flows from God's character as a covenant keeper. His mercy is not occasional grace but perpetual commitment.

cross_references.connection: The historical account of Sihon's defeat: Israel requests passage through his territory, Sihon refuses and attacks, and Yahweh gives Israel the victory. This is the event the psalm commemorates.
Moses recounts God's command to fight Sihon and His delivery of Sihon and all his people into Israel's hand, establishing the theological interpretation: this was divine will, not human conquest.

Another liturgical recitation: 'And thou gavest them kingdoms and nations...and they possessed the land of Sihon, and the land of the king of Bashan.' Sihon's defeat is remembered as part of God's faithfulness across centuries.
The parallel psalm immediately preceding Psalm 136 also mentions Sihon and Og in the same sequence, showing this historical pattern was central to Israel's liturgical memory.

commentary.historical_context: Sihon ruled the Transjordanian plateau between the Arnon River (south) and Jabbok River (north), roughly corresponding to modern central Jordan. Archaeology and ancient sources confirm this was a real kingdom with organized military structure. The defeat of Sihon opened the way for Israel to approach Canaan from the east—a vulnerability of the land that the Canaanites would have understood. Sihon's refusal to grant peaceful passage (Numbers 21:23) placed the onus on him in ancient Near Eastern diplomatic protocol; Israel was not the aggressor. This distinction mattered in how the victory was remembered: God responded to provocation and protected His people's legitimate claim to transit.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon echoes this theme of God delivering His covenant people from enemies through divine power. Alma 26:13-14 records Ammon's testimony: 'Yea, I have been all things, and have suffered all things...and this is not all; have I not assisted in bringing the Amorites to destruction?' (note the word 'Amorites'—a direct parallel to the psalm). The pattern repeats: God's servants face enemies, God remembers His covenant, deliverance comes.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 98:23-28 teaches principles of war and justified defense. When enemies refuse peaceful overtures and attack, the Lord fights for His people. This mirrors Sihon's refusal and God's response—the structure of justified divine violence.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The pattern of conquest—enemy opposes, God intervenes, land is sanctified as inheritance—prefigures the temple endowment's teaching about divine opposition to Satan and the exaltation of God's covenant people in their promised sphere.

commentary.christological_typology: Sihon's defeat foreshadows Christ's triumph over spiritual enemies. Just as Yahweh 'remembered' Israel and acted to free them from an earthly enemy, Christ's atonement remembers humanity in its bondage to sin and death, and performs the ultimate rescue. The forceful extraction from enemies (using the language of verse 24) parallels Christ's harrowing of hell and the souls He freed from captivity.
commentary.application: When we commemorate God's past faithfulness—whether in scripture, in Church history, or in our personal experience—we strengthen faith for present trials. The psalmist does not merely recall history for its own sake; the recitation of Sihon's defeat teaches the present congregation: 'God has fought for us before. He is faithful. His love endures forever.' In our own Latter-day practice, we do this when we bear testimony of the Restoration, when we rehearse personal miracles in family home evening, or when we teach our children how prayer has been answered. The repetition is not nostalgia—it is covenant pedagogy.

text_kjv: And Og the king of Bashan: for his mercy endureth for ever:

commentary.narrative: The second great Transjordanian victory follows immediately: Og, king of Bashan. Where Sihon held the central plateau, Og ruled the northern highland—the fertile Bashan region known in antiquity for its grain, cattle, and oak forests. Yet Bashan's wealth and position meant nothing against Yahweh. The psalmist pairs these two victories not because they were identical but because together they represent a complete sweep of Transjordan—all opposition eliminated, all territory opened. Og's defeat was the capstone; it removed the last major obstruction between Israel and the promised land. Deuteronomy 3:11 preserves an extraordinary detail: 'his bed was a bed of iron; is it not in Rabbath of the children of Ammon? nine cubits was the length thereof, and four cubits the breadth of it.' Og was remembered as a giant. Defeating him was not merely military victory; it was theological assertion—size and strength mean nothing before God's power.

word_study.meaning: An Amorite royal name, likely historical. The name's etymology is debated; it may relate to Ugaritic cognates meaning 'to be strong' or similar, though this is speculative. Og was a real historical figure, a king of the northern Transjordanian highlands.
word_study.significance: The pairing of Sihon and Og became fixed in Israel's memory formula. Together they represent the totality of Transjordanian opposition. By naming both individually, the psalmist witnesses to God's comprehensive victory—no enemy was overlooked or underestimated.

word_study.meaning: A region in northern Transjordan, roughly modern-day Syrian Golan and southern Hauran. Bashan was known for its fertility, forests, and high-quality cattle (Amos 4:1, Psalm 22:12). The name may derive from a root meaning 'smooth' or 'soft,' referring to its fertile soil.
word_study.significance: By mentioning Bashan specifically, the psalmist names a coveted land. Bashan was not marginal territory; it was desirable real estate. God's gift to Israel included this fertility, not as plunder but as inheritance. The prosperity of Bashan would supply Israel's abundance.

word_study.meaning: A ruler with political and military authority. In ancient Near Eastern context, a melekh commanded tribute, maintained an army, and held territory. Og's kingship was real authority, not a ceremonial title.
word_study.significance: The repetition of 'king' (Sihon was a king, Og was a king) emphasizes that Israel's conquest was not directed against disorganized peoples but against established political powers. God's victory was therefore a triumph of divine order over human organization.

cross_references.connection: The historical narrative: Og came out against Israel with his whole people, but Yahweh said to Moses, 'Do not fear him; for I have delivered him into thy hand,' and Israel defeated Og and took his land.

Moses recounts Og's defeat and adds the remarkable detail: Og's iron bed was nine cubits long, preserved in Rabbath of the Ammonites. This detail emphasizes Og's legendary size and makes his defeat a mark of God's power over the mighty.
After Og's defeat, half of Og's land goes to Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh—showing how the conquered territory is distributed as inheritance, not hoarded.
Psalm 135 immediately precedes Psalm 136 and repeats: 'Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan,' showing this pairing was a fixed liturgical formula.

Centuries later, Amos invokes Bashan's cattle as a metaphor for Israel's luxury and pride, confirming that Bashan's fertility remained part of Israel's inherited wealth and was remembered across the generations.

commentary.historical_context: Bashan in the Late Bronze Age was a prosperous highland kingdom. Archaeological evidence suggests it was more developed and wealthier than the central Transjordanian plateau. Og's kingship would have been established and stable. The defeat of such a ruler was militarily significant—not a skirmish but a campaign. Ancient Near Eastern parallels show that when scribes recorded such victories, they often emphasized the opponent's strength (size, resources, established power) to magnify the victor's achievement. Deuteronomy's note about Og's bed (9 cubits = roughly 13-14 feet) was a way of saying: 'This was no ordinary opponent.' Yet he fell. The theological message: God's power transcends human magnitude.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26 again resonates: 'And how do ye suppose that I know of their surety? Behold, I say unto you they are made known unto me by the Holy Ghost of God. Behold, I have assurance of better things' (Alma 26:16). Ammon's confidence parallels the psalmist's confidence—past deliverances guarantee future faithfulness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:7-9 addresses the Saints' suffering and reassures them: 'My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment; and then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high.' The pattern: acknowledge the enemy (Og is real and powerful), trust in God's intervention, and know that exaltation follows faithfulness.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment presents similar opposition and deliverance: the celestial room is reached only by overcoming symbolic enemies and obstacles. Og and Sihon represent the forces that block the way to inheritance; their defeat opens the path.

commentary.christological_typology: Og, described as a giant, prefigures the spiritual giants—demonic forces, principalities, powers—that Christ defeated through His atonement. The emphasis on Og's size and strength parallels the emphasis on Satan's power in modern revelation (D&C 76:28-29), yet both are overcome by the greater power of Yahweh/Jehovah. Christ's victory is more complete: He did not merely defeat enemies of a geographical territory but broke the power of death itself.
commentary.application: The psalm teaches that inherited blessings come through confrontation with real opposition. Bashan was not given freely; Og had to be defeated. Similarly, in modern spiritual life, our inheritance in the kingdom is not automatic. We inherit covenant blessings by overcoming obstacles—pride, worldliness, faithlessness. The psalm assures us that as we face our 'Og'—whatever towering obstacle blocks our way—God has proven His faithfulness through history and will not abandon us. We do not walk toward our inheritance unarmed or alone.

text_kjv: And gave their land for an heritage: for his mercy endureth for ever:

commentary.narrative: The conquest narrative culminates in a single statement: 'And gave their land for an heritage.' After reciting the defeats of Sihon and Og, the psalmist now articulates the purpose of those victories—transfer of territory. But notice the specific language: not 'gave their land as plunder' or 'conquered their land,' but 'gave their land for an heritage.' The Hebrew word nachalah (inheritance) carries covenantal weight. An inheritance is not something seized but something granted; it implies a giver with authority and a receiver with a relationship to that giver. In ancient Near Eastern royal practice, a king granted land to a loyal servant as part of their perpetual arrangement. By using nachalah, the psalmist teaches that Israel does not possess Transjordan by right of conquest alone but by divine gift. God owns the land fundamentally; He grants use and inheritance to His covenant people. This is not a trivial distinction. It means the land is a trust, held on condition of covenant faithfulness.

word_study.meaning: A simple verb meaning 'to give,' yet in Hebrew it carries the force of authoritative transfer. When a sovereign gives, the gift is absolute and binding. Natan is used repeatedly in Genesis when God gives the land to Abraham's descendants, establishing it as a covenantal act, not a commercial transaction.
word_study.significance: By using natan, the psalmist frames the transfer as a divine prerogative. The land moves from Og's rule to Israel's possession because God gives it—not because Israel is strong enough to take it. This theology protects against militarism: Israel did not conquer on its own power; God gave what He had decreed to give.

word_study.meaning: The word eretz means land or earth and with the possessive suffix means 'their land'—the territorial holdings of Sihon and Og. Eretz can mean land in a general sense, but in context it refers to the specific territories these kings controlled.
word_study.significance: The shift of possession is geographic and concrete. The psalmist is not speaking abstractly about divine power but about real land, real cities, real resources. Sihon's land and Og's land are now Israel's land. The concreteness matters: God's covenants are not merely spiritual abstractions but include material reality.

word_study.meaning: A possession held in perpetuity within a family or community. Nachalah is inherited property—land that passes from generation to generation as part of family identity. In biblical law, nachalah could not be permanently sold; it had to return to the family every jubilee year (Leviticus 25:28). The root may relate to nachal ('stream' or 'valley'), suggesting land that sustains life.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering and translator notes emphasize that the conquered land is not plunder but inheritance—not stolen goods but a gift held in trust. This is crucial theology: Israel may not exploit the land as conquered territory, selling it permanently or treating it as absolute property. It is nachalah, held as a stewardship under God, with obligations to equity and release. This concept resounds through Jewish law and ethics to this day.

cross_references.connection: The parallel psalm states the same truth: 'And gave their lands for an heritage unto Israel his people.' The repetition in consecutive psalms emphasizes the centrality of inheritance theology.

God's original covenant with Abraham: 'I am the LORD that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give thee this land to inherit it.' The land is a covenantal gift from the beginning, not a conquest prize.

Moses tells Israel: 'But the LORD hath taken you, and brought you forth out of the iron furnace...to be unto him a people of inheritance.' Israel is God's nachalah, and the land is Israel's nachalah—a mutual covenant of belonging.

The distribution of the land: 'These are the countries which the children of Israel inherited in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the heads of the fathers of the children of Israel divided for an inheritance unto them.' The conquered land is allocated as nachalah to each tribe.

The law underlying inheritance: 'The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me.' Even as Israel holds nachalah, God retains ultimate ownership; the people are stewards, not absolute proprietors.

commentary.historical_context: The term nachalah reflects ancient Near Eastern practice: when a king granted land to a loyal servant, that grant was made 'for an inheritance'—passed to the servant's heirs, held in trust. The grant came with obligations: loyalty, tribute, and proper stewardship. Israel's possession of Transjordan followed this model: the land was granted as a collective inheritance to the tribes, distributed to families, and held under covenantal obligation. Archaeological evidence shows that the highland territories of Transjordan (Sihon's and Og's lands) were indeed settled by Israelite populations in the Iron Age, though the details of conquest versus gradual settlement remain debated among scholars.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon applies nachalah theology to the Americas. Ether 2:7-9 records the Lord's promise to the Jaredites: 'And this land shall be a land of liberty unto thee...and there shall be none to molest them...if it be that ye keep my commandments.' The land is an inheritance, but it is conditional—kept or lost based on covenant fidelity. This echoes Psalm 136's theology.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:17-20 teaches: 'If ye are prepared ye need not fear...I will prepare all things, and among all these things I will give unto you revelation...that ye may be prepared in all things.' The Lord gives as an inheritance, not merely as payment. Modern revelation echoes the psalmist's language of divine giving.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ordinances teach that exaltation—the highest inheritance—is given by God to the faithful. Just as the promised land was nachalah, exaltation is an inherited glory, held in perpetuity by those who keep their covenants. The language of inheritance and stewardship runs through all temple theology.

commentary.christological_typology: The giving of inherited land prefigures Christ's giving of His kingdom. In Matthew 25:34, Christ says to the righteous: 'Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.' The kingdom is not earned but given—nachalah. It is inheritance in the fullest sense: a divine gift held in perpetuity by God's covenant people. Christ, as the fulfillment of Israel, offers not territorial land but a kingdom not of this world, an eternal inheritance.
commentary.application: The modern Latter-day Saint is invited to understand their membership in the Church and their covenants in terms of inheritance. The promises given at baptism, in the temple, in the priesthood—these are not transactions but inheritances. They are ours as we keep our part of the covenant, held in trust as nachalah. This should generate both gratitude (it is a gift) and responsibility (it is held under conditions). In practical terms: we do not 'own' our relationship with God as if it were private property; we steward it as an inheritance given for our blessing and the blessing of future generations. Just as Israel could not permanently alienate its nachalah, we cannot abandon or sell out our covenant inheritance.

text_kjv: Even an heritage unto Israel his servant: for his mercy endureth for ever.

commentary.narrative: Verse 22 specifies who receives the inheritance: 'Israel his servant.' The refrain 'for his mercy endureth for ever' continues its relentless echo. Yet this verse adds a crucial theological element. Israel is not described as 'God's chosen people' or 'God's beloved' (though these titles appear elsewhere); here, Israel is 'God's servant'—avdo in Hebrew. In modern Western thought, 'servant' can sound like a diminishment—subservience, loss of dignity. But in ancient Near Eastern political thought, being the king's servant was a position of honor and proximity. A servant is someone the king trusts, delegates to, relies upon. A king's servant carries the king's authority and speaks for the king. When Abraham is called God's servant (Psalm 105:6), it is not a humiliation but a distinction. Israel, as God's servant, is His representative on earth, the nation through which He will work His purposes. The land is given to this servant—not to a nation that seized it, not to a people who earned it, but to God's trusted agent. This framing carries profound implications: Israel's possession of the land is inseparable from its function as God's servant. Holding the land means serving God's purposes.

word_study.meaning: Inheritance, as established in verse 21. The term is repeated here for emphasis and to show that the entire verse is explicating verse 21: the heritage is specifically Israel's heritage, given to Israel as servant.
word_study.significance: The repetition of nachalah within two consecutive verses creates a parallelism: 'And gave their land for an heritage' (v. 21), 'An inheritance for Israel His servant' (v. 22). The structure shows that the defeated kings' land becomes Israel's nachalah—a transfer of inheritance.

word_study.meaning: The name meaning 'he who strives with God' or 'God prevails,' given to Jacob after his wrestling at the Jabbok (Genesis 32:28). In context, Israel designates the covenant people, the twelve tribes united under the kingship and the law of Moses.
word_study.significance: By name, Israel is defined by its wrestling with God—its struggle, its testing, its relationship. Israel is not a name of conquest but of covenant struggle. The servant who receives the inheritance is one who has struggled with and before God.

word_study.meaning: The possessive form of eved, 'servant.' In Hebrew, eved can mean a slave (held in permanent servitude), a servant (hired for a term), or a trusted agent. Context determines the nuance. When used of Israel or Abraham in relation to God, eved carries the meaning of a trusted agent—a servant through whom the master works his will.
word_study.significance: The translator notes emphasize this crucial distinction: In the ancient Near East, the king's servant was his trusted agent. Israel serves the cosmic sovereign as His representative on earth. This is not degradation but appointment to a sacred function. Israel's identity is bound up in being God's servant—not oppressed, but entrusted.

cross_references.connection: Jacob is renamed Israel after wrestling with the angel: 'Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men.' Israel's very name encodes a struggle with God and a role as mediator.

The Servant passage: 'But thou, Israel, art my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend...I have chosen thee, and not cast thee away.' Israel is God's chosen servant, held in covenant.

The covenant conditions: 'And it shall come to pass, if thou shalt hearken diligently unto the voice of the LORD thy God, to observe and to do all his commandments which I command thee this day, that the LORD thy God will set thee on high above all nations of the earth...and all these blessings shall come on thee.' Blessings follow from serving—from keeping God's word.
Another liturgical passage: 'O ye seed of Abraham his servant, ye children of Jacob his chosen.' The title 'His servant' and 'His chosen' are linked; they define Israel's identity.
Paul calls himself 'a servant of Jesus Christ,' using the same term. The apostolic office inherits the servant-agent role, representing Christ's will on earth.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern political ideology, a nation was described as the king's servant when it was in vassal relationship—owing tribute and allegiance. Yet the relationship could be benevolent. The king's servant was protected and provided for. In Israel's theology, becoming God's servant elevated the nation rather than diminished it. The term reflected not weakness but covenant status. Israel understood itself not as an independent power but as God's agent in history, carrying out His purposes. This self-understanding shaped Jewish identity and practice across centuries.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:11-13 records Ammon's declaration: 'Therefore, let us glory in the Lord, yea, and let us be exceedingly glad, for behold, the Lord hath granted unto us that we may be instruments in his hands to bring about this great work.' The Nephite missionaries understand themselves as servants, agents of God's purposes. The land is given them for service.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:29-34 teaches: 'Wherefore I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another...I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men...Nevertheless, I have forgiven you your debts; and you are released from them therefore.' The servant who receives blessing must embody forgiveness and mercy—service requires servant-like virtues. Modern revelation uses the same servant theology.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple endowment, the faithful are taught that they are servants of God, doing His work in His house. The temple garment and the temple experience establish the individual as a servant in God's kingdom. The promised inheritance comes to those who serve faithfully.

commentary.christological_typology: Israel as God's servant is ultimately a type of Christ, the Servant. Isaiah 52:13 – 53:12 describes the Suffering Servant who will be exalted despite his humiliation. Jesus, in His earthly ministry and in His atoning sacrifice, became the ultimate servant—the agent through whom God's redemptive purposes are accomplished. Matthew 20:28 records Jesus saying: 'The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.' Christ is the perfect servant, and His inheritance—all nations, all kingdoms—comes through faithful service to the Father's will.
commentary.application: For the modern Latter-day Saint, verse 22 reframes the question of what it means to be blessed by God. Blessings are not trophies for the self-glorifying; they are inheritances given to servants. The more we receive—prosperity, health, knowledge, spiritual gifts—the more we are called to serve. The verse teaches that if we are to hold inheritances (which in Latter-day theology includes the promises of exaltation, family bonds, eternal increase), we must understand ourselves as servants of God and His kingdom. This is not degrading; it is clarifying and liberating. We are not masters of our own destiny but trusted agents of a divine plan. Our inheritances are secure when we keep our covenants as His servants. Practically: when tempted to see our blessings as personal achievements or as things to hoard, we remember that we are servants holding them in trust.

text_kjv: Who remembered us in our low estate: for his mercy endureth for ever:

commentary.narrative: With verse 23, the psalm makes a decisive turn. The grand historical narrative of creation, exodus, and conquest gives way to the intimate and personal: 'Who remembered us in our lowliness.' The Covenant Rendering captures this shift: 'Who remembered us in our lowliness, for His faithful love endures forever.' The translator notes are key here: 'The psalm shifts from ancient history to present experience.' Suddenly the psalmist moves from recounting what happened to ancient Israel to addressing the congregation's present condition. 'Us'—the people singing this psalm, gathered in the temple or in liturgical assembly. 'In our lowliness'—not describing a moment in the distant past, but the people's current state. Be-shifleinu uses the root shafal ('to be low, abased, humiliated'). The people are down. They are suffering. They have known humiliation. And in that lowliness, God 'remembered' them. The verb zakhar in Hebrew does not mean 'recalled to mind' (implying God had forgotten) but 'turned His attention to with intent to act.' To be remembered by God is to be rescued. This is the theological movement of the entire verse: lowliness → remembrance → coming deliverance.

word_study.meaning: To remember, to recall, to turn one's attention to. In biblical theology, divine remembering is an act of will and intervention, not merely mental recall. When God 'remembers,' He acts to fulfill or respond. The phrase 'God remembered' is always a prelude to divine action.
word_study.significance: The translator notes cite Genesis 8:1 ('God remembered Noah'—followed by the subsiding of the flood) and Exodus 2:24 ('God remembered His covenant'—followed by deliverance from Egypt). Zakhar is a covenant term: remembrance implies action. The psalmist is not asking God to think about the people; he is asking God to act, and 'remembrance' is the theological language for that action. This verb choice is precisely calibrated to express trust in divine intervention.

word_study.meaning: The first-person plural object pronoun. 'Us' specifies that this is not a general theological statement but a direct address to the community: God remembered us—the people singing, the congregation gathered.
word_study.significance: The shift from third person (Sihon, Og) to first person (us) personalizes the theology. Each hearer becomes part of the narrative: 'God remembered us.' This is a fundamental technique of liturgical prayer—to incorporate the community into a pattern of divine remembrance and action.

word_study.meaning: From the root shafal, meaning 'to be low, to be brought low, to be abased.' Shifleinu describes a state of humiliation, defeat, or suffering. It is not neutral lowliness (like a humble spirit) but degradation imposed from without.
word_study.significance: The term contextualizes the psalmist's plea. The people are not simply poor or modest; they have been brought low. They have experienced oppression, exile, suffering—the bottom of the circumstances. Yet it is precisely in this lowliness that God is invoked to remember. This creates a poignant contrast: our worst state is the occasion for God's most vital intervention. The translator notes emphasize: 'This describes Israel at its worst, its lowest, its most defeated.'
