The plural form and the universal quantifier 'all' emphasize totality.
word_study.significance: The psalm envisions that even human authority structures — those who hold ultimate earthly power — will acknowledge and praise God. This is a radical claim: all power ultimately derives from and is answerable to God.

word_study.meaning: From yadah (to acknowledge, thank, or confess), this is the same root as in verse 1 (odekha, 'I will thank you'). The form here is future and universal: 'they will acknowledge/thank You,' spoken of all the kings of the earth.
word_study.significance: The use of yadah again links the individual's thanksgiving (v. 1) with the universal thanksgiving of the nations (v. 4). What begins as one person's grateful acknowledgment becomes the response of all humanity. Thanksgiving is the universal appropriate response to God.

word_study.meaning: Shama means 'to hear, listen, or obey.' The conditional 'when they hear' (ki shamu) indicates that the kings' thanksgiving is triggered by hearing.
word_study.significance: Hearing is not passive reception but the gateway to transformation. When the kings hear God's word, it changes them. This reflects the ancient Israelite understanding that God's word is not merely informational but performative — it accomplishes what it is sent to do (cf. Isaiah 55:11).

word_study.meaning: Imrah means 'saying, utterance, or word'; pi means 'mouth.' 'The words of Your mouth' refers to God's spoken utterances — His commandments, promises, declarations, or revelations. This is God's immediate, direct speech.
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes that it is God's own words, not human interpretation or mediation, that reaches the nations and produces thanksgiving. God's speech has inherent power and authority.

cross_references.connection: Prophesies that 'all flesh shall come to worship before me, saith the LORD' — an eschatological vision parallel to verse 4's promise that all the earth's kings will praise God.
States 'All nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord; and shall glorify thy name' — nearly identical to verse 4's vision of universal praise.
Declares 'The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ' — the fulfillment of verse 4's vision that all earthly rulers acknowledge God's supremacy.
The Lord addresses 'all the inhabitants of the earth,' declaring that His word goes forth and all must hearken — echoing verse 4's principle that God's words reach all peoples and demand response.
Prophesies that 'in that day shall the deaf hear the words of the book, and...the blind shall see' — the nations awakening to God's word, as in verse 4.

commentary.historical_context: Verses 4-5 reflect the Old Testament eschatological hope known in scholarship as 'the nations' pilgrimage to Zion' (cf. Isaiah 2:2-3, Micah 4:1-3). The vision is that in the end time, the nations will flow to Jerusalem to learn God's law and walk in His ways. This was not mere fantasy but a central theme of Israelite hope preserved in the Psalms and Prophets. In the ancient context, this would have been a radical vision: in a world of competing empires and gods, the psalmist declares that ultimately all power structures will recognize and praise the God of Israel. This reflects the Israelite conviction that their small nation was cosmically central — that the God they worshiped was not a local deity but the actual sovereign of all creation. The phrase 'when they hear the words of Your mouth' reflects ancient Near Eastern understanding of divine speech: in Mesopotamian texts, the words of the gods were thought to have inherent power to shape reality. Israel adapted this understanding to its own monotheism: only YHWH's words possess ultimate creative and transformative power.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 21:10 quotes Isaiah's vision that 'the Gentiles shall seek to' Jesus Christ and 'all the nations shall submit to him' — a Book of Mormon affirmation of verse 4's promise that all the earth's rulers will eventually acknowledge God. Alma 37:4 teaches that God's word 'shall go forth and shall not return unto him void,' echoing verse 4's principle that God's words reach all peoples and accomplish their purpose.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:4-6 declares that 'the voice of warning shall be an exceedingly great voice' and 'the arms of mercy shall be stretched out unto them; for he loveth those who will have him to be their God.' This describes the same eschatological vision: God's voice reaching all the earth, and the response being acknowledgment and thanksgiving. D&C 65:5-6 prophesies that 'the day cometh that shall crown the faithful with glory and immortal power' — the future fulfillment of verse 4's vision that all powers acknowledge God.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple is the place from which God's word goes forth to the world (Isaiah 2:3). In Latter-day Saint theology, the Temple endowment and ordinances are understood as preparing God's people to participate in the eschatological vision described in verse 4 — the bringing of all humanity to acknowledgment and praise of God. The missionary work of the Church is the means by which God's words reach the nations, though the ultimate fulfillment awaits Christ's return.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the Word of God incarnate (John 1:1, 'In the beginning was the Word'). Verse 4's vision that 'the words of Your mouth' reach all nations and produce thanksgiving is fulfilled in Christ, through whom God's ultimate word has come to the world. The Great Commission (Matthew 28:19-20) — to 'go therefore and teach all nations' — is the mechanism through which the words of God (embodied in Christ's gospel) reach the kings of the earth. Christ's Second Coming will complete verse 4's vision: all rulers and nations will acknowledge Christ as Lord (Philippians 2:10-11, 'every knee shall bow...and every tongue shall confess that Jesus Christ is Lord'). The nations' thanksgiving to God in verse 4 will ultimately be thanksgiving for Christ's redemption and reign.
commentary.application: For modern members, verse 4 is a call to faith in God's ultimate triumph and a motivation for missionary work. Practically: (1) Recognize that the gospel will eventually reach all the earth and all nations will acknowledge Christ — this is not a vain hope but a certainty grounded in God's character. (2) Engage in missionary work, knowing that when people genuinely hear God's words (the gospel message), they will respond with gratitude and thanks. (3) Do not despair when the world resists God's word — the vision is eschatological, and God's triumph is certain. (4) Trust that God's words have inherent power — your testimony, your sharing of scripture, your witness of God's character carries power to transform hearts. (5) When you encounter resistance to the gospel among powerful people (leaders, intellectuals, the wealthy), remember that even all the kings of the earth will eventually praise God — power structures and status are temporary, and God's ultimate authority is universal and certain.

text_kjv: Yea, they shall sing in the ways of the LORD: for great is the glory of the LORD.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 5 deepens and clarifies the nations' response to God's word described in verse 4. It is not merely that they will 'praise' God (yadah, acknowledge); they will 'sing' — ve-yashiru ('and they will sing'). The action is joyful, embodied, and communal. Singing is a form of corporate worship in which a group takes God's word into their mouths and makes it their own through melody and rhythm. This is the full expression of gratitude and recognition.

The substance of their song is 'the ways of the Lord' (be-darkhei YHWH). The 'ways' are not merely God's will in abstract but God's characteristic patterns of action — how He moves in history, how He judges, how He saves, how He demonstrates faithfulness. To sing 'of the ways of the Lord' is to recount and celebrate God's deeds and character as revealed in His actions. The nations' singers will be celebrating God's justice, His mercy, His power, His fidelity.

The reason for this eschatological singing is stated: 'for great is the glory of the Lord' (ki gadol kevod YHWH). Kavod (glory) is not merely reputation but the manifest, visible presence and power of God. When God's kavod is perceived, worship erupts. The nations sing because they have witnessed God's glory — His actual presence and power manifested in creation and history. The logic is direct: perceive God's glory, and praise becomes inevitable. This echoes the foundational promise of Isaiah 40:5: 'the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together.'

The verse completes the vision: individuals thank God (v. 1-3), God's word reaches the kings of the earth (v. 4), and when the nations see God's glory, they erupt in corporate singing of God's ways (v. 5). This is worship at cosmic scale — all creation recognizing and celebrating the LORD.

word_study.meaning: From shir, meaning to sing, make music, or chant. This is distinct from zamar (v. 1), which emphasizes instrumental music; shir emphasizes vocal music and the content of the song. The form here is future and plural: 'they will sing.'
word_study.significance: Singing is the complete response to revelation — not mere acknowledgment (v. 4) but joyful, embodied proclamation. Singing involves the whole person: breath, voice, and emotion are coordinated in expression of praise.

word_study.meaning: Derech (plural: derachim) means 'way, path, road, or journey.' In theological usage, 'ways' refers to God's patterns of action, God's characteristic methods of dealing with creation and His people. This is not moralistic 'living in the ways' but rather celebrating God's ways as seen in His deeds.
word_study.significance: The psalm invites singers to contemplate not merely God's existence but God's actionable character — how He reveals Himself through what He does. The 'ways of the Lord' are visible, knowable, and worthy of celebration.

word_study.meaning: Great, large, mighty, or significant. When applied to God or God's attributes, gadol indicates supreme importance and transcendent magnitude.
word_study.significance: God's glory is not merely pleasant or admirable but supremely great — beyond comparison, incomparable. The psalmist affirms that nothing in all creation approaches the greatness of God's manifest presence.

word_study.meaning: Glory, honor, or weightiness. In Hebrew, kavod originally referred to weight or substance; it came to mean the manifest, visible, substantial presence of someone. God's kavod is God's actual presence and power as it appears and acts in creation. This is not abstract reputation but visible, perceivable reality.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes that when God's glory becomes manifest — when His presence and power become visible — worship erupts inevitably. The nations sing because they see and experience God's actual presence. In Restoration theology, kavod is what Moses and Joseph Smith saw in their theophanic visions — the actual, tangible, glorified presence of God.

word_study.meaning: The covenantal name of God, revealed to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14-15). YHWH means 'I AM' or 'the one who causes to be' — God as the source and sustainer of all existence.
word_study.significance: The glory that impels universal singing is the glory of YHWH specifically, the covenantal God who bound Himself to Israel and, through Christ, to all humanity. This is not abstract divinity but the God who acts, promises, and reveals Himself.

cross_references.connection: Prophesies 'the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together' — the same vision as verse 5 that God's manifest presence will eventually be perceived universally, producing worship.
David sings 'I will sing unto thee among the nations...thy mercy and thy truth' — the identical vision of singing God's character (ways, mercy, truth) among the peoples.
Describes God's glory appearing on Mount Sinai and Israel witnessing it — the paradigm of how perceiving God's glory produces fear, worship, and acknowledgment.
The heavenly vision of the throne room in which all creation sings worship: 'Thou art worthy, O Lord' — the eschatological fulfillment of verse 5's vision of universal singing of God's glory.

Joseph Smith's vision: 'We saw the glory of the Son, on the right hand of the Father, and received of his fulness' — a Restoration theophany in which seeing God's glory produces testimony and worship.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite theology and practice, singing was a primary mode of worship and theological expression. The Psalter itself is a collection of songs, many designated for Temple worship and festivals. Archaeological evidence from ancient Near Eastern sources shows that singing was understood as a powerful form of both prayer and proclamation — the words sung were believed to carry spiritual weight and to participate in the divine order. The vision of verse 5 — that all nations will eventually sing the ways of the LORD — reflects the Israelite conviction that worship and knowledge of God would ultimately be universal, despite the current reality of a world filled with other gods and kingdoms. This was grounded not in naive optimism but in the conviction that God's glory, when fully revealed, would be undeniable and would compel worship from all quarters. The phrase 'the ways of the LORD' was familiar in Israel from the wisdom literature and from the teaching of the Torah — it referred to the revealed patterns of God's action and character that Israel had experienced and could recount.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 5:33 describes the righteous 'singing the song of redeeming love' — a Book of Mormon affirmation that perceiving God's glory and redemption produces joyful singing. 2 Nephi 22:2 similarly declares 'Behold, God is my salvation...therefore with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation' — joy and singing as the response to God's salvation and glory.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 65:11 contains the vision 'That the glory of God may be proclaimed upon the earth' — the same vision as verse 5. D&C 76:19 records Joseph Smith's account: 'the glory of the Lord was upon me' — when the glory becomes perceptible, worship is the inevitable response. D&C 128:22 includes a hymn-like passage celebrating God's ways and glory, reflecting verse 5's pattern of singing the ways of the Lord.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In Temple worship, participants witness symbolic representations of God's glory (the veil, the celestial room, the ordinances) and respond with covenantal commitment and internal praise. The Temple hymns sung during endowment sessions are, in essence, singing 'the ways of the Lord' — celebrating God's character and plan. The Latter-day Saint hymnbook, shaped by Joseph Smith's theology, contains numerous hymns that sing of God's ways and character, fulfilling verse 5's vision within the covenant community.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ's glorification (His resurrection and ascension) is the means by which God's glory becomes manifest to all creation. John 17:1 records Christ's intercessory prayer: 'Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee.' Christ's glorification is the cosmic event that produces universal worship described in verse 5. Revelation 5:13-14 depicts the vision of Christ's glory drawing all creation into song: 'Blessing, and honour, and glory, and power, be unto him that sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb for ever and ever.' The singing of the nations in verse 5 reaches its fulfillment when all creation sings to Christ and perceives His glory as the manifest presence and power of God incarnate.
commentary.application: For modern believers, verse 5 is a call to joyful song and to help others perceive God's glory. Practically: (1) Sing — in sacrament meeting, in personal worship, in family home evening. Singing coordinates the whole person in praise and helps internalize theological truth. (2) Sing about 'the ways of the Lord' — the doctrines, the principles, the character of God as revealed in scripture and personal experience. Share with others how God has acted in your life. (3) Help others perceive God's glory. When you share your testimony, use language and examples that make God's presence tangible and real, not abstract. (4) Recognize that perceiving God's glory is transformative — when people genuinely encounter God's actual presence or power, worship erupts. Seek experiences where you perceive God's reality (temple, nature, personal revelation), and let those experiences produce genuine thanksgiving and praise. (5) Sing with others — communal singing of God's character creates unity and shared testimony. The promise is that eventually all nations will sing together; the Church is the foretaste of that universal worship.

text_kjv: Though the LORD be high, yet hath he respect unto the lowly: but the proud he knoweth afar off.

commentary.narrative:
The final verse of Psalm 138 contains the theological climax and the psalm's central truth. It articulates the paradox that stands at the heart of biblical faith: God is exalted — 'high' (ram) — yet this height does not produce distance from those who are humbled and lowered (shafal). Instead, the opposite occurs. God sees the humble; He watches over them; He responds to them. But the proud and haughty (gavohah) — those who think their position or status brings them closer to God — actually find themselves at a distance (merchaq) from God. God knows them 'from afar,' which the Covenant Rendering renders as 'from a distance,' suggesting not omniscient knowledge but relational remoteness. The proud are kept at arm's length.

This verse inverts every human assumption about status and proximity to God. The world teaches that height, power, wealth, and prominence bring influence and access. The psalm declares the opposite: height and pride create distance from God, while lowliness and humility create closeness. The fundamental logic is theological anthropology: God's nature as supremely exalted does not lead Him to identify with the exalted but with the lowly. Why? Because God is great (kavod, glory), and only those who recognize their own smallness can see God as He truly is. Those who maintain a sense of importance, who defend their status, who refuse to be 'brought low' (shafal) cannot perceive God's actual greatness.

This verse also resolves the entire psalm's movement: the individual gives thanks (v. 1-3) because his soul was 'made spacious' (tarhiveni) by God's answer — he was made humble enough to see that his strength came from God, not from himself. Because God saw his need and answered, all the kings of the earth eventually will perceive God's word and glory (v. 4-5). The lowly — those who acknowledge their dependence on God — inherit the earth and the kingdom of heaven, while the proud, despite their earthly power, find themselves separated from the source of true power. This is the reversal that defines God's justice.

word_study.meaning: High, elevated, lofty, or exalted. Applied to God, this indicates supreme position, transcendence, and authority. God is positioned above all creation.
word_study.significance: The psalmist does not minimize God's transcendence. God is genuinely high and distant in the cosmic sense. The paradox is that this height does not create relational distance from the humble.

word_study.meaning: From the root ra'ah, meaning to see, perceive, or look upon. When God sees someone, He does not merely observe; He pays attention, acknowledges, and acts on their behalf. This is not distant observation but engaged awareness.
word_study.significance: God's 'seeing' the lowly is not passive but active care. To be 'seen' by God is to be cared for and responded to. The lowly are not invisible to God despite their social invisibility; rather, God gives them particular attention.

word_study.meaning: Low, lowly, brought low, or humbled. This describes both literal physical lowness and metaphorical spiritual humility or circumstantial lowliness (poverty, weakness, affliction). Those whom the world overlooks and diminishes are shafal.
word_study.significance: The psalmist uses a term that describes the actual social condition of the poor and weak, not merely an internal attitude. God's attention to the lowly extends to the materially poor, the socially marginalized, the suffering — all whom human society devalues. In Restoration theology, this connects to the doctrine that God's covenant is particularly directed toward the poor and marginalized (cf. D&C 35:13-14).

word_study.meaning: High, lofty, or proud. Unlike ram (high in position), gavohah specifically describes an inner state of pride and haughtiness — a refusal to acknowledge smallness or dependence. The proud one maintains a posture of self-sufficiency and superiority.
word_study.significance: Pride, in biblical terms, is not healthy self-esteem but a spiritual delusion: the illusion that one's importance is self-generated or independent of God. It is the refusal to be 'brought low' (shafal), to admit need or dependence.

word_study.meaning: Merchaq means 'distance, far away'; yeda means 'to know.' The phrase is ambiguous: God knows the proud from a distance (omniscience), or God keeps the proud at a distance (relational separation). The Covenant Rendering and most scholars lean toward the latter: God deliberately maintains distance from the proud.
word_study.significance: God's knowledge of the proud is not the warm, engaged knowing (yada) that describes intimate covenant relationship. Rather, it is the knowledge of one who sees but does not draw near, who maintains boundaries. The proud are kept at arm's length by God because they will not humble themselves to enter into covenant dependence.

cross_references.connection: Directly quotes this verse (or Proverbs 3:34) in the New Testament: 'God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.' Confirms that verse 6's principle is foundational NT theology.
Repeats the same principle: 'God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace to the humble' — the gospel affirmation of verse 6's reversal of human status hierarchies.
God declares 'I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit' — God's height and accessibility to the humble, matching verse 6's paradox.
Joseph Smith's vision reveals that God extends His presence to those who are humble and poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3), withholding from those who exalt themselves in pride.
Nephi refuses to murmur and maintains humility before God despite hardship, contrasting with Laman and Lemuel's pride — exemplifying verse 6's principle that humility brings divine response.

commentary.historical_context: Verse 6 articulates what scholars call 'the theology of reversal' — a central theme in both ancient Israelite wisdom literature and emerging Second Temple Judaism. This theology appears in the wisdom psalms, in Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:3-8), and in Jesus's teachings (the last shall be first, Matthew 19:30). It directly challenged the ancient near Eastern assumption that divine blessing followed social status: the king and the mighty were naturally favored by the gods; the poor and weak were disfavored. Israel's theology inverted this: the widow, the orphan, the poor — those whom society despised — were the particular concern of the one true God. This was not sentimentalism but a revolutionary claim about God's nature. It explains Israel's continued existence and identity even after losing political independence and being exiled: God's covenant was not with the nation's power structures but with the faithful remnant, often composed of the powerless and dispossessed. By the Second Temple period, reflected in texts like the Psalms of Solomon and the Dead Sea Scrolls, this theology had become even more pronounced. The 'poor' (anawim) or 'humble' (anavim) became self-designations for the faithful, pious, covenant community in contrast to the wicked and arrogant.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 32:12-16 teaches that humility and poverty are prerequisites for faith: 'Now ye may suppose that this is foolishness...But I say unto you that by small and simple things are great things brought to pass.' The humble receive divine instruction; the proud remain closed to revelation. The entire Book of Mormon emphasizes that God's covenant is with the humble and faithful remnant, not with the politically powerful.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 35:13-14 states that God's covenant is with 'the poor and the meek' and that He will 'exalt them in the last days.' D&C 112:10 warns against pride and exhorts to humility. D&C 133:57 prophesies that 'the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to restore his people' — not through the powerful but through the faithful remnant of the humble. Joseph Smith emphasized that the priesthood is not about power or status but about humble service.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In Temple worship, all participants, regardless of earthly status, wear the same white clothing and assume the same postures of submission (kneeling, bowing). The Temple rituals explicitly teach the reversal of verse 6: earthly power and status are left at the veil, and all enter equally as children of God before the altar. The Temple endowment traces the journey of humanity from exaltation and pride (Satan's rebellion) to the eventual humility required for celestial glory. Exaltation, in Latter-day Saint theology, is granted to those who become 'as a little child' (Matthew 18:3) — those who acknowledge complete dependence on and submission to God.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the ultimate exemplar of verse 6. Though Christ was 'in the form of God' and 'thought it not robbery to be equal with God' (Philippians 2:6), He 'humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross' (Philippians 2:8). Christ's incarnation, suffering, death, and resurrection are the ultimate demonstration that God is 'high' yet identifies with the lowly. Christ came not to the powerful and proud but to 'the captives, the blind...the bruised, and...liberty to them that are bruised' (Luke 4:18). Christ's parable of the Pharisee and the publican (Luke 18:10-14) explicitly teaches verse 6: the proud Pharisee, who trusts in his own righteousness, goes home unjustified; the humble publican, who 'would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast,' receives justification. The crucifixion itself enacts verse 6 cosmically: the proud and powerful condemn Jesus to death, thinking they have won; but God raises Christ from the dead and exalts Him to the right hand of power — the ultimate reversal. All creation's worship, described in verses 4-5, is ultimately worship of the humble crucified and risen Christ.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 6 is both a comfort and a call to repentance. Practically: (1) Examine your own heart for pride. Pride is the subtle conviction that your status, accomplishments, or intelligence makes you self-sufficient or removes your need to depend on God. It is the antidote to genuine faith. (2) If you are in a position of earthly power or status (professional, social, financial), be vigilant against the pride that power breeds. Remember that God 'knoweth the proud afar off' — distance from God is the consequence of pride, no matter how successful you appear. (3) Cultivate genuine humility by acknowledging your complete dependence on God daily. This is not self-deprecation but truthfulness: without God, you have no being, no capability, no redemption. (4) Welcome your seasons of weakness, poverty, or social lowliness as opportunities to become 'shafal' (brought low) in a way that opens you to God's intimate attention. God sees those whom the world overlooks; draw near to God through humility, and you will experience His regard. (5) In leadership (family, ward, workplace), use your position to identify and honor the lowly and marginalized, reflecting God's own attention to those whom society overlooks. (6) Teach your children that true power comes through humility and covenantal dependence on God, not through dominating others or accumulating status. The promise is that those who are brought low and humble themselves will eventually be exalted — not in the world's hierarchy but in God's eternal order.

text_kjv: Though I walk in the midst of trouble, thou wilt revive me: thou shalt stretch forth thine hand against the wrath of mine enemies, and thy right hand shall save me.

commentary.narrative:
The psalmist moves from public acknowledgment of God's name (verses 1-3) and confident rejoicing (verses 4-6) into the lived reality of suffering. This verse is the turning point where theology becomes biography. The psalmist does not claim exemption from trouble—he walks *through* it, *in the midst* of it (be-qerev tsarah), surrounded by danger. The verb techayeni ('you keep me alive') is not metaphorical: in the thick of mortal threat, God sustains life itself. This is not poetic flourish but the core covenant promise—that God's presence in the middle of suffering is not distant comfort but active sustenance.

The imagery shifts from walking to divine action: God stretches out His hand (shaluach yad) against the wrath of enemies. The hand of God is the instrument of covenant power throughout Scripture—it rescues, guards, and accomplishes. Here it is stretched *against* the enemies' rage (al aph oyveay), not merely for the psalmist's sake but in direct opposition to those who oppose God's people. The right hand (yeminekha), throughout the Psalms and the entire Hebrew Bible, is the hand of power, majesty, and salvation. The promise is not defense—it is decisive intervention.

word_study.meaning: The verb haleekh means 'to walk, to go, to live one's life.' The preposition be-qerev ('in the midst, in the thick of') places the subject inside the trouble, not approaching it, not remembering it past, but actively walking through it. This is immersion, not proximity.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering captures this: 'walk through the thick of trouble.' The psalmist is not on the edge of danger but in its center. This establishes the condition for the covenant promise: God meets us not at the perimeter of our struggles but at their heart.

word_study.meaning: From chayah ('to live, to keep alive, to revive'). The verb can mean physical revival from death-like condition or spiritual quickening. In the context of walking through trouble, it carries both: God restores life when death is near.
word_study.significance: This is not resurrection but resuscitation—the ongoing gift of life in the middle of threat. Covenant language: God commits not to rescue from trouble after the fact but to sustain life *while* walking through it. The tense suggests continuous action: 'You keep me alive.'

word_study.meaning: From yamin ('right, right side'). Throughout the Psalms and OT, the right hand is the hand of power, favor, and salvific action. Sitting at God's right hand is the place of greatest honor and authority (e.g., Psalm 110:1).
word_study.significance: God's right hand is not merely a symbol but the operative instrument of salvation. When the psalmist says 'Your right hand shall save me,' he invokes God's covenant commitment to act with full divine power on his behalf.

cross_references.connection: Though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me. Both verses assert God's sustaining presence in the midst of danger, not deliverance from it.

Help me, O LORD my God; O save me according to thy mercy. That they may know that this is thy hand; that thou, LORD, hast done it. Both verses depict God's hand as the instrument of salvation and a sign of His covenant care.

Thy right hand, O LORD, is become glorious in power: thy right hand, O LORD, hath dashed in pieces the enemy. The right hand as the operative power of God against enemies is established in the exodus narrative, the foundational covenant act.

Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God... my right hand of righteousness shall uphold thee. Both verses combine the promise of God's presence ('I am with thee') with the specific assurance of His right hand's support.

And now, after the many testimonies which have been given of him, this is the testimony, last of all, which we give of him: That he lives! For we saw him, even on the right hand of God. The Restoration confirms the right hand as the place of divine power and presence.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern covenant literature, the 'hand' of the deity was understood as the physical manifestation of divine will and power. Sumerian, Akkadian, and Egyptian texts depict gods stretching out their hands to protect vassals or strike enemies. The psalmist draws on this ancient imagery but personalizes it: he does not invoke an abstract divine principle but the covenant God of Israel, who has demonstrated His power through history (exodus, settlement, kingship). The phrase 'wrath of enemies' (aph oyveay) reflects the real experience of the Israelite community—threatened by neighboring peoples and internal adversaries. The promise that God would 'stretch forth His hand against the wrath' would have resonated with historical memory of deliverance: the plagues against Egypt (God's hand), the parting of the sea, the conquest of Canaan. The psalmist stands within a tradition of covenant theology where God is not a distant power but an active defender of His people.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 7:11-12 describes Christ taking upon Him the infirmities and sicknesses of His people. The promise in Psalm 138:7 that God 'keeps alive' those walking through trouble finds its fullest fulfillment in Christ's atonement—He walks through our sorrows with us, sustaining us by His power.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 78:18 states: 'For if ye are faithful in keeping my commandments, ye shall be blessed with abundance.' The promise of Psalm 138:7 that God's right hand saves the faithful connects to the Restoration principle that covenant faithfulness brings divine protection and sustenance. D&C 109:22 (Kirtland Temple prayer) affirms: 'That all things may work together for good to them that love thee.' God's completion of His work (verse 8, following) is assured for the faithful.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple theology, God's hand is the instrument of sealing and binding. The psalmist's confidence that God's hand will save him echoes the sealed member's trust that God's hand is extended to sustain and protect. The right hand of God in temple imagery represents the fullness of divine power and exaltation available to the faithful.

commentary.christological_typology: Psalm 138:7 prefigures Christ's descent into suffering on behalf of humanity. Just as the psalmist walks through trouble and is kept alive by God's hand, Christ walked through the valley of death and was sustained by His Father's power. Hebrews 2:14-18 depicts Christ taking on flesh and entering into human suffering to be a merciful and faithful high priest. The image of God's right hand stretching forth against enemies points to Christ's victorious resurrection and ascension to God's right hand (Psalm 110:1; Acts 2:33), where He intercedes for His people and extends covenant power on their behalf.
commentary.application: This verse exposes a false dichotomy many members hold: that faith means either exemption from suffering or abandonment by God. Psalm 138:7 declares a third option—God's presence and power *in the midst of* trouble. The application is concrete: when walking through illness, betrayal, doubt, or grief, the covenant promise is not that these will disappear but that God sustains life through them. His hand is actively at work against the 'wrath of enemies'—whether these are external persecutors, internal despair, or the enemy of our souls. The promise of God's right hand is not passive comfort but active intervention. A modern reader can pray this verse not as a promise of escape but as a claim on covenant care in the middle of the valley: God keeps me alive here, now, in this trouble, and His power is actively at work on my behalf.

text_kjv: The LORD will perfect that which concerneth me: thy mercy, O LORD, endureth for ever: forsake not the works of thine own hands.

commentary.narrative:
This final verse of Psalm 138 is a crescendo of theological confidence that moves from the specific (God's completion of my personal journey) to the universal (His mercy endures forever) to the intimate (He will not abandon the works of His hands). The verb yigmor ('will complete, will finish') carries profound weight in covenant theology: God does not begin and abandon. Whatever He has started in the psalmist's life—however fragmented, unfinished, or threatened by enemies—He will see through to completion. This is not optimistic thinking but the very logic of covenant relationship. God has made an investment in the psalmist; He has shaped him; therefore, He is bound by His own nature to see the work finished.

The second statement—'Your faithful love endures forever'—is the refrain from Psalm 136, now made personal. Chasdekha ('Your faithful love, Your covenant mercy') is not sentimental emotion but the steady, binding commitment that holds the covenant in place. It is not temporary or conditional; it endures le-olam ('forever, to eternity'). This shifts the focus from the psalmist's individual crisis to the character of God Himself: the grounds for confidence are not in the psalmist's strength or worthiness but in God's unchanging nature.

The third statement is the most intimate: 'Do not let go of the works of Your hands.' The image is of God as a craftsman holding His creation and the psalmist pleading with Him not to open His hands and let the work drop. The verb teref (from raphah, 'to let go, to relax, to abandon') in the negative imperative (al teref, 'do not release') makes the logic irresistible: if God made me, He is invested in me; if He is invested, He will not let go. The psalmist identifies himself as God's handiwork—ma'asei yadekha ('the works of Your hands'). This is radical vulnerability and radical confidence combined: I am entirely dependent on what God has made me to be, and precisely because I am His work, He will not abandon me.

word_study.meaning: From gamar ('to complete, to finish, to bring to an end, to accomplish'). The verb asserts that God is not a God of half-measures. What He begins, He finishes. Applied to God's work in a human life, it promises that no good work remains incomplete under God's care.
word_study.significance: This verb undergirds the entire psalm's confidence: the psalmist trusts not in his own ability to persevere but in God's commitment to finish what He started. The future tense (yigmor) expresses certainty grounded in God's nature, not in circumstances. This is one of the deepest promises in the Psalter: God sees the work through to the end.

word_study.meaning: From chesed ('covenant mercy, faithful love, steadfast kindness'). Not emotion but binding commitment. Chesed is the love that holds covenant together—it is merciful not because circumstances warrant it but because the covenant demands it. Le-olam ('forever, to eternity') intensifies this: God's chesed is not temporary or contingent but eternal.
word_study.significance: Chesed is the foundation word of the Hebrew covenant relationship. The psalmist invokes this not as a request but as a testimony: God's covenant faithfulness endures. This is the answer to 'Will God really sustain me through suffering?' Yes—because His chesed is eternal and covenant-binding.

word_study.meaning: Ma'asei means 'deeds, works, acts.' Yadekha means 'Your hands' (yad = 'hand'). The phrase denotes what God has fashioned, created, or accomplished. In this context, the psalmist identifies himself as belonging to this category: he is something God has made.
word_study.significance: To call oneself 'the works of your hands' is to claim divine craftsmanship as one's identity. The psalmist is not self-made; he is God-made. This is the theological ground for the plea: do not let go of what You Yourself have created. God's investment in His work binds Him to complete it.

word_study.term_english: forsake not / do not let go
word_study.meaning: From raphah ('to let go, to relax, to release, to abandon'). The negative imperative al teref means 'do not release, do not let drop, do not abandon.' The image is visceral: God holding something He has made, and the psalmist begging Him not to open His hands.
word_study.significance: This is one of the most intimate images of divine care in the Psalter—God as the craftsman holding His own work. The plea is grounded in logic: abandoning one's own creation would be contrary to God's nature as Creator. The covenant promise is built into the act of creation itself.

cross_references.connection: Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ. Paul applies the promise of gamar ('completion') to Christian sanctification: God will finish what He started.

The entire Psalm 136 echoes with the refrain 'for his mercy endureth for ever.' Verse 8 borrows this affirmation and makes it personal: the eternal mercy that sustained Israel as a people sustains the individual psalmist.

Even every one that is called by my name: for I have created him for my glory, I have formed him; yea, I have made him. Like Psalm 138:8, this verse establishes that God's creative act binds Him to His creation. He has made us for His glory; therefore, He will not abandon us.

And now, verily I say unto you, that through you the oracles shall be given to this generation; and in this you are blessed... for all things are subject unto me, but charity is the greatest. God's completion of His work in His people is tied to the covenant relationship (D&C 88:22-23, expanded).

Now my son, I desire that ye should refrain from your sins. For the Lord hath said that no unclean thing can enter into his kingdom; therefore how can ye be saved, except ye inherit the kingdom of God? The Book of Mormon affirms that God's work of completing His people requires their covenant fidelity.

And he loveth those who will have him to be their God; and behold, he suffereth the righteous that they may gain his kingdom. God's loving completion of His work in His people is dependent on covenant commitment.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern royal inscriptions, the language of completion (Akkadian gam-ru, 'to finish, to complete') was used of kings building temples or accomplishing military campaigns. The rhetorical force was: what I have begun, I will finish—this is a sign of my power and sovereignty. The psalmist applies this royal language to God's work in an individual human life. This represents a democratization of the royal promise: not just the king, but every covenant member can claim that God will complete His work in them. The image of God as a craftsman (yad = 'hand,' denoting skilled creation) draws on the ancient Near Eastern concept of divine artisanship—the gods fashioning the world and humanity from clay. The psalmist's plea that God not 'let go' of His handiwork evokes the imagery of divine custody and care: the God who made you holds you in His hands. This was especially comforting to Israel during exile (the historical context of many psalms): even when far from the temple and kingdom, individual Israelites could trust that God held them in His creative grip.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Moroni 10:32 states: 'Yea, come unto Christ, and be perfected in him, and deny yourselves of all ungodliness; and if ye shall deny yourselves of all ungodliness, and love God with all your might, mind and strength, then is his grace sufficient for you, that by his grace ye may be perfect in Christ.' This is the Book of Mormon's rendering of what yigmor ('completion') means: Christ perfects us, but this completion requires our covenant participation. 2 Nephi 25:23 affirms: 'For we labor diligently to write, to persuade our children, and also our brethren, to believe in Christ, and to be reconciled to God; for we know that it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do.' Grace completes what human effort cannot.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 27:13-14 contains a powerful covenantal promise: 'Wherefore, stand ye in the liberty wherewith ye are made free, and refrain from sin, that Christ may not lift up his voice against you at that awful day. And in that day ye shall do my will, for I will pour out my Spirit upon all them that believe in my name.' God's completion of His work includes the pouring out of the Spirit—the infilling that sustains covenant members. D&C 84:38 promises: 'Therefore, let thy voice and all thy teachings be established, that there may be no more contentions, and that all things may be gathered into one; that when I come I may find faith.' God completes the work of gathering and establishing faith.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, God covenants to receive us as His eternal family—His work of creation and exaltation. The endowment confirms that we are 'the works of Your hands,' sealed by priesthood authority to God's eternal family. The plea 'forsake not the works of Thine hands' echoes in temple language: God will not release or abandon those sealed to Him. Exaltation is the ultimate completion (gamar) of God's work—bringing His children to eternal life with Him.

commentary.christological_typology: Psalm 138:8 points to Christ as the ultimate completion of God's work. Christ is described in Hebrews 10:14 as the one who 'hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.' The promise that God will complete what concerns us finds its fulfillment in Christ's atoning work, which completes the law and makes possible eternal progress. Colossians 1:15-20 portrays Christ as 'the image of the invisible God... and by him all things consist.' Christ is both the means by which God's work is completed and the proof that God does not abandon His handiwork. His incarnation is God saying: 'I will not let go of My creation.' His resurrection is the assurance that what God has made will not be left incomplete or lost to death. In John 19:30, Christ's final utterance—'It is finished' (tetelestai, 'completed')—is the ultimate enactment of the promise in Psalm 138:8: God's work is completed through the Atonement.
commentary.application: This verse is for members in seasons of incompleteness—spiritual struggles that feel unresolved, sins that feel unforgiven, wounds that seem unhealable, vocations that feel stalled, or relationships that are broken. The covenant promise is radical: God is not a God of half-measures. What He has started in you, He will finish. You are not the project He will abandon. But the promise carries an implicit condition: it applies to those who remain in covenant with Him ('Your faithful love endures forever' speaks to mutual commitment). The modern application is to stop trying to perfect yourself by your own effort and instead trust that God's chesed ('faithful love') is bound to complete you. This is the difference between self-improvement and sanctification. Self-improvement says, 'I must do better.' Sanctification says, 'God has started a work in me, and He will finish it if I remain covenant-faithful.' The plea 'forsake not the works of Thine hands' is not a fearful begging but a grounded claim: I am God's handiwork, sealed in covenant, and He will not let go. This is especially powerful for those who feel themselves falling apart—spiritually, emotionally, or morally. The remedy is not self-recrimination but a return to covenant and a trust that God holds you in His creative grip.

text_kjv: O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me.

commentary.narrative: Psalm 139 opens with one of Scripture's most profound claims about divine knowledge. The psalmist addresses God directly and immediately establishes the central theme: God has searched him exhaustively and knows him completely. The verb 'searched' (chaqar in Hebrew) carries the sense of deliberate, thorough investigation—the kind of deep excavation a miner performs to extract precious ore from the earth. This is not passing acquaintance or surface observation. The psalmist has been subjected to divine scrutiny that reaches into the deepest places of his being. The second verb, 'known,' affirms that this search has reached its conclusion; God's investigation is complete, and the result is comprehensive knowledge. Together, these two verbs establish that the psalmist stands before a God who is neither distant nor ignorant, but intimately and exhaustively familiar with him.
commentary.narrative_continued: The choice to open the psalm with direct address—'O LORD'—is significant. The psalmist is not theorizing about God's omniscience in the abstract. He is confessing a personal reality: God has searched *me*, and God knows *me*. This moves the doctrine of divine knowledge from theological proposition to lived experience. The psalmist is not defensive or evasive; instead, he launches into this confession with a kind of wonder mixed with vulnerability. He acknowledges that he stands before One who sees everything—every hidden thing, every secret motive, every unspoken thought. This opening sets the emotional and spiritual tone for the entire psalm: awe in the face of divine omniscience, coupled with the paradoxical comfort that this all-seeing God still addresses him.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: In the ancient Near Eastern context, kings and gods were said to 'know' their subjects—meaning they had authority over them and understood their affairs. But the language here reverses the power dynamic subtly: it is God who searches the psalmist, not the psalmist who seeks God. The psalmist is the object of divine investigation. Yet this vulnerability does not produce distance or alienation in the psalm; rather, the tone oscillates between fear and intimacy. The reader should recognize that the psalmist is grappling with a mystery: how can I bear being so completely known? And yet, paradoxically, how can I survive being unknown to the God who made me?

word_study.meaning: to search, investigate, probe, explore thoroughly; used of mining precious metals from the earth (Job 28:3), of examining a matter closely (Proverbs 25:2), and of God's investigation of persons. The root implies depth and systematic thoroughness—not a glance but an excavation.
word_study.significance: The verb establishes that God's knowledge is not superficial or incomplete. He has gone to the deepest layers of the psalmist's being. The Covenant Rendering's choice to render this as 'searched' rather than 'known' preserves the active, investigative quality of the Hebrew verb. In LDS theology, this aligns with the doctrine that God's knowledge extends to all things, past, present, and future (D&C 38:2), and that He is acquainted with all our thoughts and intents (Alma 18:32).

word_study.meaning: to know, to be acquainted with, to perceive, to recognize. In its completed form (vatteda), it indicates that knowledge has reached its full state—God has investigated and now possesses complete knowledge. The verb can mean cognitive knowledge, relational intimacy, or both.
word_study.significance: The combination of 'searched' and 'known' creates a temporal sequence: first investigation, then complete knowledge. The psalmist is not claiming that God merely observes; he claims that God has come to know him in his totality. This dual verb structure emphasizes both the process (search) and the result (knowing). In Hebrew, yada often carries intimate, relational connotations—to 'know' one's spouse, to 'know' God's ways. Here, God's knowledge of the psalmist is personal, not mechanical.

cross_references.connection: The psalmist again marvels that God 'knowest' him and takes account of him, expressing wonder at divine attention to a finite human being. This creates a bookend to Psalm 139's opening affirmation of God's exhaustive knowledge.

King Lamoni's servant explains that God 'knoweth all the thoughts and intents of the heart,' a direct application of Psalm 139's claim to the Book of Mormon context. God's knowledge extends not just to actions but to inner thoughts.

The Lord affirms that He 'knoweth all things, and there is not anything save I know it.' This modern revelation reiterates the omniscience proclaimed in Psalm 139:1, grounding it in Restoration doctrine.
The prophet echoes the psalmist's theme: 'Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the LORD' — affirming that God's presence and knowledge are inescapable and universal.

The New Testament declares that God's word 'is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart...neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight.' This links divine omniscience to judgment and accountability.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern world, a god's 'knowing' a person was considered a mark of favor and authority. Egyptian texts describe the pharaoh as 'known' by the gods; similarly, Mesopotamian texts speak of deities who 'know' their worshippers. However, Psalm 139 inverts this: the God of Israel does not merely 'know' the psalmist in the sense of recognizing his status or role. Rather, God has conducted an exhaustive investigation into the psalmist's entire being—his thoughts, movements, and hidden places. This represents a uniquely Israelite understanding of divine omniscience: not as distant, administrative knowledge, but as intimate, penetrating knowledge. The language of 'searching' and 'knowing' would have resonated with Israelite subjects who lived under a king's authority and were subject to judgment. To stand before such a God was simultaneously to experience awe (fear of judgment) and comfort (the assurance of being known by the one true God rather than abandoned or invisible).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, this doctrine appears repeatedly. Alma teaches that the Lord 'knoweth all the thoughts and intents of the heart' (Alma 18:32), and Nephi speaks of God's ability to perceive 'all things, both past, present, and future' (1 Nephi 9:6). The Book of Mormon emphasizes that no sin can be hidden from God (Alma 12:3), which reiterates the psalmist's vulnerability before divine knowledge. Yet it also affirms that God's knowledge is paired with mercy and redemption through Christ.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:2 ('I know all things') and D&C 35:3 establish that the God revealed in the Restoration possesses the same omniscience proclaimed in Psalm 139. Furthermore, D&C 88:41 teaches that light is the medium of God's knowledge: 'The light shineth in darkness, and the darkness comprehendeth it not...the light is in all things, and giveth light to all things.' This suggests that God's ability to 'search' is bound up with His fundamental nature as light and intelligence. Joseph Smith taught that 'God is a being of complete knowledge and perfect understanding' and that intelligence is eternal matter organized by God's power (D&C 93:29-36).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, the covenant member stands before God in a state of nakedness and vulnerability—a bodily enactment of the spiritual truth expressed in Psalm 139:1. The rituals of the temple align the member with the psalmist's confession: before God, one cannot hide; all is known. The temple also teaches that this complete knowledge, rather than producing shame and rejection, becomes the basis for transformation through covenants. One stands known and fully seen, and then is clothed in new garments—suggesting that divine omniscience, though potentially overwhelming, is paired with divine acceptance and redemption.

commentary.christological_typology: In the Psalter's narrative structure, verses that emphasize God's complete knowledge often prefigure Christ, who in the New Testament is revealed as the One who 'knoweth all things' (John 21:17). Jesus embodies the psalmist's wonder at divine omniscience—He reads the thoughts of the Pharisees (Matthew 12:25), knows what is in man (John 2:25), and calls people by names that reveal His penetrating knowledge of their hearts (as with Peter, Nathanael, and the Samaritan woman). Psalm 139's theme of being searched and known finds its ultimate referent in the consciousness of Christ, who sees into all hearts and who came not to condemn but to call sinners to repentance (John 3:17). For the Christian reader, confessing that God has searched and known him means recognizing in that divine gaze the eyes of the incarnate Christ.
commentary.application: Modern members of the Church live in an age of unprecedented information collection and surveillance. Psalm 139:1 invites believers to redirect their anxiety about being 'tracked' or 'known' by earthly systems toward a reckoning with the more ultimate reality: they are already fully known by God. This knowledge should produce not paranoia but peace. If God has searched you and knows you completely—including your struggles, doubts, and hidden sins—and has nevertheless provided a Savior and invited you into His covenant, then you are truly loved. The application is to stop hiding. Confess what is already known. Seek forgiveness from the One who sees you completely. And paradoxically, in surrendering the exhausting effort to hide from God, one finds freedom and rest. This verse also challenges shallow repentance: you cannot fool God with outward conformity when your heart remains unchanged. But it also offers hope: there is nothing about you—nothing in your past, nothing in your secret thoughts, nothing in your deepest shame—that God has not already seen and accounted for in His plan of mercy.

text_kjv: Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising: thou understandest my thought afar off.

commentary.narrative: Having announced that God has searched and known him (verse 1), the psalmist now provides the first set of concrete examples of what this comprehensive knowledge entails. The verb 'knowest' (yada) appears again, now applied to the most ordinary, daily aspects of human existence: sitting and rising. This is not poetic hyperbole; it is a deliberate choice of the most mundane activities to make a radical point. Between every moment of sitting down and standing up lies the entirety of human daily life. The psalmist is using a merism—a figure of speech that encompasses the whole by naming opposite extremes—to claim that God's knowledge covers every instant of the psalmist's waking existence. When I rest, God knows it. When I rise, God knows it. Nothing escapes His notice.
commentary.narrative_continued: The second half of the verse shifts the focus inward: 'thou understandest my thought afar off.' The word 'thought' (re'i in Hebrew) is ambiguous and theologically rich. It can mean 'thought, purpose, intention' or derive from a root meaning 'to shepherd, to tend.' Either reading is profound. If it means 'thought,' then God understands the inner workings of the psalmist's mind—his deliberations, intentions, and plans—and He knows them from 'afar off' (me-rachoq), meaning not merely from a distance in space but from a distance in time. God knows the thought before the psalmist fully forms it. If re'i derives from 'shepherd,' then God tends the psalmist's thoughts as a shepherd tends sheep, caring for them and directing them. Both readings affirm that God's knowledge penetrates into the invisible realm of human consciousness and intention.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The verse thus establishes God's omniscience in two domains: the physical (sitting and rising) and the mental (thoughts and intentions). No part of the psalmist's existence—neither his outward actions nor his inward musings—escapes divine scrutiny. This creates a deepening sense of exposure. It is one thing to believe that God 'knows' in a general sense; it is another to confess that He knows when I sit, when I rise, and what I am thinking. The progression from verse 1 (God has searched and knows me) to verse 2 (God knows my every action and thought) moves from the abstract to the concrete, from the general to the specific. Each verse will continue this descent into ever-deeper layers of human interiority and vulnerability.

word_study.meaning: literally, 'my sitting and my rising.' Shavat means to sit, dwell, settle; qum means to rise, stand, get up. The merism encompasses all of human daily activity—everything from resting to acting.
word_study.significance: This is the classic Hebrew use of merism to express totality. Just as 'night and day' means 'all the time' or 'heaven and earth' means 'everything,' so 'sitting and rising' means the complete daily rhythm of human existence. By naming only these two opposite poles, the psalmist implies that everything in between—work, speech, thought, movement, rest—is also encompassed in God's knowledge. The Covenant Rendering preserves this meristic structure with 'sit' and 'rise,' which aids the English reader in recognizing the figure of speech.

word_study.meaning: Banta is 'You understand' or 'You perceive' (from binah, 'understanding, insight'). Re'i is ambiguous: it can mean 'my thought, my purpose, my intention' (from ra'ah in the sense of 'to consider') or it can mean 'my thought' in connection with shepherding (from ra'ah, 'to shepherd'). The root ambiguity is intentional in Hebrew poetry, allowing multiple layers of meaning simultaneously.
word_study.significance: Binah, understanding, suggests not just cognitive awareness but penetrating insight—the kind of understanding that comes from experience and relationship. To 'understand' the psalmist's thoughts is to grasp not just what he thinks but why, what it means, what it tends toward. The ambiguity of re'i enriches this: God both perceives the psalmist's inner thoughts AND tends them as a shepherd tends his flock. This makes divine omniscience not cold or distant but relational and caring. In the LDS context, this aligns with the teaching that God is not merely an observer but an active participant in the lives of His covenant people, guiding their thoughts and intentions toward righteousness.

word_study.meaning: from a distance, from far away. But in this context, it does not mean God is distant; rather, it means God knows the thought before it arrives, from a distance in time or in the process of forming.
word_study.significance: This phrase emphasizes God's foreknowledge and prescience. He does not wait for the thought to be completed and then know it; He knows it while it is still forming, 'from a distance.' This anticipatory knowledge—knowing what a person will think before they think it—is a mark of divine omniscience that exceeds merely observing present reality. In Restoration theology, this connects to God's ability to see all things (D&C 38:2) and to Joseph Smith's teaching that God dwells in the eternal now, where past, present, and future are equally present to His knowledge.

cross_references.connection: The eyes of the LORD are in every place, beholding the evil and the good.' Like Psalm 139:2, this affirms God's universal, constant surveillance of human action and moral character.

The LORD said to Samuel, 'I look on the heart,' in contrast to human judgment that looks 'on the outward appearance.' This aligns with Psalm 139:2's claim that God understands thoughts and intentions, not merely external conduct.
God 'knoweth all the thoughts and intents of the heart.' This Book of Mormon affirmation directly parallels the psalmist's claim in 139:2 that God understands his thoughts.
The word of God is 'a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.' The New Testament links God's omniscience to the power of His word to penetrate human consciousness.

The teachings recorded here affirm that God's knowledge extends to all things past, present, and future, providing the Restoration context for understanding Psalm 139:2's claim of God's anticipatory knowledge.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, as in many cultures, sitting and rising were not merely physical actions but symbolic of states of being. 'Sitting' often represented rest, judgment, or peace; 'rising' represented action, war, or engagement. The merism 'sitting and rising' thus encapsulates not just temporal continuity but the totality of a person's states and conditions. In the royal psalms and in the psalms of lament, the claim that God knows the worshipper's actions and thoughts would have had particular resonance for Israelites who lived under law codes and temple oversight. They were accustomed to accountability before authorities, but Psalm 139:2 moves accountability to a transcendent plane: God is the ultimate witness, the final authority on what one knows and intends. This would have been both comforting (God truly sees injustice and will judge it) and terrifying (no deception is possible). The psychological insight of the verse—that God knows not just what we do but what we think—represents a sophisticated understanding of moral accountability that reaches beyond mere behavior to the hidden intentions of the heart.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 2:24, Lehi teaches that the Lord 'remembereth all the covenants which he hath covenanted with our fathers,' suggesting a God whose memory (and thus knowledge) is comprehensive and faithful. In Alma 41:7, Alma affirms that 'all things shall be restored to their proper order...according to the justice and mercy of God,' implying that God knows and will account for all human thoughts and intents. The Book of Mormon consistently presents omniscience not as abstract doctrine but as the basis for divine justice and mercy toward individual persons.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:6-13 teaches that Christ is 'in all things, and through all things, and by him all things are made' and that 'the light which is in all things...giveth light to all things.' This provides a metaphysical basis for understanding how God can know all thoughts: because light (intelligence, consciousness) pervades all creation, and Christ as the source of that light knows all. D&C 6:16 promises 'I will tell you in your mind and in your heart, by the Holy Ghost'—suggesting that God's knowledge of and communication with His people reaches into the deepest recesses of consciousness. Section 121:45 teaches that righteous thoughts generate power in the heavens, implying that God is aware of and responsive to human thoughts.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony presents God as the ultimate witness who cannot be deceived. A member stands before the altar and covenants before Him; there is nowhere to hide, no room for insincerity. The temple encapsulates the truth of Psalm 139:2: God knows your sitting and your rising, your outward conformity and your inward intention. The covenant of truthfulness in the temple directly addresses the psalmist's insight that God knows thoughts and intents; the member pledges to align thought, word, and deed in integrity before God.

commentary.christological_typology: In Matthew 9:4, Jesus says to the Pharisees, 'Wherefore think ye evil in your hearts?' The Gospels repeatedly emphasize that Jesus 'knew what was in man' (John 2:25) and could read the thoughts of those around Him. This demonstrates that the divine omniscience described in Psalm 139:2 is embodied in the incarnate Christ. Jesus reads the heart as God reads the heart—He knows the internal disposition behind external action. For Christians, this means that Christ's knowledge of the psalmist in Psalm 139 is not abstract; it is the personal, searching knowledge of the One who came to call sinners to repentance and who offers redemption precisely because He knows us fully and loves us still.
commentary.application: In the modern world, where many people carefully curate their external image on social media while harboring private doubts, resentments, and lusts, Psalm 139:2 strikes with particular force. You cannot hide your thoughts from God. This verse calls the believer to radical honesty about their inner world—not to perfection, but to integrity. It is not enough to behave well outwardly if your thoughts are corrupt. Conversely, if your thoughts are genuinely turned toward God, no outward circumstance can separate you from Him. The application is to bring your whole self—thoughts, intentions, hidden struggles—into the presence of God in prayer and covenant. Stop the exhausting work of managing your image. Confess to God what He already knows. Invite Him to guide your thoughts toward truth and righteousness. This creates a condition of radical vulnerability before God that, paradoxically, produces freedom. When nothing is hidden, there is nothing to fear being discovered. And when you know that God knows your thoughts and still offers Himself as your refuge, faith becomes possible.

text_kjv: Thou compassest my path and my lying down, and art acquainted with all my ways.

commentary.narrative: The psalmist continues to specify the modes and dimensions of God's comprehensive knowledge, now employing two more concrete images that deepen the sense of divine surveillance. The verb 'compassest' typically means 'to go around, to encircle, to surround,' but here it is used in the sense of examining or scrutinizing closely. The TCR rendering, 'You sift my traveling and my resting,' captures the deeper Hebrew meaning: the verb is zerita, from the agricultural term for winnowing grain—sifting to separate the wheat from chaff. This image suggests that God does not merely observe the psalmist's path and resting; He sifts through them, examining them meticulously, extracting the significant from the insignificant, the pure from the impure. Nothing passes through this divine sieve unexamined.
commentary.narrative_continued: The words 'path and lying down' (orchi ve-riv'i) form another merism parallel to 'sitting and rising' in verse 2, but with subtle differences. 'Path' (orach) refers to the way one travels, one's journey, one's course through life—not just the physical route but the metaphorical path of one's choices and direction. 'Lying down' (riv'ah) refers to rest, to sleep, to the cessation of activity. Together, they span not just time but the modes of human existence: traveling (active engagement with the world) and resting (vulnerability and withdrawal). The image is of a life lived on a path, with rest periods along the way, and God carefully winnowing through all of it. Then the verse concludes with a generalizing statement: 'art acquainted with all my ways.' The verb hiskantah means 'to be accustomed to, to be familiar with, to make oneself intimate with through repeated exposure.' This is not sudden or new knowledge; it is the deep familiarity that comes from long, sustained attention.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: What makes verse 3 particularly striking is the accumulation of imagery. Verses 1-2 moved from general (God has searched and known me) to specific (He knows my sitting, rising, and thoughts). Verse 3 continues this descent into increasing specificity and concreteness. By verse 3, the psalmist is not merely stating doctrine; he is enumerating the evidence of God's knowledge with the precision of one who has carefully observed the divine gaze. Each new image—searching, knowing, understanding thoughts from afar, sifting paths and rest, being familiar with all ways—adds layers to the portrait of divine omniscience. The cumulative effect is to create an almost overwhelming sense of exposure. The psalmist is not complaining; he is marveling. And yet, there is a note of intensity that borders on discomfort. How can one live under such scrutiny?

word_study.meaning: to sift, winnow, scatter; to examine by sifting grain to separate wheat from chaff. The verb implies sorting, examining, and distinguishing the valuable from the worthless.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'sift' is theologically rich. God does not passively watch the psalmist's journey; He actively examines it, distinguishing the righteous from the unrighteous elements of the psalmist's life and choices. This connects to themes of divine judgment and refining fire in other psalms (Psalm 17:3, 26:2). In LDS context, this aligns with the concept of judgment and refinement: God examines not just the surface of our lives but the substance, distinguishing genuine faith from pretense, real obedience from superficial conformity.

word_study.meaning: path, way, journey, course; the route one travels, but also metaphorically, one's manner of living, one's choices, one's trajectory through life. The word encompasses both the literal way and the moral direction.
word_study.significance: In Hebrew wisdom literature, 'way' or 'path' is often used metaphorically for one's moral and spiritual direction (Proverbs 4:26, 'Ponder the path of thy feet'). When God examines the psalmist's 'orach,' He is assessing not just the physical route but the moral trajectory. Has the psalmist walked the way of righteousness or unrighteousness? The verb zerita applied to orach suggests that God is constantly refining and examining the psalmist's life choices.

word_study.meaning: lying down, resting, sleeping; the state of rest and vulnerability when a person relinquishes activity and control.
word_study.significance: The merism 'path and lying down' captures all states: active and passive, awake and asleep, engaged and vulnerable. The psalmist is asserting that God's knowledge covers him even when he is defenseless in sleep. This would have had particular resonance for ancient worshippers who understood sleep as a vulnerable state when demons or evil spirits might threaten. But here, the message is that even in sleep, the psalmist is under God's watchful care and examination.

word_study.meaning: to be accustomed to, to be intimate with, to be familiar with through repeated exposure and experience. The verb suggests knowledge that has accumulated over time through sustained familiarity.
word_study.significance: Unlike the more active verbs in earlier verses (searched, knows, understands), hiskantah suggests a passive, relational familiarity—the deep knowledge that comes from living with someone, from sustained relationship. God has not merely observed the psalmist once; He has accumulated intimate knowledge of him through time. This adds a dimension of relationship and continuity to divine omniscience: God does not know the psalmist as a stranger might observe a stranger; He knows him as one deeply invested in the relationship.

cross_references.connection: Examine me, O LORD, and prove me; try my reins and my heart.' This psalm similarly asks God to scrutinize and examine the psalmist's life and character, paralleling the 'sifting' image of Psalm 139:3.

Ponder the path of thy feet.' This wisdom literature passage echoes the language of 'path' (orach) and emphasizes the moral significance of one's way or course, just as Psalm 139:3 suggests God examines our paths.

Yet thou knowest me: thou hast seen me, and tried mine heart toward thee.' This prophetic text combines the verbs 'know,' 'see,' and 'try' to express the comprehensive divine examination that parallels Psalm 139:3.
In this Doctrine and Covenants vision, all people are shown to the faithful who are saved in the celestial kingdom, implying God's complete knowledge and judgment of each person's path and character.

And if ye call on the Father, who without respect of persons judgeth according to every man's work...pass the time of your sojourning here in fear.' This New Testament passage connects God's comprehensive knowledge of our ways to His role as judge.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern royal ideology, a king was said to 'know' all the lands and peoples under his dominion—meaning he had complete authority and oversight over them. Psalm 139:3, by applying this language to God's relationship with an individual, democratizes divine knowledge: not just nations and kingdoms are under God's scrutiny, but each individual's path and resting places are examined by Him. The image of winnowing (sifting) would have been familiar to any agrarian society, where the grain harvest was a crucial annual event. The psalmist draws on this universal experience to illustrate spiritual reality: just as a farmer separates grain from chaff through careful sifting, so God separates the righteous from the unrighteous elements in human life. This suggests a God who is not indifferent or distant but actively engaged in the moral refinement of His people.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 2:19, 'And it came to pass that the LORD spake unto me, saying: Thou art blessed, Nephi, because of thy faith.' The Book of Mormon emphasizes that God knows individual persons by name and knows their faith, suggesting the intimate familiarity described in Psalm 139:3. In Alma 37:35, Alma advises his son Helaman, 'Let all thy doings be unto the LORD...Counsel with the LORD in all thy doings,' implying that God is aware of and involved in all our paths and choices.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:36-40 teaches that God dwells 'in all things' and that His 'voice is Spirit,' suggesting the omnipresent awareness of the psalmist's paths and resting places. Section 6:30 promises that 'I will go before your face, I will be on your right hand and on your left,' suggesting God's intimate familiarity with each person's journey. Section 59:21 teaches that God grants increase to those who remember to 'stand in the place which I have appointed' and keep His commandments, implying His detailed knowledge of each person's walk.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple washing and anointing rituals, which bless 'all the affections of the heart' and anoint one 'that all thy paths and thy footsteps may be made sure,' directly invoke the language of Psalm 139:3. The temple recognizes that God examines and knows all one's paths and seeks to bless them through covenant. The temple thus transforms the potentially threatening surveillance of Psalm 139 into a blessing: God knows your paths in order to sustain and guide them toward exaltation.

commentary.christological_typology: In Revelation 2:23, the risen Christ says, 'I am he which searcheth the reins and hearts: and I will give unto every one of you according to your works.' This echoes the language of Psalm 139:3—God examines (or sifts) the inner reins and heart—and attributes this searching function to Christ Himself. The examination of paths and the testing of hearts, described in Psalm 139:3, become the function of the incarnate Christ in the New Testament. His resurrection and ascension do not diminish His intimate knowledge of individual believers; rather, they enable it. Christ knows the path each believer walks and will examine whether they have walked it in faith and obedience.
commentary.application: Modern believers often compartmentalize their lives—work self, family self, church self, private self—and imagine that at least the private self is hidden from view.
