The participle 'is building' (boneh) emphasizes ongoing action—this is not a future promise but a present reality. The psalmist witnesses and celebrates God's work of restoration. The two parts of the verse address the twin disasters of exile: the physical destruction of Jerusalem and the scattering of the people. God's response encompasses both the land and the people; neither is abandoned. The 'outcasts' (nidche Yisrael) are literally the 'driven away' or 'expelled ones'—those forcibly removed during the Babylonian conquest and exile. By naming this specific historical catastrophe and announcing God's active reversal of it, the psalmist invites his community to understand their current moment as one of divine intervention. The people singing this psalm are themselves part of the answer to their own prayer for restoration.

word_study.meaning: Participle of banah (to build, to construct). The participle form indicates ongoing, continuous action rather than a completed act.
word_study.significance: The psalmist does not say 'The LORD built Jerusalem' (past tense, finished) or 'will build' (future, uncertain). Instead, 'is building' captures God in the act. For the post-exilic community watching stones rise on the Temple Mount, this language resonates with lived experience. The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'is building' preserves this immediacy.

word_study.meaning: The city of peace (from yireh, 'to see,' and shalom, 'peace'), though the etymology is disputed. Historially and theologically, Jerusalem represents God's chosen dwelling place and the center of covenant life.
word_study.significance: Jerusalem is not merely a geographic location but the symbol of God's covenant with Israel, the place of the Temple and the throne of David. To rebuild Jerusalem is to restore the entire theological and political identity of Israel.

word_study.meaning: To gather, to assemble, to collect. The verb suggests bringing scattered things back into unity.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes restoration of community. Exile had fractured Israel into diaspora communities across the ancient world. God's act is to re-assemble, to make one people again. This is not individual salvation but communal restoration.

word_study.meaning: Plural of nadach (to drive away, to expel, to scatter). The nidche are the driven-away ones, the forcibly expelled.
word_study.significance: The term carries the weight of violence and trauma. These are not migrants who chose to leave but exiles torn from their homeland. God's gathering of them is not mere immigration policy but redemption of the oppressed. The Covenant Rendering's 'scattered' captures this sense of violent dispersion.

cross_references.connection: Describes God gathering the lambs in his arms and carrying them in his bosom, echoing the tender re-gathering of the scattered people.
The Lord says, 'I will be found of you...and I will turn away your captivity,' promising the exact restoration that Psalm 147:2 celebrates as present reality.
Jesus promises to gather Israel: 'Blessed are the Gentiles...that they may be numbered among my people.' The pattern of gathering is central to Restoration theology.
The Lord announces His work to 'gather together all things...which are scattered abroad,' extending the biblical pattern into latter-day restoration.

commentary.historical_context: The historical backdrop is the Babylonian exile (586 BCE) and the return authorized by Persia's Cyrus the Great (538 BCE). The destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BCE was catastrophic: the Temple was burned, the walls destroyed, and much of the population—especially the elite—was deported to Babylon. The return was not sudden or complete. Over decades, groups made the long journey back. The city and Temple had to be rebuilt piece by piece. Zerubbabel led the rebuilding of the Temple; Nehemiah later oversaw the rebuilding of the walls. For those living through this period, the psalmist's words were not pious sentiment but eyewitness reporting. They could point to construction projects, to returning families, to the re-establishment of sacrificial worship. Archaeological evidence confirms this post-exilic rebuilding phase, with layers of construction visible at Jerusalem's ancient sites. The psalm captures the theological meaning of these mundane historical events: God had not abandoned His people, and their return was His act of restoration.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly emphasizes gathering as a central covenant principle. 2 Nephi 9:2 speaks of the covenant God made with Israel to gather them 'in the last days.' Alma 10:17 references God's determination 'to gather his people together.' The Restoration doctrine of gathering—particularly the gathering to Zion—directly echoes this pattern in Psalm 147:2. Joseph Smith taught that gathering is always a sign of God's favor and the beginning of a new covenant cycle.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:7-8 contains Christ's declaration that He comes 'to gather together all things...which are scattered abroad, to redeem the house of Israel.' D&C 45:39 teaches that 'the gathering together...shall be in this land,' connecting Old Testament restoration patterns to Latter-day Saint gathering theology. D&C 133:26-34 poetically describes the Lord commanding His people to 'go ye out from Babylon,' directly echoing Jeremiah and Psalm 147.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The rebuilding of Jerusalem centers on the Temple (the Zerubbabel Temple, later Herod's Temple). For Latter-day Saints, the gathering has similarly centered on temples—from Kirtland to Nauvoo to Salt Lake City. The principle is the same: God gathers His people around sacred space where covenants are made and renewed. The promise that God is 'building up Jerusalem' parallels the Church's temple-building program as a sign of God's continuing work of restoration.

commentary.christological_typology: In Christian theology, the restoration of Jerusalem and the gathering of Israel find their ultimate fulfillment in the gathering of believers into the body of Christ. Hebrews 12:22-24 describes the Church as coming to 'Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem,' suggesting that Christ's work is the ultimate gathering and restoration. The psalmist's celebration of God's building project anticipates Christ as the 'chief corner stone' (Ephesians 2:20) who gathers a new Israel.
commentary.application: For modern Saints, this verse affirms that God is actively engaged in gathering His covenant people. This is not merely a historical fact about the return from exile but an ongoing pattern of divine action. When members of the Church leave sin, return to covenants, or are baptized into the fold, they participate in this eternal gathering. The verse teaches us to recognize God's hand in historical events and in our personal spiritual returns. In practical terms, it suggests that genuine repentance is always possible because God is continuously in the business of gathering and restoration. We should also recognize that this gathering is communal, not merely individual. We are gathered as a people into covenant, not isolated into personal salvation.

text_kjv: He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.

commentary.narrative: Verse 3 deepens the reason for praise by shifting from collective, political restoration (the rebuilding of a city, the regathering of a nation) to personal, emotional healing. The God who rebuilds walls also heals broken hearts. The 'broken in heart' (shevure lev) refers not to a temporary sadness but to those whose inner life has been shattered—by exile, grief, betrayal, loss, or trauma. This is the language of wholeness fractured. The verb 'heals' (rofe) employs medical imagery: the Lord is a physician. The follow-up image of 'binding up wounds' (mechabesh) continues the medical metaphor with even greater specificity. Mechabesh is the technical term for bandaging a wound—a hands-on, intimate act of care. The psalmist is saying that God does not merely restore political structures; He reaches into the internal wounds of individual believers. The parallelism of the verse is deliberate: 'the brokenhearted' and 'their wounds' are two ways of describing the same spiritual and emotional damage. Exile had broken more than a city; it had broken people. This verse promises that those inner fractures will be tended by God Himself.

word_study.meaning: Definite participle of rapha (to heal, to restore, to make whole). The article 'ha' ('the') emphasizes God as THE healer. The participle indicates ongoing healing action.
word_study.significance: The image of God as healer is foundational in Hebrew thought. Exodus 15:26 introduces God as 'the LORD that healeth thee' (Yahweh-rophe). Here, healing is not a special or occasional act but God's characteristic work. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes present tense: 'He heals.'

word_study.meaning: The broken ones of heart; those whose heart (lev—the center of emotion, will, and intellect in Hebrew thought) is shattered, fractured, crushed.
word_study.significance: This is not minor sadness but fundamental brokenness. The noun shevar means 'a break, a fracture.' To be shevure lev is to have one's inner self broken beyond one's own power to repair. This is where divine intervention becomes necessary and meaningful. For exiles, this brokenness was both literal (loss of home, family) and psychological.

word_study.meaning: From the root chavash (to bind up, to bandage, to wrap). This is a specific medical act: the careful wrapping of a wound to hold it together and promote healing.
word_study.significance: The verb carries the concreteness of physical care. God does not merely sympathize with wounds; He tends them actively. The image suggests that healing requires ongoing attention—wounds must be properly bound and kept clean. Jeremiah 30:12-13 uses this same vocabulary to describe Israel's incurable wound, making this psalm's promise of binding-up all the more poignant.

word_study.meaning: Plural construct: the sorrows, pains, or wounds (from atzav, to hurt, to pain). The term refers to physical or emotional pain, often from injury.
word_study.significance: The word carries both the physical and emotional dimensions of trauma. For exiles, wounds were both literal (hardship of travel, loss of home) and metaphorical (grief, psychological damage). God's care extends to all these dimensions of human suffering.

cross_references.connection: God reveals Himself as 'I am the LORD that healeth thee' (Yahweh-rophe), establishing healing as a divine name and characteristic.
The suffering servant is anointed to 'bind up the brokenhearted,' using identical language to Psalm 147:3 and describing Christ's healing mission.
Christ 'will take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people...that his bowels may be filled with mercy,' describing the Savior's intimate participation in human suffering and healing.

The Lord teaches that faith and healing go together: 'And the elders of the church...shall lay on hands...and the prayer of faith shall save the sick,' institutionalizing the divine healing principle.

commentary.historical_context: The imagery of broken hearts and binding wounds resonates deeply in a post-exilic context. The Babylonian exile (586 BCE) was not merely a military defeat; it was a profound psychological and spiritual crisis. For the exiled population, the trauma included: separation from homeland, destruction of the Temple (where God's presence was believed to dwell), loss of political autonomy, and the theological crisis of apparent divine abandonment. The Psalter itself reflects this emotional landscape—psalms of lament, confusion, and despair are interspersed throughout. Yet by the time Psalm 147 was likely composed (in the early post-exilic period, or possibly later), the community was experiencing return and restoration. The invitation to recognize God as 'the healer of the broken in heart' was addressing a real, ongoing crisis: the psychological and spiritual wounds that exile had inflicted did not heal automatically when people returned to the land. Physical restoration of walls and Temple was faster than emotional and spiritual healing. The psalm validates the internal wounds while announcing their divine treatment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 4:2-3 describes the people becoming 'deeply penitent' with 'broken hearts and contrite spirits,' then receiving God's spirit and healing. The pattern is consistent: spiritual brokenness leads to recognition of divine power, which brings healing. Ether 15:30-31 describes spiritual healing in the midst of profound violence and loss. The Book of Mormon repeatedly shows that God's healing power is most evident in contexts of deep suffering.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:2 teaches that the Savior 'has all power, all wisdom, and all understanding; he knoweth all things...and all the souls are precious unto him.' This foundational doctrine supports the promise that no broken heart escapes God's notice or care. D&C 58:2-4 teaches Saints to 'be believing' even in affliction, because the Lord will 'sanctify affliction' for our gain.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The healing of broken hearts is central to the temple's purpose. In Latter-day Saint theology, the temple is a place of wholeness and restoration—the place where individual and communal covenants are renewed, where fragmentation is healed through ordinances. The binding up of wounds echoes the language of sealing—making whole what was separated.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 61:1 explicitly connects this healing promise to Christ: 'The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me...he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted.' Jesus Himself applies this prophecy to His ministry (Luke 4:18). The wounded and broken who come to Christ find in Him the ultimate fulfillment of God's role as healer. The image of binding up wounds foreshadows Christ's atonement, which addresses not only sins but the deep wounds that sin (our own and others') inflicts on human hearts.
commentary.application: This verse invites modern believers to bring their deepest, most personal pain to God. In a culture that often encourages self-sufficiency and resilience, the psalm makes space for acknowledging that some wounds are too deep for self-help. Broken hearts—from grief, betrayal, abuse, loss—are not signs of weakness but the human condition requiring divine intervention. The verse teaches that healing is real and available, though it often requires time (like the process of binding and caring for a physical wound). Modern Saints should recognize that pastoral care in the Church—compassionate listening, service, prayer—is a participation in God's work of binding up wounds. If your heart is broken, the psalm invites you not to hide it or pretend resilience, but to bring it to God, the healer. If you encounter broken hearts in others, you become an instrument of God's healing through compassion and care.

text_kjv: He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names.

commentary.narrative: Verse 4 introduces a dramatic shift in scale and imagery. After speaking of God's restoration of Jerusalem and His healing of broken hearts, the psalmist now directs attention to the vastness of the cosmos—to the stars themselves. The parallelism is stark: the same God who heals individual broken hearts also numbers the stars. This is not a digression but a deepening of the theological point. The verse establishes a contrast between what appears infinite (the stars, presumably uncountable in ancient astronomy) and what God sees with perfect clarity and completeness. God 'tells the number' (mone mispar) of the stars—a census, a complete accounting. But more intimately, He 'calleth them all by their names'—each star has a name, and God knows each one individually. This moves beyond mere numerical knowledge to personal knowledge. The image suggests that God's attention is not exhausted by the cosmos; His care for the individual is not diminished by the vastness of creation. The psalmist is reassuring the community: if God knows each star by name, surely He knows each member of His people by name. Isaiah 40:26 contains nearly identical language, reinforcing this as a major theological motif: the God of infinite cosmic knowledge is also the God of intimate personal care.

word_study.meaning: Determining or counting the number. Mone (participle of manah, to count, to number) mispar (number, count). Together: to take a census, to number completely.
word_study.significance: The emphasis is on completeness and accuracy. This is not an approximation but an exact count. The Covenant Rendering's 'He determines the number' captures the sense that God is taking an inventory, leaving nothing out of His reckoning. This matters theologically: God's knowledge is not vague or general but precise.

word_study.meaning: Stars, celestial bodies. In ancient Near Eastern thought, stars were often understood as divine beings or at least as manifestations of divine order.
word_study.significance: Stars represent the visible limit of human knowledge and counting. To ancient observers, the stars seemed infinite. By claiming God numbers them, the psalm asserts that what seems infinite to humans is finite and completely known to God. This is a statement about the gap between human and divine knowledge.

word_study.term_english: calleth them all by their names
word_study.meaning: To each of them names he calls; to call by name. Yikra (he calls) shemot (names) lekulam (to all of them). This moves from quantity to identity.
word_study.significance: In Hebrew thought, knowing someone's name means knowing their essence, their identity, their character. To call by name is an act of intimate knowledge and relationship. God not only knows how many stars there are; He knows what each one is. This is the language of personal relationship extended to cosmic scale. The Covenant Rendering's 'He calls each of them by name' emphasizes the individuality preserved within the totality.

cross_references.connection: Nearly identical language: 'Lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things...he calleth them all by names by the greatness of his might.' This is the other major occurrence of this cosmic-personal imagery.
God tells Abram to 'look toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them,' using the inability to count stars as a metaphor for the numberless offspring God will give.
Jesus teaches that God knows when a sparrow falls, and then says 'ye are of more value than many sparrows,' connecting cosmic knowledge to personal care.
The Lord declares that all things 'are governed by law' and 'by me all things are governed,' extending the principle of divine ordering from stars to all creation.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern cosmology, the stars held profound significance. They were understood as markers of divine order—the heavens were the realm of the gods, and the stars were manifestations of cosmic order (often associated with the zodiac in Mesopotamian astronomy). The ability to number or predict the stars was considered a mark of divine or royal wisdom. The psalmist draws on this cultural background but inverts it: it is not human wisdom or royal power that numbers the stars, but God alone. The astronomical knowledge available in the post-exilic period was sophisticated enough (influenced by Babylonian astronomy during the exile) that the psalmist's audience would have understood the genuinely overwhelming nature of stellar observation. Yet the claim remains: not one star escapes God's attention. This would have resonated powerfully in a post-exilic context where the community had experienced divine abandonment or at least apparent abandonment. If God had not forgotten a single star, surely He had not forgotten His people.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:15-16 describes Ammon's wonder at the power of God: 'Who can glory too much in the Lord? Yea, who can say too much of his great power, and of his mercy, and of his long-suffering towards the children of men?' The Book of Mormon frequently emphasizes God's intimate knowledge. 2 Nephi 11:5 teaches that God 'doeth all things...with wisdom and in order; for his paths are straight, and his course is one eternal round.' The concept of cosmic order pointing to divine care is consistent throughout.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:24 describes the vision of the celestial kingdom and references stars: 'And again we beheld the terrestrial kingdom.' The connection between stellar imagery and divine knowledge is consistent with Latter-day Saint cosmology. D&C 88 (the 'Olive Leaf' revelation) explicitly teaches the governing principles of all things, connecting order, law, and divine knowledge.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In Latter-day Saint thought, the stars appear in temple symbolism and in the doctrines of premortal existence and eternal progression. The teaching that God knows each individual by name echoes covenant language—the temple experience involves God knowing and calling each member by name as they make covenants. The personal and the cosmic are reconciled through temple ordinances.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is often understood as the organizing principle of creation and the one through whom God knows all things. Colossians 1:16-17 teaches that 'by him were all things created...and by him all things consist.' The intimate knowledge of stars by name points to Christ as the one who sustains and knows all creation. In Revelation 1:16 and 2:1, Christ holds stars in His hand, suggesting both care and authority. The verse anticipates that Christ's redemptive work will restore the personal-cosmic connection broken by sin.
commentary.application: This verse offers profound comfort to modern believers. In a age of mass society where individuals often feel anonymous and insignificant, Psalm 147:4 affirms that God knows you by name. You are not a statistic, not one face among millions lost in anonymity. The God who knows each star by name knows you. Your name is not generic—God knows your particular identity, your story, your struggles. This is especially meaningful when you feel small or forgotten. The verse also invites us to wonder at creation. When modern Saints look at photographs from the James Webb Space Telescope or consider the vastness revealed by cosmology, Psalm 147:4 invites us not to feel insignificant but to recognize that the God who created and sustains this incomprehensible cosmos has chosen to know us personally. The verse teaches that size is not the measure of value or importance in God's economy. Finally, the verse suggests a way to pray: you can come to God knowing that you do not have to explain who you are or what matters about you. God already knows. Your prayer is not information to a distant deity, but communion with one who knows you completely.

text_kjv: Great is our Lord, and of great power: his understanding is infinite.

commentary.narrative: Verse 5 draws a conclusion from the previous verses, synthesizing them into an explicit declaration of God's magnitude. The verse uses the superlative degree—'great' (gadol) appears twice, and 'understanding is infinite' (ein mispar) captures what cannot be measured or numbered. This verse announces the implications of what has been observed: if God rebuilds cities, heals broken hearts, and numbers stars, then He must be incomparably great and powerful. But the verse adds a crucial dimension: God's greatness is not only power (koach) but also understanding (tevunah). Tevunah refers not to mere information but to wisdom, discernment, the ability to see and comprehend reality as it truly is. The ironic juxtaposition is masterful: verse 4 mentioned that God numbers the stars, but verse 5 says His understanding cannot be numbered. The one who counts everything is Himself uncountable. God's greatness is not exhausted by what can be measured or catalogued; it extends into dimensions of wisdom and understanding that transcend all categories. The phrase 'our Lord' (adonenu) maintains the personal relationship: despite this cosmic greatness, God is 'ours,' belonging to the community that sings this psalm.

word_study.meaning: Great, large, powerful, important. Used to describe physical size, importance, power, or dignity. In theological contexts, it emphasizes God's transcendence and supremacy.
word_study.significance: The term appears twice in the verse ('Great is our Lord and of great power'), creating emphasis through repetition. In Hebrew poetry, this kind of doubled expression intensifies the meaning. God is not just powerful; His power is measured on a scale beyond human categories.

word_study.meaning: Power, strength, might, force. The ability to effect change or accomplish purpose. In theological contexts, divine koach is the power that creates and sustains all things.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'great in power' (rav-koach) is used throughout Scripture to describe God's might. It is the power demonstrated in the acts mentioned in verse 2 (building Jerusalem) and verse 3 (healing broken hearts). But verse 5 insists this power operates in conjunction with understanding.

word_study.meaning: Understanding, discernment, wisdom, insight. From the root bin (to distinguish, to separate, to understand). It refers to the capacity to perceive, analyze, and comprehend reality with precision.
word_study.significance: Unlike knowledge (yada), which is familiarity with facts, tevunah is the wisdom to understand how things fit together and what they mean. God's tevunah is not merely the accumulation of facts but the penetrating wisdom that sees all things as they truly are. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes 'His understanding has no limit,' stressing the qualitative as well as quantitative dimensions.

word_study.meaning: There is no number; without number, uncountable, infinite. A negation (ein) followed by mispar (number, count), expressing that something exceeds all quantification.
word_study.significance: This exact phrase appears in verse 4 ('his understanding has no number'), creating a poetic echo. It emphasizes that what cannot be enumerated or categorized cannot be limited or diminished. God's understanding is not just greater than human understanding; it is categorically different.

cross_references.connection: As the heaven is high above the earth, so great is his mercy toward them that fear him,' using the same language of incomparable greatness applied to God's compassion.
The everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary; there is no searching of his understanding,' declaring the inscrutability of God's wisdom.

O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!' The New Testament echoes this sense of God's transcendent understanding.

The Doctrine and Covenants describes light as truth and the organizing principle of all creation: 'He that ascended up on high...received all things...truth is knowledge of things as they are,' identifying understanding with divine truth.

commentary.historical_context: In post-exilic Judaism, there was an intensified interest in the transcendence and majesty of God. The experience of exile had raised acute theological questions: How could a God of such power have allowed the Temple to be destroyed? Had God been defeated by Babylonian deities? The response, reflected in texts like Psalm 147 and Second Isaiah (Isaiah 40-55), was to emphasize God's transcendence even more emphatically. God's greatness and understanding were beyond all categories—neither defeat nor exile could diminish them. This represents a theological development in Jewish thought: an increasing emphasis on God's transcendence alongside (not instead of) God's intimate care for the individual. Verse 5 articulates this sophisticated balance: God is incomprehensibly great and wise, yet this same God builds up Jerusalem and heals broken hearts (verses 2-3). There is no contradiction; God's transcendence and immanence are held together in a paradox that later theologians would struggle with and refine.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:35 declares, 'Now behold, who can glory too much in the Lord? Yea, who can say too much of his great power, and of his mercy, and of his long-suffering towards the children of men?' This captures the same sentiment—the impossibility of exaggerating God's greatness. Jacob 4:8 teaches that God's judgments are 'inscrutable,' emphasizing the limits of human understanding when confronted with divine wisdom.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:114-118 describes the vision of the celestial kingdom and emphasizes that the things shown cannot be uttered, suggesting the transcendent nature of God's understanding. D&C 19:9-12 teaches that Christ's suffering comprehends all things: 'For behold, I, God, have suffered these things for all, that they should not suffer if they would repent.' This suggests that God's understanding extends to dimensions of suffering and redemption beyond human comprehension.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple theology, the concept of 'mysteries' plays an important role—certain dimensions of divine truth are revealed only in the temple to those who are prepared. Psalm 147:5 affirms that God's understanding necessarily exceeds what any individual or community can fully comprehend. The temple invitation is to grow in understanding (tevunah) by participating in God's ordinances and covenants.

commentary.christological_typology: In Christian theology, Christ is understood as the wisdom of God incarnate (1 Corinthians 1:24, 'Christ...the wisdom of God'). Colossians 2:3 describes Christ as the one in whom 'are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.' Verse 5's affirmation of God's infinite understanding points toward Christ as the full expression of divine wisdom. The paradox of infinite understanding expressed in finite, human form in the Incarnation represents the ultimate unfolding of this verse's logic.
commentary.application: Modern believers can take confidence from this verse in several ways. First, it affirms that God's wisdom is not limited by time or circumstance. When life presents situations that seem insurmountable or unclear, this verse invites you to trust in a divine understanding that transcends your own. You do not need to see the whole plan; you can trust the wisdom of one whose understanding is infinite. Second, the verse teaches humility about human wisdom. In a culture that often emphasizes self-sufficiency and the value of individual judgment, this psalm reminds us that there are dimensions of reality and truth that exceed our capacity to comprehend. This is not an invitation to intellectual laziness but to combine human understanding with submission to divine wisdom. Third, the verse connects God's greatness to His care: this is the same infinite understanding that was devoted to numbering your life and knowing your name (verse 4). That infinite mind is fixed upon you with infinite care. The application is to pray not only for solutions you can understand, but to bring your deepest questions and confusions to a God whose understanding exceeds all categories.

text_kjv: The LORD lifteth up the meek: he casteth the wicked down to the ground.

commentary.narrative: Verse 6 returns from the cosmic and philosophical dimensions of God's greatness to the moral and social dimensions of His work. It presents a stark contrast: God lifts up the meek while casting down the wicked. This is not a new motif in the Psalter—the reversal of social positions is a recurring theme. But in the context of Psalm 147, it grounds the abstract affirmations about God's power and understanding in concrete moral action. God's greatness is not merely theoretical; it is demonstrated in how He relates to human society. The 'meek' (anavim) are the humble, the afflicted, those without earthly power or status. The 'wicked' (resha'im) are those who oppose God's order, who exploit the vulnerable. The verb imagery is physical: meodded ('sustains, encourages, supports') suggests an upward lifting, while mashpil ('brings low, casts down') suggests the opposite motion. The parallelism is precise—what is done for the meek is precisely the opposite of what is done to the wicked. This is moral order manifest in social reality. For the post-exilic community, this verse would have carried particular resonance. Israel had experienced being cast down by a more powerful nation; this psalm assures them that the wicked oppressor will be brought low while God's people, though currently humble, will be lifted up. The verse affirms that moral order is not arbitrary but rooted in God's character and action.

word_study.meaning: Sustains, supports, encourages, strengthens. From the root aded (to support, to help), the participle describes ongoing divine support. This is not a one-time lift but continuing encouragement.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'sustains' is more precise than 'lifts up,' which might suggest a momentary action. Meodded describes God as a constant support. The word appears in Psalm 41:3 in connection with God's care for the sick and weak. It emphasizes God's role as sustainer, not merely rescuer.

word_study.meaning: The humble, the afflicted, the meek, the poor. The plural of anav (humble, meek, afflicted). In biblical thought, anavim can refer to those literally poor or those spiritually humble.
word_study.significance: Throughout the Psalter, the anavim are those whom God favors and protects. The term carries both a social and spiritual dimension: the economically vulnerable are often the spiritually open. The anavim represent those who recognize their dependence on God because earthly supports have failed them. For exiles, this would have been an immediate identity: they were the anavim, the reduced and humbled.

word_study.meaning: Brings low, humbles, casts down, reduces. From the root shaphal (to be low, to be brought low). The participle indicates God's action in reducing the wicked to their proper place.
word_study.significance: This verb is the precise opposite of the upward motion implied in meodded. It describes a leveling, a bringing down to the ground (adei-aretz, 'to the ground, even to the dust'). The wicked are brought low, stripped of their power and status. This is the principle of reversal that permeates biblical thought.

word_study.meaning: The wicked, the wrongdoers, those who act against God's order. From the root rasha (to be wicked, to condemn, to be guilty). Resha'im are not merely morally deficient but actively hostile to divine order.
word_study.significance: Throughout the Psalter, resha'im are the enemies of God and of God's people. They represent the forces that work against justice and covenant. Their being cast down is presented not as cruelty but as the necessary maintenance of moral order. God does not permit wickedness to prevail indefinitely.

word_study.meaning: Earth, ground, land. In this context, the ground represents the lowest position, the place of humiliation and defeat.
word_study.significance: The preposition 'adei' ('even to, down to') emphasizes the totality of the descent. The wicked are brought not merely low but to the earth itself—stripped of all elevation and dignity. This echoes the creation narrative where humans are made from earth (adamah), suggesting a return to a fundamental, humbled state.

cross_references.connection: Hannah's song: 'The LORD maketh poor, and maketh rich: he bringeth low, and lifteth up. He raiseth up the poor out of the dust,' presenting the same reversal pattern in thanksgiving for God's intervention in her life.

Mary's Magnificat: 'He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree...filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away,' echoing this verse in a New Testament context.

Alma describes the humble as 'stripped...of pride,' and promises that God 'pour[s] out his Spirit more abundantly upon a people which willeth to believe in your words...than upon a people which believeth not.'
The Lord warns that the wicked 'shall feel mine arm, which shall be a terror unto them,' affirming the principle that God opposes the wicked while supporting the humble.

commentary.historical_context: The principle of reversal reflected in this verse is deeply rooted in ancient Near Eastern thought and biblical tradition. In Egyptian literature, the concept of ma'at (cosmic order and justice) included the principle that the god would overthrow chaos (represented by enemies and the wicked). Similarly, in Mesopotamian thought, the gods upheld order (cosmos) against disorder (chaos). Biblical authors drew on these cultural resources while giving them specific theological meaning: God's reversal of social positions is not arbitrary power but expression of moral and covenantal order. For the post-exilic community, this verse offered hope grounded in moral principle, not mere sentiment. They had experienced being 'cast down' by a superior military power. This psalm assures them that such apparent triumph of power over righteousness is temporary; God ultimately maintains moral order. Historical reality in the post-exilic period bore this out: Babylon itself was conquered by Persia (539 BCE), and the Persians, paradoxically, permitted the Jewish return. The 'wicked' oppressor was indeed brought low; the humble exiles were sustained.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon is suffused with this principle of reversal. Alma 5:26-27 teaches that those who are humble 'shall be brought forth by the angels to a place which is called the first resurrection, that they may have glad tidings; But behold, I say unto you, the wicked shall be cast out from the presence of God.' The pattern is identical: humility leads to exaltation; wickedness leads to reduction. This principle structures multiple narratives in the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 63:32-34 teaches that 'the day cometh that they who will not hear the voice of the Lord, neither the voice of his servants...must be brought low in the dust.' D&C 38:15 declares, 'I have sent forth the fulness of my gospel by the hand of my servant Joseph; and in weakness have I blessed him.' God works through the humble and brings the wicked to account. The reversal is God's consistent pattern.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony includes the principle of reversal and elevation. Those who enter the temple approach God, moving from outer to inner, from lower to higher chambers, symbolizing spiritual elevation. Conversely, those who reject covenants and continue in wickedness are separated from these blessings. The temple enacts this principle of reversal in ritual form.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's life and mission exemplify this pattern of reversal in radical form. He began in humility (born in a manger, descended from humble circumstances) and was exalted (resurrected and glorified). Conversely, the wicked leaders of His time were brought to account (the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE fulfilled predictions of their downfall). Philippians 2:8-9 describes Christ being 'humbled' in death but then 'highly exalted,' enacting the reversal pattern in His own person. Moreover, Christ identifies with the anavim (the humble and afflicted): 'Blessed are the poor in spirit' (Matthew 5:3), making clear that His kingdom reverses worldly valuations. Revelation 12 depicts the ultimate casting down of Satan and the elevation of the faithful.
commentary.application: This verse invites modern believers to understand God as the defender of justice and the protector of the vulnerable. If you are among the 'meek'—economically struggling, socially marginalized, spiritually dependent on God's grace—this verse assures you that God sees you and sustains you. You are not forgotten or abandoned. God's economy reverses the world's valuations: the world elevates the powerful and wealthy, but God elevates the humble and faithful. This should affect how we act: we should align ourselves with God's moral order by defending the vulnerable, opposing exploitation, and refusing to exploit others for power or wealth. If you find yourself tempted to wield power over others or to trust in wealth and status for security, this verse calls you to turn from that path. The 'wicked' in this verse are not merely those who violate rules, but those who set themselves against God's order by oppressing the vulnerable and exalting themselves. The application is both comforting (if you are suffering or vulnerable) and warning (if you are tempted to oppress or exalt yourself). Finally, the verse teaches us to view history and current events with theological perspective. Apparent victories of powerful, wicked regimes are temporary. God's reversal may come through natural historical processes (as with Babylon) or through divine intervention. Either way, righteousness and justice ultimately prevail because they are grounded in God's character, not merely human preference.

text_kjv: Sing unto the LORD with thanksgiving; sing praise upon the harp unto our God:

commentary.narrative: Psalm 147:7 opens the second major section of this hymn with an imperative call to vocal and instrumental worship. The psalmist summons the congregation to respond to God's cosmic and intimate care (detailed in verses 2-6) with gratitude expressed through song and the kinnor (lyre). This is not mere entertainment or aesthetic appreciation; the todah (thanksgiving offering/acknowledgment) was a specific sacrificial genre in Israel's worship system—a formal declaration before the assembled community that God had heard and answered. The verb 'enu carries the sense of 'answer' or 'respond,' suggesting that human praise is itself a response to God's prior action. The shift from third-person description of God's works (verses 2-6) to direct second-person command (verse 7) moves the psalm from proclamation to participation.

word_study.meaning: To sing, to respond, to answer; carries the sense of answering a call or responding to someone's voice. In worship contexts, it means to sing back to God—a responsive song.
word_study.significance: The verb choice emphasizes that worship is relational—not a monologue but a dialogue. God speaks through his works; the congregation answers through song. This reflects the covenantal framework where God acts and Israel responds with acknowledgment.

word_study.meaning: In the context of a confession or public acknowledgment; todah as a noun refers both to the act of giving thanks and to a specific peace offering in Israel's temple system—a sacrifice that involved a communal meal and public testimony.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering clarifies that todah is not merely emotional gratitude but covenantal acknowledgment—a formal recognition before witnesses that God is faithful and worthy of trust. This deepens the sense of worship as a community act with legal/covenantal weight.

word_study.meaning: A stringed instrument, typically translated 'harp' or 'lyre'; the instrument associated with David and foundational to Israelite temple music. Smaller and more portable than later harps, it was played by plucking strings.
word_study.significance: The kinnor is David's instrument (1 Samuel 16:23), linking this psalm to the Davidic tradition and kingship. Its presence here sanctifies instrumental music as a legitimate mode of worship—not mere accompaniment but an essential vehicle of praise.

cross_references.connection: Both psalms explicitly connect thanksgiving (todah) with singing and joyful response; 100:2 uses the same root 'enu ('make a joyful noise') and frames it as covenantal acknowledgment.
David plays the kinnor, establishing the lyre as the instrument of prophetic anointing and divine presence—the instrument that soothes Saul and connects the player to God.

The todah offering is formally described here: a peace offering with thanksgiving that includes bread and a communal meal, underscoring that the psalm's call to 'sing with thanksgiving' invokes the full sacrificial/communal act.

Paul exhorts believers to let 'the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord'—echoing the todah tradition of corporate, grateful response.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, instrumental worship was central to temple practice, not peripheral or decorative. The kinnor appears in multiple contexts—from shepherd music (1 Samuel 16:16) to formal temple worship (2 Chronicles 5:12). Archaeological evidence from Levantine sites confirms that stringed instruments similar to the kinnor were common in Iron Age religious and royal contexts. The todah offering represents a distinctive Israelite innovation: whereas many ancient Near Eastern cultures emphasized propitiatory or votive sacrifice, the todah is explicitly joyful, communal, and testimonial—a sacrifice designed to publicize God's faithfulness and to bind the community together in shared acknowledgment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:8 captures the spirit of this verse: 'Now when our hearts were depressed, and we were about to turn back, behold, the Lord comforted us, and said: Go forth and do as I have commanded you, and I will make much of you'—leading to rejoicing and thanksgiving. The Nephite emphasis on public testimony and communal praise mirrors the todah tradition.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 25:12 instructs Emma Smith: 'And verily I say unto thee that thou shalt lay aside the things of this world, and seek for the things of a better.' Yet verse 12 also allows: 'Wherefore, be faithful; and let thy soul delight in the song of the heart, the song of righteousness.' Music and thanksgiving are explicitly linked as forms of spiritual devotion and covenant keeping.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The directive to praise 'with thanksgiving' on the kinnor echoes temple worship practices. In LDS temples, hymns and sacred music facilitate worship and covenant experience. The principle remains: instrumental and vocal music, combined with grateful hearts, constitute legitimate and powerful worship before God.

commentary.christological_typology: The call to answer God's voice with song finds its fulfillment in the Church as the Bride of Christ. Revelation 5:8-10 describes the redeemed singing a new song before the throne, responding to Christ's redemptive work. The todah structure—public acknowledgment of God's saving acts—prefigures the Eucharistic/sacramental tradition where the Church responds to Christ's sacrifice with gratitude and testimony.
commentary.application: For the modern covenant member, verse 7 challenges the privatization of gratitude. 'Sing unto the Lord with thanksgiving' is not a command to feel grateful in isolation but to express thanks publicly, corporately, with full engagement of voice and (metaphorically) heart-instrument. In a secular age that often mutes religious expression, the psalm invites the faithful to make their gratitude audible and visible—in family home evening hymns, in sacrament meeting participation, in formal and informal testimony. The emphasis on the kinnor reminds us that music is not decorative but covenantal—a language through which the soul responds to God's reality.

text_kjv: Who covereth the heaven with clouds, who prepareth rain for the earth, who maketh grass to grow upon the mountains.

commentary.narrative: Verse 8 returns to the theme of God's providential care, now focusing on atmospheric and terrestrial cycles. The three participles ('covereth,' 'prepareth,' 'maketh grow') form a unified sequence describing what modern meteorology calls the water cycle but what the psalmist presents as divine orchestration. The clouds cover the sky—an act of preparation, not concealment. The rain nourishes the earth—an act of intentional provision. The grass grows on the mountains—an act of fertilization and life-giving. This verse does not present nature as autonomous or indifferent but as the direct outcome of God's purposeful action in each moment. The inclusion of the mountains (not just fertile lowlands) underscores that God's provision extends even to marginal, difficult terrain where human control is weakest. The cumulative effect is to demonstrate God's attentiveness to creation's physical needs.

word_study.meaning: Participle of kasah; to cover, to conceal, to veil. Can carry both protective and obscuring connotations—covering can mean hiding or sheltering.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's use of 'covers' rather than 'concealeth' emphasizes the protective sense: clouds do not obscure God's work but execute it. The sky is 'covered' as an act of preparation, not punishment.

word_study.meaning: Participle of kun; to establish, to prepare, to make ready. Often used of building or constructing; implies intentional setup and purposeful arrangement.
word_study.significance: God does not merely 'send' rain; he 'prepares' or 'establishes' it—suggesting deliberate orchestration and timing. The term carries connotations of covenant-keeping (fun is used of God establishing his covenant in Genesis 6:18).

word_study.meaning: Participle of tsamach; to make grow, to cause to sprout, to bring forth. Used of vegetation bursting forth from the earth.
word_study.significance: This verb emphasizes causation and life-giving power. Grass does not grow autonomously; God causes it to grow. This reinforces the active, present-tense nature of divine Providence—not a distant Creator but an engaged sustainer.

cross_references.connection: Jesus teaches that God 'maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust'—affirming the indiscriminate, universal nature of God's atmospheric provision described in this psalm.

Jesus points to the birds and the lilies as evidence of God's providential care: 'Consider the birds of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap... yet your heavenly Father feedeth them.' This echoes the psalm's logic that God sustains creation without human intervention.

The Lord's speech in Job uses identical imagery: 'Who hath divided a watercourse for the overflowing of waters, or a way for the lightning of thunder; to cause it to rain on the earth, where no man is?'—affirming that God's providential rain falls even in uninhabited wilderness.
Elijah's declaration that God will send rain (and his servant's report of clouds forming) demonstrates the practical belief that weather is under God's direct control, not natural law alone.

The land of promise is described as one 'which the LORD thy God careth for: the eyes of the LORD thy God are always upon it'—making the provision of rain not coincidental but covenantally intentional.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern world, rainfall was the most immediate and unpredictable manifestation of divine power. The Levantine climate is Mediterranean—winter rainfall, long dry summers. Drought and famine were existential threats. Egyptian and Mesopotamian cultures had elaborate rain and storm deities (Baal, Adad, Indra) precisely because meteorological control was seen as the supreme exercise of divine power. The psalmist's insistence that Israel's God (YHWH) controls the water cycle—not a specialized storm deity—represented a radical claim of monotheistic supremacy. The specific mention of grass growing on mountains reflects the subsistence herding economy of Israel: mountain pastures, accessible only seasonally, were vital grazing land. The grass that grew on mountains after winter rains was literally the difference between livestock survival and famine.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 8:1 describes how Lehi 'saw the heavens open, and he thought he saw God sitting upon his throne, surrounded with numberless concourses of angels'—a vision often followed by teachings about God's direct governance. Alma's sermon at Zarahemla emphasizes God's active sustenance of the earth (Alma 30:44): 'All things denote there is a God; yea, even the earth, and all things that are upon the face of it, yea, and its motion, yea, and also all the planets which move in their regular form do witness that there is a Supreme Creator.'
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:6-13 presents God's power in terms of active, continuous causation: 'He that ascended up on high, as also he descended below all things... by him, and through him, and of him, the worlds are and were created, and the inhabitants thereof are begotten sons and daughters unto God.' The language mirrors verse 8's description of God actively causing creation's processes to function.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment celebrates God's active role in creation and sustenance. The waters (representing the chaos before creation) are explicitly subject to God's will. The principle that God actively maintains creation—not merely initiates it—is central to temple theology. Joseph Smith taught that God's power is continuous and present, not passive or historical.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the agent of creation: 'All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made' (John 1:3). The rain, the clouds, the grass growing on mountains—all manifest Christ's ongoing creative power. In John 4:14, Christ offers living water that 'shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.' The promise of sustenance in verse 8 finds its spiritual fulfillment in Christ, who satisfies all spiritual hunger and thirst.
commentary.application: Modern believers in a scientifically advanced culture often struggle to maintain the sense of divine presence described in this verse. We understand cloud formation, precipitation cycles, photosynthesis. But the psalm invites a deeper vision: behind every 'natural' process stands an agent of intentional love. The covenant member might practice 'vertical reading'—seeing in everyday weather patterns the signature of God's active care. When rain comes after drought, when crops flourish despite difficult terrain, these become occasions not for mere meteorological observation but for gratitude and recognition of divine Providence. In a culture that tends to compartmentalize faith and science, verse 8 invites integration: God works through natural law; natural law is the mode of his care.

text_kjv: He giveth to the beast his food, and to the young ravens which cry.

commentary.narrative: Verse 9 narrows the focus from the cosmic (rainfall and mountain grass) to the intimate and particular: God feeds individual animals. The parallel structure ('to the beast...and to the young ravens') moves from domesticated livestock (behemah—cattle, sheep) to wild scavengers (young ravens), encompassing creation's full spectrum. The critical detail is that the ravens 'cry out' (yiqra'u)—their cry is not mere animal noise but a supplication that God 'hears' and 'answers' through provision. The verb yiqra' ('to call out, to cry, to invoke') is the same root used for human prayer and divine response. By applying it to the ravens, the psalmist elevates animal need to the level of religious petitioning: the young ravens' hunger-cry is a prayer that God honors. This is not sentimentalizing nature but recognizing that all creation's dependence on God constitutes a kind of worship. The contrast between 'giving' (noten—an active, personal verb) and the ravens' need underscores God's attentiveness to what humans might overlook or deem insignificant.

word_study.meaning: Participle of natan; to give, to provide, to grant. Emphasizes active, ongoing provision rather than a single act of bestowal.
word_study.significance: The present participle form suggests continuous, habitual provision—God is perpetually giving. This is not a past creative act but a present, sustained relationship of care.

word_study.meaning: Livestock, animals, beasts; typically refers to domesticated creatures (cattle, sheep, goats) but can include wild animals. Represents life that is dependent and non-rational.
word_study.significance: The choice of behemah—a term that can include both herded and wild creatures—emphasizes that God's provision crosses the boundary between the domesticated realm (where humans might assist) and the wild realm (where human provision is impossible).

word_study.meaning: Literally 'children/sons of the raven'; young ravens, raven chicks. Specifically juvenile birds, representing creatures most vulnerable and dependent.
word_study.significance: Ravens were considered unclean animals under Levitical law (Leviticus 11:15) and were known as scavengers. Yet God feeds them. The psalm's inclusion of 'unclean' creatures emphasizes that God's care transcends cultic purity categories—all of creation is included in divine Providence.

word_study.meaning: They call out, they cry, they invoke. From the root qara', which is used both for human prayer/petition and for the cries of animals in distress.
word_study.significance: By using this verb for the ravens' hunger-cry, the psalmist treats animal need as a form of petition that God honors. This elevates creation's dependence to a covenantal relationship where cry and response are exchanged.

cross_references.connection: The Lord asks Job: 'Who provideth for the raven his food? when his young ones cry unto God, they wander for lack of meat.' This is a direct parallel to Psalm 147:9, using identical language and logic—God's provision for young ravens is presented as evidence of divine wisdom and care.

Jesus says: 'Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat... Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap... yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they?' Jesus explicitly quotes the logic of this psalm—animal provision is proof of God's care for human beings.

Luke records: 'Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings? and not one of them is forgotten before God... Fear not therefore: ye are of more value than many sparrows.' The principle of verse 9—that God attends to small creatures—proves that God attends to human beings.

Peter exhorts: 'Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.' The assurance rests on the theological premise established in this verse—that God actively cares for creation's needs, so believers can entrust their cares to him.

The Lord reveals: 'The beasts of the field and the fowls of the air, and that which cometh of the earth, is ordained for the use of man for food and for raiment' yet emphasizes that all are under God's dominion and care—establishing human stewardship within a larger framework of divine Providence.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the raven was widely recognized as a vulnerable creature dependent on scavenging. Unlike domesticated animals (which communities herded and protected), ravens represented the wildness and unpredictability of nature. The theological challenge was acute: How does a covenant God who commands Israel's loyalty also tend creatures outside the covenantal community? The psalmist's answer elevates this as a sign of God's supremacy—the very creatures most independent of human control are fed by God. This would have been especially striking in the context of Ancient Near Eastern theology, where gods often represented particular domains (storm gods for rain, harvest gods for grain, etc.) or particular peoples (national gods). The Israelite God's care for creatures universally and indiscriminately suggested a power that transcended all such limitations. The specific mention of ravens (nevim in Hebrew, associated with uncleanness and marginality) may deliberately emphasize inclusion of the ritually impure in God's care—a radical statement about the scope of divine love.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Nephite understanding of stewardship emphasized God's ownership of creation. Alma 30:44 declares: 'All things denote there is a God; yea, even the earth, and all things that are upon the face of it, yea, and its motion, yea, and also all the planets which move in their regular form do witness that there is a Supreme Creator.' The care for animals is part of this witness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 59:17-20 instructs: 'And it pleaseth God that he hath given all these things unto man... but it is forbidden to waste them, and to withhold them from the needy... for the beasts of the field and the fowls of the air, and that which cometh of the earth, is ordained for the use of man for food and for raiment, and that he might have abundance.' The Lord's providential care for creatures establishes a framework for righteous stewardship—humans are not owners but caretakers of what God provides.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The creation account in temple liturgy emphasizes God's direct role in bringing forth all life. The covenant to multiply and replenish the earth includes a covenant of stewardship over 'the beasts of the field, and the fowls of the air, and every living thing.' This verse reinforces that stewardship is grounded in the reality that all creatures belong ultimately to God.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ consistently used animal imagery to teach about God's providential care (Matthew 6:26; Luke 12:6-7). More profoundly, Christ's Atonement extends redemptive care to all creation: Romans 8:19-21 speaks of creation itself being 'delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God.' The feeding of the ravens prefigures the cosmic redemption wrought through Christ, in which all creation is restored and sustained through him (Colossians 1:16-17).
commentary.application: For modern disciples, verse 9 invites a radical reframing of worry. If God feeds creatures that cannot pray in words, that cannot farm or plan, that lie outside human economy and often human sympathy (ravens were unclean, undesirable)—then human anxiety about provision becomes a failure of faith. The verse also challenges indifference to animal suffering. If God 'gives to the beast his food,' then deliberate starvation, neglect, or unnecessary cruelty toward animals represents a violation of the divine order that this verse describes. In a practical sense, the covenant member might practice recognizing moments when provision arrives unexpectedly—a job offer, a timely gift, a solved problem—not as luck or chance but as the echo of the same divine attentiveness described in verse 9. The principle extends to spiritual provision: God feeds the soul through prayer, scripture, community, guidance—not because the soul has earned it but because God is the kind of being who provides.

text_kjv: He delighteth not in the strength of the horse: he taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man.

commentary.narrative: Verse 10 marks an abrupt and theologically significant shift. After describing God's providential care for the physical world and its creatures (verses 2-9), the psalm now directly critiques the values of militarism and human self-reliance. The two images—the horse and the legs of a warrior—represent the primary military technologies of the ancient world: mounted cavalry (the warhorse being the most expensive and devastating weapon of ancient warfare) and heavy infantry (the trained, muscular soldier). The parallelism ('delighteth not...taketh not pleasure') creates an emphatic negation: God's approval does not rest on military prowess. This is not merely a statement that God prefers peace to war, but a more fundamental theological claim: God does not value what human military culture values. The repetition of negatives ('lo...lo') hammers the point home. For an ancient Israelite reader, this would have been countercultural. Military strength was the foundation of national security, royal legitimacy, and territorial control. Kings were praised for their military exploits. Yet the psalmist insists that military might does not impress God. Verse 11 will clarify what does impress God—not strength but fear and trust.

word_study.meaning: Participle of chaphats; to delight in, to take pleasure in, to be pleased with, to find satisfaction in. Implies personal preference and approval.
word_study.significance: God does not merely 'tolerate' military power; he actively does not find pleasure in it. The verb emphasizes that God's values are contrary to militarism—not indifferent but actively disapproving.

word_study.meaning: Strength, might, power, valor, heroic strength. Often used of warrior prowess and military capability. Can also mean 'mighty deeds' or 'acts of valor.'
word_study.significance: Gevurat is not weakness or frailty but positive, impressive human power. God's rejection of it is even more striking—he does not just tolerate but explicitly rejects what human culture celebrates as admirable.

word_study.meaning: Horse; specifically the warhorse used in military campaigns. Horses were rare, expensive, imported (often from Egypt), and represented the highest military technology of the ancient world.
word_study.significance: The horse was not merely transportation but the symbol of military supremacy. Kings were repeatedly warned against multiplying horses (Deuteronomy 17:16; 1 Kings 10:26-29). Its mention here carries symbolic weight—God rejects the entire apparatus of military might, symbolized by its most prestigious weapon.

word_study.meaning: Legs, thighs, shanks; specifically the muscular lower body of a warrior. Refers to the physical strength and running capability that made a soldier effective.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering clarifies that 'legs' refers to warrior capability—the ability to run into battle, to stand firm, to pursue enemies. It represents human military prowess at the individual level, as the horse represents it at the technological level.

cross_references.connection: The law of the king explicitly forbids multiplying horses: 'He shall not multiply horses to himself... Neither shall he greatly multiply to himself silver and gold.' God establishes a principle that military accumulation is contrary to theocratic kingship.

Samuel declares to King Saul: 'Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.' The prophet rejects Saul's confidence in military offerings and substitutes trust in obedience—the same revaluation of values that verse 10 presents.

Isaiah condemns those who 'go down to Egypt for help... they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD! Yet he also is wise, and will bring evil, and will not call back his words: but will arise against the house of the evildoers, and against the help of them that work iniquity. Now the Egyptians are men, and not God; and their horses flesh, and not spirit.'—expressing the same theological principle: military might (embodied in Egyptian horses) is 'flesh, not spirit,' and cannot replace trust in God.

A companion psalm declares: 'There is no king saved by the multitude of an host: a mighty man is not delivered by much strength. An horse is a vain thing for safety: neither shall he deliver any by his great strength.' This directly parallels verse 10's rejection of military reliance.

The prophet hears: 'Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts'—establishing a principle that continues into the Restoration: God's work is accomplished through his power, not human military or physical might.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, particularly during the Iron Age, the warhorse represented military supremacy. Egypt controlled the international horse trade and supplied horses to lesser powers (including Israel) for enormous expense. A chariot and horses cost the equivalent of a small estate. Assyrian reliefs glorify the king's cavalry and military machinery. Yet the Israelite tradition was unique in repeatedly warning against military accumulation and emphasizing trust in God over military preparation. This reflected Israel's actual vulnerability (small, geographically exposed) and theological conviction (God as the real source of security, not horses or chariots). The Davidic tradition, despite David being a warrior, consistently emphasized that God—not weapons—secured victory (1 Samuel 17:47). The psalmist was working within this prophetic critique of militarism that runs through Israel's wisdom literature and prophecy. In the context of Persian rule (when this psalm may have been composed), military weakness was Israel's actual condition; the psalm reframes this as theological virtue—trust in God rather than in horses and warriors.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon consistently critiques reliance on military strength. Alma 2:30 records: 'And it came to pass that [Amlici] rent that he had rent his garment; and he ran and told the people all these things which had happened unto his people, and to his king and his judges... And it came to pass that the people were exceedingly astonished at the words which he had spoken... the people cried out with one voice, saying: Yea, we believe all the words which thou hast spoken.' More tellingly, Alma 44:3-4 presents Moroni's challenge to Amalickiah: 'Behold, I am Moroni, chief captain of the armies of the people of Nephi... Yea, I would that ye should understand that I come not against you to shed blood.' The ethical warrior recognizes that God, not military might, determines outcomes.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 105:3 records the Lord's rebuke after the Missouri conflict: 'And my people must needs be chastened until they learn obedience, if it must needs be, by the things which they suffer.'—establishing that even physical persecution is preferable to relying on carnal weapons. D&C 98:33-47 contains the 'law of the Lord' concerning self-defense and forgiveness, establishing principles that limit military response and prioritize moral authority over military might.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment sequence progresses from physical creation through moral education to spiritual reality. The principle that God values faithfulness over strength, trust over prowess, is woven into temple symbolism. The temple represents a kingdom not defended by military arms but by truth and covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's rejection of military Messianism is directly connected to this verse. When the disciples asked if Christ would restore the kingdom (Acts 1:6), he redirected them to spiritual rather than political-military restoration. Christ's temptation in Matthew 4 included an offer of 'all the kingdoms of the world' if he would worship Satan—precisely the military-political power that verse 10 rejects. Christ's refusal mirrors the psalm's logic: true power comes through obedience to God, not through control of horses, weapons, or armies. Christ's choice of the cross—apparent defeat and powerlessness in human military terms—reveals that God's power operates according to principles radically different from human militarism (1 Corinthians 1:25).
commentary.application: For modern believers, verse 10 invites reflection on what forms of 'strength' we unconsciously trust. In a militarized global culture, we may internalize the assumption that security comes from military might, wealth, or power. The verse challenges this. More personally, we might ask: Do I trust in my own capabilities (legs), my professional status (horse of our era), my financial security? Verse 10 does not condemn capability or provision but rejects the spiritual error of locating ultimate security there. The covenant member is invited to a counterintuitive stance: admitting dependence, vulnerability, and the insufficiency of all human strength as the ground of true trust in God. Practically, this might manifest as willingness to forgive rather than retaliate, to trust rather than to control, to wait on God rather than to force outcomes through personal will. In an era of political polarization and militarism, the verse invites a prophetic stance: confidence not in human strength or military might but in God's ultimate authority and justice.

text_kjv: The LORD taketh pleasure in them that fear him, in those that hope in his mercy.

commentary.narrative: Verse 11 completes the rhetorical movement begun in verse 10. If God does not delight in military strength, then what does please him? The answer: fear of God and hope in his faithful love (chesed). The structure is intensely parallel: verse 10 negates (what God does not value), and verse 11 affirms (what God does value). This creates a values-reversal that would have struck the ancient reader with force. In place of external prowess comes internal disposition. In place of capability comes vulnerability-before-God. The 'fear of the LORD' (yir'at YHWH) is not terror but reverence, awe, and appropriate submission—the foundational religious attitude in Israelite wisdom literature. The phrase 'those who hope in his faithful love' (ha-meyachalim le-chasdo) introduces the verb yachal, meaning to wait, to hope, to linger in expectation. These people are not passive but actively oriented toward God's chesed (faithful love, steadfast mercy, covenant loyalty). They have staked their identity and security on what God promises, not on what human strength can achieve. The verse posits a radical anthropological claim: humans please God not through achievement but through the stance of reverent trust. This is covenantal theology at its core—the relationship between God and his people is not transactional (do this, receive that) but relational (trust him, receive his chesed).

word_study.meaning: Participle of ratsah; to take pleasure in, to be pleased with, to delight in, to accept favorably. Emphasizes voluntary approval rather than command or obligation.
word_study.significance: God's pleasure is not coerced but freely given to those who fear and hope in him. The verb suggests personal satisfaction and relational warmth—God is pleased with certain kinds of human beings.

word_study.meaning: Those who fear him; yirah (fear) in Hebrew encompasses awe, reverence, religious submission, and appropriate fear. Not terror but the fundamental religious posture of acknowledging God's supremacy.
word_study.significance: In Israelite wisdom literature, 'the fear of the LORD' is the beginning of all knowledge (Proverbs 1:7). It is not psychological fear but covenantal awareness—recognition of who God is and what humans owe to God.

word_study.meaning: Those who wait; yachal means to wait, to hope, to linger in expectation, to endure in patient trust. Active patience directed toward a future fulfillment.
word_study.significance: This is not passive resignation but active, focused waiting. These people 'wait for' God's chesed—they orient their entire existence toward receiving and experiencing his faithful love. The verb suggests anticipation and readiness.

word_study.meaning: Chesed: covenant loyalty, faithful love, steadfast mercy, loving-kindness. One of the most important words in biblical theology, describing God's commitment to his covenant people despite their unworthiness.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering preserves 'faithful love' to capture that chesed is not sentimental emotion but covenantal commitment. God's chesed is guaranteed by his nature (his covenant), not dependent on human performance. To 'hope in his chesed' is to stake one's security on what God has promised to be and to do.

cross_references.connection: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge'—establishing fear of God as the foundational religious posture that enables all other wisdom and virtue.
'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding'—reinforcing that fear of God and hopeful trust lead to true understanding.
'Oh how great is thy goodness, which thou hast laid up for them that fear thee'—affirming that God's chesed is specifically 'laid up' for those who fear and trust him.

Paul writes: 'Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his: and, Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity'—echoing the principle that those who fear God and hope in his faithfulness are known and kept by him.
'God is love (agape)'—the New Testament's fullest articulation of the principle that verse 11 asserts: God delights in and is defined by his faithfulness toward those who trust him.

Alma teaches: 'And now as I said concerning faith—faith is not to have a perfect knowledge of things; therefore if ye have faith ye hope for things which are not seen, which are true'—directly paralleling the verb yachal ('to hope') in verse 11, applied to spiritual hope.

commentary.historical_context: In the religious worldview of the ancient Near East, gods were often portrayed as capricious, demanding propitiation through elaborate ritual and sacrifice. The relationship between deity and human was transactional and hierarchical—the god received honor and sacrifice; the human received protection or favor. Israel's distinctive theological claim, reflected repeatedly in the Psalms and Prophets, was that YHWH valued internal disposition over external performance. The prophetic critique of empty sacrifice (Amos 5:21-24; Isaiah 1:11-17; Hosea 6:6) expressed this revolution: God prefers obedience and trust to multiplied sacrifices. The fear of the LORD combined with hope in his chesed represented a new anthropological possibility: ordinary people could please God through the existential stance of trusting him, without needing priestly mediation or elaborate ritual. This democratized access to divine favor. It also created a framework in which justice and righteousness (mishpat and tzedakah) became central to covenantal relationship, because true fear of God was inseparable from ethical behavior.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma's sermon on faith (Alma 32) presents hope and trust in Christ as the pathway to knowledge and growth. Alma 32:21-23 teach that faith is hoping for things not seen, and that faith must be nurtured. The parallelism with verse 11 is striking: those who 'hope in his faithful love' are those in whom God's pleasure resides. Moroni 10:3-4 similarly connect hope (anticipation of Christ's guidance) with the Holy Ghost's witness—the Restoration's version of the 'fear of the LORD and hope in chesed' dynamic.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 12:8 affirms: 'Therefore, do the things which I have commanded you, and I will pour out my Spirit upon you in all things.' The underlying covenantal principle is the same: obedience (fear of God) and trust (hope in his faithfulness) result in divine approval and blessing. D&C 88:63 teaches: 'Draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you; seek me diligently and ye shall find me'—establishing the relational reciprocity between human trust and divine presence.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant involves exactly this dynamic: an individual's fear of God (reverent submission to covenants) combined with hope in God's faithful love (trust that the Lord will sustain them through ordinances and promises).
